And the many-texture case -- 1.66x where one texture got 5.0x -- is RenderBatch construction, which is the one part of this path a native implementation would not obviously help, because the batches have to come back to Python either way.

Two things the pricing established that outlive the verdict. One crossing per sprite is the cheap shape: 20,000 individual pushes cost 2.3 ms, while one call taking the frame as ten lists costs 1.47 ms but needs 6.36 ms of Python to build them. RFC-0003 states "one crossing per system per frame" as a design law, and here it is the more expensive of the two. And scalars cross almost free while containers do not: 0.092 us for a three-argument call, 0.114 us for an eleven-argument one, 0.405 us for a seventeen-argument one whose real cost is the three Python lists among them. Argument count barely registers; marshalling a list does.

What would reopen it: a design where the native side owns sprite state and the ECS writes into it on change, so a frame with few moving sprites crosses almost nothing. That is a different boundary from the one priced here -- it needs notify_component_changed plumbing and it runs into Decision 3, since a sprite is an ECS entity that game code reads. It has not been priced, and this item should not be read as having priced it. 5. Projectiles alone — declined at 2.0x, with the ratio recorded here so the decision is re-checkable rather than re-arguable. 6. Marco 1's maths half — still dropped, for the reasons in ADR 0003: the hot Vector2 traffic is all inside the systems above, and the code outside them does 1-8 vector operations a frame.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
Port by module, as RFC-0003 proposed. Rejected: it was wrong three times out of three, in both directions. It would have shipped sparks at 1.4x and skipped the flow field, which is the largest win in the engine by an order of magnitude.

Keep the per-subsystem accelerate= default. Rejected under Decision 4: it makes gameplay depend on build state. The argument for it is consistency with the two landed pools, which is why those are being retrofitted onto the switch rather than left as the exception.

Require bit-exact cross-store parity. Rejected as unachievable, not merely expensive -- see Decision 4. Pursuing it would mean reimplementing CPython's set probing in Rust, and the thing it would buy is better bought by recording which store ran.

Make everything native and drop the Python implementations. Rejected: it forfeits pip install pyguara working without a Rust toolchain, which is the engine's main distribution advantage and the reason the extension was made optional in the first place.

docs.title: ADR 0005: System.update is the fixed step, and keeps its name
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-18

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The engine has two update channels, and the names for them are inverted between the two halves of the API.

fixed rate display rate Scene fixed_update(fixed_dt) update(dt) System update(dt) variable_update(dt)

SceneManager.fixed_update() calls scene.system_manager.update(fixed_dt) and then scene.fixed_update(fixed_dt); SceneManager.update() calls scene.system_manager.variable_update(dt) and then scene.update(dt). So update means the opposite thing depending on which object you are holding, and a developer who has just written one is primed to misread the other.

An external audit raised this as a defect and proposed renaming System.update to fixed_update.

docs.title: Why the collision exists
docs.text: Systems ticked on the fixed step before there was a variable channel to offer them. When one was added it could not take the free name, so it became variable_update on an opt-in VariableStepSystem protocol, and the already-correct System.update kept the name it had.

docs.title: What makes a rename dangerous rather than merely churny
docs.text:
A rename here is not a refactor with a compiler to lean on. System is a runtime_checkable Protocol, so conformance is checked by method name at runtime, and nothing annotates itself as implementing it. Renaming the method would therefore:

  • Silently re-time every system that was not updated. A class still defining update keeps satisfying System — SystemManager would call the new name, find nothing, and the system would simply stop ticking, with no error anywhere. 55 def update(self, dt definitions exist under pyguara/ alone, plus every system in games/ and in any game built on the engine.
  • Break the one thing the asymmetry buys. Scene.fixed_update and System.update being spelled differently is what lets a reader see, at a call site, whether they are looking at a scene hook or a system tick.

Mypy does not help: strict mode is on for pyguara/, but a structural protocol nobody inherits from has nothing to check against. The failure mode is a system that quietly never runs, which is the worst shape a regression can take in a frame loop.

docs.title: What is actually wrong
docs.text:
Not the names — the documentation. System.update's own docstring read:

Update system logic.

Args: dt: Delta time in seconds since last update

Every word of that is true of either channel. The fixed-step meaning was written down in exactly one place: the class docstring of VariableStepSystem — the one protocol a system does not have to implement in order to have update called on it. A reader who implements System and nothing else, which is every system in the engine, never passes the sentence that would tell them what they just wrote.

The same bare docstring is copied onto InitializableSystem.update and CleanupSystem.update, so all three entry points into the API are equally silent.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Do not rename System.update. The inversion stays.

Instead:

  1. Every protocol in pyguara/systems/protocols.py that declares update states in its own docstring that it is the fixed step, names Scene.update as the opposite channel, and cites this ADR.
  2. VariableStepSystem.variable_update says which step it is in words, rather than only describing its dt as "seconds since the last rendered frame" and leaving the reader to infer it.
  3. tests/test_system_step_naming.py pins those docstrings, so the bare copies cannot come back.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
The asymmetry is now a documented contract rather than an accident. A reader meeting System.update learns which step it is from the thing they are already reading.

The cost is that the documentation has to carry what the name cannot. That is load-bearing prose, which is why it is tested. A docstring test is an unusual thing to write; it is justified here because the docstring is the only mechanism conveying a fact that a mistake about re-times a game loop.

The hazard is reduced, not removed. Someone can still write def fixed_update on a system and watch it never be called. That is a different gap — there is no diagnostic for a system defining a method no protocol declares — and it is not solved by naming.

If this is ever revisited, the safe sequence is: accept both names on SystemManager for a release, warn on the old one, then drop it. Not a rename in place.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
Rename System.update to fixed_update. Rejected above: silent re-timing, no compiler or type checker to catch it, and the breakage lands in third-party game code.

Rename Scene.update to variable_update instead. Worse. Scene is the class every tutorial and every demo subclasses, update is the first method anyone overrides, and the same structural-typing problem applies — Scene.update is @abstractmethod, so an outdated override would at least raise, but it would raise in every game at once for a naming preference.

Accept both names on System, dispatching to whichever exists. Two spellings for one hook, forever, and isinstance against a runtime_checkable protocol compares names — so a system defining both, or neither, becomes ambiguous rather than wrong. The engine would be carrying the confusion in code instead of in a docstring.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• pyguara/systems/protocols.py — the protocols and their docstrings.
  • pyguara/systems/manager.py — update() and variable_update(), the two channels.
  • tests/integration/test_scene_owned_systems.py — pins the wiring: a system recording each channel separately, driven three frames to one fixed tick so neither can stand in for the other.
  • tests/test_system_step_naming.py — pins the docstrings.

docs.title: ADR 0006: The wheel ships the extension, so native is the default store
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-20
  • Amends: ADR 0003 (the crate's packaging), ADR 0004 Decision 4 (what the engine-wide switch is protecting against)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR 0003 built the native accelerator as a crate that is not wired into pyproject.toml: cargo build --release produced a library, uv sync kept working without a Rust toolchain, and pyguara/native.py used the extension when it found one. That was the right shape for a spike whose milestone was still a question.

It is the wrong shape for a shipped engine, and the reason is in the numbers ADR 0004 recorded. A flow field recomputes 46-53x faster; a flock of 1000 agents goes from 16 ms a tick -- 96% of a 16.7 ms frame -- to 1.9 ms. Those are not optimisations, they are the difference between a crowd the engine can carry and one it cannot. Under build-it-yourself packaging, every one of them is a lottery decided by whether the person who installed PyGuara happened to have cargo on their machine.

That also leaves Decision 4 defending against a condition the packaging created. Decision 4 exists because "the same game, same code, same seed, diverges between a machine that built the extension and one that did not", and an engine-wide, observable switch is the right answer to that given the divergence. Removing the divergence is better than reporting it.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
maturin replaces hatchling as the build backend, and the compiled extension ships inside the wheel. pip install pyguara is native on every platform the wheel matrix covers; nobody runs cargo to get the performance the documentation promises.

Three mechanical consequences, each verified rather than assumed:

1. The extension moves inside the package. A mixed python/rust project requires the module to live under the Python package, so the importable name is pyguara.pyguara_core_rs rather than a top-level pyguara_core_rs. The crate, the cargo library, the #[pymodule] and the module keep one spelling -- which is why the name stutters rather than being shortened to a private _core under the package. pyproject.toml and native.py both have to agree on it, so test_the_module_name_matches_the_one_maturin_installs reads the former and asserts the latter: a mismatch would make the import fail, the target/ fallback answer in a checkout, every test still pass, and an installed PyGuara run pure Python while reporting nothing wrong.

2. One wheel per platform, not per platform and interpreter. The crate already built against abi3-py312, so a single wheel serves 3.12 and 3.13. Verified by installing the 3.12-built wheel under 3.13 and checking native.store_name() -- it reports native. The Linux row was verified the whole way: built in maturin's own manylinux container, it tags as cp312-abi3-manylinux_2_17_x86_64.manylinux2014_x86_64, and installed into an empty venv with no toolchain it recomputes a flow field through the native store (vector_at returning the correct diagonal). Built against the host instead, the wheel tags manylinux_2_35 and maturin refuses manylinux2014 outright -- too-recent GLIBC_2.3x symbols -- which is why manylinux: auto and its container matter and a locally built wheel is not the artifact to ship. Five wheels are built: Linux x86_64 and aarch64, macOS x86_64 and arm64, Windows x64. Windows x86/arm64 and Linux armv7/s390x/ppc64le are deliberately absent, because pygame-ce and pymunk ship no wheels there and an installable PyGuara wheel for a platform the engine cannot run on is a trap.

3. The hatchling pin retires with the backend. That pin (hatchling>=1.27,<1.28) existed because 1.28 emits Metadata-Version: 2.5, which released twine/pkginfo reject. maturin 1.15 emits 2.4 and twine check passes on its wheel, so the workaround is not carried over -- and the release workflow now runs twine check on every artifact, which asserts what the pin used to stand in for.

docs.title: What this does not change
docs.text:
native.py stays absent-tolerant, and the pure-Python implementations stay. They are not dead code:

  • PYGUARA_NO_NATIVE=1 is the first thing to try when a bug might be the accelerator's, and what the parity suites use. It does not reach the native audio backend, which has no Python counterpart: PYGUARA_AUDIO_BACKEND=pygame is the equivalent there (ADR 0004, Decision 4).
  • native_acceleration = "off" is a supported setting, and SpatialHash has a documented access pattern where Python is faster (ADR 0004, Decision 7).
  • A platform outside the matrix installs from the sdist, and a developer may have a checkout with nothing built yet.

Decision 4's engine-wide switch therefore stands exactly as written. What changes is that auto now resolves to native for essentially every installed game rather than for whoever had a toolchain, so the divergence it reports has become rare instead of routine.

docs.title: The cost, stated
docs.text:
A source build now needs a Rust toolchain where none was needed before. This is not a side effect to be minimised; it is the price, and it falls on three groups:

  • Contributors. uv sync compiles the crate. A checkout without cargo no longer produces a working environment at all -- previously it produced one that silently ran Python.
  • The sdist. pip install pyguara --no-binary and any platform outside the five wheels compile the crate themselves.
  • Downstream builds that pin --no-binary by policy.

The mitigation is the wheel matrix itself: the platforms a PyGuara game actually ships on are covered, so almost nobody performs a source build.

The sdist also needed trimming. maturin's default is the whole git checkout -- 1156 files, including assets/, games/, docs/, tests/ and two agent scratch directories, where hatchling shipped 404. [tool.maturin] exclude brings it to 414: the package, the crate, Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, pyproject.toml, the readme, the licence and the changelog, which is everything a source build needs and nothing else.

docs.title: What this introduces, and what guards each thing
docs.text:
Shipping a compiled artifact adds failure modes that are silent by construction -- an engine running Python where native was expected installs, imports, runs every demo, and is merely slower. Each one gets a guard rather than a note:

failure mode guard a wheel built without the extension in it wheels.yml opens the archive and asserts a .so/.pyd/.dylib is present -- which works for the cross-compiled rows too, as they cannot run their own wheel CI never compiling the crate, so every parity suite skips fixed as a side effect: make install builds it. Plus a step that calls configure(REQUIRED), the engine's own mechanism for refusing to run Python by accident the pure-Python store rotting now that nobody runs it a python-fallback job runs the unit suite under PYGUARA_NO_NATIVE=1 maturin develop defaulting to a debug build, which is slower than Python and would fail every perf guard make native passes --release an installed extension outranking a newer cargo build --release, so edited Rust is silently not running documented in native.py, and asserted by test_an_installed_extension_wins_over_a_cargo_build -- the fix is maturin develop, not another cargo build

The first of those is the one worth dwelling on. Before this change the pipeline had no cargo step at all: the five Track R subsystems were merged by a CI run that compiled nothing, skipped every parity suite, and reported green. CI was precisely the contributor-without-Rust that AGENTS.md warns about.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
Publish the accelerator as its own wheel (pyguara_core_rs), with pyguara staying pure Python and depending on it under platform markers. This keeps a toolchain-free source build and a py3-none-any wheel. Rejected: two distributions means two version matrices, and an install where the accelerator does not match the engine version is a parity violation nothing would detect -- the two implementations have to agree, and that is only checkable when they ship together.

Keep build-it-yourself (the status quo). Rejected: it makes the engine's headline performance a property of the installer's machine, and it is the condition Decision 4 was written to cope with rather than one worth preserving.

Ship both a pure-Python wheel and platform wheels. A py3-none-any wheel is a valid install candidate on every platform, so resolvers would hand it to people who could have had the extension, reintroducing the lottery with extra steps.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• uv sync is the one-step build; make native (maturin develop --release) rebuilds in place after editing Rust. cargo build --release still works and is still found, but is now the second place looked at.
  • Every CI job that installs the project installs a Rust toolchain, cached with Swatinem/rust-cache.
  • wheels.yml is a reusable workflow called by both ci.yml and release.yml, so what a release publishes is built by the same job that verified it on the branch.
  • AGENTS.md's claim that "nothing in this repository requires" a Rust toolchain is now false and has been rewritten. ADR 0003's "not wired into pyproject.toml" and its warning about maturin build overwriting the real package are superseded here: module-name is set, which is what that warning asked for.
  • W29 (Nuitka, source protection only) now has a PyO3 extension to verify against, which the plan already listed as a risk alongside pymunk's CFFI.

docs.title: ADR 0007: Networking is a listen server over an authenticated Rust transport
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-01
  • Plan: project/backlog/active/network_multiplayer.md, which carries the measurements and the phases this ADR only summarises

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The first user is Reclaimer, an online co-op action RPG with hordes and heavy projectile counts, for about 4 players. One player hosts from their own machine.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
1. A listen server, and the host decides everything. Clients send input and display state, predict their own character, and interpolate everyone else.

Lockstep was rejected. It needs bit-identical results across machines, which nothing has tested for pymunk or for floats across x86 and ARM, and which the Python and native stores do not give (ADR 0004, Decision 5). Everyone also waits for the slowest player, and every machine has to run the whole horde.

2. Rust below the line, Python above it. Sockets, packets and reliability are native. Anything that reads or writes ECS components stays Python unless a measurement earns a port. Moving snapshot encoding to Rust was priced at 1.2-1.9x, because the component reads are half its cost and cannot move, so it stays in Python.

The reason for the Rust transport is not speed. A thread that never needs the GIL keeps acknowledging while Python stalls, and memory safety suits parsing data from the internet.

3. A backend, not a store. It has no Python counterpart, so it loads through native.require_extension() and PYGUARA_NO_NATIVE=1 does not turn it off (ADR 0004, Decision 4). pyguara.net imports cleanly without the extension and fails with a clear message only when a session starts.

4. renet and renetcode, behind a hardening layer. Both are pure Rust and already sans-IO. They delivered everything in order on all 200 seeds at up to 40% loss, and they replace a reliability layer we would otherwise have to write and fuzz. quinn-proto was rejected because ring brings C and assembly, which ADR 0006 has so far avoided.

Neither is safe as shipped, and each of these was reproduced against the versions Cargo.toml pins exactly:

Problem Who can trigger it Guard in rust/src/net/core.rs One datagram with a sequence length over 8 panics renetcode Anyone, before any authentication plausible() One datagram too short for its MAC panics renetcode Anyone, before any authentication plausible() Slices of one message claiming different num_slices panic renet Someone holding the invite catch_unwind, dropping that peer One malformed packet disconnects a peer in bare renet Anyone, if renet were exposed Only renetcode-authenticated bytes reach it A lost first keepalive deadlocks a join while traffic flows: the host admits a player whose client times out. 19 of 100 seeded joins at 20% loss The network itself The client confirms, and the host holds traffic and reports nothing until it does A message the sender accepts can overflow the receiver, which charges whole slices against the same limit and disconnects Any large send Reliable sends only fill half a channel's limit A reliable message overtakes the session's welcome, on another channel, and is dropped: a client could join and never see 200 existing enemies Loss during a join ClientSession holds early messages until it is admitted

These were not reported upstream, by the owner's decision. So a new version of either crate needs its parsers re-read and tests/test_net_hostile.py re-run, and a fix cannot be assumed.

5. Joining takes an invite, carrying a random 256-bit session key. A client mints its own connect token under that key, so only invited players can connect and traffic is encrypted. An all-zero key, which is what renetcode's Unsecure mode uses, is refused.

  • The token's server address is a fixed placeholder on both sides. Secure mode checks it against the host's public addresses, and a host behind NAT does not know its own.
  • Token time counts from zero with a 10-year expiry, so no wall clock is compared and a guest's wrong clock cannot refuse them. A replayed token gains nothing: its keys are sealed inside, and one token cannot be used from a second address.

There is no forward secrecy: anyone holding the invite who also recorded the handshake can read that session. So an invite is a secret, and a new one is made per session.

6. Only authenticated traffic counts against a peer. A UDP source address is spoofable, so throttling or kicking by address before the MAC check would let a stranger remove a real player with forged packets. Unauthenticated datagrams share one global budget, which can delay a joiner and nothing else.

7. A sans-IO core under one mutex. The core takes datagrams and a time step, and returns datagrams and messages, with no socket, thread or clock inside. A seeded in-process network can therefore drive the code that ships. The socket thread and Python share it through a Mutex held for microseconds, rather than through queues in each direction.

8. Snapshots are complete states, read directly from components. No movement system calls notify_component_changed, so replication can't rely on it. A lost snapshot costs nothing, because the next one is whole, which gives a client convergence for free. Delta encoding stays out until a measurement asks for it: at 500 entities a client costs 0.88 Mbit/s.

9. Spawns and despawns run on the delayed timeline. They are applied when the render clock reaches their tick, in order, so things appear and vanish in step with the motion around them. A spawn that has arrived but not been applied keeps its records.

10. Visibility is per player, decided by Replicated.owner. A drop's entity is never sent to anyone but its owner, which saves bandwidth and leaves nothing to find in a hacked client.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Protocol changes need make native, and a stale build is easy to miss, so pyguara.net compares a protocol version with the extension and names make native in the error.
  • A joining player waits about one round trip longer, for the confirmation.
  • A reliable channel's usable backlog is half its configured limit.
  • A game message picks up frame-rate latency on top of the network's: on loopback, a reliable echo takes 50-67 ms against a 7 ms link round trip, from polling once a frame and the socket thread's 8 ms tick at each end. Phase 3 should measure what that does to input, and the thread could flush a send at once if it matters.
  • Prediction and the rest are later phases of the plan.

docs.title: ADR 0008: The columnar world spike
docs.text: Status: In progress -- increments 1 and 2 measured; criterion 1 met. No decision yet. Date: 2026-11-10 Scope: This fork only. Wedeueis/pyguara is unchanged by any of it.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR 0004 ports one boundary at a time and leaves state in Python. Its own numbers show where that stops: native flocking spends 63% of its tick crossing, a native render batcher was deferred at 7.4-8.9x because batches must come back, and snapshot encoding priced at 1.2-1.9x because component reads cannot move. Decision 3 names what would change that -- "a design where the native side owns sprite state" -- and says it has not been priced.

This spike prices it. The proposal is that component state lives in native, typed, contiguous columns; that a native system reads and writes them in place; and that Python reaches them one value at a time through a view, or as NumPy arrays over the same memory.

It was given four exit criteria before any code was written:

  1. CPU render path at 20,000 sprites: 39.2 ms -> under 4 ms.
  2. Native flocking at 1,000 agents: 1.86 ms -> under 0.8 ms.
  3. Per-entity attribute access from Python no more than 1.5x slower than today.
  4. All demos render and the visual snapshots are unchanged.

docs.title: What increment 1 built
docs.text:
rust/src/world.rs and pyguara/columnar/, standing beside the object ECS and wired into nothing:

  • Entity ids are 64-bit: slot index low, generation high. A despawned id never resolves again.
  • One sparse set per component, rows in insertion order. Removal tombstones a row and flush() compacts in order, which is EntityManager's deferred-removal rule and keeps the ordering #324 depends on.
  • A schema derived from the dataclass: float -> f8, int -> i8, bool -> u1, Vector2 -> two f8. Anything else is refused by name, and that component stays in the object ECS.
  • arrays() hands back NumPy arrays over the column memory, no copy. While one is alive, a change that would move that memory raises BufferError.
  • view() is a native descriptor per field on a generated subclass of a native RowView.
  • Per-column write counters, the automatic form of notify_component_changed.
  • add_scaled, one native system working in place, as the stand-in for the systems the later increments port.

tests/test_columnar_world.py holds 38 tests. tools/columnar_probe.py reproduces every number below.

docs.title: Measured
docs.text: WSL2, CPython 3.12, release build, minimum of several rounds.

docs.title: Bulk work: 290x to 1000x
docs.text:
position += velocity * dt over every entity, milliseconds per tick:

Entities Object ECS, Python loop Columns, NumPy Columns, native 10,000 12.28 0.019 (633x) 0.042 (292x) 100,000 137.39 0.136 (1007x) 0.385 (357x)

NumPy beats the native loop because add_scaled joins two sparse sets by entity -- a gather per row -- while NumPy adds two contiguous arrays that happen to be aligned. That is the archetype-table argument in one row, and it is worth 3x here.

docs.title: Spawning: 7x to 9x
docs.text:
Two components per entity, milliseconds:

Entities Object ECS Columnar 10,000 141.9 21.2 6.7x 100,000 1961.5 214.6 9.1x

Still one crossing per add. A bulk insert from arrays is the obvious next step and has not been written.

docs.title: Per-entity access: criterion 3 fails
docs.text:
Nanoseconds per access, through a view the caller already holds:

Object ECS Columnar view Read a scalar field 7 (slots dataclass) 67 9.5x slower Read a Vector2 37 (Transform.position) 170 4.7x slower Write a Vector2 94 (Transform.position) 88 parity Make a view -- 297

Reads miss the 1.5x bar by a wide margin, and the floor is structural. A native method call that does nothing but check a generation costs 46 ns, which is already more than Transform.position costs in full. The first version, built on Python properties, read a vector in 350 ns; moving to native descriptors halved that, and what is left is the crossing (about 60 ns) plus building the Vector2 (about 105 ns, against 210 ns for Vector2(x, y) itself).

Writes are at parity only because Transform's setter is expensive: it marks a subtree dirty. Against a plain dataclass a view write is 10x slower too.

docs.title: What this means
docs.text:
The bulk numbers say native ownership is worth far more than any port ADR 0004 priced. The access numbers say it cannot be the only way game code touches a component: a system that walks 1,000 entities reading twenty fields each pays about 1.2 ms more per frame through views than through objects.

That splits components into two kinds rather than refuting the design.

  • Bulk-consumed state -- transforms for rendering, velocities, anything a native system or an array expression reads -- gains two to three orders of magnitude and loses nothing that matters, because its consumers stop going through per-entity access at all.
  • Per-entity logic state -- cooldowns, inventories, AI blackboards -- should stay Python objects. It was never going to be a column anyway if it holds a string or a list.

Three ways to lower the read floor exist and none is built:

  1. Stable-address storage. Chunked columns never move, so a view could hold a memoryview and a row and index it directly, with no native call. It also retires the BufferError rule, since nothing an array points at would ever be reallocated. The cost is that a column stops being one contiguous array.
  2. Scalar-first APIs. Most of a vector read is constructing the Vector2. Code that wants x should be able to ask for x.
  3. Free Vector2 from pymunk.Vec2d. ADR 0003 measured this and declined it while pymunk is the physics backend.

docs.title: Not yet measured, and what decides the spike
docs.text:
Criteria 1, 2 and 4 are untouched. Criterion 1 is the one that decides: render extraction over columns is the largest single cost the design claims to remove, and it is the first consumer that reads Transform in bulk rather than per entity.

Increment 2 is therefore a columnar Transform and Sprite, a native extraction that sorts, batches and packs instances from them, and the 20,000-sprite frame measured against the 39.2 ms in docs/guides/performance.md.

docs.title: Increment 2: sprites drawn from columns
docs.text:
Criterion 1 is met: 1.7 ms against the 4 ms bar.

ColumnarSprite and ColumnarTransform (pyguara/columnar/render.py) hold the fields Scene.render reads from Sprite and Transform. The native SpriteExtraction (rust/src/extract.rs) reads them in place, joins the two tables, places and sorts each sprite by Scene.render's and RenderQueue's rules, and pushes each instance into the NativeGpu through the same function NativeGpu.sprites uses. tests/test_columnar_render.py holds the instance bytes equal to the object path's, ties and all.

Building the frame's instances at 20,000 sprites:

Objects Columns One texture 51.3-52.2 ms 1.62-1.75 ms 30-32x Texture changes every sprite 156-170 ms 2.00-2.06 ms 76-83x

The object side here includes the scene's component reads and the hand-over to NativeGpu.sprites, so it is larger than the 39.9 ms in docs/guides/performance.md, which stops at the batches.

What it leaves out, each of which keeps a sprite in the object ECS: atlas regions, materials, Transform parenting (the column is a world position), and anything the object Sprite holds that is not a number.

Criterion 4 holds for what exists: nothing on the object path changed except that NativeGpu.sprites now calls the shared per-sprite function, and the pixel and snapshot suites pass. Criterion 2, flocking over columns, is not built.

docs.title: Wiring it into the ECS: postponed
docs.text:
Measured before building (2026-11-18), with tools/frame_probe.py: no demo and not Reclaimer draws sprites through Scene.render. Each overrides render and draws by hand, and Reclaimer draws rectangles and shapes. Their frame time is native GPU work, not Python: update and fixed update are under 2.5 ms in every demo. A per-entity read through a held view costs 177 ns against 50 ns for Transform.position.

So columns in EntityManager would make no current game faster and would make per-entity reads 3.5x slower. Postponed by the user's call, until a game draws thousands of sprites through Scene.render; that game is then measured before and after.

docs.title: Decisions taken in this increment
docs.text: Recorded with their alternatives in .claude/decision-log.md: sparse sets over archetypes, f8 for Python floats, the export-pinning rule, no Python fallback, native descriptors, and building Vector2 through tuple's own constructor.

docs.title: ADR 0009: A native mirror of static solids, and what running Reclaimer on the fork showed
docs.text: Status: Superseded (2026-11-18). The mirror lived in PymunkEngine, and went with it when pymunk was retired; Rapier answers the same queries natively, moving bodies included (roadmap 6e). Date: 2026-11-10

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The fork exists to make the engine much faster without risking Wedeueis/pyguara. The plan led with native, columnar component storage (ADR 0008). The instruction that followed was narrower and more useful: make the current Reclaimer run on the fork, unchanged, with no bugs, and much faster.

So Reclaimer was profiled before anything else was built, and the profile disagreed with the plan.

At 200 enemies, one player, one rendered frame cost 16.8 ms. Where it went, from a cProfile run (shares, not timings -- the profiler inflates everything):

Share of the frame CharacterMover asking the physics engine about walls 31% Enemy AI, mostly line-of-sight rays and Vector2 arithmetic 20% Immediate-mode drawing from the game's view code 27% Vector2 operators, spread across all of the above about 18%

A wall probe was the largest single cost in the game. CharacterMover moves a box one whole pixel at a time and asks overlap_box once per pixel per axis, and the pymunk backend answered each by constructing a pymunk.Body and a pymunk.Poly in Python before Chipmunk was called. The owner had already ruled, on 2026-11-09, that this waits for a native sweep rather than a Python fix.

None of it was component storage. Columnar storage would not have moved any row of that table.

docs.title: Decision 1 -- Mirror, and answer only when certain
docs.text:
PymunkEngine keeps a native copy (rust/src/solids.rs) of the boxes of its static, unrotated, non-sensor box shapes, and answers three questions from it: a box overlap, a whole swept move, and whether a ray misses.

The mirror does not reimplement Chipmunk. Every answer is one of three:

  • certainly clear,
  • certainly this one box, or
  • ask Chipmunk.

A probe within a millionth of a pixel of a box's edge is the third. So is a probe overlapping several boxes, because which one Chipmunk names first depends on the insertion history of its spatial index. A ray is answered only when it misses; a possible hit goes to Chipmunk, which owns the hit point and the normal.

The consequence is the reason for the design: the fast path cannot disagree with the slow one. It can only decline. There is no tolerance in tests/test_native_solids_parity.py, and no float operation of Chipmunk's that this code has to match.

Rejected: reimplementing Chipmunk's box and segment queries bit-exactly. That is a parity obligation against a library this project does not own, renewed on every pymunk upgrade.

docs.title: Decision 2 -- The mirror steps aside rather than approximating
docs.text:
It exists only while every solid in the space is something it holds exactly. One dynamic or kinematic body, one circle, one rotated wall, one body without an entity id, and _static_solids() returns None and every query goes to Chipmunk as before.

That is precisely a world of level geometry, which is what a character mover sweeps against and what Reclaimer's Solids is. A richer space keeps its old behaviour and its old cost.

Geometry is read from each shape's cached bounding box, not recomputed from the body. Chipmunk does not reindex a static body that is repositioned, so its own queries keep answering from the old place; the mirror shares that, because the alternative is to be right where the reference is wrong.

docs.title: Decision 3 -- Identical includes the types
docs.text: The Python loop does arithmetic on whatever it is given, so an integer position stays an integer through it. The native sweep computes in floats and converts back, because 70 and 70.0 compare equal and encode differently on the wire. The parity suite compares types as well as values.

docs.title: Decision 4 -- Fast paths for Vector2, held to the code they replace
docs.text:
Vector2 subclasses pymunk.Vec2d. Each operator built a Vec2d -- which checks its operand with isinstance(other, numbers.Real), an abstract-base-class test -- and then a second Vector2 from it.

For another Vector2, or a plain float or int, the operators now do the same floating-point operations in the same order and construct once. Anything else takes the old route unchanged. Camera2D.world_to_screen got the same treatment, and Entity.get_component lost a typing.cast call.

ADR 0003 declined a native Vector2 and optimised its call sites one at a time instead. This is neither: the class stays a Vec2d, and every call site gets faster at once.

docs.title: Decision 5 -- The top-down step in one call
docs.text:
Added after the rest, once the sweep was native and a second profile was taken. At 200 enemies TopDownSystem.update still cost 1.28 ms of a 6.6 ms rendered frame -- 6.4 us a body, nearly all of it the Python around the sweep: collider_bounds, two scaled vectors, the skinned half extents, a MoveResult, the offset taken back off.

The engine now offers step_bodies, and TopDownSystem hands it every body it is about to move in one call. The native side does step_body's arithmetic in the same order on the same doubles and runs the existing sweep for each, so a body it answers for ends where step_body would have put it, to the bit. Anything it declines -- a probe too close to call -- goes through step_body as before, as does any body whose centre is not a pair of floats or whose velocity or remainder is not a plain float or int (Decision 3's reason).

Batching is exact rather than merely close because of Decision 2: the mirror exists only while every solid is static, so no body's move can change what another's sweep sees, and the order bodies are stepped in cannot matter. Separation, whose order does matter, is untouched.

One trap is recorded because the parity suite has a test for it and nothing else would: with no collider, step_body uses the position as the centre and adds no offset. Adding a zero offset is not the same, since -0.0 + 0.0 is +0.0. So the centre crosses the boundary already offset, and only the subtraction on the way back happens natively.

step_body itself is unchanged, because client prediction replays it one body at a time and must agree with the host.

Checked by tests/test_native_topdown_step_parity.py, comparing on repr so that neither -0.0 against 0.0 nor 70 against 70.0 can pass, with a count that fails if the batch declines everything. Four sabotages were built: the skin dropped and the offset added twice in Rust, the centre type check and the no-collider centre removed in Python. Each fails at least one test; the last two only their dedicated ones.

docs.title: Measured
docs.text:
WSL2, CPython 3.12, release build. Reclaimer at commit 88b2604, unchanged apart from pointing its dependency at this fork.

A host's tick with four players, over a simulated 100 ms link:

Enemies Original Fork 24 2.81 ms 0.93 ms 3.0x 100 7.34 ms 2.32 ms 3.2x 200 13.97 ms 4.28 ms 3.3x

One rendered frame, one player, enemies in sight:

Enemies Original, mean / p95 Fork, mean / p95 24 5.64 / 7.45 ms 4.24 / 5.31 ms 1.3x 100 10.65 / 15.56 ms 6.07 / 7.50 ms 1.8x 200 16.78 / 26.36 ms 8.24 / 9.44 ms 2.0x

One swept move against five walls: 64 us to 4 us.

Decision 5 alone, measured with it switched off and on in the same build (the host's own part of a four-player tick, and one rendered frame, one player, by a different harness from the tables above):

Off On TopDownSystem.update, 200 enemies 1.28 ms 0.51 ms 2.5x Host tick, 100 enemies, four players 2.39 ms 2.05 ms 1.17x Host tick, 200 enemies, four players 4.64 ms 3.83 ms 1.21x Rendered frame, 200 enemies 6.66 ms 6.15 ms 1.08x

The 900-tick hash of every position, remainder and their types, at 40 and 150 enemies and at 150 with three guests, is identical before and after, and every one of the 156,000 body-steps in the frame run was answered by the batch.

docs.title: How "no bugs" was checked
docs.text:
• Reclaimer's own suite: 630 passed against the fork.
  • The engine's suite: 8,260 passed.
  • A seeded fight, hashed every tick for 900 ticks, at 40 and at 150 enemies: every position, every sub-pixel remainder and the game's own Simulation.state_hash(). Identical between the original engine code and the fork, and identical with the mirror switched on and off.
  • Sabotage. Three deliberate breakages of solids.rs were built and run. The parity suite caught one of them. Rounding ties away from zero rather than to even, and ignoring a ray's radius, both left 146 tests green -- a random float almost never lands on a tie or within a pixel of a face. TestWhatSabotageFound now aims at both, and each breakage fails five or six tests.

Two regressions were introduced and caught by existing tests before anything was committed. They are recorded because both are shapes worth recognising:

  • The body adapter was given a bound method of the engine to report a move. Studio deep-copies RigidBody handles to snapshot a scene, and the copy followed the method into the engine. It is now a shared flag.
  • getattr(engine, "sweep_box", None) is satisfied by a MagicMock, which nine tests pass as an engine. The mover now accepts a tuple and nothing else.

docs.title: What is left, and why it is a different kind of work
docs.text:
After these changes the 200-enemy frame is 53% rendering and 47% simulation, and what remains in each is per-entity Python:

  • the game's view code issuing one draw_rect per enemy part. Measured since: draw_world is 2.6 ms of the 6.6 ms frame, about 1.5 ms of it in the renderer's calls and 1.0 ms the view's own per-enemy Python, so a batched drawing call alone could take back about 1.2 ms;
  • enemy brains and state machines, now the largest part of a tick;
  • a guest interpolating every replicated field of every entity each frame: about 2.8 ms a frame at 200 enemies under the profiler, which inflates it, so read that as a ranking and not a cost.

None of that can be made faster from underneath without changing what the calling code does. That is where ADR 0008's columnar world and a batched drawing interface come in, and both mean changes to Reclaimer, not only to the engine.

docs.title: Not verified
docs.text: Everything here ran headless, on SDL's dummy video driver. A capture proves the simulation and the render path; it does not prove a window on a screen, and nobody has played the fork.

docs.title: ADR 0010: The container is a service registry
docs.text:
• Status: proposed
  • Date: 2026-11-14

Not accepted, and nothing here is built, except decisions 3 and 4 below: ADR 0012 settled and built those on their own, for phase 3. It changes the DI container, which AGENTS.md lists among the core systems to ask about first, and it deletes public API. It is scheduled after the fork merges back into pyguara; see project/backlog/active/engine_completion_roadmap.md, phase 6.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
pyguara/di/ is about 840 lines: a reflection-based container that auto-wires constructors from type hints, three lifetimes (SINGLETON, TRANSIENT, SCOPED), a DIScope with disposal, a run scope spanning scenes, registration decorators, and circular-dependency detection.

Counted on next at 6154b5a, outside pyguara/di/ itself:

Feature Engine Games Tests register_instance 41 23 74 register_singleton (auto-wired) 5 7 21 register_transient 0 0 17 register_scoped 0 0 16 @singleton / @transient / @scoped 0 0 0 create_scope 1 0 15 container.get(...) 65 173 145

So the container is, in use, a typed registry of singletons that were built before they were registered, read through get.

  • Transient, scoped and the decorators are exercised only by their own tests.
  • The one create_scope call is Scene.resolve_dependencies, which gives every scene a scope that nothing registers a scoped service into.
  • Auto-wiring serves five classes, all in bootstrap.py: InputManager, SceneManager, UIManager, AudioManager and Application. (The seven in games/ are boot_process, which wires by hand on purpose.)
  • Game code does not inject; it looks up. Of the 173 container.get calls in games/, 118 ask for one of five services: UIManager (35), SceneManager (33), Application (24), EventDispatcher (16) and InputManager (10).
  • 34 # type: ignore[type-abstract] comments exist because get(type[T]) is typed for a concrete class and the engine's interfaces are Protocols.

docs.title: What the container does earn
docs.text:
Three things, and they are why it is not simply removed:

  1. Backend selection. bootstrap.py chooses pygame or wgpu, native or pygame audio, and registers the choice under IRenderer, IAudioSystem and IInputBackend. That lookup is what lets game code obey "never import the rendering backend".
  2. Attachment. attach_studio(app.container), the agent harness and the headless tools find a running game's services by type.
  3. Substitution in tests. The 74 register_instance calls in tests/ replace real services with fakes.

A module-level global, or passing every service by hand, loses all three.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Reduce the container to what is used, and name it for what it is.

  1. DIContainer becomes a typed service registry. It keeps register_instance, get and is_registered. TRANSIENT, SCOPED, DIScope, the run scope, the decorators, auto_register, the reflection over constructors and the resolution stack are deleted. Roughly 840 lines become roughly 100.
  2. The five auto-wired services are constructed explicitly in bootstrap.py. A wrong argument is then a type error at the call, not a resolution failure at startup.
  3. Scene gains typed accessors for the services nearly every scene reaches for: the UI manager, the scene manager, the application, the input manager. event_dispatcher is already an attribute; the engine supplies it, so a scene's constructor stops taking one.
  4. scene.container.get(T) stays as the escape hatch for everything else, documented as a service locator. Application.container is the public way in; nothing reads _container.
  5. get accepts a Protocol. One typing change removes the 34 type-abstract ignores. Whether by overload or by a small typed key is settled when it is written, against what mypy strict accepts.
  6. It is renamed ServiceRegistry, with DIContainer kept as an alias for one release.

Systems are unchanged. A system already takes what it needs through its constructor, and the scene that owns it builds it. That is constructor injection with no container in it, and it stays the pattern.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Breaking. register_transient, register_scoped, create_scope, begin_run_scope, Scene.scope and the decorators go. Nothing in the engine or games/ uses them, but a game outside this repository might; the changelog entry is marked breaking.
  • The run scope (#65) goes with them. It was built for a roguelike run that outlives its floor transitions, and nothing uses it. A game that needs one owns a plain object and registers it with register_instance; ending the run is replacing it.
  • About fifty tests are deleted, being tests of the deleted features. The thread-safety test stays: registration and lookup still need the lock an earlier audit found missing.
  • A scene's constructor signature changes, which touches every scene in games/ and in Reclaimer. Mechanical, and the one-call entry point in the roadmap's phase 4 wants the same change, so they land together.
  • The README stops claiming "native Dependency Injection." What is left is more modest and is what was always there.
  • A dependency cycle among the five services is no longer detected at run time. It cannot occur: they are built in order, in one function, and a cycle would not type-check.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
Keep it as it is. It works, it is tested, and it costs nothing at run time. Rejected because the cost is in what a newcomer has to learn: three lifetimes and a scope hierarchy presented as the engine's architecture, of which a game uses none.

Remove the container; pass services by hand or hold them in module globals. Rejected for the three reasons under "What the container does earn". Globals in particular would let game code import a backend's module to reach its service.

Go the other way: real injection everywhere. Scenes declare their services as constructor parameters and the container builds them. This is what the existing machinery was designed for. Rejected because scenes are constructed by game code, with arguments of their own (a level, a save slot), in 30,000 lines of demos that do not work that way, and because it deepens the reflection rather than removing it.

Keep the lifetimes, hide them from the docs. Rejected: code that is kept is code that is maintained and tested, and an undocumented feature is the worst of both.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• project/backlog/active/engine_completion_roadmap.md, phases 3, 4 and 6.
  • docs/core/dependency-injection.md, which this replaces when accepted.
  • REFACTOR_STATE.md, the DI iteration, for the missing-lock finding.

docs.title: ADR 0011: One Rust engine, with Python as its interface
docs.text:
• Status: accepted as a direction (the user's call, 2026-11-14). No port below is approved by it; each still has to pass ADR 0004's rule.
  • Date: 2026-11-14
  • Supersedes: the position of ADR 0003, that the native core is an accelerator kept beside a Python implementation. ADR 0003's measurements stand and are relied on here.
  • Amends: ADR 0004, Decisions 4 and 5, for subsystems that end up with one implementation.
  • Plan: project/backlog/active/engine_completion_roadmap.md, phase 6.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR 0003 answered RFC-0003 by narrowing it. The crate would be an accelerator, not a rewrite: absent-tolerant, with a Python implementation of every native subsystem kept, tested for parity, and selected by one engine-wide switch (ADR 0004, Decision 4). Replacing pymunk was "a separate decision" and "a project, not a milestone"; a Rust Vector2 was shelved.

That was right for what was true in October. Four things have changed.

  1. The extension always ships. ADR 0006 put it inside the wheel and rejected a pure-Python wheel, so there is no supported install without it. The Python stores were kept for a machine that had not built the extension, and that machine is now a source checkout with nothing compiled, or a platform outside the wheel matrix.
  2. Rust is already the platform layer, with no Python twin. The wgpu renderer, the window, input, gamepads, image decoding, text, the audio mixer, the network transport and the Steam binding are backends in Rust and nothing else. ADR 0004 had to be amended to say its switch governs stores, not backends. The engine is no longer a Python engine with a native accelerator; it is two engines sharing a package.
  3. The twins have a measured price and a measured failure. Five parity suites, three tiers of agreement that differ per subsystem, and a second implementation of every change. And SpatialHash defaulting to native silently turned the flocking suite's Python reference into the native one: 69 tests passed with the grid's distance test deliberately broken (ADR 0004, Decision 7).
  4. A real game now sets the costs. Profiling Reclaimer named what is expensive, and none of it was on RFC-0003's list: a guest interpolating every replicated field of every entity each frame, and one Python call per drawn primitive.

So the question ADR 0003 answered, "should some of this be native?", is settled by what was built. The open one is what the engine is.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The backend is one Rust engine. Python is the interface a game is written in. Where a backend subsystem is better in Rust it is replaced there, whether it is Python today or a third party's C, and it then has one implementation.

docs.title: 1. What is the interface, and stays Python
docs.text:
Scenes and their lifecycle, the service registry (ADR 0010), the event bus, the UI builder, the gameplay kits, prefabs, Studio and the CLI. This is where a game's author works, where iteration speed matters more than execution speed, and where ADR 0004's T_pinned lives. None of it is a candidate.

Gameplay kits are not ported. They are the code a game reads, copies and changes.

docs.title: 2. What makes a backend subsystem a candidate
docs.text:
ADR 0004's Decision 1 to 3 and 6 are unchanged: fix the algorithm first, price the ceiling with the ratio rule, and port a boundary, not a function. This ADR adds no exemption from measurement. It changes two things about how the answer is read.

Unification now counts. Under ADR 0003 a port had to pay for itself in milliseconds and for a second implementation forever, so a 2x port was declined. Where a port replaces its Python or C predecessor, the second cost is gone, and removing a dependency or a duplicate is a benefit to be weighed. A port may be accepted on those grounds with a modest speedup. It may not be accepted on those grounds if it is slower in a regime a consumer actually runs.

The unit to move is a system with its data. ADR 0008 measured bulk work on native columns at 290x to 1000x and per-entity reads from Python at 4.7x to 9.5x slower. So state that Python reads one object at a time stays in Python until the system that reads it moves too. A native type that Python touches per entity, per frame, is the wrong boundary.

docs.title: 3. One implementation, once native is the only install
docs.text:
A two-store subsystem keeps only its Rust implementation. This retires, for that subsystem:

  • its Python store from the shipped package;
  • accelerate= on its constructor;
  • its share of native_acceleration and PYGUARA_NO_NATIVE.

The parity obligation becomes a correctness obligation. ADR 0004's Decision 5 defined correct as "agrees with Python". With no Python store there is no such definition, so before a store is retired its parity suite is converted, not deleted:

  • the bit-exact and constructed-geometry tiers become golden vectors: the inputs, and the outputs the two stores last agreed on;
  • the sabotage tests stay, and must still fail when the Rust is broken;
  • the Python implementation may survive under tests/ as an executable reference where a golden vector cannot express the property. It is then test code: never imported by the engine, never a fallback.

A store whose suite cannot be converted this way is not retired.

native_acceleration ends as required. When the last two-store subsystem is retired the switch has nothing to choose between, and an engine that cannot load its extension fails at startup naming why.

docs.title: 4. Third-party C is replaced when it is what holds something back
docs.text:
pygame is already replaced on the wgpu path. It becomes an optional extra once wgpu is the default backend, and leaves dev when the pixel tests hold wgpu to golden images in place of the software renderer.

pymunk is replaced by a Rapier backend behind IPhysicsEngine. Not for speed; nothing measured says pymunk is slow. The reasons are:

  • it is the last backend the engine does not own;
  • cross-machine determinism, which rollback netcode would need and Chipmunk through CFFI does not offer;
  • it is the reason Vector2 is a tuple (ADR 0003, finding 1), and so the reason every position in the engine depends on a physics library.

ADR 0003 called this "a project, not a milestone", and that has not changed. Rapier runs beside pymunk, held to the existing physics tests, until it reproduces joints, queries, triggers, collision events, one-way platforms and the swept character mover. Then it becomes the default, and pymunk is retired.

The retirement was planned for a release after the default switch, so games could switch back for one release. It shipped in the same release instead (the user's call, 2026-11-18): the only game on the engine, Reclaimer, pins an engine commit and moves when it bumps that pin. A config naming pymunk stops at startup with an error naming rapier.

docs.title: 5. Vector2 follows physics, and is not a performance item
docs.text:
A Rust Vector2 is only possible once pymunk is gone, because pymunk's C layer accepts tuples and nothing else.

It should not be sold as an optimisation. ADR 0003 counted the traffic: outside the hot systems a frame performs 1 to 8 vector operations, and inside them the data has moved or is moving to native arrays, where no Python vector is built at all. A PyO3 call costs 50 to 100 ns against today's 290 ns add, so the gain on a single operation is perhaps 3x, on traffic that is nearly absent.

Its justification is the dependency: a maths type that is the engine's own. It is done only if the audit ADR 0003 asked for and never ran, of everything that relies on Vector2 being a tuple (unpacking, indexing, hashing, equality against a literal tuple), comes back cheap. If it does not, Vector2 becomes a plain Python tuple subclass of the engine's own, which removes the dependency with no boundary at all.

docs.title: Order
docs.text:
Dependency order; the roadmap's phase 6 carries sizes and "done when".

  1. Retire the Python stores, one subsystem at a time (Decision 3).
  2. pygame becomes an extra.
  3. Replication and interpolation in Rust.
  4. Batched drawing.
  5. Physics on Rapier.
  6. Vector2, after 5.
  7. Columnar components (ADR 0008), with 4 as their first consumer.
  8. Golden pixel tests; pygame dropped.

Items 3 and 4 come before physics because they have a measured cost in a real game behind them today, and Rapier does not.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
A source build with no Rust toolchain stops being a degraded engine and becomes no engine. ADR 0006 already made the toolchain the price of a source build; this removes what the fallback bought. A contributor who cannot build the crate cannot run the affected subsystems.

A platform outside the wheel matrix loses the Python path. Today that is anything but Linux x86_64 and aarch64, macOS x86_64 and arm64, and Windows x64. Such a platform builds from the sdist or does not run.

Debuggability moves. A Python store can be stepped through and patched from a game. A Rust one cannot, so a retired subsystem owes its users what the Python source gave them for free: errors that name the input at fault, and state that can be read back from Python.

The Python interface is a compatibility surface now. If the backend can change underneath it, the interface is what a game depends on. A game written against it before a port must run after it, and a port that needs a signature to change says so as a breaking change.

Rapier changes results once. It will not settle a stack as Chipmunk does. Every replay, golden frame and seeded test containing a rigid body changes on the switch, and a game tuned on pymunk's feel is retuned.

Parity sabotage loses a witness. Two independent implementations catch a transcription slip that one implementation and its own recorded output cannot. Golden vectors captured while the stores still agree keep what was known; they do not catch a defect both stores shared.

Less code, and fewer rules. Five Python stores, five parity suites and the per-subsystem agreement tiers go. So does the section of docs/agents/native-extension.md that exists to explain them.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
Keep ADR 0003's position. Defensible, and cheaper this quarter. Rejected because its premise is gone: the twins exist for an install that is no longer supported, and they have already hidden a broken native path behind a green suite once.

Rewrite the engine in Rust, with Python bindings generated from it. What RFC-0003 was read as proposing. Rejected for the reason ADR 0003 gave: the ECS, events, scenes and kits are T_pinned, the interface is what the engine is for, and 30,000 lines of demos and a shipping game are written against it.

Move the ECS to Rust first, and everything else onto it. The architecturally tidy order. Rejected on ADR 0008's measurement: per-entity access from Python gets slower, and the profile of a real game showed columnar storage would not have moved any of its costs. It stays last, behind a consumer that needs it.

Keep pymunk and stop at the rest. A reasonable place to stop, and the plan can stop there: items 1 to 4 and 8 do not depend on physics. Not chosen as the end state because it leaves Vector2 tied to a physics library and rollback netcode out of reach, but nothing earlier in the order is wasted if 5 and 6 are never built.

docs.title: Not decided here
docs.text:
• Whether rollback netcode is wanted. It is the strongest reason for item 5 and the one that would move it up the order.
  • What the Python interface's stability promise is, and from which version. This ADR creates the need for one.
  • Which crate versions, and whether Rapier's determinism feature costs performance that matters here. Measured when item 5 starts.

docs.title: ADR 0012: How a scene reaches the engine's services
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-14

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Game code had no single way to reach a service. Scenes called self.container.get(T) 173 times in games/, and 118 of those asked for one of five services: UIManager (35), SceneManager (33), Application (24), EventDispatcher (16) and InputManager (10). The repository's own main.py read the private app._container, although Application.container already existed, and a dozen tests did the same.

ADR 0010 proposes shrinking the container into a typed service registry. It is scheduled for phase 6 of project/backlog/active/engine_completion_roadmap.md and is not accepted. Phase 3 needs only the part of it that decides how game code asks, which is what this ADR settles, ahead of the rest.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Scene has typed accessors for the four common services: application, scene_manager, ui_manager and input_manager. event_dispatcher is already an attribute.
  2. Each accessor looks the service up in the scene's container when read. It is not stored at resolve time. A test that substitutes a service in the container is then seen by the scene, and a container missing one of the four still resolves every scene that does not ask for it.
  3. Before resolve_dependencies() an accessor raises SceneNotReadyError, a RuntimeError naming on_enter() as the earliest place to ask. start_coroutine() raises the same error, for the same reason.
  4. self.container.get(T) stays, as the escape hatch for every other service: effects, the physics engine, persistence, the render graph.
  5. Application.container is the public way in from outside a scene. Nothing in the repository reads app._container.

The demos in games/ use the accessors throughout.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• No breaking change. self.container.get(UIManager) still works; the accessor is the documented spelling.
  • 86 lookups in games/ became attribute reads, and the scene code they sit in names its dependency by type annotation, so an IDE completes it.
  • A scene subclass that defines its own attribute named application, scene_manager, ui_manager or input_manager now collides with a read-only property. None in games/ or Reclaimer does.
  • The scene constructor still took the event dispatcher when this was accepted. It is optional now: the engine supplies the application's own in resolve_dependencies(), which is what pyguara.run(MyScene) needs.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
Constructor injection. A scene declares the services it needs as constructor parameters and the container builds it. Rejected for the reason ADR 0010 gives: scenes are constructed by game code, with arguments of their own (a level, a save slot), and the container cannot supply those. It would also deepen the reflection ADR 0010 means to remove.

Keep self.container.get(T) as the only way. It works, but every call is a lookup by type that mypy types loosely, and it presents the container as something every scene must understand. The four accessors cover two thirds of the calls.

Resolve the four in resolve_dependencies() and store them. Rejected: see point 2 of the decision.

An accessor for every registered service. Rejected: the list would grow with each subsystem and still need an escape hatch for a game's own services.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• ADR 0010, which proposes the rest of the container's reduction and carries the counts this one starts from.
  • docs/core/scenes.md, "Reaching the engine's services".

docs.title: Branching and pull requests
docs.text:
Moved out of AGENTS.md on 2026-11-14, unchanged, so that file stays short enough to read every session. AGENTS.md keeps the rules; this has the reasons and the detail.

Every independent branch is cut from main. Not from another feature branch, and not from whatever happens to be checked out.

git checkout main && git pull --ff-only
git checkout -b <type>/<scope>-<subject>

docs.title: Stack only for a real dependency
docs.text:
Base a branch on another one only when it genuinely cannot build or be reviewed without it — it edits the same functions, or relies on an API the parent introduces. "It came next chronologically" is not a dependency.

When you do stack, say so in the PR body: name the parent, state the dependency, and note the merge order.

Why this matters here: GitHub retargets a stacked PR only when its base branch is deleted on merge. delete_branch_on_merge is enabled on this repository, so that now happens automatically — but merging a stack out of order still lands children in the wrong place, and a stack more than two deep compounds every rebase. Independent branches have neither problem.

docs.title: Merging
docs.text:
• Merge commits, not squash and not rebase-and-merge. Commits are split deliberately (fix: separately from docs: and large mechanical churn) so they review independently, and squashing destroys that. Rebase rewrites the SHAs that verification notes refer to.
  • Merge a stack bottom-up, so each child retargets before its own turn.
  • If a branch falls behind main, rebase it — git rebase origin/main — rather than merging main into it.

docs.title: Before opening a PR
docs.text:
The full suite, the linter and the type checker must all pass:

pytest && ruff check . && mypy pyguara

When a branch carries several commits, each one should pass on its own, not merely the tip.

docs.title: Once a PR is open, the branch is frozen
docs.text:
Do not push more commits to a branch after its PR is up for review. The PR can merge at any moment — delete_branch_on_merge then removes the branch, and a later git push to that name recreates it as a zombie: commits that are not in main, sitting on a branch with no open PR, that nothing will ever merge. This has happened repeatedly.

Anything that comes after — review feedback, an extra test, a tracker or docs fix, the next phase of an audit — goes on a new branch cut from main with its own PR (or a stacked branch if it is a genuine dependency, per above). Before pushing to any pre-existing branch, confirm its PR is still open:

gh pr view <branch> --json state,title   # MERGED / CLOSED -> new branch from main

On handoff, say which it is: "PR is final, nothing else coming" versus "still adding X, do not merge yet" — so a fast merge is never a gamble.

docs.title: The changelog is its own pull request
docs.text:
A feature or fix PR does not edit CHANGELOG.md. Every PR used to add its entry at the top of ### Added, the same lines every other open PR was adding to, so each merge put the rest in conflict. In November 2026, five PRs open at once needed eight replacement branches between them, for nothing but changelog lines.

Instead:

  • The PR body carries the entry, drafted by whoever made the change, under a ## Changelog heading. Write it exactly as it should appear in the changelog, with its section (Added, Changed, Fixed, Removed); the changelog PR adds the PR number. Write None for a change nothing outside the repository sees (tests, CI, internal refactors).
  • A changelog PR collects them. Cut a branch from main (docs/changelog-<date>). List what merged since the last changelog PR, copy each ## Changelog section into [Unreleased], and edit the result into one readable list. Do this periodically, whenever several PRs have merged, and always before tagging a release.
gh pr list --state merged --base main --search "merged:>YYYY-MM-DD" \
  --json number,title,mergedAt --limit 100
gh pr view <number> --json body -q .body   # the ## Changelog section

A PR that changes nothing but the changelog conflicts with nothing else, and since only one is open at a time, it never conflicts with itself.

docs.title: The decision log works the same way
docs.text:
.claude/decision-log.md had the same problem: every PR appended to its end, and every merge put the next PR in conflict.

  • While working, log choice points in .claude/decision-log.local.md, the moment each is resolved. That file is git-ignored, so writing to it can't touch any PR.
  • Copy the PR's entries into its body under ## Decisions, one ### heading per entry, with the same Context, Alternatives, Chose and Tags lines. The reviewer approves or overrides them there.
  • The same collecting PR appends them to .claude/decision-log.md, with the PR number and whether the user approved each one. A collecting PR may carry both files, or each in its own PR; either way it is the only open PR that edits them.
gh pr view <number> --json body -q .body   # the ## Decisions section

docs.title: Cleaning up
docs.text: After a PR merges, delete any local branch that tracked it (git fetch --prune clears the remote-tracking ref; git branch -d <branch> the local one). Periodically reconcile: git branch -a against gh pr list --state merged — a branch with a merged PR and no follow-up work is dead weight, remote (git push origin --delete <branch>) and local both.

docs.title: Seeing and hearing the engine
docs.text: Moved out of AGENTS.md on 2026-11-14, unchanged, so that file stays short enough to read every session. AGENTS.md keeps the rules; this has the reasons and the detail.

docs.title: Seeing what the engine draws
docs.text:
An agent cannot look at a window. tools/agent_view.py boots a demo headlessly, drives it, and writes PNG frames to .agent-view/:

uv run python tools/agent_view.py --list
uv run python tools/agent_view.py guara_falcao --frames 120 --shot 1 --shot 119
uv run python tools/agent_view.py guara_falcao --click 400,265@30 --shot 80

A capture proves the render path works. It does not prove a window appears on screen -- those have already diverged here, when vsync silently promoted the display to an OpenGL surface that never presented software blits. Read docs/guides/agent-visual-inspection.md before reporting on either.

docs.title: Hearing what the engine plays
docs.text:
The same problem one sense over: an agent cannot listen to a speaker. tools/audio_capture.py captures the mixed output to a file instead of handing it to a device, and reports what came out. The pygame mixer is opened on SDL's disk driver; the native mixer, the default, owns its device, so it is rendered offline in the same format (capture_native):

uv run python tools/audio_capture.py --asset games/quintal_cerrado/assets/audio/seed.wav --wav
uv run python tools/audio_capture.py --seam --laps 5 --stall 0.35

A capture proves the output path works -- the clip decoded, the bus volumes applied, and something other than silence reached the far end. It cannot hear an ALSA underrun or a muted system mixer, exactly as a frame capture cannot see a blank window. A wholly silent capture is flagged, for the reason a flat frame is.

--seam measures whether a queued loop joins with no gap and no dropped sample, which is the assumption W28b's staging rests on and what tests/integration/test_audio_output.py pins.

docs.title: Docstrings
docs.text:
A docstring says what the thing does and how to call it, as true of the code today. It is reference text for someone who has never seen the project's history.

make lint checks this page's rules: ruff holds the format, and tools/check_docstrings.py holds the content, of docstrings and of comments.

docs.title: The shape
docs.text:
def find_path(self, start: Vector2, goal: Vector2) -> list[Vector2]:
    """Return the shortest walkable path between two world positions.

    The path runs through cell centres and includes both ends. Diagonal
    steps are never taken between two blocked cells.

    Args:
        start: Where the path begins, in world units.
        goal: Where it ends, in world units.

    Returns:
        The waypoints in order, or an empty list when no path exists.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If either position is outside the grid.
    """
  1. Summary line: one sentence on the same line as the opening quotes, ending in a full stop. Imperative for a function ("Return the..."); a noun phrase for a class or module.
  2. Body: optional, at most 8 lines of prose. What a caller cannot see from the signature: units, ordering, what is mutated, what is cached, what is not thread-safe.
  3. Sections, Google style, in this order: Args:, Returns: or Yields:, Raises:, Example:. A dataclass or component lists its fields under Attributes:.
  4. Raises: lists what the function raises, and nothing it does not.
  5. A section is not required where the summary already says it. A typed function with one obvious argument needs no Args:.
  6. A private helper (_name) needs one line, or none when its name says it.

Studio shows the first line of a component's docstring, and of each enum member's, in component_schema. The summary has to make sense alone.

docs.title: What does not belong
docs.text:
Not in a docstring Rule Where it goes More than 8 lines of prose before the first section DS001 A page under docs/, linked in one line What the code used to do, or the bug behind a change DS002 The regression test's docstring; the commit message **Bold** emphasis DS003 Nowhere. Put the important sentence first An issue, PR, RFC or work-item number DS004 The commit message and the PR A benchmark figure DS005 docs/guides/performance.md The name of a test DS006 Nowhere. The test finds the code, not the reverse The project's process: an audit, a spike, the fork, who decided DS007 The ADR, if the decision still binds

Also not in a docstring, though no rule can check it: an argument for why the design is right. If the decision still constrains the code, it is an ADR, and the docstring may name it ("See ADR 0009").

A constraint that binds the next editor stays, stated as a rule and without its story.

# No: the story.
"""...
Grouping used to be by identity, which split a deserialised material
into its own batch (#212). It is by id now, and
`test_two_materials_with_the_same_id_stay_in_one_batch` pins that.
"""

# Yes: the rule.
"""...
Grouping is by `material_id`, not identity, so a copied or deserialised
material batches with its original.
"""

docs.title: Where the rules apply
docs.text: Directory Format (ruff D, Google convention) Docstring content Comment content pyguara/ Yes DS001 to DS007 DS002, DS004, DS005 tests/ No DS001 and DS003. A regression test may name its issue and tell the bug's story, briefly No games/, tools/ No No No

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
A # comment in pyguara/ may explain why the code is the way it is, at whatever length that takes. It follows three of the rules above: it does not say what the code used to do (DS002), cite an issue or work item (DS004) or quote a benchmark figure (DS005). Consecutive comment lines are read as one block.

A finding in a comment is reported under the definition around it, with #comment after the name.

docs.title: Running the check
docs.text:
uv run python tools/check_docstrings.py              # what CI runs
uv run python tools/check_docstrings.py pyguara/ai   # one directory

A finding prints as path:line: DS00n message: 'matched text' (name).

There is no baseline: every docstring and comment in scope meets the rules, and a new finding fails the check. The check can still read a tools/docstring_baseline.txt, for the day its scope grows to a directory with existing findings; --write-baseline creates one and --prune-baseline shrinks it.

docs.title: When a rule is wrong
docs.text: The content rules are patterns, and a pattern can match something the rule is not about: 16.67 ms in the contract of a frame clock, for one. Reword the docstring if that costs nothing. Otherwise add the entry to tools/docstring_allowlist.txt with a reason after it.

docs.title: Domain Docs
docs.text: How the engineering skills should consume this repo's domain documentation when exploring the codebase.

docs.title: Before exploring, read these
docs.text:
• CONTEXT.md at the repo root, or
  • CONTEXT-MAP.md at the repo root if it exists — it points at one CONTEXT.md per context. Read each one relevant to the topic.
  • docs/adr/ — read ADRs that touch the area you're about to work in. In multi-context repos, also check src/<context>/docs/adr/ for context-scoped decisions.

If any of these files don't exist, proceed silently. Don't flag their absence; don't suggest creating them upfront. The /domain-modeling skill (reached via /grill-with-docs and /improve-codebase-architecture) creates them lazily when terms or decisions actually get resolved.

docs.title: File structure
docs.text:
Single-context repo (most repos):

/
├── CONTEXT.md
├── docs/adr/
│   ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│   └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/

Multi-context repo (presence of CONTEXT-MAP.md at the root):

/
├── CONTEXT-MAP.md
├── docs/adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
└── src/
    ├── ordering/
    │   ├── CONTEXT.md
    │   └── docs/adr/                  ← context-specific decisions
    └── billing/
        ├── CONTEXT.md
        └── docs/adr/

docs.title: Use the glossary's vocabulary
docs.text:
When your output names a domain concept (in an issue title, a refactor proposal, a hypothesis, a test name), use the term as defined in CONTEXT.md. Don't drift to synonyms the glossary explicitly avoids.

If the concept you need isn't in the glossary yet, that's a signal — either you're inventing language the project doesn't use (reconsider) or there's a real gap (note it for /domain-modeling).

docs.text:
If your output contradicts an existing ADR, surface it explicitly rather than silently overriding:

docs.title: Issue tracker: GitHub
