Fingerprinting the walls and weights costs 0.03-0.06% of a recompute (2.7 us against 5.0 ms at 30x20; 77 us against 241 ms at 160x160), so soundness is free and there is no invalidation contract to forget.

What that does to the native port is worth stating, because it is not "never mind". The guard removes the redundant recomputes; a genuine one still costs what the table above says. On a 30x20 grid that is a 5 ms spike every fifth of a second, survivable. On 96x96 it is a single 85 ms stall -- five frames dropped the moment a goal moves. So the port's justification moves from throughput to worst-case latency: it turns a five-frame hitch into a sub-millisecond one. ADR 0004's Decision 6 says to settle the algorithm before the boundary, and this is what that looks like in practice -- the guard did not remove the case for porting, it changed what the porting is for.

docs.title: Ported. 85 ms to 1.6 ms
docs.text:
FlowFieldService is backed by the native sweep when the extension is built, measured end to end -- a fresh service per round, so the wall-mask upload is paid rather than skipped:

Grid Cells Python native share of a frame 30x30 900 7.519 0.162 46x 45% -> 1.0% 64x64 4096 36.449 0.739 49x 219% -> 4.4% 96x96 9216 85.586 1.629 53x 513% -> 9.8%

FlowFieldService has since lost its Python store (ADR 0011, Decision 3), so the "Python" column is now what tests/reference/flow_field.py costs. One ratio moved with it. The fingerprint that decides whether to skip is still Python, and the sweep it is weighed against is Rust:

Grid fingerprint and skip recompute skip as a share 64x64, both in Python (before) 0.012 ms 36.449 ms 0.03% 64x64, sweep in Rust (now) 0.012 ms 0.745 ms 1.6%

Still fifty times cheaper than what it avoids, and tests/performance/test_perf_pathfinding.py guards it at 10%.

The five-frame hitch is a tenth of a frame. Note what that does not change: the guard above is still what keeps a per-tick caller off the recompute path at all, because 1.6 ms sixty times a second is still 10% of every frame for a field that did not change.

The field never comes back to Python, and that is the whole reason the margin is this size. Nothing outside FlowFieldService reads an individual cell -- vector_at and cost_at are the only ways in -- so the cost map and the descent field both stay native and there is no download. ADR 0004 calls this opacity, and it is the difference between this row and flocking's, which has to hand every agent's position back every tick -- measured, 57x against 9x.

Those ratios are against a Python store that has since got faster. GridGraph.get_neighbors was inlined afterwards, which the native sweep does not use, so the numerator moved and the native column did not:

Grid Python native 32x32 5.16 0.195 26x 64x64 22.48 0.765 29x 96x96 52.18 1.641 32x

vector_at got cheaper too, by 5.7x (3.27 us -> 0.575 us), and the boundary had to be picked for it to. A crossing that returned the descent neighbour would have made the method slower: the lookup was never the cost. Four Vector2 operations after it are 3.1 us of the 3.27, against 0.044 us for a crossing. So the direction is computed natively and the whole method is one crossing.

Bit-exact, not close. The pools compare with a tolerance because they hold f32 and a spark half a pixel off is a spark. A flow field steers gameplay, so tests/test_flow_field_reference.py asserts equality on every cell of every grid it builds. Three things make that reachable: f64 on both sides, GridGraph.get_neighbors' order replicated exactly (the descent pass takes the first strictly-cheaper neighbour, so the order is the tie-break), and the fact that a Dijkstra cost map is order-independent given non-negative weights.

Reproduce with uv run python tools/price_native_boundary.py, or uv run pytest tests/performance/test_perf_pathfinding.py -m slow for the table.

Two things to know before trusting a re-measurement. Use a real texture object, not a MagicMock: the Python path hashes and compares the texture once per particle, which is cheap for a real object and pathological for a mock -- it inflated an early version of this table to a fictitious 325x. And the native pool stores f32 where Python uses f64, so positions drift sub-pixel over a lifetime; the parity tests bound that rather than ignoring it.

docs.title: Procedural generation -- Wave Function Collapse
docs.text:
generate_wfc over a four-state terrain palette (water-sand-grass-rock, each touching its neighbours in the chain), 4-directional adjacency:

Grid Cells scan and sort entropy heap 16x16 256 11.37 1.38 8.2x 24x24 576 68.37 3.34 20.5x 32x32 1024 213.28 6.12 34.8x 48x48 2304 1063.98 14.76 72.1x 64x64 4096 3494.79 27.22 128.4x

The multiple grows with the grid because what changed is the complexity class, not a constant. Per 4x the cells:

16 -> 32 32 -> 64 what that is scan and sort 18.8x 16.4x quadratic entropy heap 4.4x 4.4x near-linear

The algorithm was 95% overhead, and none of it was the algorithm. WFC repeatedly collapses the lowest-entropy undecided cell, and finding that cell was done by listing every undecided cell and sorting it -- once per collapse. At 48x48 that is 2221 collapses over 2304 cells: 0.709 s in list.sort, 2.57 million calls to the sort key, and 7.69 million calls to len, against 0.014 s in propagate, which is the constraint propagation the algorithm is actually made of.

It now keeps a heap keyed on (entropy, row-major position), lazily invalidated: narrowing a cell pushes a fresh entry rather than rewriting the old one, and an entry is live only while its recorded entropy still matches its cell. Sound because possibilities only shrink, so a superseded entry is always larger than the live one and sorts behind it. After the change propagate is the largest line in the profile, which is what it should have been all along.

Output is unchanged, bit for bit. The selection order decides which cell collapses next, so a plausible-but-different structure still yields a valid grid obeying every rule -- a different one, from the same seed. Ten shapes are pinned by digest in tests/test_kits_procgen_wfc.py, including the RNG's end state, because a reordering could land the same grid while leaving the stream elsewhere.

docs.title: What this did to the native case
docs.text:
Procgen was listed beside pathfinding as RFC-0003's best-value claim, and ADR 0004 recorded that nobody had measured it. Measured and then fixed, the candidate is gone:

T_py T_cross T_pinned ceiling wfc, 64x64 25.640 0.006 0.373 67.7x

67.7x looks like an easy yes and is a no, for two reasons the ratio alone does not carry. It is once per generated level, so 67.7x of 25 ms saves 25 ms when a floor is created -- against a second implementation to maintain forever. And T_pinned is 98% of the floor: generate_wfc returns dict[Cell, S], so every cell becomes a Python dict entry under a tuple key whoever filled it in.

Before the fix the same row read 3.5 seconds, where a port would have looked unavoidable. This is the third row where ADR 0004's Decision 6 -- the algorithmic question before the boundary -- changed the verdict and not merely the reasoning.

docs.title: A* -- what one query costs
docs.text:
AStarPathfinder.find_path corner to corner over a GridGraph, 12% walls scattered, 8-directional with corner-cutting refused:

Grid Cells ms / query path share of a frame 32x32 1024 1.68 41 cells 10% 64x64 4096 5.98 78 cells 36% 96x96 9216 13.63 114 cells 82%

So a single repath across a 96x96 floor is most of a frame. That is the number to design against: a game that repaths on a timer, staggered, is fine; one that repaths a crowd on an event is not.

Where it went was the graph, not the search: at 96x96 get_neighbors was 55% of a 20.09 ms query, cost 19%, the heuristic 6%, and the heap operations rounding error, with 51 agents each repathing to their own target at 305 ms. Inlining get_neighbors' bounds and wall tests took a third off, with the yield order untouched because the native flow field replicates it bit-exactly. The figures in the next paragraph predate that.

Not a native candidate, and the ratio is not why. T_cross for a flow-field-shaped boundary -- the grid native, endpoints and path across -- is 0.005 ms, which prices the ceiling at 4250x. That figure is evidence that the boundary is not the problem and nothing more: the formula divides by a crossing that has gone to zero, so it stops describing anything a port would achieve. See ADR 0004, Decision 1.

Two things decide it instead. The expensive case here -- many agents converging on one goal -- is already native and already O(1) per agent: that is what the flow field is, at 1.6 ms for a whole 96x96 field against 20 ms for one A* query. And AStarPathfinder solves any Graph[Node], while a native implementation could only serve GridGraph; its 74% in get_neighbors and cost is precisely the part that cannot cross for a caller-supplied graph. A port would be a second solver, not this one made faster.

GridGraph.get_neighbors itself is a real Python target -- it is also the Python flow field's hot path -- but its yield order is replicated bit-exactly by rust/src/flowfield.rs and pinned by tests/test_flow_field_reference.py, so it is its own careful piece of work rather than a line in this one.

docs.title: ParticleSystem / Sparks update -- milliseconds per frame
docs.text:
All three self-contained pools -- particles, sparks and projectiles -- pre-allocate their slots and hand them out, so they allocate nothing per frame. They do walk their whole capacity every frame, live slots and dead alike, and that reads like the thing to fix.

Measured, it is not:

Pool Capacity Live ms / update us / slot particles 1000 0 0.024 0.024 particles 1000 10 0.046 — particles 1000 1000 2.196 2.196 particles 4000 0 0.104 0.026 particles 4000 4000 9.020 2.255 sparks 1000 0 0.011 0.011 sparks 1000 1000 2.849 2.849 sparks 4000 4000 11.454 2.863

A dead slot costs one boolean test: 0.024 us. A live one costs 2.2 us, ninety times as much. So an idle 1000-slot pool costs 0.024 ms -- nothing -- and compacting the pool to skip dead slots would buy back exactly that.

The cost is the per-element arithmetic. 4000 live particles take 9 ms and 4000 sparks 11.5 ms, over half a 16.7 ms frame for one pool. That is where a vectorised rewrite would have to win, and it is the opposite of where the "walks the whole capacity" reading points.

Defensible scale on this machine: roughly 1000 live particles at 60 Hz (2.2 ms) alongside everything else a frame does; 4000 is not reachable.

Those are the Python pools. Both pools now exist only in Rust, where the same update costs about a quarter of a percent as much and the dead-slot argument stops mattering in either direction. Each table's two columns were measured in one run, the Python one from tests/reference/ (which is faster today than the table above records):

Sparks update Capacity Live Python pool (before) Rust pool (now) idle 1000 0 0.0103 ms 0.0007 ms full 1000 1000 1.246 ms 0.0027 ms full, 4x 4000 4000 5.004 ms 0.0103 ms ParticleSystem update Capacity Live Python pool (before) Rust pool (now) idle 1000 0 0.0236 ms 0.0007 ms full 1000 1000 2.137 ms 0.0061 ms full, 4x 4000 4000 8.552 ms 0.0240 ms

An idle Rust spark pool is 26% of a full one and an idle Rust particle pool 11.5%, where the Python pools' were about 1%, because a live element is now nearly as cheap as a dead slot. The "idle is under a fifth of full" guard is therefore gone from tests/performance/test_perf_pools.py: it existed to say compacting a pool is the wrong optimisation, and at 6 us for a full pool that is not a question. Both pools are still held to linear scaling with capacity (3.8x and 3.9x for 4x).

docs.title: Replication on a guest -- milliseconds per 60 Hz frame
docs.text:
A guest decodes each 20 Hz snapshot and, every frame, writes every remote entity's state blended between the two snapshots around the render tick. Measured with a Transform of a 16-bit QuantisedVector position and an 8-bit Angle rotation, every entity moving, one machine, best of three:

Entities Before: snapshots Before: update Before: total Now: snapshots Now: update Now: total 200 0.144 0.531 0.675 0.115 0.148 0.263 2.6x 500 0.547 1.504 2.051 0.303 0.400 0.703 2.9x

What moved. A component whose every field interpolates is decoded, kept and blended by NativeInterpolator (rust/src/replica.rs), which then calls one generated writer per component. Components with a discrete field stay on the Python path, and the two are held bit for bit equal by tests/test_net_native_interpolation.py.

Why not more. Writing 200 Transforms through their property setters costs 0.081 ms however the values were computed, and the snapshot loop that keeps a Python record per entity, for digests and discrete fields, is most of the rest. A tighter Python path, tried first, bought 1.2x. The port misses ADR 0004's 5x bar; what would clear it is component data that does not have to be written back to Python at all, which is roadmap item 6g.

docs.title: Rendering, CPU side
docs.text: These are the portable figures, and the surprise is where the time goes.

docs.title: Batcher.create_batches — milliseconds
docs.text:
Sprites Case Before After 1000 one texture 2.22 0.32 6.99x 1000 transformed 2.10 0.32 6.64x 1000 tinted 2.25 0.33 6.75x 1000 10 textures 3.65 1.54 2.36x 5000 one texture 11.86 1.73 6.85x 5000 transformed 11.56 1.97 5.88x 5000 10 textures 19.47 8.66 2.25x 20000 one texture 54.94 10.98 5.00x 20000 transformed 54.00 13.85 3.90x 20000 tinted 55.48 12.44 4.46x 20000 10 textures 103.88 62.40 1.66x

The CPU batcher was the bottleneck at scale, not the GPU — 54.9 ms at 20000 sprites, more than four times the entire GL path for the same batch — and almost none of it was the grouping. The "after" column is the same loop with three pieces of waste removed, producing batches that are identical field by field:

What it was doing What it costs (world * zoom) + offset with Vector2 arithmetic 2.8–3.9x collecting rotations, scales, colours and source rects for every command, then discarding all four if the batch's flag stayed false ~20% testing the tint through Color.__eq__, which builds two tuples per command ~25% reaching the material_id property when neither command has a material ~5%

The first one is the finding worth carrying elsewhere. Each Vector2 intermediate is a real object allocated and dropped inside the loop; doing the same two float operations on the components is bit-exact and three to four times faster on its own. The cost was never the loop.

The second row explains a measurement that used to look backwards: the tinted case was slower than the untinted one, because an untinted frame paid the comparison on every command and never the append. It is now the other way round.

What this does not help is the many-texture case — 1.66x at 20000 across ten textures. With a batch break on nearly every command the cost moves into RenderBatch construction, which none of the four changes touch. Texture switching at a fixed 8000 commands: 21.8 ms with one texture, 31.6 ms with ten, 32.2 ms with fifty, so batch breaks cost about 50% and almost all of it is paid going from one texture to a handful.

Only the first row has a test. test_the_screen_transform_is_not_done_with _vectors times the batcher against a copy of the old loop in the same process, asserted at 2x against a measured 5x. The other three are each ~5–25%, which on a shared runner is noise, so they are argued in the class docstring instead — reverting any of them leaves the suite green, and the test says so rather than implying coverage it does not have.

docs.title: RenderQueue.sort — milliseconds
docs.text:
Commands Time 2000 0.59 8000 2.87

Linear and cheap. The per-command lambda and tuple allocation in the sort key are real, but at 8000 commands they cost under 3 ms, so no action is warranted — recorded here so the question does not get re-opened from first principles.

docs.title: The whole CPU frame — milliseconds at 20000 sprites
docs.text:
The number that matters for deciding anything, because a native render batcher would replace all four stages at once and quoting one of them would be the mistake ADR 0004 Decision 7 names.

Stage Before After RenderSystem.submit — build a command per renderable, push it 18.90 18.90 RenderQueue.sort 2.91 2.91 Batcher.create_batches 47.74 8.16 pack_sprite_instances 9.25 9.25 total 78.80 39.22

2.01x on the frame, with the batcher's share falling from 61% to 21%. What is left is dominated by submit, which is now 48% of it: a RenderCommand is a slots=True dataclass with nine fields, and building 20000 of them costs about 0.95 µs each against the 0.21 µs of attribute reads that feed them.

docs.title: Two pieces of headroom, recorded rather than taken
docs.text:
The instance pack is list-shaped, and the shape is most of the cost. The pack spends its time turning Python lists of tuples into arrays, and numpy is much faster at a flat list:

Converting 20000 rows Time asarray(list of 2-tuples) 3.74 asarray(flat list).reshape(-1, 2) 1.10 frombuffer(array('f', flat)) 0.64 asarray(list of 4 int tuples) 6.24 asarray(flat ints).reshape(-1, 4) 3.28

The whole pack measures 13.33 ms with the lists as RenderBatch carries them and 6.16 ms with every column arriving flat — 2.2x. Not taken, because it means changing RenderBatch.destinations from list[tuple[float, float]] to a flat list, and len(batch.destinations) is how every backend and several tests get the sprite count. That is a protocol change across three renderers, not a tweak, and it wants its own workstream.

Batch-break cost is RenderBatch construction. The many-texture rows above are allocation-bound: 20000 commands across ten textures build roughly 20000 dataclasses with five lists each. A batcher that reused batch objects across frames, or that carried runs as (start, count) into shared columns, would attack that — and it is the one part of this path a native implementation would not obviously help with either, since the batches have to come back to Python.

docs.title: Visibility culling headroom
docs.text: Sorting and batching 8000 commands of which roughly a tenth are on screen costs 25.2 ms. RenderSystem has no visibility rejection at all, so all of that is paid. This is the number a culling change would have to beat; it is recorded rather than acted on, because for a game where everything is on screen anyway culling buys nothing, and the trade only pays in a large scrolling world.

docs.title: Sprites from columns — milliseconds to build a frame
docs.text:
ADR 0008's deciding criterion: the CPU side of a 20,000-sprite frame, under 4 ms. The object side is everything between the components and the GPU's instance list: Scene.render's loop, RenderSystem.submit, the sort, the Batcher and WgpuRenderer.render_batch into NativeGpu.sprites. The columnar side is one ColumnarSpriteRenderer.draw, which reads the same fields from columns and pushes the same instances (tests/test_columnar_render.py compares the bytes). Rendering the frame is the same on both and left out.

Every sprite has a transform, a turn, a scale and a tint. Ten textures means the texture changes on every sprite, which is the worst case for batching. Best of seven, three fresh processes, WSL2, RTX 3050 through D3D12; tools/columnar_probe.py reproduces it.

Sprites Textures Objects Columns 1,000 1 2.09 0.093 23x 5,000 1 11.42 0.415 28x 20,000 1 51.3–52.2 1.62–1.75 30–32x 1,000 10 5.34 0.113 47x 5,000 10 29.46 0.531 55x 20,000 10 156–170 2.00–2.06 76–83x

Criterion 1 is met: 1.7 ms against the 4 ms bar. The object frame here is larger than the 39.9 ms "CPU frame" above because that one stops at the batches, and this one includes the scene's component reads and the hand-over to NativeGpu.sprites.

What it is worth today: nothing measured. No demo and not Reclaimer draws sprites through Scene.render, so this path is not on any of their frames. tools/frame_probe.py runs each demo headlessly, uncapped, under the FrameProfiler. Means over 300 frames after a 60-frame warm-up, in milliseconds, WSL2 on the GL adapter:

Demo Work Fixed Update Render Sprites through Scene.render net_horde 16.18 2.34 0.07 13.70 0 guara_falcao 35.51 0.07 0.15 35.21 0 tamandua_murundus 44.62 0.31 1.18 43.00 0 true_coral 46.07 0.14 0.37 45.47 0 vinagre_matilha 13.41 0.44 0.17 12.71 0

The render phase is native GPU work (end_frame, present, fullscreen effects), not Python. Wiring columns into EntityManager is postponed until a game draws thousands of sprites this way; see ADR 0008.

docs.title: Rendering, GL side
docs.text: Machine-dependent — see the caveat at the top. Recorded because the split between Python and GPU work is itself informative.

docs.title: Many primitives in one call -- milliseconds to hand them over
docs.text:
WgpuRenderer.draw_rect once per rectangle, against draw_rects with one array, on an offscreen 1280x720 wgpu frame, best of 30. Only the time to hand the primitives to the frame is counted; the GPU work is the same either way. "Building" includes filling a fresh float32 array from positions the game already holds, which is the realistic case.

Rectangles One call each One array One array, building it 400 0.106 0.021 (5.2x) 0.041 (2.6x) 4000 1.037 0.114 (9.1x) 0.176 (5.9x)

The per-call figure, 0.26 us a rectangle here, is the cost next_engine_plan.md measured at 0.4 us on native Windows. A batch row runs the same native drawing code as a draw_rect call, which is why the frames are byte-identical (tests/test_graphics_primitive_arrays.py).

docs.title: Instanced sprite draw — milliseconds
docs.text:
All on the transform path, so the pack column is genuinely a component of the end-to-end column rather than a figure from a different code path.

Sprites End-to-end …of which: instance pack Pack share Pack, as a row loop 1000 1.86 0.40 21% 0.85 5000 3.33 1.99 60% 4.46 20000 11.62 8.07 69% 17.47

The Python pack still dominates at scale, but it no longer runs a row at a time. The last column is the row loop the path used to run, measured at the same widths for comparison: filling the instance array with numpy column writes instead is about 2.2× faster at 20000, and that alone took the whole 20,000-sprite draw from roughly 16 ms to 11.6 ms. The pack's share fell from four fifths to a bit over two thirds — it is still where the time is, so anything further done to this path should still be aimed at it, and the remaining cost is dominated by turning Python lists of tuples into arrays.

docs.title: draw_text — milliseconds per frame, 20 strings
docs.text:
draw_text rasterises a string with pygame.font and uploads it as a GL texture. It used to release that texture at the end of the call, reasoning that "a fresh piece of text has nothing to reuse anyway" -- true of a string seen once, and wrong about what actually calls it. FloatingText redraws the same damage numbers every frame for the life of the entry, and the debug overlays redraw whole static panels, so the common case was twenty uploads and twenty frees per frame for pixels identical to the previous frame's.

Real GL, standalone context, min of 5 rounds of 120 frames:

20 strings per frame released per call cached the same 20 strings each frame 9.98 1.03 20 brand-new strings each frame 11.10 16.44

The steady-state case is where the engine actually lives, and it gives back 9 ms of a 16.7 ms frame.

The second row is the honest cost, and it is not the bound's fault -- it measures the same at a limit of 32, 64, 128 and 256. Releasing inside the call meant the driver freed a block and immediately allocated one the same size, over and over, which an allocator handles about as well as it handles anything. Caching decouples the two: a miss allocates a new texture while freeing one from hundreds of frames ago, and the reuse is gone. So text that never repeats pays ~45% more than it did.

That is accepted rather than solved. Twenty entirely new strings every frame already cost 11 ms before this change -- two thirds of the frame -- so it was not a case anything could ship with, and the shape that is shipped is the first row. A string that changes every frame on its own (an FPS counter) is one miss, not twenty.

Two limitations worth knowing: the cache is bounded by entry count, not bytes, so 256 long strings hold more than 256 short ones; and these textures are the renderer's own, outside ResourceManager, so they do not count towards its cache budget.

docs.title: The UI overlay — milliseconds per frame, and why the HUD does not matter
docs.text:
(Measured on the ModernGL backend, since retired; the wgpu UI renderer draws widgets as primitives and has no such upload.) The ModernGL UI renderer was a hybrid. Every widget is rasterised by pygame onto an offscreen surface, and present() uploads that whole surface as a texture and composites it as a fullscreen quad. So the cost of a UI frame is set by the window area, not by what the UI drew.

That is not a figure of speech. One draw_text in the corner and a forty-nine-primitive HUD — panels, bars, an eight-slot item belt, a minimap, a six-line stat block — cost the same, because the rasterising is the part that scales with content and the rasterising is 3% of it:

1280x720 one label a full HUD (49 primitives) rasterise the widgets 0.006 0.330 everything else 10.9 9.8

Real GL, standalone context, pytest-benchmark minimum. The machine is a 3050 behind Mesa-on-D3D12, so the upload number is a driver number and will differ by an order of magnitude elsewhere; the CPU numbers below transfer.

Where the frame went, before and after:

Whole UI frame, ms 1280x720 1920x1080 before 10.1 26.7 after 5.8 12-14 43% faster ~50% faster

The 1080p figure is a range because it is: repeated runs on this machine land between 11.6 and 13.8 ms, where the 720p one holds to within 5%. Reported as measured rather than as the prettiest run.

Two full-surface CPU copies stood in front of the upload, and neither was buying anything:

  • pygame.transform.flip, to turn the surface upside down for OpenGL. The quad's v coordinate now runs 1 at the bottom of the screen instead, so the sampler does it for nothing.
  • pygame.image.tobytes(surface, "RGBA"), to normalise the surface's pixels. A 32-bit pygame surface is already a contiguous block of B,G,R,A pixels with no row padding, so present() hands GL the surface's own memory and sets the texture's swizzle to BGRA. The texture unit reorders for free.
Measured alone, ms 1280x720 1920x1080 the two CPU copies 3.4 12.7 the raw upload that remains 5.8 12.5

The copies are the portable half — same cost on any machine with the same pixel count. The end-to-end saving (4.3 ms at 720p) is a little larger than the copies measured alone, because the old path also allocated a flipped Surface and a bytes object every frame.

What is left is the upload itself, and only instancing removes it. At 720p a UI frame still costs 5.8 ms whether it draws one label or a HUD — a third of a 16.7 ms budget, bought by an FPS counter. Drawing the primitives as instanced SDF shapes instead would make the cost proportional to the UI, but the shape shader (shaders/shape.frag) has no rounded-rect and no polygon SDF today, while border_radius has 30 live call sites in this repository. That is workstream W16 proper, tracked as #334 rather than guessed at. It also carries a decision that is not an engineering one: pygame's rasteriser and an SDF shader disagree about antialiasing, rounded corners and line caps, so every shipped HUD would change slightly.

docs.title: Instance layout width
docs.text:
Packing and uploading 20000 instances, at each width the layout has had:

Floats per instance Time 7 (position and transform only) 9.29 ms 11 (with a per-instance tint) 9.72 ms 15 (with an atlas UV rect) 9.85 ms

A few percent per widening, and the steps are small enough that the 11→15 one lands inside run-to-run noise about as often as not — measured across repeats it ranged from 0.07 ms to 0.44 ms, against a standard deviation of roughly 0.15–0.39 ms. The ordering is consistent; the size of each gap is not.

That is why the GL sprite path carries both the tint and the UV rect unconditionally, rather than keeping extra shader programs for batches that want neither — a plain sprite broadcasts white into the four colour columns and (0,0)/(1,1) into the four UV columns, which is free once the pack is vectorised. A uniform would instead force a per-batch state change, which for the UV rect would defeat the entire purpose: an atlas exists so that sprites with different regions share one draw call.

The bytes uploaded are 1.2 MB per frame at 20,000 sprites.

docs.title: Resource loading, and the GIL
docs.text:
What decides the shape of asynchronous loading here. pygame-ce decodes images in SDL with the GIL released; json parses with it held. So "load assets on a worker thread" is right for one and a pessimisation for the other, and the difference is measured rather than assumed.

Per item, 24 items, 4 worker threads, CPython 3.12.10 (a standard GIL build -- Py_GIL_DISABLED is unset), 12 logical CPUs:

Operation Sequential 4 threads Speed-up GIL pygame.image.load, 2356×1824 jpg 30.87 ms 10.58 ms 2.92× released pygame.image.load, 1024×1024 png 6.91 ms 2.05 ms 3.37× released …plus convert_alpha + tobytes 15.12 ms 7.93 ms 1.91× mostly released json.loads, ~4k entries 4.64 ms 6.51 ms 0.71× held open().read(), 2.5 MB, page-cached 0.17 ms 0.84 ms 0.20× n/a

Three things follow.

One image decode can cost more than a frame. 30.87 ms for a 2356×1824 jpg is nearly two 60 Hz frames, so a scene that loads a dozen textures on entry stalls for a third of a second. This is the cost asynchronous loading exists to move.

Threading pays for image decode and costs for JSON. 2.9–3.4× against 0.71×: offloading a GIL-holding parse adds contention and returns nothing, so it finishes slower than doing it inline. A loader therefore opts in to threaded decode rather than getting it by default.

asyncio is the wrong tool for this problem. It overlaps I/O waits, and there is no wait here worth overlapping -- reading 2.5 MB costs 0.17 ms while decoding it costs 30.87 ms. The expense is CPU, which an event loop cannot parallelise on a GIL build; it would also mean running an event loop inside a synchronous frame loop. A thread pool for the phases that release the GIL, plus a time-budgeted main-thread pump for everything else, is what the measurements support.

The last row measures thread-pool overhead, not disk: 2.5 MB out of the page cache costs 0.17 ms, less than the ~0.7 ms it takes to hand the work to a pool. Quoted so nobody reads it as "file I/O does not parallelise".

docs.title: The garbage collector
docs.text:
CPython's cycle collector runs a full collection now and then, and a full collection walks every container object in the process: every module, class, function, asset, component and system. Nearly all of those were made while loading and stay alive until the scene ends, so the walk finds nothing and still costs a frame.

Measured on Reclaimer's host (four players, three of them guests over a simulated network, 50 enemies), about 80,000 tracked objects, 1200 ticks:

Full collections 95th percentile 99th percentile Worst tick Left alone 21 6.2 ms 18.8 ms 25.2 ms Frozen once the room had loaded 22 5.5 ms 6.9 ms 9.3 ms Frozen mid-fight 22 5.2 ms 6.7 ms 7.8 ms

Left alone, every tick over 15 ms in that room was a full collection: about one every 0.8 s, each adding 15 to 20 ms. Freezing doesn't make collections rarer, it makes them cheap, because what was frozen is no longer walked. Freezing once the room had loaded did nearly as well as freezing mid-fight, since what a game makes during play is a small part of what it holds.

So the application does it for you: PerformanceConfig.freeze_on_scene_change (on by default) runs pyguara.application.memory.settle_memory() after the first frame of any new set of scenes. That unfreezes what it froze last time, runs one full collection, which frees the cycles the old scene left, and freezes what's left. The unfreeze matters: a cycle among frozen objects is never collected while frozen, so freezing alone would keep every scene's cyclic garbage forever.

The engine sees scene changes and nothing else. A game that loads more inside a running scene, such as a level built on demand or a world that arrives over the network, calls settle_memory() itself once the load is done.

docs.title: Vector2 in Rust
docs.text: Vector2 moved from a pymunk.Vec2d subclass to a class in the native extension (roadmap 6f), measured 2026-11-18 on the same machine and interpreter, main against the branch. It holds its components both as f64, for arithmetic, and as the Python floats x and y return, so a read hands back an existing object as a tuple field does.

docs.title: One operation -- nanoseconds, best of seven
docs.text:
Operation pymunk subclass Rust Vector2(x, y) 226 122 1.9x a + b 279 84 3.3x a * 2.0 262 94 2.8x a / 2.0 275 89 3.1x a.x 21 13 1.6x x, y = a 42 72 0.6x a.length 128 35 3.7x a.normalize() 361 81 4.5x a.distance_to(b) 335 44 7.6x a.dot(b) 223 41 5.4x a.lerp(b, 0.5) 408 96 4.2x a == b 24 21 1.1x hash(a) 51 52 1.0x

Unpacking is the one thing that got slower. A tuple unpacks without a call; anything else goes through __iter__. In a loop that runs per entity, read v.x and v.y, which are now the fastest way in. Indexing, v[0], is about 15% slower than a tuple's for the same reason.

Two designs were measured and dropped on the way. With f64 fields and PyO3 getters, a.x cost 33 ns and the CPU render sweeps lost 20-35%; with double member descriptors it cost 31 ns, because each read allocates a float. Holding the float objects is what made reads cheaper than a tuple's.

docs.title: Whole sweeps -- milliseconds, best of two fresh processes each
docs.text:
Sweep pymunk subclass Rust FlockingSystem, 1000 agents, native 1.66 1.25 1.33x FlockingSystem, 3000 agents, native 5.22 4.28 1.22x FlockingSystem, 1000 agents, Python 12.54 9.91 1.27x Batcher, 20000 sprites, one texture 8.69 6.61 1.31x CPU frame, 5000 sprites 9.10 8.67 1.05x CPU frame, 20000 sprites 40.53 39.91 1.02x Render submission, 20000 22.68 22.39 1.01x RenderQueue.sort, 8000 3.65 3.58 1.02x SpatialHash.query_radius, 10000, native 4.06 3.78 1.07x Swept character probe, 50 46.99 44.03 1.07x Flow field recompute, 96, Python 51.26 50.92 1.01x

Nothing is slower measured this way. Run inside one long pytest session, several rows read 10-20% slower instead, sort among them, which touches no vector: main ran its sort in 2.87 ms there against 3.65 ms in a fresh process, so what moved is the state earlier benchmarks leave behind, not the sort. Compare these numbers process by process.

docs.title: Smaller measurements
docs.text:
Figures that used to live in docstrings and comments, kept here because each explains a choice in the code.

What Measured The choice it explains Vector2.__add__ against adding two floats 452 ns against 69 ns (6.5x) on the pymunk-based class; 84 ns against 69 ns on the Rust one flock_force and Batcher do their inner-loop arithmetic on floats and build a Vector2 only at the boundary Uploading a 96x96 grid's walls and weights to the native flow field 0.18 ms, against a 1.36 ms recompute FlowFieldService uploads the whole graph when its contents change, with no incremental path A circular wipe's cover at 1280x720, as a fan of 68 quads 1.04 ms, with every seam blended twice under a translucent cover circular_cover_points returns one self-touching polygon: 0.3 ms, and no seams The same cover as two scanline rectangles per row 1,440 draw calls; 2.62 ms opaque, 5.89 ms translucent As above EntityManager.create_entities(20000) against a create_entity() loop 1.06x, within noise; an inlined copy of the registration measured 1.21x create_entities goes through add_entity(); it is a convenience, not a fast path Spawning 4,000 entities with one cached query registered, before QueryCache stopped copying its result set per component added 214 ms, against 40 ms with no cached query The cache updates in place RenderSystem.submit of 20,000 sprites, before and after it honoured Sprite.flip_x/flip_y 21.3-21.9 ms before, 22.5-23.3 ms after (about 0.05 us a sprite); 25.9-27.0 ms when every sprite is flipped A flip becomes a negative scale in submit, so no backend needs a second flag; an unflipped sprite pays only the two reads A pool of 700 entities each carrying a FlockingAgent, all matching queries while idle, in games/tamandua_murundus about 18 frames per second, against about 60 once idle entities were disabled EntityPool disables an idle entity, so it matches no query A Python flocking tick at 1,000 agents, with the Python spatial index and with the native one 16.6 ms against 9.8 ms FlockingSystem's Python path still pins its index to accelerate=False, so the Python path is Python throughout FlowFieldService.vector_at in Python 3.27 us, 97% of it four Vector2 operations The native path answers the whole lookup in one call Physics at 4 substeps 0.65 ms an update at 200 dynamic bodies, 2.5 ms at 500 4 is the default; 1/2/4 substeps stop a body crossing a 10px wall up to about 200/400/900 px/s The frame profiler, recording one frame (seven timestamps), 2026-11-16 2.2 us, against nothing when it is off It can stay on in a shipped build: 0.013% of a 60 Hz frame The frame profiler's overlay, summarising 120 frames and laying out its rows every frame, before the summary was cached 157 us a frame The overlay shows one summary for 15 frames: 33 us a frame, before the renderer's own cost for the text

docs.title: What the test suite guarantees
docs.text:
tests/performance/ runs in two tiers, and they exist for different reasons.

Guards (-m "performance and not slow", ~3 s) assert a complexity class, never a wall-clock time. Each measures the same operation at N and at a multiple of N in the same process, and asserts the ratio between them. That cancels machine speed out entirely, which is what makes them safe on a shared CI runner: a laptop, a loaded container and a CI box all agree that a linear algorithm costs roughly 4× for 4× the work, even while disagreeing about every absolute number involved. They catch a change of complexity class — the kind of regression that is invisible in review and fatal at scale — and deliberately do not catch a 2× constant-factor slowdown.

Sweeps (-m "performance and slow") assert nothing. They are pytest-benchmark runs at sizes too large for CI, and their only job is to produce the tables above.

Neither tier should ever run under coverage. Tracing every line costs more than the code being timed and turns every measurement into noise; both make targets pass --no-cov.

A machine with no GL context skips the GL tier rather than failing it.

docs.title: Zero to Hero: Making your First PyGuara Game
docs.text:
Welcome to the Zero to Hero tutorial series for the PyGuara Game Engine! This guide takes you step-by-step through the structure and concepts of PyGuara using the tutorial modules under the games/ folder of the repository.

By the end of this guide, you will understand how the engine boots up, how to design code around the Entity-Component-System (ECS) mindset, how to hook up input maps and handle events, how to integrate physical simulation via Pymunk, how to construct constraint-based UI scene graphs, and finally, how to compile and distribute your game as a standalone binary.

docs.title: 🗺️ Tutorial Roadmap
docs.text:
The tutorial is structured into six parts: 1. The Boot Sequence (games/boot_process): Initializing the engine, Dependency Injection, and starting your first Scene. 2. The ECS Mindset (games/ecs_mental_model): Composing game objects using pure data components and executing logic with Systems. 3. Input Mapping & Events (games/input_events): Binding keyboard controls to logical actions and using the event queue for decoupled communication. 4. Physical Simulation (games/physics_integration): Adding rigid bodies, colliders, and collision listeners. 5. UI & Scene graphs (games/ui_scene_graph): Organizing menu layouts, panels, and responsive widgets. 6. Standalone Compilation: Building and packaging the final game executable using pyguara build.

games/ has seven tutorial modules. The two this guide does not walk through are games/asset_pipeline (loading sprites with .meta files through ResourceManager) and games/tilemap_authoring (building a level from a Tiled map). Each is short enough to read directly, and games/README.md describes both.

docs.title: 🛠️ Part 1: The Boot Sequence (games/boot_process)
docs.text:
Before we can render characters or handle physics, we must initialize the engine. In PyGuara, this is done using Dependency Injection (DI) and a bootstrap configuration file.

The entry point of any PyGuara game performs the following core steps: 1. Configures logging. 2. Bootstraps the DI container. 3. Retrieves the global Application instance from the container. 4. Initializes the starting Scene. 5. Runs the game loop.

docs.title: The Entry Point (main.py)
docs.text:
import logging
from pyguara.application.application import Application
from pyguara.events.dispatcher import EventDispatcher
from games.boot_process.bootstrap import configure_game_container
from games.boot_process.scenes import BootScene

def main():
    # 1. Configure logging
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

    # 2. Bootstrap Dependency Injection
    container = configure_game_container()

    # 3. Resolve the Application
    app = container.get(Application)

    # 4. Create the starting scene
    event_dispatcher = container.get(EventDispatcher)
    start_scene = BootScene(event_dispatcher)

    # 5. Run the Game Loop
    app.run(starting_scene=start_scene)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: The Bootstrap Wiring (bootstrap.py)
docs.text:
Inside bootstrap.py, we instantiate the central DIContainer and register our managers, window backends, and renderers. Because PyGuara is completely decoupled, we can register any concrete implementation that conforms to our protocols (e.g., IRenderer or UIRenderer):

from pyguara.di.container import DIContainer
from pyguara.events.dispatcher import EventDispatcher
from pyguara.config.manager import ConfigManager
from pyguara.graphics.window import Window, WindowConfig
from pyguara.graphics.backends.pygame.pygame_window import PygameWindow
from pyguara.graphics.backends.pygame.pygame_renderer import PygameBackend
from pyguara.graphics.backends.pygame.ui_renderer import PygameUIRenderer
from pyguara.graphics.protocols import IRenderer, UIRenderer
from pyguara.input.manager import InputManager
from pyguara.scene.manager import SceneManager
from pyguara.resources.manager import ResourceManager
from pyguara.ui.manager import UIManager
from pyguara.systems.manager import SystemManager
from pyguara.scripting.coroutines import CoroutineManager
from pyguara.application.application import Application

def configure_game_container() -> DIContainer:
    container = DIContainer()
    container.register_instance(DIContainer, container)

    # Event System (The Backbone)
    event_dispatcher = EventDispatcher()
    container.register_instance(EventDispatcher, event_dispatcher)

    # Central Config
    config_manager = ConfigManager(event_dispatcher)
    config_manager.load()
    container.register_instance(ConfigManager, config_manager)

    # Window & Graphics Configuration
    win_config = WindowConfig(title="Module 1: Boot Process", screen_width=800, screen_height=600)
    window_backend = PygameWindow()
    window = Window(win_config, window_backend)
    window.create()
    container.register_instance(Window, window)

    # Renderer implementations conform to IRenderer & UIRenderer protocols
    renderer = PygameBackend(window.native_handle)
    container.register_instance(IRenderer, renderer)

    ui_renderer = PygameUIRenderer(window.native_handle)
    container.register_instance(UIRenderer, ui_renderer)

    # Core Systems registered as Singletons
    container.register_singleton(InputManager, InputManager)
    container.register_singleton(SceneManager, SceneManager)
    container.register_singleton(ResourceManager, ResourceManager)
    container.register_singleton(UIManager, UIManager)
    container.register_singleton(SystemManager, SystemManager)
    container.register_singleton(CoroutineManager, CoroutineManager)
    container.register_singleton(Application, Application)

    return container

This module wires the engine by hand, on the software renderer, to show what the container holds. It is not how a game starts. A real game calls create_application(), or create_container() when it needs to add its own services first: both read config/game_config.json and build the configured backend, which is wgpu by default. The capstone demos' bootstrap.py files (for example games/guara_falcao/bootstrap.py) show that form, and Project Structure has the template.

```python from pyguara.application import create_application from pyguara.events.dispatcher import EventDispatcher

app = create_application() app.run(BootScene(app.container.get(EventDispatcher))) ```

docs.title: 🧩 Part 2: The ECS Mindset (games/ecs_mental_model)
docs.text:
Instead of writing classic Object-Oriented inheritance trees (like a Player class that inherits from PhysicsObject which inherits from GameObject), PyGuara leverages a strict Entity-Component-System (ECS) composition architecture.

  • Entity: A lightweight ID container (simply an identification number).
  • Component: Pure data container with no logic whatsoever.
  • System: Pure logic execution. Systems query entities containing specific components and manipulate their data.

docs.title: 1. Defining Components (components.py)
docs.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pyguara.ecs.component import Component
from pyguara.common.types import Vector2, Color

@dataclass
class Transform(Component):
    position: Vector2

@dataclass
class Sprite(Component):
    color: Color
    size: Vector2

This module defines its own tiny Transform and Sprite so nothing is hidden. In a game, use the engine's (pyguara.common.components.Transform, pyguara.graphics.components.Sprite), and write your own components as @dataclass(slots=True) classes that inherit from BaseComponent, which rejects a component that declares a method.

docs.title: 2. Creating a System (systems.py)
docs.text:
To process movement logic, we create a MovementSystem. In its constructor, we register our query to enable high-performance $O(1)$ query caching:

from pyguara.ecs.manager import EntityManager
from pyguara.common.types import Vector2
from games.ecs_mental_model.components import Transform

class MovementSystem:
    def __init__(self, entity_manager: EntityManager):
        self._em = entity_manager
        # Speed up lookups from O(N) to O(1) by caching this query
        self._em.register_cached_query(Transform)

    def update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        # Loop through entities possessing the Transform component
        for entity in self._em.get_entities_with_cached(Transform):
            transform = entity.get_component(Transform)

            # Update coordinate state (diagonal movement at 100 px/sec)
            speed = 100.0
            new_x = transform.position.x + speed * dt
            new_y = transform.position.y + speed * dt

            # Wrap around boundaries
            if new_x > 800: new_x = 0
            if new_y > 600: new_y = 0

            transform.position = Vector2(new_x, new_y)

docs.title: 3. Assembling the Scene (scenes.py)
docs.text:
In the scene's on_enter method, we register the system, spawn an entity, and attach components to it:

from pyguara.scene.base import Scene
from pyguara.common.types import Vector2, Color, Rect
from games.ecs_mental_model.components import Transform, Sprite
from games.ecs_mental_model.systems import MovementSystem

class ECSScene(Scene):
    def on_enter(self) -> None:
        self.movement_system = MovementSystem(self.entity_manager)

        # Spawn our visual entity
        hero = self.entity_manager.create_entity("hero")
        hero.add_component(Transform(position=Vector2(100, 100)))
        hero.add_component(Sprite(color=Color(255, 0, 0), size=Vector2(50, 50)))

    def update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        self.movement_system.update(dt)

    def render(self, world_renderer: IRenderer, ui_renderer: UIRenderer) -> None:
        world_renderer.clear(Color(30, 30, 30))

        # Custom immediate rendering loop (Usually handled by RenderSystem)
        for entity in self.entity_manager.get_entities_with(Transform, Sprite):
            transform = entity.get_component(Transform)
            sprite = entity.get_component(Sprite)

            rect = Rect(transform.position.x, transform.position.y, sprite.size.x, sprite.size.y)
            world_renderer.draw_rect(rect, sprite.color)

docs.title: 🎮 Part 3: Input Mapping & Events (games/input_events)
docs.text:
PyGuara decouples player input from the engine loop using semantic action bindings and a pub/sub event dispatcher.

  1. InputManager: Maps keyboard, mouse, or gamepad inputs (e.g. SPACE) to virtual actions (e.g. "dash").
  2. EventDispatcher: Broadcasts event payloads across systems. Systems can subscribe to actions without holding references to windows or input devices.

There is no physics in this part. The square moves because you are holding a key, full stop — Part 4 below is where a body first moves under forces, and doing a rough version of it here would only teach the wrong answer one section early.

docs.title: 1. Registering Action Bindings
docs.text:
Inside your scene's on_enter:

from pyguara.input.manager import InputManager
from pyguara.input.types import InputDevice, ActionType
from pyguara.input.keys import SPACE, A, D, S, W

input_manager = self.container.get(InputManager)

# HOLD for the directions: true for as long as the key is down.
for action in ("move_up", "move_down", "move_left", "move_right"):
    input_manager.register_action(action, ActionType.HOLD)
# PRESS for the dash: it happens once, on the way down.
input_manager.register_action("dash", ActionType.PRESS)

input_manager.bind_input(InputDevice.KEYBOARD, W, "move_up")
input_manager.bind_input(InputDevice.KEYBOARD, S, "move_down")
input_manager.bind_input(InputDevice.KEYBOARD, A, "move_left")
input_manager.bind_input(InputDevice.KEYBOARD, D, "move_right")
input_manager.bind_input(InputDevice.KEYBOARD, SPACE, "dash")

docs.title: 2. Translating Inputs to Events (systems.py)
docs.text:
We create an InputBridgeSystem that intercepts input mappings and turns them into game-specific results. Note that it does two different things, and the difference matters:

  • a held direction becomes state on a component — "am I still holding left" is a question about now, not about a moment;
  • a pressed dash becomes an event — it happened once, and anything that cares should hear about it once.

Reaching for an event where state was wanted (or the reverse) is the commonest way this wiring goes wrong.

from pyguara.events.dispatcher import EventDispatcher
from pyguara.input.events import OnActionEvent
from games.input_events.events import DashEvent

class InputBridgeSystem:
    def __init__(self, entity_manager, dispatcher: EventDispatcher, player_id: str):
        self._em = entity_manager
        self._dispatcher = dispatcher
        self._player_id = player_id
        self._held: set[str] = set()
        # Subscribe to standard engine action events
        self._dispatcher.subscribe(OnActionEvent, self.on_action)

    def on_action(self, event: OnActionEvent) -> None:
        pressed = event.value > 0.5

        if event.action_name in _DIRECTIONS:   # state
            if pressed:
                self._held.add(event.action_name)
            else:
                self._held.discard(event.action_name)
            self._write_direction()
            return

        if event.action_name == "dash" and pressed:   # event
            self._dispatcher.dispatch(DashEvent(self._player_id, distance=80.0))

docs.title: 3. Handling Gameplay Events in PlayerSystem
docs.text:
PlayerSystem knows nothing about keys or actions — only about the Movement component and the gameplay event. That is what lets the same system be driven by a gamepad, a replay or an AI without a line changing here:

class PlayerSystem:
    def __init__(self, entity_manager: EntityManager, dispatcher: EventDispatcher):
        self._em = entity_manager
        dispatcher.subscribe(DashEvent, self.on_dash)

    def on_dash(self, event: DashEvent) -> None:
        """One instant hop the way the player is facing."""
        entity = self._em.get_entity(event.entity_id)
        if entity is None or not entity.has_component(Movement):
            return
        movement = entity.get_component(Movement)
        direction = movement.direction
        if direction.length == 0:
            direction = Vector2(1, 0)   # standing still: dash right
        transform = entity.get_component(Transform)
        transform.position = transform.position + direction * event.distance

    def update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        for entity in self._em.get_entities_with(Transform, Movement):
            transform = entity.get_component(Transform)
            movement = entity.get_component(Movement)
            # Position, straight from intent. Nothing is integrated here --
            # `dt` is only what makes a held key cover the same distance per
            # second on any machine.
            transform.position = transform.position + movement.direction * (
                movement.speed * dt
            )

PlayerSystem is registered with the scene's own SystemManager (self.system_manager.register(...)), so it is ticked for you every fixed step — the scene's update() has nothing to call by hand.

docs.title: 🏃 Part 4: Physical Simulation (games/physics_integration)
docs.text:
For advanced simulation, PyGuara runs the Rapier rigid body engine, in its native extension. Rather than calculating gravity manually, physical objects register RigidBody and Collider components. The PhysicsSystem automatically simulates rigid body calculations and mirrors the resulting coordinates back onto Transform components.

For a player or NPC, use CharacterBody with CharacterMover instead of a dynamic RigidBody — it gives crisp, non-bouncy movement with ground and wall detection. See docs/physics/character-movement.md. The dynamic-body example below is for props and projectiles.

docs.title: 1. Attaching Physical Components
docs.text:
from pyguara.physics.components import RigidBody, Collider
from pyguara.physics.types import BodyType, ShapeType

# Create a dynamic falling circle
ball = self.entity_manager.create_entity("ball")
ball.add_component(Transform(position=Vector2(400, 100)))
# RigidBody carries mass and body type; friction/restitution live on the
# Collider's PhysicsMaterial.
ball.add_component(RigidBody(body_type=BodyType.DYNAMIC, mass=1.0))
# Collider dimensions are [radius] for a circle, [width, height] for a box.
ball.add_component(Collider(shape_type=ShapeType.CIRCLE, dimensions=[20.0]))

docs.title: 2. Managing Static Ground Boundaries
docs.text:
Static physics boundaries prevent entities from falling into the void:

ground = self.entity_manager.create_entity("ground")
ground.add_component(Transform(position=Vector2(400, 500)))
# Static body does not move under gravity or collisions
ground.add_component(RigidBody(body_type=BodyType.STATIC))
# Box collider bounds
ground.add_component(Collider(shape_type=ShapeType.BOX, dimensions=[800, 40]))

docs.title: 🖥️ Part 5: UI Scene Graphs & Layouts (games/ui_scene_graph)
docs.text: Creating buttons, health bars, and overlay dialogs requires a layout-agnostic framework to handle resolution adjustments automatically. PyGuara provides a constraint-based UI layout system.

docs.title: 1. Building responsive buttons and panels
docs.text:
You instantiate UI widgets, attach declarative LayoutConstraints, and add the roots to the UIManager. The manager runs a layout pass over every root before it draws (and again after a window resize), so a constrained element's position/size are placeholders -- the constraints decide the final rect.

from pyguara.common.types import Vector2
from pyguara.ui.manager import UIManager
from pyguara.ui.components import Panel, Button
from pyguara.ui.constraints import LayoutConstraints
from pyguara.ui.types import UIAnchor

# 1. Grab UIManager from DI Container
ui_manager = self.container.get(UIManager)

# 2. A panel covering the centre 50% x 60% of the screen.
#    position/size are placeholders; the constraint wins.
panel = Panel(Vector2(0, 0), Vector2(10, 10))
panel.constraints = LayoutConstraints(
    anchor=UIAnchor.CENTER,
    width_percent=0.5,
    height_percent=0.6,
)
ui_manager.add_element(panel)

# 3. A button centred inside the panel's content rect.
button = Button("Start Game", Vector2(0, 0))
button.constraints = LayoutConstraints(
    anchor=UIAnchor.CENTER,
    width_percent=0.3,
    height_percent=0.1,
)

def on_click(btn: Button):
    print("Transitioning to main level scene...")
    # Scene transition command (via SceneManager)

button.on_click = on_click
panel.add_child(button)

If you mutate something a layout depends on after the first frame -- a label's text, an element's visible flag -- call ui_manager.invalidate_layout() so the next render re-runs the pass.

docs.title: 📦 Part 6: Standalone Compilation (pyguara build)
docs.text: Once your game is complete, you will want to share it with players without requiring them to install Python or Pip. PyGuara provides a packaging utility built directly into its Command Line Interface.

docs.title: How to Compile Your Game
docs.text:
The pyguara build command compiles your entry script, copies all associated assets (like images, sound clips, and configurations), resolves external dynamic libraries, and outputs a ready-to-run folder.

# Basic directory-based build
uv run pyguara build games/guara_falcao/main.py --output dist/guara_falcao

# Compact single-executable build
uv run pyguara build games/true_coral/main.py --onefile --output dist/true_coral

docs.title: Build Options Reference
docs.text:
• -o, --output: Specifies the destination directory for the package (default: dist/).
  • -n, --name: Changes the final binary name (defaults to the entry script's filename).
  • --onefile: Merges all resources and Python script libraries into a single file executable.
  • --windowed: Suppresses the OS command shell terminal console on boot (default behavior).
  • --icon: Bundles a custom application icon (e.g. icon.ico for Windows or icon.icns for macOS).
  • -a, --assets: Explicitly specifies directories containing game assets (textures, music, shaders) to package with the executable.
  • --dry-run: Prints the PyInstaller command that would run, without building.

See Command-Line Tools for the full option list and for pyguara atlas, the sprite-atlas packer.

Now you have all the knowledge required to bootstrap, design, script, and publish your own 2D games using the PyGuara game engine! Keep exploring the examples under the games/ folder to study advanced scripts, spatial audio routing, and the in-engine debug overlays.

docs.title: Kits
docs.text:
pyguara/kits/ is the opt-in layer. Core is what every game needs; a kit is a genre's vocabulary, packaged so a game that wants it can import it and a game that doesn't never pays for it. Nothing in core imports a kit, and kits reach each other only through core event dispatch — never a direct import.

The kits that exist today: action_combat, effects, stats, projectiles, procgen, spawn, loot, progression, the two movement policies platformer_movement (coyote time, jump buffer, wall jump) and topdown_movement (soft separation between actors), plus the smaller echolocation, pack and trail.

Only progression is documented here so far. The rest are documented in their own module docstrings; pages get written as each kit is audited.

  • Progression — experience, levels, upgrade offers, pickup magnet

docs.title: Progression kit
docs.text:
pyguara.kits.progression — experience and levels, the upgrade pick a level-up offers, and the pickup magnet.

The genre this comes from asks for five separable things. Three are in the kit; the other two are deliberately not:

In the kit Stays with the game Experience, levels, the curve The level-up UI scene The upgrade offer and what's been taken The upgrade content: names, weights, recipes The pickup magnet Any weapon / item / inventory model

docs.title: Experience and levels
docs.text:
from pyguara.kits.progression import Experience, Geometric, grant_experience

player.add_component(Experience())
curve = Geometric(base=100.0, growth=1.25)

levels = grant_experience(dispatcher, player.id, xp, curve, amount=250.0)

Data component plus a free function, matching StatBlock/get_stat and Health/apply_damage — the component holds the numbers and the behaviour that mutates them lives beside it, not on it.

Carry-over is kept. Crossing a level costs exactly that level's price and the remainder counts toward the next, so a single large grant lands in the same place as the same total delivered in pieces. One grant can cross several levels — a boss early in a run — and each crossing gets its own LeveledUp.

Experience.pending_levels counts levels reached but not yet spent. The kit never spends them: it has no idea what a level is worth. The game decrements it as it hands out whatever a level buys.

max_level caps progression. At the cap current stops accumulating, because a bar filling toward a level that will never arrive is worse than a full one — but total keeps counting, because an end-of-run screen should report everything collected.

docs.title: Curves
docs.text:
LevelCurve is a Protocol, so a bespoke curve is one method with nothing to import and nothing to inherit from.

Curve Shape Linear(base, step) Each level costs a fixed amount more than the last. Geometric(base, growth) Each level costs a fixed multiple of the last. Table(costs) Costs read off a list a designer wrote. Past the end, the last entry repeats.

docs.title: Events, not callbacks
docs.text:
dispatcher.subscribe(LeveledUp, lambda event: scene_manager.push(LevelUpScene()))

This is the load-bearing decision in the kit: it's how a level-up scene gets pushed without the kit knowing that scenes, or UI, or upgrade cards exist.

ExperienceGained carries the settled numbers and is dispatched before the LeveledUps it caused, so a listener redrawing an experience bar has already done it by the time another pushes a scene over the top.

docs.title: Upgrades
docs.text:
from pyguara.kits.progression import Upgrade, UpgradeRecord, offer, take

pool = [
    Upgrade(key="whip", apply=lambda eid: boost(eid, "damage", 0.1), max_taken=None),
    Upgrade(key="bracer", apply=lambda eid: boost(eid, "armor", 5)),
    Upgrade(
        key="evolved_whip",
        apply=lambda eid: give_evolved_whip(eid),
        requires={"whip": 5, "bracer": 1},
    ),
]

cards = offer(rng, pool, record, count=3)   # the 1-of-3 pick
take(record, cards[chosen], player.id)

Upgrade.apply is an opaque callable. The kit never learns that "+10% move speed" means a StatBlock modifier, or that "pierce" means an Effect — the game writes the closure. So this package imports neither kits.stats nor kits.effects while composing perfectly with both, and with whatever a game invents that neither anticipated. There is a test that parses the package's imports and fails if that is ever quietly spent.

offer() does not reimplement weighted selection. It filters by eligibility and delegates to common.random.weighted_choice, sampling without replacement so a card cannot appear twice in one pick. A late run that has exhausted its pool offers two cards rather than raising.

The same seed and the same record produce the same offer, which is what lets a run be replayed.

Weapon evolution needs no new type. requires plus UpgradeRecord.taken is the mechanism — "evolved whip requires whip ×5 and the bracer" is a requires of {"whip": 5, "bracer": 1}. That's what earns requires its place in an otherwise minimal kit, and it takes evolution trees out of the "needs an item model" column entirely.

take() updates the record before running the closure, so an upgrade that scales with its own stack count sees the take it is part of.

docs.title: The pickup magnet
docs.text:
from pyguara.kits.progression import Attracted, Magnet, MagnetSystem

player.add_component(Magnet(radius=120.0, speed=120.0, acceleration=600.0))
orb.add_component(Attracted(payload=5.0, collect_radius=12.0))
orb.add_component(SpatialTracked())

magnets = MagnetSystem(entity_manager, dispatcher, spatial_index)

Not a physics interaction. A magnet is a radius query and a velocity — no collider, no body, no contact resolution. An orb passes through walls on its way to the player, which is what the genre wants and what keeps a thousand of them affordable. A game that needs pickups to respect geometry gives them a Collider and doesn't use this.

It's the second consumer of the shared SpatialHash (kits/projectiles was the first), which is the point: attraction is a "what is near me" question, and that index answers it in one cell walk rather than a scan over every orb on the field. Entities must be tracked in it the usual way (SpatialTracked + SpatialIndexSystem); this system never inserts into the index itself.

Collecting dispatches PickupCollected carrying the orb's opaque payload and marks the pickup inactive. Destroying it is left to the game, which may want to pool it, play something on it, or fade it out. A typical listener calls grant_experience() with the payload.

Attracted.active exists so a just-dropped orb can sit inert for a moment instead of flying straight back into whoever dropped it.

docs.title: Character movement: the switch to CharacterMover, resolved
docs.text: PyGuara used to move platformer characters as dynamic rigid bodies with assigned velocity. That is no longer true: characters are now moved by CharacterMover, a swept collide-and-slide mover, and carry no physics body at all. This document records why the old approach was replaced, the decision that unblocked the switch, and the shape the engine ended up with.

docs.title: Where we were
docs.text:
PlatformerSystem read input, worked out a desired velocity, and assigned it to the body:

rigidbody.handle.velocity = Vector2(new_velocity_x, new_velocity_y)

Chipmunk then stepped the world and resolved whatever overlaps resulted. That was the source of a whole family of bugs, because a character pressed into geometry is inside it until the solver pushes it back out.

Measured in guara_falcao, jumping while running:

depth reached 8.95px into the floor recovery rate ~0.04px per tick time visibly sunk over 3 seconds

Substepping, a raised penetration-recovery rate, and merging tile colliders all helped without fixing the cause; jumping while moving still penetrated. Every bug in this family — sinking, seam catching, wall creep, tunnelling — came from asking a rigid-body solver to move something that was not really a rigid body.

docs.title: The decision that unblocked the switch
docs.text: Before wiring the mover in, one question had to be answered: what should a character still be able to do physically (be knocked back? push crates? ride platforms?), because that decides how much of the dynamic-body world had to be rebuilt rather than deleted. Checked against the actual code at the time: none of the three existed as working features — Hazard.knockback_force was declared and read by nothing, crates weren't implemented in guara_falcao at all (GDD-only), and moving platforms had no system driving them. The decision made: build full physical parity anyway — knockback, platform riding, and crate pushing — using Celeste's model as the reference (Maddy Thorson's "Celeste and TowerFall Physics"): integer-pixel positions with a float remainder accumulator, and solids that explicitly carry/push the actors touching them, rather than leaning on Chipmunk friction or a continuous bisection sweep.

docs.title: What shipped
docs.text:
CharacterMover (pyguara/physics/character_mover.py) sweeps a character one whole pixel at a time. A float remainder accumulates sub-pixel motion every call (gravity at 900px/s² is rarely a whole number of pixels per tick); only the whole-pixel part is ever stepped, and every pixel stepped is tested, so tunnelling is impossible and there is nothing to bisect for — the last free whole pixel is the resting position. CharacterMover.probe() is the same overlap primitive used one pixel off in a direction, without moving: Celeste's OnGround() is exactly CollideCheck(Position + Vector2.UnitY), not a raycast, and it's what ground detection uses now.

CharacterBody (pyguara/physics/components.py) replaces RigidBody for a character: velocity, ground state, and knockback state, with no shape registered with the physics engine at all. That is what makes the old ground-ray self-detection bug class structurally impossible rather than guarded against — the character has nothing to detect.

SolidMover/SolidSystem (pyguara/physics/solid_mover.py, solid_system.py) are the other half: how the world moves a character that isn't driving. Built on Celeste's Solid.MoveHExact/MoveVExact rather than a swept move — a rider or a pushed actor is placed directly at the position a solid's motion dictates (the solid already decided exactly where it's going), then checked for whether that position is clear of everything except the solid that moved it. If not, it's squished: flagged on CharacterBody.squished and reported via OnActorSquished, since what a squish means (damage, death, nothing) is a game decision, not a physics one. A MovingSolid is still an ordinary RigidBody/Collider as far as Chipmunk is concerned, so genuinely dynamic bodies keep colliding with it normally.

Pushing is Pushable, a marker on a MovingSolid: when CharacterMover's sweep is blocked by one, PlatformerSystem asks SolidMover.try_move() to shove it by the distance the block left untravelled, retrying the character's own move once if the shove succeeds. try_move() excludes the pushing character from the reactive carry/push pass that follows — without that, a pushed crate immediately shoves back at whoever just pushed it, which is exactly the shape a first version of the test for this caught.

Knockback is apply_knockback() (pyguara/kits/platformer_movement/system.py): consumed as velocity, not an impulse. It overrides CharacterBody.velocity directly and suppresses input control for a short window, during which the velocity decays back toward zero and gravity keeps acting underneath it — an ordinary hit-stun. games/guara_falcao's HazardSystem now calls it, which is what finally gives Hazard.knockback_force something to do.

System ordering (GameplayScene.fixed_update() in guara_falcao) became: whatever authors a solid's motion (a patrol script) → sync kinematic transforms into the engine, so a query this same tick sees where a solid already is → SolidSystem carries/pushes whatever a solid touched → PlatformerSystem moves the character against that now-current geometry → PhysicsSystem steps whatever is still a genuine Chipmunk dynamic body. PhysicsSystem.sync_kinematic_transforms() was split out of update() to make the middle of that sequence possible.

Two details worth keeping in mind, both handled:

  • A box resting exactly flush counts as overlapping in Chipmunk's shape_query — a touching contact is an overlap. SKIN (0.05px) is the allowance applied to every query box so a resting contact doesn't poison the next step's query; it never changes where anything actually settles.
  • Ground/wall detection, riding, and pushing all assert exact pixel positions in tests now, not pytest.approx(..., abs=0.1) — there is no bisection settling near the answer any more, so there's no reason to tolerate one.

docs.title: Where these live
docs.text:
CharacterMover is core: axis-separated sweep-and-resolve, no gravity assumption, no genre vocabulary. Every genre with character-based movement needs it, and #99 proved the point — it needed zero changes to serve 8-directional top-down motion.

PlatformerController/PlatformerSystem and TopDownBody/TopDownSystem are kits (pyguara/kits/platformer_movement, pyguara/kits/topdown_movement). Coyote time and wall-jumping answer a platformer's questions; actor-vs-actor separation answers a top-down game's. Neither belongs to the other, and core belongs to both.

A character that something else steps, such as a player controller or network prediction calling step_body itself, sets TopDownBody.moved_elsewhere. TopDownSystem then leaves its movement alone, so it isn't moved twice, and it still takes part in separation. Separation pushes positions directly, so it can push an actor into a wall; for a crowd in a level, give the actors a separation force instead (FlockingSystem's does this) and leave separation_radius at zero.

Import them from the kit, and register the component yourself if you want it in prefabs — core does not register a kit's components:

from pyguara.kits.platformer_movement import PlatformerController, PlatformerSystem

container.get(ComponentRegistry).register(PlatformerController)
