docs.title: Spatial Queries
docs.text:
Every question a game asks the physics world that is not "step the simulation" is a spatial query: what did the player click, which enemies are in the blast radius, does this doorway fit the crate, what does the laser pass through. They are read-only — nothing moves — and they run against the same broadphase the solver uses, so they are cheap.

All of them live on IPhysicsEngine, which bootstrap.py registers as a singleton; resolve it from the DI container (container.get(IPhysicsEngine)) or take it in a system constructor.

docs.title: The queries
docs.text:
Method Shape asked Returns Reach for it when raycast(start, end, ...) a line segment nearest RaycastHit or None line of sight, ground probe, a single hitscan shot raycast_all(start, end, ...) a line segment list[RaycastHit], near→far a piercing shot or laser that passes through several targets point_query(point, ...) one point list[entity id], most-enclosed first click-picking — "what is under the cursor?" overlap_box(centre, half_extents, ...) an axis-aligned box first entity id or None a mover's per-step "is this space blocked, and by what?" overlap_box_all(centre, half_extents, ...) an axis-aligned box list[entity id] a box-shaped melee swing, a marquee selection overlap_circle(centre, radius, ...) a circle list[entity id] explosion radius, aggro range, a radial melee arc region_query(bounds, ...) a Rect's bounding box list[entity id] a fast first cut of a large world before a precise test

Common parameters, on every query:

  • mask — a collision bitmask. A shape whose category is outside the mask is ignored, exactly as for raycast. Defaults to "hit everything".
  • ignore_entity_id — one entity to leave out of the results, normally the querier itself (a character probing for ground would otherwise find its own collider).

Shared behaviour:

  • Sensors are never returned. A sensor (Collider(is_sensor=True), or a TriggerVolume) is meant to be passed through; use the trigger events for those.
  • An entity is reported once, even if it carries several colliders.
  • The list queries return [] when nothing matches; raycast / overlap_box return None.

docs.title: Precise vs. broad-phase
docs.text: region_query is the odd one out: it tests bounding boxes, not shapes. A circle or a rotated polygon whose bounding box pokes into the rectangle is reported even though the shape itself does not touch it. That is the point — it is the cheapest possible "roughly what is around here", meant to narrow a big world down to a handful of candidates that you then confirm with overlap_circle, overlap_box_all, or your own maths. Every other query on this page tests the real shape.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
from pyguara.physics.protocols import IPhysicsEngine
from pyguara.common.types import Rect, Vector2

engine = container.get(IPhysicsEngine)

# Click-picking: topmost entity under the mouse in world space.
picked = engine.point_query(world_mouse)
if picked:
    select(picked[0])

# Explosion: everything within 120px, minus the bomb itself.
for entity_id in engine.overlap_circle(blast_centre, 120.0, ignore_entity_id=bomb.id):
    apply_damage(entity_id, falloff(blast_centre, entity_id))

# Piercing shot: hit every body along the line, nearest first.
for hit in engine.raycast_all(muzzle, muzzle + aim * 800):
    damage(hit.entity_id)
    if not pierces(hit.entity_id):
        break

# "Can the crate fit through here?" — a solid in the doorway means no.
blocked = engine.overlap_box(doorway_centre, Vector2(16, 24), ignore_entity_id=crate.id)

docs.title: Determinism
docs.text: The queries read the world; they do not advance it, and they take no random input, so they are safe to call from anywhere in a frame and do not affect deterministic replay. raycast / raycast_all cast a line of zero width, so a hit lands exactly where the line meets the shape.

docs.title: Physics System
docs.text: PyGuara simulates physics with Rapier, in the native extension, behind the IPhysicsEngine protocol. It replaced pymunk (Chipmunk2D); see Coming from pymunk.

docs.title: RigidBody
docs.text:
Represents a physical object the physics engine simulates. - Dynamic: Affected by forces and gravity. - Static: Immovable (walls, ground). - Kinematic: Moved by code but affects dynamic bodies (platforms).

A player character is the exception — it should carry a CharacterBody, not a RigidBody. See Platformer characters below.

docs.title: Collider
docs.text: Defines the collision shape and properties. - Shapes: BOX, CIRCLE. - Properties: Friction, Restitution (bounciness), Density. - Trigger: is_sensor=True makes it a non-solid trigger volume.

docs.title: PhysicsSystem
docs.text: The PhysicsSystem synchronizes the ECS Transform component with the physics engine's bodies. - Pre-Step: Updates the engine's bodies if ECS transforms changed (Kinematic/Manual). - Step: Advances simulation (dt). - Post-Step: Updates ECS transforms from the engine's bodies (Dynamic).

docs.title: Substepping
docs.text:
The world runs no continuous collision detection, so in principle a body moving velocity × dt in one solver step can pass through anything thinner than that jump. physics.substeps (default 4) splits each tick into that many solver steps to shorten it.

In practice Rapier keeps thin walls solid without them. Measured with tests/integration/test_collision_robustness.py's fire_at_wall and one substep, an 8px box stops at a 10px wall at 20,000 px/s (333px a step), and a 1px box at a 1px wall. Only a circle of 1 or 2px fired into a wall as thin, at 20,000 px/s, came out just past it. Chipmunk tunnelled at 1,200 px/s through that 10px wall with one substep. Fast projectiles should still use raycast rather than lean on the solver.

docs.title: The engine
docs.text:
physics.backend names the engine, and rapier is the only one. Bootstrap logs it with the substep count (physics: rapier, 4 substeps). It covers bodies, circle and box colliders, materials, collision layers and groups, sensors, collision events, forces and impulses, every query, every joint type, one-way platforms and the native swept mover (sweep_box, step_bodies).

A game that builds a physics world of its own -- a room's walls kept apart from the main world, say -- should make it with pyguara.physics.create_physics_engine(config.physics), so it is configured as the main one is.

Refused rather than ignored: segment and polygon colliders, and a max_force on any joint but a motor, which Rapier can cap only on a motor. Both raise NotImplementedError.

docs.title: Coming from pymunk
docs.text:
pymunk was the engine until 0.8. physics.backend = "pymunk", in a config file or as PYGUARA_PHYSICS_BACKEND, now stops the game at startup with RetiredBackendError. PymunkEngine is gone; RapierEngine or create_physics_engine replaces it. Chipmunk's two tunings, physics.penetration_recovery and physics.sleep_time_threshold, are gone with it, and a config file that still sets them loads with a warning naming each key. The pymunk package is no longer a dependency: Vector2 is the engine's own, in the native extension.

What a game notices:

  • Collision events are reported after each solver step, not during it. A pair whose on_collision_begin returns False is resolved for one solver step before it stops being; Chipmunk stopped at once.
  • A ray is a line, where Chipmunk's had a radius of one pixel.
  • Results differ: Rapier settles a stack differently, so a replay or a golden frame with rigid bodies in it changed with the switch.
  • With a collision system attached, which every game started through create_application has, Rapier steps a pile of falling boxes in about a fifth of pymunk's time, and its swept mover keeps its speed with moving bodies in the world; see performance.

docs.title: Collision Handling
docs.text:
Collisions generate events via the CollisionSystem, which bootstrap.py wires to the physics engine. Subscribe on the EventDispatcher:

  • OnCollisionBegin / OnCollisionPersist / OnCollisionEnd: two solid (non-sensor) colliders touching.
  • OnTriggerEnter / OnTriggerStay / OnTriggerExit: something overlapping a sensor collider.
def on_collision(self, event: OnCollisionBegin):
    print(f"Entities {event.entity_a} and {event.entity_b} collided!")

The engine reports a contact pair in its own order and tells CollisionSystem which side owns the sensor; the trigger events always come out with trigger_entity set to the sensor's entity and other_entity the body that entered it, regardless of that order.

docs.title: Spatial queries
docs.text: Collision events tell you what is touching what. To ask the world a question directly — what did the player click, who is in the blast radius, does this space fit — use the read-only queries on IPhysicsEngine (raycast, raycast_all, point_query, overlap_box, overlap_box_all, overlap_circle, region_query). They are documented on their own page: Spatial Queries.

docs.title: Trigger volumes
docs.text:
A TriggerVolume component is the high-level way to use a sensor: it keeps a live entities_inside set and supports tag filtering and one-shot deactivation. It needs three systems running -- PhysicsSystem, CollisionSystem, and TriggerSystem (the last is opt-in; create one and tick it each frame). TriggerSystem gives the entity the pieces it needs to enter the simulation:

  • a sensor Collider matching the volume's shape, and
  • a static RigidBody, if the entity has none -- PhysicsSystem only registers shapes for entities that have a body. Add your own KINEMATIC RigidBody instead if the trigger has to move with a platform.
zone = entity_manager.create_entity()
zone.add_component(Transform(position=Vector2(400, 300)))
zone.add_component(TriggerVolume(
    shape_type=ShapeType.BOX, dimensions=[100, 100], tags={"player"},
))
# ...later, any frame:
if zone.get_component(TriggerVolume).contains_entity(player.id):
    ...

docs.title: Joints
docs.text:
Joint connects two entities' RigidBody bodies -- pin, distance, spring, slider. The component is pure data; pyguara.physics.joint_system.JointSystem is what turns it into a real constraint. Like PhysicsSystem it is opt-in: create one and tick it each fixed step, after PhysicsSystem.update().

from pyguara.physics.joints import create_pin_joint

bob.add_component(create_pin_joint(target_entity_id=anchor.id))

JointSystem builds the constraint once both entities have a body in the engine (retrying on later ticks until then), and destroys it when either entity is removed or the Joint component is taken off its entity. Factory helpers: create_pin_joint, create_distance_joint, create_spring_joint, create_slider_joint, plus create_rope_chain for a segmented rope.

docs.title: Platformer characters: CharacterMover, not RigidBody
docs.text:
A platformer character is the one thing that should not be a RigidBody. Assigning it velocity and letting the solver resolve overlap after the fact is what produces sinking, seam catching, wall creep and tunnelling — a character pressed into geometry is briefly inside it until the solver pushes it back out.

Instead, give it a CharacterBody (velocity, ground state, knockback) and a Collider used only for its dimensions — no shape is registered with the physics engine at all. PlatformerSystem sweeps it every tick with CharacterMover, which advances one whole pixel at a time and stops flush the instant a step would overlap something, so penetration cannot occur by construction.

The same model extends to what the character touches:

  • MovingSolid + SolidSystem carry or push any CharacterBody a moving platform touches (riding on top, or shoved from the side).
  • Pushable, added to a MovingSolid, lets a character shove it — a crate, say — instead of just stopping at it.
  • apply_knockback() overrides a character's velocity for a short, decaying window, for hits and explosions.

RigidBody is still the right choice for everything else — crates before they're pushed, ragdolls, projectiles, the level's static geometry. See docs/physics/character-movement.md for why this split exists and the defects it fixes.

docs.title: pyguara.assets
docs.text:
One way to read a game's files, whether they are loose or packed.

pyguara build can bake the assets into one pack (a ZIP), which is mounted at run time over the folder it was made from. Every engine loader reads through this module. A pack holds paths relative to its root, and a path is looked up in a pack only if it lies under that root, so the same paths work loose or packed. The last mounted pack is consulted first, then the earlier ones, then the disk. Packs are read-only.

Example

from pyguara import assets

assets.mount_pack("Reclaimer.pak", root=game_dir) assets.read_bytes(game_dir / "assets/sprites/hero.png") # the pack assets.read_bytes("saves/slot1.save") # the disk

docs.title: pyguara.crash
docs.text:
Crash reports: an unhandled exception leaves a file behind, and says where.

The report holds the traceback, the engine and Python versions, the platform, which native store was in force, and whatever the engine noted on the way, such as the renderer. It is written to the player's data directory, and holds paths from their machine.

Opt-in, because the directory is named after the game. Install it before the application is built, so a failure at startup is reported too.

Example

from pyguara.crash import install_crash_reporter

install_crash_reporter("Reclaimer") app = create_application() app.run(TitleScene(...))

docs.title: CrashReporter dataclass
docs.text:
The installed hook: where reports go, and the hook it chains to.

Built by install_crash_reporter(), not directly.

Attributes:

Name Type Description app_name str

The game's name, written into each report.

directory Path

Where reports are written. Created on the first crash, not at install, so a game that never crashes leaves nothing.

keep int

How many reports to keep; older ones are deleted on write.

previous_hook ExceptHook

The sys.excepthook this one replaced and calls after writing, so the traceback still reaches stderr.

last_report Path | None

The most recent report written, or None.

docs.title: note
docs.text:
note(key: str, value: object) -> None

Record a fact for any crash report written from now on.

The engine notes what it learns while starting -- the renderer chosen, for one -- so a report says what was running, not only where it failed. A game may note its own: the level, the build id. A later note under the same key replaces the earlier one.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default key str

A short name, written as key: value.

required value object

Anything; written with str().

required

docs.title: clear_notes
docs.text:
clear_notes() -> None

Forget every noted fact. For tests, and for a game that restarts.

docs.title: install_crash_reporter
docs.text:
install_crash_reporter(
    app_name: str,
    app_author: str | None = None,
    *,
    directory: Path | None = None,
    keep: int = 20,
) -> CrashReporter

Write a report for any exception that would otherwise end the program.

Replaces sys.excepthook and chains to the one it replaced, so the traceback still prints where there is a console. Installing again replaces the earlier reporter rather than stacking a second.

Covers the main thread. An exception in another thread does not end the program, and is not reported.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default app_name str

The game's name: the directory name, and the report's first line.

required app_author str | None

Vendor name, used only on Windows. Defaults to app_name.

None directory Path | None

Where to write, instead of crashes/ in the per-user data directory.

None keep int

How many reports to keep. At least 1.

20

Returns:

Type Description CrashReporter

The installed reporter, whose directory says where reports go.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If app_name is empty or keep is below 1.

uninstall_crash_reporter() -> None

Put back the hook install_crash_reporter() replaced. A no-op if none.

docs.title: pyguara.errors
docs.text:
Error-handling types shared across engine subsystems.

Kept at the top level, importing nothing from the engine, so any subsystem can depend on it without creating a cycle -- di in particular must not import events, and events must not import log.

docs.title: ErrorHandlingStrategy
docs.text:
Bases: Enum

What a subsystem does when user-supplied code raises.

Used by EventDispatcher for handlers and filters, and by DIContainer for constructor introspection. A single definition, because two enums with the same members are not interchangeable: comparing one subsystem's RAISE against another's silently evaluates false.

Attributes:

Name Type Description LOG

Log the error and carry on. Graceful degradation in production.

RAISE

Log the error and re-raise it. Fail fast in development, and the default everywhere.

IGNORE

Swallow the error silently. Tests and narrow edge cases only.

Example 
from pyguara.errors import ErrorHandlingStrategy

dispatcher = EventDispatcher(error_strategy=ErrorHandlingStrategy.LOG)
container = DIContainer(error_strategy=ErrorHandlingStrategy.LOG)

docs.title: pyguara.native
docs.text:
The compiled extension, found once and required.

Every backend subsystem the engine ships is implemented in the extension and has no Python counterpart, so there is no store to choose: an engine that cannot load it stops at bootstrap and says why. See ADR 0011.

This module imports nothing from pyguara but the extension itself, so it can be consulted from anywhere, including before bootstrap.

Building the extension is covered in AGENTS.md and docs/adr/0006-shipping-the-native-extension.md.

docs.title: STORE_NAME module-attribute
docs.text:
STORE_NAME = 'native'

What a replay records as the store it was made with.

There is one. A replay recorded before the Python stores were retired may say "python"; see Application's playback check.

docs.title: CooldownNode
docs.text:
Bases: DecoratorNode

Refuse to run a child again until a delay has elapsed.

The cooldown starts when the child finishes, not when it starts, so a long-running action is not cut short. A child that returns RUNNING is left alone.

Reads context.dt, as WaitNode does, so time spent paused does not count.

Example

docs.title: ParallelNode
docs.text:
Bases: CompositeNode

Executes all children simultaneously.

Returns SUCCESS if success_threshold children succeed. Returns FAILURE if failure_threshold children fail. Returns RUNNING otherwise.

A child that has finished is latched: its result is remembered and it is not ticked again until this node itself resolves. latch=False re-ticks every child on every tick, for children that are all idempotent polls.

Example

parallel = ParallelNode( ... children=[move_to_target, scan_for_enemies, play_animation], ... success_threshold=2, ... failure_threshold=2 ... )

docs.title: RandomSelector
docs.text:
Bases: CompositeNode

Try children in a shuffled order until one succeeds.

A selector picks by priority, which makes a guard dog predictable. This picks by chance, which is what idle variation, attack choice and barks want.

The order is reshuffled when the node starts, not on every tick, so a child that returns RUNNING keeps its turn rather than being abandoned mid-action.

Example

RandomSelector([bark, sniff, scratch])

docs.title: ReactiveSelectorNode
docs.text:
Bases: SelectorNode

A selector that re-checks higher-priority branches every tick.

SelectorNode resumes at the child that was RUNNING, so a higher-priority branch that becomes viable mid-action does not take over. This node re-ticks from the top, so the first viable branch wins on every tick. The pre-empted child is reset().

Example

ReactiveSelectorNode([ ... SequenceNode([is_health_low, flee]), ... SequenceNode([is_enemy_close, attack]), ... ActionNode(patrol), ... ])

docs.title: ReactiveSequenceNode
docs.text:
Bases: SequenceNode

A sequence that re-checks its guards every tick.

SequenceNode resumes at the child that was RUNNING, so a condition at the front is checked once. This node starts from the first child on every tick, so a guard holds for as long as the branch runs. When a failing guard pre-empts a RUNNING child, that child is reset(), so it does not resume half-finished later.

Example

ReactiveSequenceNode([ ... ConditionNode(is_player_visible), ... ActionNode(chase), ... ActionNode(attack), ... ])

docs.title: RepeaterNode
docs.text:
Bases: DecoratorNode

Repeats child N times or infinitely.

Example

repeater = RepeaterNode(ActionNode(patrol), count=5)

docs.title: OR infinite:
docs.text: repeater = RepeaterNode(ActionNode(patrol), count=-1)

docs.text:
get_neighbors(node: GridNode) -> Iterator[GridNode]

Yield valid neighbors.

Diagonal moves refuse to cut a solid corner: both orthogonal cells flanking the diagonal must be walkable (in bounds and not a wall), matching the deleted GridMap's behavior -- an out-of-bounds flanking cell blocks the diagonal too, not just an actual wall.

This is the largest Python cost in grid pathfinding, so it reads the grid directly instead of calling in_bounds and is_passable up to six times per candidate. The yield order is load-bearing: rust/src/flowfield.rs replicates it bit-exactly.

docs.title: ReactiveSequenceNode
docs.text:
Bases: SequenceNode

A sequence that re-checks its guards every tick.

SequenceNode resumes at the child that was RUNNING, so a condition at the front is checked once. This node starts from the first child on every tick, so a guard holds for as long as the branch runs. When a failing guard pre-empts a RUNNING child, that child is reset(), so it does not resume half-finished later.

Example

ReactiveSequenceNode([ ... ConditionNode(is_player_visible), ... ActionNode(chase), ... ActionNode(attack), ... ])

docs.title: ReactiveSelectorNode
docs.text:
Bases: SelectorNode

A selector that re-checks higher-priority branches every tick.

SelectorNode resumes at the child that was RUNNING, so a higher-priority branch that becomes viable mid-action does not take over. This node re-ticks from the top, so the first viable branch wins on every tick. The pre-empted child is reset().

Example

ReactiveSelectorNode([ ... SequenceNode([is_health_low, flee]), ... SequenceNode([is_enemy_close, attack]), ... ActionNode(patrol), ... ])

docs.title: ParallelNode
docs.text:
Bases: CompositeNode

Executes all children simultaneously.

Returns SUCCESS if success_threshold children succeed. Returns FAILURE if failure_threshold children fail. Returns RUNNING otherwise.

A child that has finished is latched: its result is remembered and it is not ticked again until this node itself resolves. latch=False re-ticks every child on every tick, for children that are all idempotent polls.

Example

parallel = ParallelNode( ... children=[move_to_target, scan_for_enemies, play_animation], ... success_threshold=2, ... failure_threshold=2 ... )

Bases: CompositeNode

Try children in a shuffled order until one succeeds.

A selector picks by priority, which makes a guard dog predictable. This picks by chance, which is what idle variation, attack choice and barks want.

The order is reshuffled when the node starts, not on every tick, so a child that returns RUNNING keeps its turn rather than being abandoned mid-action.

Example

RandomSelector([bark, sniff, scratch])

docs.title: pyguara.ai.flocking_system
docs.text:
System for boid flocking: cohesion, alignment, separation, and seek.

Sums cohesion, alignment, separation, and an optional seek target into one steering force per agent, each tick.

Kept as a sibling of SteeringSystem rather than a new dispatch branch on it: a flock needs neighbor queries and a sum of forces every tick, while SteeringSystem is a closed dispatch over exactly one behavior per entity. An entity can carry both components (e.g. the jaguar uses plain SteeringAgent flee/evade while the pack uses FlockingAgent).

docs.title: FlockingAgent dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: StrictComponent

Per-entity boid tuning and runtime velocity.

Attributes:

Name Type Description max_speed float

Maximum movement speed.

max_force float

Maximum steering force (turn speed/acceleration).

mass float

Used to calculate acceleration (Force / Mass).

velocity Vector2

Current velocity of the agent.

neighbor_radius float

Distance within which other FlockingAgents count as flockmates for cohesion/alignment.

separation_radius float

Distance within which flockmates push apart. Usually smaller than neighbor_radius.

cohesion_weight float

Blend weight for steering toward the flock center.

alignment_weight float

Blend weight for matching the flock's heading.

separation_weight float

Blend weight for pushing apart from close flockmates. Kept high relative to the others by default -- a weak separation relative to cohesion/seek is what produces visible jitter as agents fight over the same space.

seek_weight float

Blend weight for seek_target, e.g. a flow-field direction or an assigned flanking vector. Zero if unused.

seek_target Vector2 | None

Optional external steering target (world position); ignored when seek_weight is zero.

enabled bool

Whether this agent should be updated at all.

docs.title: FlockingSystem
docs.text:
Ticks every FlockingAgent toward its neighbors, each frame.

Neighbor query, weighted force sum, F=ma integration: the same integration shape as SteeringSystem.

The flock is steered by the native extension, in one crossing per tick. There is no Python implementation; see ADR 0011, Decision 3.

The sweep is Gauss-Seidel, so its order is part of the simulation. It follows entity insertion order, so a seeded flock ticks the same way every run.

Example

system_manager.register(FlockingSystem(entity_manager), priority=150)

docs.title: flock_force
docs.text:
flock_force(
    position: Vector2,
    agent: FlockingAgent,
    neighbors: Iterable[tuple[Vector2, Vector2]],
) -> Vector2

Sum cohesion, alignment and separation in a single pass.

Equivalent to calling SteeringBehavior.cohesion, .alignment and .separation and summing the weighted results, in one iteration over the neighbours.

The arithmetic is on floats, not Vector2, on purpose: this loop runs once per neighbour per agent per tick. Distances are compared squared, so there is at most one sqrt per neighbour. seek is not included; it depends on a caller's target, not on the neighbourhood.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default position Vector2

The steering agent's own world position.

required agent FlockingAgent

The agent, read for its radii, weights and velocity.

required neighbors Iterable[tuple[Vector2, Vector2]]

(position, velocity) per flockmate, self excluded.

required

Returns:

Type Description Vector2

The weighted sum of the three neighbourhood forces.

add_transition(

    to_state: str,
    predicate: Callable[[StateMachine], bool] | None = None,
    *,
    on_event: str | None = None,
) -> None

Declare a transition outside the states themselves.

A transition table keeps "what follows what" in one place, so a state can be reused in several machines and a machine can be built from data.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default from_state str | None

The state this applies to, or None for "any state" -- the usual home for on_damaged style interrupts.

required to_state str

Where to go.

required predicate Callable[[StateMachine], bool] | None

Called with this machine each update; the transition fires when it returns True. None means "always", which only makes sense together with on_event.

None on_event str | None

Fire only when this event has been posted since the last update. Combined with predicate, both must hold.

None

If neither a predicate nor an event is given, which would be a transition that fires unconditionally every tick and so a state that can never be stayed in.

docs.title: pyguara.ai.pathfinding.flow_field
docs.text:
Multi-source Dijkstra cost maps and flow fields.

dijkstra_map answers "how far is every reachable node from the nearest of these goals" in one sweep -- the substrate a horde of enemies, units converging on a rally point, or a tower's targeting all want without each running its own A* search. flow_field turns that cost map into a per-node "which neighbor gets me closer" lookup, so an agent following it does one dict lookup a tick instead of a search.

Generic over any Graph[Node], exactly like AStarPathfinder -- a grid is the common case, but nothing here assumes one.

docs.title: pyguara.ai.pathfinding.flow_field_service
docs.text:
A cached flow field over a GridGraph, queried in world space.

The field is computed and held in Rust: a GridGraph is flat integer state, and nothing outside this class reads a cell, so the cost map and the descent field never come back to Python and only a query crosses the boundary. See docs/adr/0011-one-rust-engine-python-interface.md.

For a graph that is not a grid, flow_field.py has the same two steps as plain functions over any Graph[Node].

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
A sequence of tweens, waits, callbacks and parallel groups.

Built by chaining -- each method returns the timeline -- and run by start() plus update(dt) each frame, or by handing it to a TweenManager.

Steps are composed before start(). Appending to a running timeline is allowed and the new step simply runs when reached; appending to a finished one does nothing until it is started again, which is the same rule a Tween follows.

Halt immediately, without firing on_complete.

Every step is halted, not only the current one, so a parallel group that was interrupted does not leave its members running.

docs.title: update
docs.text:
update(dt: float) -> bool

Advance the timeline by dt.

A step that finishes with time left over hands the remainder to the next one in the same call. A step that takes no time (a callback, an empty parallel group, a zero wait) also runs in the same call, so then(tween).call(f) calls f on the frame the tween ends.

At most one full pass over the steps happens per call, so a looping timeline of instant steps cannot spin here.

required

Type Description bool

True while still running, False once finished -- the contract

docs.title: Tween dataclass
docs.text:
Animates a value from start to end over a duration.

Supports different easing functions, delays, loops, and callbacks.

The endpoints may be two numbers, two Vector2, two Color, or two equal-length tuples/lists of numbers. current_value comes back as the type that went in: a Vector2 endpoint yields a Vector2, a Color endpoint a Color with its channels rounded and clamped.

Two Tween instances are equal only if they are the same object.

Example

docs.title: Animate position from (0, 0) to (100, 50) over 1 second
docs.text: tween = Tween( ... start_value=(0.0, 0.0), ... end_value=(100.0, 50.0), ... duration=1.0, ... easing=EasingType.EASE_OUT_QUAD ... ) tween.start()

docs.title: In update loop:
docs.text: tween.update(dt) position = tween.current_value

apply Callable[[Any], None]

Writes a value to the destination. A closure rather than an (object, attribute) pair because the destination may be a read-only property, or a slotted value type that can only be replaced on its parent -- the same reason tools.tweakable.TweakableLeaf carries one.

The Transform this binding switched into visual interpolation, or None if it did not. Set only when the binding drives transform.position on a transform that was not already interpolating, so TweenSystem can put it back when the tween ends and never clears a flag something else owns.

docs.title: TweenSystem
docs.text:
Advances every entity's Tweener bindings and writes their values.

Registered on each scene's own SystemManager, in the engine priority band, so it runs before the scene's own update sees the result.

A finished binding is dropped the tick it finishes, after its final value has been written -- so a tween to an exact destination lands on that destination rather than one frame short of it.

docs.title: resolve_property
docs.text:
resolve_property(entity: Entity, path: str) -> TweenTarget

Resolve a dotted path against an entity into a readable destination.

The first segment names a component the way entity.transform does; the rest walk attributes from there, so "transform.position", "sprite.color" and "sprite.color.a" all work.

The write goes through the last container, replacing the final attribute rather than mutating it. That is the only approach that works for a value type: Vector2 is immutable and Color's channels are clamped on construction, so neither can be changed in place.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default entity Entity

The entity to resolve against.

required path str

Dotted path, e.g. "transform.position".

required

Returns:

Type Description TweenTarget

The destination.

Raises:

Type Description PropertyPathError

If the path is empty, has no attribute part, or names something the entity does not have. Raised rather than logged: a typo'd path means the effect silently never happens, and a tween that quietly does nothing is worse to debug than one that refuses to start.

docs.title: tween_property
docs.text:
tween_property(
    entity: Entity,
    path: str,
    to: Any,
    duration: float,
    easing: EasingType = EasingType.LINEAR,
    *,
    delay: float = 0.0,
    loops: int = 0,
    yoyo: bool = False,
    on_complete: Callable[[], None] | None = None,
    replace: bool = True,
) -> Tween

Tween one of an entity's properties from its current value to to.

The start point is read from the property itself, so a call interrupting an earlier tween of the same path begins from wherever it had got to -- which is what makes a knockback retargeted mid-flight look continuous rather than snapping back.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default entity Entity

The entity to animate.

required path str

Dotted path, e.g. "transform.position".

required to Any

The destination value, of the property's own type.

required duration float

Seconds.

required easing EasingType

Which curve.

LINEAR delay float

Seconds to wait before moving.

0.0 loops int

0 once, -1 forever, N extra repeats.

0 yoyo bool

Alternate direction each loop.

False on_complete Callable[[], None] | None

Called once when the tween finishes.

None replace bool

Stop any tween already running on this exact path first. On by default, because two tweens writing the same property every frame is never what anyone wanted: the last writer wins and the result depends on binding order.

True

Returns:

Type Description Tween

The Tween, for pause(), stop() or inspection.

Raises:

Type Description PropertyPathError

If path does not resolve.

docs.title: pyguara.animation.timeline
docs.text:
Composing tweens in sequence and in parallel.

A Timeline has the same update(dt) -> bool contract as a Tween, so TweenManager holds either, and a timeline can be a step inside another timeline.

Example

(Timeline() .then(wind_up) .wait(0.05) .call(spawn_hitbox) .parallel(knockback, screen_shake) .then(recover) .start())

docs.title: Animatable
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Something a TweenManager can tick.

Satisfied by Tween and Timeline alike, which is what lets a manager hold both and a timeline hold a timeline. Deliberately the contract Tween already had rather than a new one: update returning False to mean "done, drop me" is how the manager already decides what to remove.

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
A sequence of tweens, waits, callbacks and parallel groups.

Built by chaining -- each method returns the timeline -- and run by start() plus update(dt) each frame, or by handing it to a TweenManager.

Steps are composed before start(). Appending to a running timeline is allowed and the new step simply runs when reached; appending to a finished one does nothing until it is started again, which is the same rule a Tween follows.

docs.title: update
docs.text:
update(dt: float) -> bool

Advance the timeline by dt.

A step that finishes with time left over hands the remainder to the next one in the same call. A step that takes no time (a callback, an empty parallel group, a zero wait) also runs in the same call, so then(tween).call(f) calls f on the frame the tween ends.

At most one full pass over the steps happens per call, so a looping timeline of instant steps cannot spin here.

Seconds since the last call.

required

True while still running, False once finished -- the contract

docs.title: Tween dataclass
docs.text:
Animates a value from start to end over a duration.

Supports different easing functions, delays, loops, and callbacks.

The endpoints may be two numbers, two Vector2, two Color, or two equal-length tuples/lists of numbers. current_value comes back as the type that went in: a Vector2 endpoint yields a Vector2, a Color endpoint a Color with its channels rounded and clamped.

Two Tween instances are equal only if they are the same object.

Example

docs.title: Animate position from (0, 0) to (100, 50) over 1 second
docs.text: tween = Tween( ... start_value=(0.0, 0.0), ... end_value=(100.0, 50.0), ... duration=1.0, ... easing=EasingType.EASE_OUT_QUAD ... ) tween.start()

docs.title: In update loop:
docs.text: tween.update(dt) position = tween.current_value

docs.title: pyguara.animation.tweener
docs.text:
Tweening an entity's own properties, ticked by the engine.

tween_property starts a tween on a dotted property path, and TweenSystem advances it and writes the value back each step.

TweenSystem is a scene system, not a container service, so its tweens end with the scene whose entities they animate.

Example

tween_property(entity, "transform.position", to=target, duration=0.3, easing=EasingType.EASE_OUT_QUAD)

Raised when a property path does not resolve on an entity.

docs.title: Binding dataclass
docs.text:
One tween, plus where to write its value.

Attributes:

Name Type Description animatable Animatable

The tween (or timeline) driving the value.

apply Callable[[Any], None]

Writes a value to the destination. A closure rather than an (object, attribute) pair because the destination may be a read-only property, or a slotted value type that can only be replaced on its parent -- the same reason tools.tweakable.TweakableLeaf carries one.

path str

The path this binding was created from, for messages and for stop_property().

interpolated Transform | None

The Transform this binding switched into visual interpolation, or None if it did not. Set only when the binding drives transform.position on a transform that was not already interpolating, so TweenSystem can put it back when the tween ends and never clears a flag something else owns.

docs.text:

docs.title: TweenSystem
docs.text:
Advances every entity's Tweener bindings and writes their values.

Registered on each scene's own SystemManager, in the engine priority band, so it runs before the scene's own update sees the result.

A finished binding is dropped the tick it finishes, after its final value has been written -- so a tween to an exact destination lands on that destination rather than one frame short of it.

docs.title: resolve_property
docs.text:
resolve_property(entity: Entity, path: str) -> TweenTarget

Resolve a dotted path against an entity into a readable destination.

The first segment names a component the way entity.transform does; the rest walk attributes from there, so "transform.position", "sprite.color" and "sprite.color.a" all work.

The write goes through the last container, replacing the final attribute rather than mutating it. That is the only approach that works for a value type: Vector2 is immutable and Color's channels are clamped on construction, so neither can be changed in place.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default entity Entity

The entity to resolve against.

required path str

Dotted path, e.g. "transform.position".

required

Returns:

Type Description TweenTarget

The destination.

Raises:

Type Description PropertyPathError

If the path is empty, has no attribute part, or names something the entity does not have. Raised rather than logged: a typo'd path means the effect silently never happens, and a tween that quietly does nothing is worse to debug than one that refuses to start.

docs.title: tween_property
docs.text:
tween_property(
    entity: Entity,
    path: str,
    to: Any,
    duration: float,
    easing: EasingType = EasingType.LINEAR,
    *,
    delay: float = 0.0,
    loops: int = 0,
    yoyo: bool = False,
    on_complete: Callable[[], None] | None = None,
    replace: bool = True,
) -> Tween

Tween one of an entity's properties from its current value to to.

The start point is read from the property itself, so a call interrupting an earlier tween of the same path begins from wherever it had got to -- which is what makes a knockback retargeted mid-flight look continuous rather than snapping back.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default entity Entity

The entity to animate.

required path str

Dotted path, e.g. "transform.position".

required to Any

The destination value, of the property's own type.

required duration float

Seconds.

required easing EasingType

Which curve.

LINEAR delay float

Seconds to wait before moving.

0.0 loops int

0 once, -1 forever, N extra repeats.

0 yoyo bool

Alternate direction each loop.

False on_complete Callable[[], None] | None

Called once when the tween finishes.

None replace bool

Stop any tween already running on this exact path first. On by default, because two tweens writing the same property every frame is never what anyone wanted: the last writer wins and the result depends on binding order.

True

Returns:

Type Description Tween

The Tween, for pause(), stop() or inspection.

Raises:

Type Description PropertyPathError

If path does not resolve.

docs.title: step
docs.text:
step() -> bool

Run exactly one frame, and report whether to run another.

Each frame measures its own duration, clamps it to physics.max_frame_time, accumulates it, and runs as many fixed-rate updates as that buys before rendering once.

time_scale and paused scale the measured duration, not fixed_dt, so slow motion means fewer fixed steps per real second. While a replay loaded via load_replay() drives the game, each frame's duration comes from the recording and the scale is ignored.

Exceptions propagate; run() owns the logging and the shutdown().

Returns:

Type Description bool

True while the loop should continue -- the app is running and the

bool

window is open. False once either stops being true, so

bool

while app.step(): pass terminates exactly where run() does.

bool

Also False when called before begin().

docs.text: Application setup and dependency wiring.

docs.title: Configure module-attribute
docs.text:
Configure = Callable[[GameConfig], None]

A hook to adjust configuration before anything is built from it.

Called once, after ConfigManager.load() and before the window, the renderer or the physics engine exist -- which is the only point where changing display.backend or display.screen_width still decides anything. A game uses it to name its window and pick its backend without reimplementing the wiring that follows:

def _configure(config: GameConfig) -> None:
    config.display.title = "My Game"
    config.display.backend = RenderingBackend.WGPU

docs.title: Setup module-attribute
docs.text:
Setup = Callable[[DIContainer], None]

A hook to add to the wired container, before the application is built.

Called once, after the engine has registered its services and before Application exists. A game uses it to register services of its own or to add passes to the RenderGraph:

def _setup(container: DIContainer) -> None:
    container.register_instance(Inventory, Inventory())


pyguara.run(TitleScene, setup=_setup)

docs.title: RegisterSections module-attribute
docs.text:
RegisterSections = Callable[[ConfigManager], None]

A hook to register game-defined config sections, before anything loads.

Called once before ConfigManager.load(), which is the only point at which register_section() can still do anything: from_dict() builds only the sections the registry knows about, so a registration after the load has already discarded whatever the file said about them.

Configure is the hook after the load, for adjusting values. This one is for declaring what values there are.

def _sections(config_manager: ConfigManager) -> None:
    config_manager.register_section("balance", BalanceConfig)


pyguara.run(MyScene, configure=_configure, register_sections=_sections)

docs.title: NoGraphicsAdapterError
docs.text:
Bases: RuntimeError

The wgpu renderer, the default, found no GPU to draw with.

Raised at startup rather than falling back to the software renderer: the two look different -- pygame has no lighting or post-processing -- so a silent switch would change how the game looks on that machine.

Where a frame's time goes, measured by the frame loop itself.

FrameProfiler records how long each phase of Application.step() took over the last couple of seconds, and draw_frame_profile() shows it through the UIRenderer. It needs no developer tooling, so it works in a shipped build: debug.enable_profiler in the game's config turns it on.

docs.title: pyguara.application.memory
docs.text:
Keeping Python's garbage collector out of the frame.

A full collection walks every container object in the process. A game holds tens of thousands, nearly all made while loading and alive until the scene ends, so the walk can cost more than a frame.

settle_memory() unfreezes, collects, and then calls gc.freeze(), which moves everything still alive out of the collector's reach. The Application calls it whenever the scenes it runs change (PerformanceConfig.freeze_on_scene_change); a game calls it after any load the engine cannot see.

docs.title: settle_memory
docs.text:

Collect everything, then freeze what's alive so full collections skip it.

Call it after loading, between frames: it runs one full collection, which costs about as much as the stall it prevents.

Returns:

Type Description int

How many objects are frozen now.

Provides: - Low-level audio playback via IAudioSystem - High-level AudioManager for game audio - Entity-attached audio via AudioSource component - Spatial audio support

docs.title: AudioEffect module-attribute
docs.text:
AudioEffect = LowPassFilter | HighPassFilter | Reverb

One DSP effect on a bus.

A closed union rather than a protocol: an effect is a description a backend interprets, not behaviour it calls, and a backend has to match on the kind to configure its own DSP chain either way. Adding an effect is therefore a deliberate protocol change, which is what stops one backend inventing an effect the others cannot see.

Responsibilities: - Play/stop audio based on component state - Update spatial audio positions each frame - Handle auto-play on component attach - Clean up audio when entities are destroyed

A backend was asked for something it cannot do.

Raised rather than ignored. A mixer that cannot pitch-shift and accepts pitch=1.2 anyway reports success for a sound that plays at its original speed, and the caller has no way to find out -- the same "guard that returns a wrong answer" the engine has removed elsewhere.

Every capability has a default value that means "not asked for" (pitch=1.0, loop_start=None, no bus effects), so this can only fire for a caller that asked on purpose. A caller that would rather degrade than fail reads IAudioSystem.capabilities first.

docs.title: SoundHandle dataclass
docs.text:
An opaque reference to one playing sound.

token is minted by the audio system, means nothing to a caller, and is never reused within a process -- which is the entire point. A mixer channel number is recycled the instant its sound ends, so an int held for a few frames can address a sound the holder never started: stop_sfx(7) stops whatever is on channel 7 now. A handle that has ended simply stops resolving, and the methods that take one become no-ops.

Attributes:

Name Type Description token int

Process-unique identifier. Treat it as opaque; its value carries no information and may change meaning between releases.

docs.title: UnsupportedAudioCapability
docs.text:
Bases: AudioError

A backend was asked for something it cannot do.

Raised rather than ignored. A mixer that cannot pitch-shift and accepts pitch=1.2 anyway reports success for a sound that plays at its original speed, and the caller has no way to find out -- the same "guard that returns a wrong answer" the engine has removed elsewhere.

Every capability has a default value that means "not asked for" (pitch=1.0, loop_start=None, no bus effects), so this can only fire for a caller that asked on purpose. A caller that would rather degrade than fail reads IAudioSystem.capabilities first.

Attributes:

Name Type Description capability

The capability that was requested.

backend

Class name of the audio system that declined it.

docs.title: AudioManager
docs.text:
High-level audio manager that coordinates the audio system.

Provides: - Convenient resource loading and playback - Volume management (master, SFX, music) - Music playback control (play, pause, stop) - Sound effect playback with tracking - Event integration for audio state changes

Example

audio_mgr = AudioManager(audio_system, resource_mgr, event_dispatcher) audio_mgr.play_sfx("sounds/jump.wav", volume=0.8) audio_mgr.play_music("music/bgm.ogg", loop=True) audio_mgr.set_master_volume(0.7)

docs.title: set_sfx_limit
docs.text:
set_sfx_limit(
    path: str,
    *,
    max_voices: int | None = None,
    min_interval: float = 0.0,
) -> None

Limit how much of one sound plays at once.

Ten hits landing in one frame would otherwise start ten copies of the same clip together, which is one sound, much louder. A play the limit holds back is dropped, not queued: the copies already playing are the sound of that moment, and a late one would be heard after it.

Both arguments at their defaults remove the limit.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default path str

The sound, as play_sfx names it. play_sfx_clip is limited by its clip's path.

required max_voices int | None

The most copies playing together, or None for no cap.

None min_interval float

Seconds that must pass between two starts.

0.0

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If max_voices is below 1, or min_interval is negative or not finite.

docs.title: pyguara.audio.placeholder
docs.text:
Placeholder sound effects, built from simple tones, before any real ones exist.

Short synthesized stand-ins (a thud, a blip, a hiss) made with the standard library and written as .wav files. There are two ways in: functions that build and combine samples, and recipes, the same tree as data. docs/systems/cli.md describes the recipe format and the pyguara sounds command.

Output is deterministic. Noise draws from a stream seeded by the sound's own name, so editing one sound never changes another's bytes.

Example

hit = envelope(mix(transient(0.03, 0.5, rng), sine(140.0, 0.12, 0.6)), decay_rate=20.0)

docs.title: AudioEffect module-attribute

AudioEffect = LowPassFilter | HighPassFilter | Reverb

One DSP effect on a bus.

A closed union rather than a protocol: an effect is a description a backend interprets, not behaviour it calls, and a backend has to match on the kind to configure its own DSP chain either way. Adding an effect is therefore a deliberate protocol change, which is what stops one backend inventing an effect the others cannot see.

docs.title: AudioCapability
docs.text:
Bases: Flag

What an audio backend can actually do.

A backend declares the optional features it supports here and raises UnsupportedAudioCapability for the rest. Every capability has a request that means "not asked for" (pitch=1.0, loop_start=None, an empty effect list), so a game that uses none of them runs on any backend.

Attributes:

Name Type Description NONE

No optional capability. What PygameAudioSystem reports.

PITCH

Per-play playback-rate change (pitch on play_sfx).

LOOP_POINTS

Looping between two points inside a clip rather than over the whole file.

BUS_EFFECTS

DSP attached to a bus (set_bus_effects).

docs.title: SoundHandle dataclass
docs.text:
An opaque reference to one playing sound.

token is minted by the audio system, means nothing to a caller, and is never reused within a process -- which is the entire point. A mixer channel number is recycled the instant its sound ends, so an int held for a few frames can address a sound the holder never started: stop_sfx(7) stops whatever is on channel 7 now. A handle that has ended simply stops resolving, and the methods that take one become no-ops.

Attributes:

Name Type Description token int

Process-unique identifier. Treat it as opaque; its value carries no information and may change meaning between releases.

docs.text:
Tracks information about a currently playing sound.

Used for channel management, priority-based stealing, and spatial updates.

handle is the identity callers hold; channel_id is where the sound happens to be playing, which the mixer owns and recycles.

docs.title: NativeAudioSystem
docs.text:
An audio system on the native mixer (rust/src/mixer.rs).

The mixer owns the device and plays voices; this class decides what they are. Buses, spatial attenuation and voice priorities follow PygameAudioSystem. It adds continuous pitch, sample-exact loop points, and bus volumes that reach sounds already playing.

Selected by AudioConfig.backend. With no output device, the mixer runs against a silent clock and sounds still end on time; output says which.

Pack multiple sprite images into a single texture atlas using a shelf-packing algorithm. Generate both the packed image and JSON metadata for runtime loading.

docs.text:
Build command for creating standalone executables.

Wraps PyInstaller to package PyGuara games into distributable executables, automatically bundling assets and engine runtime.

Usage

pyguara build game.py --output dist/ pyguara build game.py --name MyGame --onefile pyguara build game.py --assets assets/ --icon icon.ico

Build a standalone executable from a PyGuara game.

ENTRY_POINT is the main Python file of your game (e.g., main.py).

Examples: # Basic build pyguara build main.py # Custom output and name pyguara build main.py --output builds/ --name MyGame # Single file with icon, in any format Pillow reads pyguara build main.py --onefile --icon assets/logo.png # Include multiple asset directories pyguara build main.py -a assets/ -a levels/ # Ship the assets as one pack rather than loose files pyguara build main.py --pack

docs.title: pyguara.cli.dist
docs.text:
Store distribution templates for a built game.

pyguara build produces an executable; these commands write the files a store upload needs. They generate scripts and print what to run. They do not upload: that needs steamcmd or butler and a store account.

Usage

pyguara dist icons logo.png --out build/icons pyguara dist steam --app-id 480 --depot-id 481 --content dist/MyGame pyguara dist itch --target studio/my-game --content dist/MyGame

PyInstaller does not convert: it wants .ico on Windows and .icns on macOS and fails or warns on anything else, which is why a project with a single logo.png cannot be built for Windows without this step. Pillow is already a core dependency, so no new one is needed.

The image to convert. Square and at least 256x256 is what every target wants; smaller is accepted and produces fewer .ico sizes.

required

Generates the app and depot VDFs, an upload wrapper for both shells, a README with the manual steps, and the development-only steam_appid.txt -- outside the content root, because shipping it lets a customer bypass the Steam client.

docs.title: pyguara.cli.pack
docs.text:
Baking asset folders into one pack, for pyguara build --pack.

A pack is a ZIP whose entries are the folders' files, each under its folder's own name -- assets/sprites/hero.png -- which is where PyInstaller's --add-data would have put the loose file in the bundle. A frozen game mounts it with the bundle as its root (pyguara.assets), so every path the game's code builds finds the packed file.

Reproducible: entries are sorted and carry a fixed timestamp, so the same folders bake to the same bytes.

docs.title: pyguara.cli.studio
docs.text:
pyguara studio: the authoring surface from a terminal.

Three subcommands:

  • instructions writes or checks the AGENTS.md family. It needs no engine, so it runs in CI.
  • ops serves the operation surface as JSON lines on stdio.
  • mcp serves the same operations over the Model Context Protocol.

ops and mcp speak on stdout, so nothing else may write to it. _protocol_stdout() hands the real stdout to the server and points sys.stdout at stderr before the engine is imported.

docs.text:
Sprites drawn from columns, in one native call per frame.

ColumnarSprite and ColumnarTransform hold the fields Scene.render reads from Sprite and Transform, as columns. ColumnarSpriteRenderer pushes every visible sprite into a NativeGpu by the same rules and the same arithmetic as the object path, without a RenderCommand or a RenderBatch in between.

docs.title: pyguara.columnar.world
docs.text:
ColumnarWorld: component state held in native columns.

The columns live in Rust (rust/src/world.rs). This is a spike beside the object ECS, not wired into EntityManager, scenes or systems; see ADR 0008.

arrays() returns NumPy arrays over the column memory itself. While one is alive, anything that would move that memory (an add that grows the column, a flush with removals pending) raises BufferError. Removal is deferred, as in EntityManager: the rows leave the columns at the next flush.

Example

world = ColumnarWorld() entity = world.spawn() world.add(entity, Position(Vector2(1.0, 2.0)))

world.view(entity, Position).value = Vector2(3.0, 4.0) # one entity xs = world.arrays(Position)["value.x"] # every entity world.add_scaled(Position, "value.x", Velocity, "value.x", dt)

docs.title: Transform
docs.text:
Bases: StrictComponent

Position, rotation and scale in 2D space, with optional parenting.

A transform may be parented to another, in which case its stored values are local to that parent and the world_* properties resolve the chain. World values are cached and recomputed lazily: a setter marks the subtree dirty, and the next world_* read rebuilds only what it needs.

Angles are in radians throughout, except rotation_degrees. Behaviour (set_parent, teleport, look_at, the coordinate conversions) is free functions beside this class.

Attributes:

Name Type Description interpolate

Whether the renderer draws this between fixed ticks. Set automatically by PhysicsSystem for bodies it creates, which are the transforms that need it: they advance at the fixed rate, so drawing the raw tick position stutters on any display not locked to it. Leave it off for a transform a system moves every frame in variable-rate update() -- that is already frame-exact, and interpolating it mixes two clocks and adds judder instead of removing it. Use teleport() for moves that are not motion.

previous_position Vector2

Position at the previous fixed tick, maintained by SceneManager.fixed_update() while interpolate is set.

docs.title: teleport
docs.text:
teleport(transform: Transform, position: Vector2) -> None

Move without drawing the journey.

A normal position change is interpolated, so the renderer draws the entity partway between where it was and where it now is. That is what makes ordinary motion smooth, and exactly wrong for a move that is not motion: a respawn, a level load, wrapping around a screen edge. Those would be drawn as a streak across everything in between for one frame.

This sets both the current and previous position, leaving nothing to interpolate across.

required position Vector2

required

docs.text:

    transform: Transform, alpha: float

Return where this transform should be drawn between two ticks.

A transform with interpolate set is drawn between its position at the previous fixed tick and the current one, by how far the frame sits between them. That removes the stutter of a fixed-rate body on a display running at another rate, and costs one tick of latency. A transform that has not opted in is drawn where it is.

Checks for the optional libraries a backend is built on.

pygame is not installed by pip install pyguara. The software renderer and the pygame audio backend need it, and each asks here before importing it, so a missing install is reported by name with the command that fixes it.

docs.title: pyguara.common.grid
docs.text:
Integer grid-cell math: coordinates, distances, neighbours, line walks.

Cell is a plain tuple[int, int], so it unpacks as x, y = cell and works as a dict key, as grid code across the engine expects (ai.pathfinding.grid.GridNode, a SpatialHash bucket key).

docs.title: pyguara.common.modifiers
docs.text:
A stacking, source-tracked numeric value: base + flat + percent + override.

ModifiableValue knows how several tagged contributions combine into one number, and nothing about what the number means; stat names are kits/stats' job. It is a plain value type, not wired to events.

It has no duration or expiry. A temporary buff is kits/effects' job: the effect removes its own modifier when its timer elapses.

docs.title: ModifierType
docs.text:
Bases: Enum

How a Modifier's value combines into a ModifiableValue.

docs.title: Modifier dataclass
docs.text:
One tagged contribution to a ModifiableValue.

Attributes:

Name Type Description value float

The contribution's magnitude. Its meaning depends on mod_type -- a flat amount, a fraction for the two percent types (0.1 for +10%), or the replacement value for OVERRIDE.

mod_type ModifierType

How this modifier combines with the others.

source Any

Whatever identifies where this modifier came from -- typically an item id, an effect instance, or a status name. Compared with ==, never by identity, so a plain string works as well as an object. ModifiableValue.remove_source() removes every modifier sharing a source in one call, which is the primary removal path: a caller unequipping an item or clearing a status doesn't track which individual Modifiers it added.

docs.title: ModifiableValue
docs.text:
A base value plus stacking modifiers, recomputed lazily.

strength = ModifiableValue(10.0)
strength.add_modifier(Modifier(5.0, ModifierType.FLAT, source="ring"))
strength.add_modifier(Modifier(0.2, ModifierType.PERCENT_ADD, source="buff"))
strength.value  # (10 + 5) * (1 + 0.2) == 18.0
strength.remove_source("ring")
strength.value  # (10 + 0) * (1 + 0.2) == 12.0

docs.title: pyguara.common.random
docs.text:
A serializable random-number stream.

RandomStream wraps random.Random so gameplay code holds an explicit source of randomness that can be seeded and snapshotted, unlike the global random module.

restore_state() accepts state that has been through JSON, where the tuples random.Random.getstate() returns come back as lists.

docs.title: weighted_choice
docs.text:
weighted_choice(
    rng: RandomStream, choices: Sequence[tuple[T, float]]
) -> T

Pick one item from choices, weighted by each entry's own weight.

Originated in kits/loot (drop tables); moved here once kits/procgen needed the same primitive for Wave Function Collapse's per-cell state pick -- a generic RNG utility, not a loot-specific one.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default rng RandomStream

Seeded stream driving the roll.

required choices Sequence[tuple[T, float]]

(item, weight) pairs. Weights need not sum to 1 -- each item's odds are its own weight over the total. A weight of 0 is never picked (in practice; only an exact floating-point boundary hit could select it, which does not happen).

required

Returns:

Type Description T

One item from choices.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If choices is empty, or every weight is 0 or less.

docs.title: pyguara.common.spatial
docs.text:
A uniform-grid spatial hash for fast "what's near this point" queries.

Positions are bucketed into fixed-size cells, so a radius or rectangle query looks at a handful of cells. Callers supply any key (usually an entity id) with a position and an optional filter mask. It is a broad-phase index: query_radius confirms exact distance, but nothing here knows a key's size or shape.

The index is held in Rust and has no Python implementation. See docs/agents/native-extension.md for what it promises and what it does not, the result order among them.

docs.title: SpatialHash
docs.text: Buckets keys by position into fixed-size cells for range queries.

docs.title: query_point
docs.text:
query_point(
    point: Vector2, mask: int = _FULL_MASK
) -> list[K]

Every key sharing point's cell, filtered by mask.

No distance test: a key anywhere in the cell counts, so what comes back depends on where the cell boundaries fall. That makes it the one query whose result is sensitive to cell_size.

docs.text:

    center: Vector2, radius: float, mask: int = _FULL_MASK

The order of the result is not defined. A caller that wants a particular one of several results must pick it (by distance, by id), not take the first.

docs.title: query_rect
docs.text:

Every key whose position lies inside bounds.

Half-open, following Rect.contains_point: the left and top edges are inclusive and the right and bottom exclusive, as pygame.Rect.collidepoint has it.

docs.title: pyguara.common.types
docs.text:
Foundational value types for the PyGuara engine.

Vector2, Color and Rect are the primitives every other subsystem shares. Vector2 is implemented in the native extension; the class body here is its signature for type checkers. Color and Rect are plain dataclasses; no rendering backend is imported here.

Y increases downwards, matching SDL and the engine's default gravity, so "up" is negative Y. Every direction helper here and in Transform follows that.

An RGBA colour, one byte per channel.

A backend-agnostic value type. Channels are coerced to int and clamped to 0-255 on construction, so colour arithmetic that overshoots -- a fade, a brightness multiplier, an out-of-range HSV conversion -- saturates instead of handing a backend a value it cannot represent.

docs.title: push_profile
docs.text:
push_profile(
    name: str,
    overrides: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] | None = None,
) -> bool

Layer a named set of overrides over the current configuration.

A profile is a batch of update_setting() calls applied atomically and reversibly: the same type checks, the same validator veto, and pop_profile() restores exactly what was underneath -- which plain assignment cannot, since the previous value is gone the moment it is overwritten.

That reversibility is the whole point. A difficulty preset, an accessibility profile and a roguelike's run modifiers are all the same shape: a set of values that applies for a while and then stops.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default name str

Profile name. Must not already be active.

required overrides dict[str, dict[str, Any]] | None

section -> setting -> value. Omit to resolve the name from the config file's "profiles" block or a previous define_profile().

None

Returns:

Type Description bool

True if the layer was applied. False leaves the configuration

bool

exactly as it was -- the push is all-or-nothing, since a

bool

difficulty preset that applied two of its three settings would

bool

be worse than one that applied none.

Game-defined sections are hoisted out of custom to the top level, so the document reads the same whether a section came from the engine or the game, and from_dict() need not know which it was.

    overrides: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] | None = None,
) -> bool

Layer a named set of overrides over the current configuration.

A profile is a batch of update_setting() calls applied atomically and reversibly: the same type checks, the same validator veto, and pop_profile() restores exactly what was underneath -- which plain assignment cannot, since the previous value is gone the moment it is overwritten.

That reversibility is the whole point. A difficulty preset, an accessibility profile and a roguelike's run modifiers are all the same shape: a set of values that applies for a while and then stops.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default name str

Profile name. Must not already be active.

required overrides dict[str, dict[str, Any]] | None

section -> setting -> value. Omit to resolve the name from the config file's "profiles" block or a previous define_profile().

None

Returns:

Type Description bool

True if the layer was applied. False leaves the configuration

bool

exactly as it was -- the push is all-or-nothing, since a

bool

difficulty preset that applied two of its three settings would

bool

be worse than one that applied none.

docs.title: pop_profile
docs.text:
pop_profile(name: str | None = None) -> bool

Peel one layer back off, restoring what was underneath it.

Removing a layer from the middle of the stack is legal and deliberate: run modifiers are independent, so dropping one must not require dropping the ones pushed after it.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default name str | None

Profile to remove. Omit to remove the most recent, which is a no-op on an empty stack. A named profile that is not active is reported either way: asking for one by name says the caller believed it was applied.

None

Returns:

Type Description bool

True if a layer was removed.

docs.title: to_dict
docs.text:
to_dict() -> dict[str, Any]

Serialize config to dictionary.

Game-defined sections are hoisted out of custom to the top level, so the document reads the same whether a section came from the engine or the game, and from_dict() need not know which it was.

Enums are reduced to their .value throughout. asdict() leaves RenderingBackend as a plain Enum instance (unlike LogLevel, an IntEnum that is already JSON-safe) and json.dump() then rejects it; doing it generically means the next enum field added anywhere, including in a game's own section, does not repeat that bug.

Unknown keys are ignored and logged rather than raising, so a config written by a newer engine still loads. Nested values are coerced back to their declared types -- Color from its dict form, enums from their string or integer value -- which plain construction would not do.

The input is never mutated.

The populated config. Sections absent from data keep their

docs.title: pyguara.dev
docs.text:
Development tools.

Asset hot-reload -- watch loaded assets on disk and re-import them live during development. See docs/systems/dev.md.

docs.title: AssetReloadWatcher
docs.text:
Watches every loaded asset's file and reloads it when it changes.

The watch set follows the ResourceManager cache: :meth:drain periodically reconciles it, so assets loaded after :meth:start are picked up and evicted ones are dropped.

Callers that already hold the previous resource instance keep that stale object -- reload() swaps the cache entry, it does not mutate the old one. Re-load() after a reload to pick up the new instance.

Example

watcher = AssetReloadWatcher(resource_manager) watcher.start()

docs.title: each frame, on the main thread:
docs.text: reloaded = watcher.drain() ... watcher.stop()

docs.title: pyguara.dev.asset_reload
docs.text:
Asset hot-reload: watch loaded assets on disk and re-import them live.

Bridges :class:~pyguara.dev.file_watcher.PollingFileWatcher to :meth:ResourceManager.reload. A file change is detected on the watcher's polling thread, queued, and applied on the thread that calls :meth:drain -- the game loop -- because ResourceManager is not safe to mutate from under a running frame.

Development-only. Off by default; Application.enable_asset_hot_reload() turns it on and SandboxApplication calls that automatically.

docs.title: pyguara.di
docs.text:
Dependency Injection package.

Provides a lightweight, type-safe container with support for lifecycle management (Singleton, Scoped, Transient), circular dependency detection, and automatic dependency resolution.

docs.title: DIContainer
docs.text:
Reflection-based dependency injection container.

Services are registered against an interface type and constructed by reading their constructor's type hints. Three lifetimes are supported: SINGLETON (one per container), SCOPED (one per DIScope) and TRANSIENT (a fresh instance per request).

Registration and resolution are guarded by a reentrant lock, so a service is constructed at most once even under contention. Cycle detection state is thread-local.

docs.title: run_scope property
docs.text:
run_scope: DIScope | None

The active run scope, or None outside of one.

A run spans multiple scenes -- floor transitions in a roguelike, say -- so it is not tied to any single Scene's lifetime the way Scene.scope is. Every scene already holds self.container, so scene code reaches the current run's scope as self.container.run_scope with no extra plumbing.

docs.title: DIContainer
docs.text:
Reflection-based dependency injection container.

Services are registered against an interface type and constructed by reading their constructor's type hints. Three lifetimes are supported: SINGLETON (one per container), SCOPED (one per DIScope) and TRANSIENT (a fresh instance per request).

Registration and resolution are guarded by a reentrant lock, so a service is constructed at most once even under contention. Cycle detection state is thread-local.

docs.title: run_scope property
docs.text:
run_scope: DIScope | None

The active run scope, or None outside of one.

A run spans multiple scenes -- floor transitions in a roguelike, say -- so it is not tied to any single Scene's lifetime the way Scene.scope is. Every scene already holds self.container, so scene code reaches the current run's scope as self.container.run_scope with no extra plumbing.

docs.title: ErrorHandlingStrategy
docs.text:
Bases: Enum

What a subsystem does when user-supplied code raises.

Used by EventDispatcher for handlers and filters, and by DIContainer for constructor introspection. A single definition, because two enums with the same members are not interchangeable: comparing one subsystem's RAISE against another's silently evaluates false.

Attributes:

Name Type Description LOG

Log the error and carry on. Graceful degradation in production.

RAISE

Log the error and re-raise it. Fail fast in development, and the default everywhere.

IGNORE

Swallow the error silently. Tests and narrow edge cases only.

Example 
from pyguara.errors import ErrorHandlingStrategy

dispatcher = EventDispatcher(error_strategy=ErrorHandlingStrategy.LOG)
container = DIContainer(error_strategy=ErrorHandlingStrategy.LOG)

docs.title: pyguara.ecs
docs.text:
Entity Component System core.

  • Entity: a uniquely identified container for components.
  • Component: the structural protocol every component satisfies.
  • BaseComponent: the base class; rejects logic methods when a subclass is defined. StrictComponent is an alias for it.
  • EntityManager: registration, lifecycle and querying for one world.
  • ChildOf: ownership, so destruction cascades. Transform parenting is the spatial relation.
  • EntityPool/Poolable: pooling for entities that spawn often.

docs.title: BaseComponent
docs.text:
Reference implementation of the Component protocol.

Subclasses that declare logic methods raise TypeError at class definition time. Set _allow_methods = True on a subclass to opt out -- debt to migrate rather than a supported answer. StrictComponent is this class under an older name; either base gives the same check.

__slots__ keeps per-instance overhead low. Dataclass subclasses should declare @dataclass(slots=True); non-dataclass subclasses should declare their own __slots__.

The owning entity, or None while detached.

Retained name for what BaseComponent now does by default.

Components have always been meant to be data-only; until this became the default, the rule was a warning nothing acted on and StrictComponent had no adopters outside tests. The name is kept so components already using it keep working, and because it reads as an intention at a definition -- but it adds nothing to BaseComponent.

Prefer BaseComponent for new components.

docs.title: EntityManager
docs.text:
Central database for the entities in one world.

Queries are backed by an inverted index (ComponentType -> {EntityID}), so matching entities are found by set intersection rather than by scanning every entity.

Entity removal is a two-step process. remove_entity() makes an entity soft-dead immediately; flush_pending_removals() physically cleans up its index entries at the frame boundary. Keeping the index stable for the whole frame is what makes every query safe to iterate while systems destroy entities.

docs.title: remove_entity
docs.text:
remove_entity(entity_id: str) -> None

Soft-destroy an entity: immediate, terminal, not reusable.

The entity leaves the registry and its manager callbacks are detached before this returns; further mutation of it raises. Physical index cleanup is deferred to flush_pending_removals(). Subscribers from subscribe_entity_removed() are notified here, while the entity's components can still be read.

Destruction cascades: every entity whose ChildOf points at this one is removed too, depth first. Removing an unknown id is a no-op.

docs.title: flush_pending_removals
docs.text:
flush_pending_removals() -> None

Clean up index entries for entities soft-removed since the last flush.

Call once per frame at the frame boundary, never mid-frame: holding the index stable for the duration of a frame is what keeps that frame's queries safe to iterate.

docs.title: clear
docs.text:
clear() -> None

Remove every entity from the world, then flush the indexes.

Each entity is taken through remove_entity(), so subscribe_entity_removed() callbacks fire and downstream state (physics bodies, render batches, spatial indexes) is torn down, then flush_pending_removals() empties the inverted index and every cached query. The world is left empty and safe to repopulate -- the intended entry point for reloading a scene from disk, instead of clearing the internal dicts by hand (which leaves cached queries and subscribers out of sync).

The callback fires synchronously from remove_entity(), at the moment of soft-death and before index cleanup, so it can still read the removed entity's components. Exceptions propagate to the caller of remove_entity(); a subscriber that may fail should handle its own errors.

Subscribing a callback that is already subscribed is a no-op, so a scene whose dependencies are resolved twice does not double-notify.

docs.title: EntityPool
docs.text:
Pre-allocates entities once, then hands them out and takes them back.

Every entity is created once, at construction, via factory. acquire() and release() toggle Poolable.is_active and move an entity between the available and active sets; nothing is destroyed. Capacity is fixed: acquire() returns None once exhausted.

An idle entity is disabled, not stripped. It keeps every component, and EntityManager excludes it from every query until it is acquired again. get_active() returns entities in acquisition order.

The identity check is deliberate. Looking the id up and comparing the stored object with is keeps exactly the semantics the old list membership test had, rather than trusting an id to be unique across every pool sharing an EntityManager.

Components are data-only containers; logic belongs in systems, or in a free function beside the component (Transform/set_parent, Health/apply_damage). BaseComponent raises TypeError when a subclass declares a logic method. StrictComponent is the same class under an older name.
