Retained name for what BaseComponent now does by default.

Components have always been meant to be data-only; until this became the default, the rule was a warning nothing acted on and StrictComponent had no adopters outside tests. docs.title: pure_query
docs.text:
pure_query(method: F) -> F

Mark a component method as a side-effect-free read of its own fields.

A method that only reads the component it is called on hides no behaviour, so the data-only rule allows it when it is marked.

A pure query may not mutate anything, may not reach a system, a backend or the event dispatcher, and may not touch another entity's state. Anything that does is logic and belongs in a system.

Example 
@dataclass(slots=True)
class EntityTags(StrictComponent):
    tags: set[str] = field(default_factory=set)

    @pure_query
    def has_tag(self, tag: str) -> bool:
        return tag in self.tags

docs.title: EntityManager
docs.text:
Central database for the entities in one world.

Queries are backed by an inverted index (ComponentType -> {EntityID}), so matching entities are found by set intersection rather than by scanning every entity.

Entity removal is a two-step process. remove_entity() makes an entity soft-dead immediately; flush_pending_removals() physically cleans up its index entries at the frame boundary. Keeping the index stable for the whole frame is what makes every query safe to iterate while systems destroy entities.

The entity leaves the registry and its manager callbacks are detached before this returns; further mutation of it raises. Physical index cleanup is deferred to flush_pending_removals(). Subscribers from subscribe_entity_removed() are notified here, while the entity's components can still be read.

docs.text:

docs.title: clear
docs.text:
clear() -> None

Remove every entity from the world, then flush the indexes.

Each entity is taken through remove_entity(), so subscribe_entity_removed() callbacks fire and downstream state (physics bodies, render batches, spatial indexes) is torn down, then flush_pending_removals() empties the inverted index and every cached query. The world is left empty and safe to repopulate -- the intended entry point for reloading a scene from disk, instead of clearing the internal dicts by hand (which leaves cached queries and subscribers out of sync).

For anything that spawns and despawns often: bullets, wave-spawned enemies, particles as entities. Mechanism only: what a pooled entity is (its components, its reset logic) is the caller's factory.

docs.text:
Bases: StrictComponent

A pooled entity's factory must attach this itself -- EntityPool reads and writes it, but never adds one on a caller's behalf, since what else the entity needs (a reset position, a lifetime) is the factory's job regardless.

docs.title: EntityPool
docs.text:
Pre-allocates entities once, then hands them out and takes them back.

Every entity is created once, at construction, via factory. acquire() and release() toggle Poolable.is_active and move an entity between the available and active sets; nothing is destroyed. Capacity is fixed: acquire() returns None once exhausted.

An idle entity is disabled, not stripped. It keeps every component, and EntityManager excludes it from every query until it is acquired again. get_active() returns entities in acquisition order.

docs.title: pyguara.ecs.query_cache
docs.text:
Incremental result caching for hot-path ECS queries.

The inverted index in EntityManager already makes component lookup O(1), but intersecting several index sets still costs work on every call. A query registered here keeps its result materialised and updates it as components are attached and detached, so the per-frame read is a plain iteration, in the same reproducible order as an uncached query: see EntityManager._component_index.

Only register queries that run every frame; each registered query adds bookkeeping to every component add and remove that touches one of its types.

docs.title: QueryCache
docs.text:
Maintains materialised entity-id sets for registered component queries.

Caches stay synchronised through the two hooks EntityManager calls on every component change. Entity removal uses the same path: when flush_pending_removals() cleans up a removed entity, it calls on_component_removed() once per component type the entity carried.

This caches final intersection results; it does not implement archetypes.

Example 
entity_manager.register_cached_query(Transform, RigidBody)

for entity in entity_manager.get_entities_with_cached(Transform, RigidBody):
    ...

docs.title: pyguara.ecs.relations
docs.text:
Entity-to-entity relations: who owns whom.

Distinct from Transform parenting. A Transform parent is spatial: "my position is expressed relative to yours". ChildOf is ownership: "when you are destroyed, so am I". A health bar above an enemy wants both; a spawner's minions want ownership with no spatial relationship.

An entity that wants both attaches a ChildOf and sets its Transform parent.

docs.title: ChildOf dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: BaseComponent

Marks an entity as owned by another, for cascade destruction.

Attach it through EntityManager.set_parent() rather than add_component(), and change it the same way. The manager keeps a reverse index (parent -> children) so a cascade costs nothing per destroy, and that index is maintained from set_parent() and from the component add/remove hooks -- assigning parent_id in place bypasses both and leaves the index describing a parent that no longer claims this entity. The same contract entity._components has always had.

Attributes:

The id of the owning entity.

docs.title: pyguara.events
docs.text:
Event system: the dispatcher, its contracts, and the engine's own events.

Subscription is by type and matches subclasses, so subscribing to KeyboardEvent receives both KeyDownEvent and KeyUpEvent.

docs.title: EventDispatcher
docs.text:
Routes events to subscribers, with priority, filtering and queueing.

Subscription is by type, and dispatch walks the event's MRO: a handler subscribed to a base class receives every subclass too, and one subscribed to object receives everything. Handlers from the whole MRO merge into one priority-ordered pass.

queue_event() is safe to call from any thread. Everything else (dispatch(), subscribe(), unsubscribe(), clear_subscribers()) must run on the main thread, which drains the queue via process_queue().

The same callable may be subscribed more than once -- with different priorities or filters, say -- and will then run once per subscription.

docs.text:
dispatch_after(delay: float, event: Event) -> None

Dispatch event once delay seconds of game time have passed.

The delay is measured in whatever time advance() is fed, which Application scales by time_scale and zeroes while paused. So a pending event waits out a pause and runs at half speed in slow motion.

A delay of zero or less dispatches on the next advance(), not immediately; use dispatch() to deliver now.

required event Event

docs.title: advance
docs.text:
advance(dt: float) -> None

Advance pending dispatch_after timers and fire what is due.

Called once per frame by Application, with the same scaled delta the physics accumulator gets.

An event whose handler schedules another delayed event does not also fire this call: the new one is appended to the list being rebuilt, so it starts its own delay from the next advance(). That is what stops a zero-delay chain from spinning inside one frame.

The same callable may be subscribed more than once -- with different priorities or filters, say -- and will then run once per subscription.

required handler EventHandler[E]

required priority int

Optional predicate; the handler runs only if it returns True.

None owner object | None

Remove the subscription after its first delivery. The handler still runs; it simply does not run again.

False

docs.title: dispatch_after
docs.text:
dispatch_after(delay: float, event: Event) -> None

Dispatch event once delay seconds of game time have passed.

The delay is measured in whatever time advance() is fed, which Application scales by time_scale and zeroes while paused. So a pending event waits out a pause and runs at half speed in slow motion.

A delay of zero or less dispatches on the next advance(), not immediately; use dispatch() to deliver now.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default delay float

Seconds of game time to wait.

required event Event

The event to dispatch when the delay elapses.

required

docs.title: advance
docs.text:
advance(dt: float) -> None

Advance pending dispatch_after timers and fire what is due.

Called once per frame by Application, with the same scaled delta the physics accumulator gets.

An event whose handler schedules another delayed event does not also fire this call: the new one is appended to the list being rebuilt, so it starts its own delay from the next advance(). That is what stops a zero-delay chain from spinning inside one frame.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default dt float

Seconds of game time elapsed since the last call.

required

docs.title: ErrorHandlingStrategy
docs.text:
Bases: Enum

What a subsystem does when user-supplied code raises.

Used by EventDispatcher for handlers and filters, and by DIContainer for constructor introspection. A single definition, because two enums with the same members are not interchangeable: comparing one subsystem's RAISE against another's silently evaluates false.

Attributes:

Name Type Description LOG

Log the error and carry on. Graceful degradation in production.

RAISE

Log the error and re-raise it. Fail fast in development, and the default everywhere.

IGNORE

Swallow the error silently. Tests and narrow edge cases only.

Example 
from pyguara.errors import ErrorHandlingStrategy

dispatcher = EventDispatcher(error_strategy=ErrorHandlingStrategy.LOG)
container = DIContainer(error_strategy=ErrorHandlingStrategy.LOG)

docs.title: Camera2D
docs.text:
A 2D Camera component that defines the viewable area of the game world.

It handles Zoom and Panning math. It does NOT render anything; it simply provides the transformation the renderer applies.

There is one world-to-screen transform: screen = world * zoom + screen_offset(viewport). world_to_screen, screen_to_world and get_view_bounds are built on it. Rotation is not supported.

Attributes:

Name Type Description position Vector2

The center of the camera in World Coordinates.

zoom float

The scale factor (1.0 = 100%, 2.0 = 200%).

docs.title: position property writable
docs.text:
position: Vector2

The centre of the camera in world coordinates.

While a view override is held this is the override, so that a game drawing by hand from camera.position follows the editor's view exactly as the render pipeline does. The game's own writes keep landing underneath, where release_view finds them.

docs.title: view_overridden property
docs.text:
view_overridden: bool

Whether something other than the game is driving the view.

docs.title: view_position property
docs.text:
view_position: Vector2

Where the camera actually looks this frame.

position plus the current shake displacement. Every transform -- screen_offset, and get_view_bounds through it -- is expressed against this, not against position, so a shake moves the picture without moving the camera: position stays the value follow(), frame_targets() or the game last set, and bounds clamping has a stable thing to clamp.

bounds: Rect | None

The world box the view is kept inside, or None for unbounded.

docs.title: zoom property writable

zoom: float

The scale factor: 1.0 is natural size, 2.0 twice as large.

The override while one is held, for the same reason position is.

docs.title: frame_targets
docs.text:
frame_targets(
    targets: list[Vector2],
    padding: float = 0.0,
    min_zoom: float = 0.1,
    max_zoom: float = 4.0,
    smooth_time: float = 0.0,
    adjust_zoom: bool = True,
) -> None

Keep several points on screen at once, zooming to fit.

The co-op camera. Call it every frame with the players' current positions; the camera centres their bounding box and picks the zoom that fits it, between min_zoom and max_zoom.

Framing and follow() are mutually exclusive -- both decide position, so holding both would make the result depend on the order of two lines inside update(). Starting one cancels the other. With adjust_zoom, framing also cancels an in-flight zoom_to(), which it would otherwise overwrite every frame.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default targets list[Vector2]

World points to keep in view.

required padding float

World-space margin around their bounding box.

0.0 min_zoom float

How far out the camera will go before letting someone off screen.

0.1 max_zoom float

Ceiling, so one target does not zoom to infinity.

4.0 smooth_time float

Seconds of smoothing on position and zoom; 0 snaps.

0.0 adjust_zoom bool

False to centre the targets without touching zoom.

True

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If targets is empty, or the zoom range is not a positive interval.

Attributes:

Name Type Description deadzone Rect

Rectangle where target can move without camera moving.

max_speed float

Maximum camera movement speed in pixels/second.

smooth_time float

Smoothing factor (smaller = more responsive).

lookahead float

Seconds of the target's own velocity to lead by. The camera derives that velocity from how far the followed point moved since the last frame -- the caller does not have to hand it over -- and smooths it with smooth_time, because a raw per-frame delta is noisy enough to make the view jitter. 0 disables lookahead; 0.2-0.4 is the usual range for a runner, where the point is to show more of what the player is about to hit than of what they have already passed.

docs.title: Batcher
docs.text:
Group sorted render commands into draw batches.

Consecutive commands sharing a texture and a material become one batch, so a backend issues one draw call per group. Rotation, scale, tint and atlas source rect are optional parallel columns, filled only from the first command in a batch that needs one.

Grouping is by material_id, not object identity, so a copied or deserialised material batches with its original. The loop works on floats, not Vector2; see docs/guides/performance.md.

docs.title: create_batches
docs.text:
create_batches(
    sorted_commands: list[RenderCommand],
    camera: Camera2D,
    viewport: Viewport,
) -> list[RenderBatch]

Group compatible commands into batches to minimize draw calls.

Commands are grouped by (texture, material_id), and only consecutive ones -- the caller is expected to have sorted, which RenderQueue.sort does on (layer, sort_group, z_index, material_id).

A batch carries transform, tint and source-rect columns only when some command in it needs them, so a backend can keep a fast path for plain sprites. Those columns are either empty or exactly as long as destinations; nothing in between.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default sorted_commands list[RenderCommand]

The frame's commands, already sorted.

required camera Camera2D

Supplies the zoom and the world-to-screen offset.

required viewport Viewport

The region being drawn into.

required

Returns:

Type Description list[RenderBatch]

One batch per run of compatible commands, in command order.

docs.title: sort
docs.text:
sort() -> None

Sorts the queue in-place to ensure correct visual stacking.

Sorting order:

  1. Layer: background to UI.
  2. Sort group (Sprite.sort_group): coarse ordering within the layer.
  3. Depth (z_index): a y-sorted command carries its world Y here.
  4. Material ID: groups commands at equal depth for the batcher.

The sort is stable, so commands equal on every key keep their submission order.

docs.title: resize
docs.text:
resize(width: int, height: int) -> None

Adopt a new drawing size.

width and height are read-only, so before this there was no way to tell a renderer the window had changed -- and the ModernGL one builds its orthographic projection from them. A renderer left on the size it was constructed with maps the original pixel rectangle onto the new framebuffer, stretching the world by the ratio between the two aspect ratios: a circle came out an ellipse.

Implementations whose size is read from something else -- a pygame surface is its own size -- have nothing to store, and say so.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default width int

The new width in pixels.

required height int

The new height in pixels.

Restrict subsequent drawing to rect, in screen coordinates.

Nesting intersects: a push inside an active clip narrows to the overlap of the two, so a scroll container can live inside another. An empty intersection clips everything away.

Every push must be matched by a pop_clip(). A widget that draws between the two should do it in a try/finally, or an exception leaves the clip set for the rest of the frame.

docs.text:

Restores the clip to whatever was in force before that push, which may be another clip or none at all. A pop with nothing pushed is a no-op rather than an error: a widget that pops in a finally should not turn one bug into two.

A utility for slicing sprite sheet images into individual frames.

This class loads a sprite sheet image and can slice it into a grid of equal-sized frames. It uses Pillow for image manipulation, making it independent of the rendering backend (Pygame or ModernGL).

Example

factory = container.get(TextureFactory) sheet = SpriteSheet("assets/sprites/player.png", factory) frames = sheet.slice_grid(32, 32) # 32x32 pixel frames

docs.title: Or with a PIL Image directly (useful for testing):
docs.text: img = Image.new("RGBA", (64, 64)) sheet = SpriteSheet.from_image(img, factory, "test_sheet")

docs.title: clip
docs.text:
clip(
    name: str,
    frame_width: int,
    frame_height: int,
    row: int = 0,
    count: int = 0,
    fps: float = 10.0,
    *,
    loop: bool = True,
    mode: PlaybackMode | None = None,
    loop_count: int = 1,
    frame_events: dict[int, tuple[str, ...]] | None = None,
    margin: int = 0,
    spacing: int = 0,
) -> AnimationClip

Build an AnimationClip from one row of the grid.

slice_grid() returns a flat row-major list, so building a clip meant slicing frames[8:16] by hand and getting the arithmetic right every time -- friction rather than architecture, and the one place a sprite sheet's layout leaks into game code.

A row, not an arbitrary span, because that is how sprite sheets are actually laid out: one action per row. Use slice_grid() plus a slice for anything stranger.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default name str

The clip's name, e.g. "walk_down".

required frame_width int

Width of a single frame in pixels.

required frame_height int

Height of a single frame in pixels.

required row int

0-based row index.

0 count int

How many frames to take from that row. 0 takes the whole row.

0 fps float

The clip's frame rate.

10.0 loop bool

Whether the clip loops. Ignored if mode is given.

True mode PlaybackMode | None

Explicit PlaybackMode, for ping-pong or play-N-times.

None loop_count int

How many loops LOOP_TIMES runs.

1 frame_events dict[int, tuple[str, ...]] | None

Frame index to event names, as AnimationClip takes them. Indices are relative to this clip, not to the sheet -- frame 0 is the first frame of the row.

None margin int

Blank border between the sheet edge and the grid.

0 spacing int

Blank gutter between adjacent frames.

0

Returns:

Type Description AnimationClip

The clip, with its frames already sliced.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the row is out of range, or the requested count exceeds what the row holds. Both mean the caller's idea of the sheet disagrees with the sheet, and a clip quietly short of frames animates wrongly rather than visibly failing.

Nine-patch sprites divide an image into 9 sections (corners, edges, center) that can be scaled independently while preserving corner details.

Nothing here imports a backend or the resource manager. The caller hands over a texture it has already resolved, as ui.components.Image takes one.

docs.title: NinePatchSprite dataclass
docs.text:
Nine-patch sprite component for scalable UI rendering.

A nine-patch sprite divides a texture into 9 sections: - 4 corners (fixed size, never stretched) - 4 edges (stretched in one direction) - 1 center (stretched in both directions)

This allows UI elements like buttons and panels to scale properly without distorting corners.

Path to the texture atlas/sprite image

source_rect Rect | None

Source rectangle in the texture (entire image if None)

Nine-patch division metrics

min_size Vector2 | None

Minimum render size (prevents over-shrinking)

docs.title: texture_size
docs.text:
texture_size(texture: Any) -> tuple[int, int]

Report a texture's pixel size, whichever shape of texture it is.

The two halves of the engine wrap a texture differently and both reach a UIRenderer: the world side passes a resources.Texture, with width and height properties, while the UI side's draw_texture takes Any and the real backends require the raw pygame.Surface, which answers get_width(). ui.components.Image is handed the latter. Rather than pick one and make the other a type error far from here, ask for either -- and say so, since a caller reading texture: Any has no way to know what is acceptable.

Name Type Description Default texture Any

A resources.Texture, or a backend surface.

required

Type Description tuple[int, int]

(width, height) in pixels.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

If it is neither. Raised here, at the boundary, naming what was passed -- the alternative is an AttributeError from inside a slice loop that has already drawn four of nine patches.

docs.text:
render_ninepatch(
    renderer: UIRenderer,
    ninepatch: NinePatchSprite,
    texture: Any,
    x: int,
    y: int,
    width: int,
    height: int,
    color: Color | None = None,
) -> int

Render a nine-patch sprite: nine draws, one per slice.

Corners keep their pixel size at any destination size, edges stretch along one axis and the centre stretches along both.

A slice with no extent is skipped. metrics.left == 0 makes three of the nine destination rects zero-width, and an edge as thick as half the destination leaves the centre empty; both are ordinary.

required width int

Width to render at. Clamped up to the minimum by get_dest_rects, so the corners never overlap.

Height to render at, likewise.

Optional tint, passed through to every slice.

None

Type Description int

How many slices were drawn, 0 to 9.

docs.title: pyguara.graphics.primitives
docs.text:
Many rectangles, circles or lines, drawn from arrays in one call.

Each row of an array draws exactly what the matching draw_rect, draw_circle or draw_line call would, truncation to whole pixels included. On a PrimitiveArrayRenderer the array crosses to the GPU in one call; on any other renderer the rows are drawn one call at a time. Colours are 0 to 255, coordinates are screen pixels, values are read as float32, and an outline of 0 fills. The columns are in the example.

Example

docs.title: rects:   x, y, width, height, red, green, blue, alpha, outline
circles: x, y, radius, outline, red, green, blue, alpha
lines:   start_x, start_y, end_x, end_y, width, red, green, blue, alpha
docs.text: rows = numpy.zeros((len(enemies), 9), dtype=numpy.float32) rows[:, 0:2] = positions rows[:, 2:4] = (8, 8) rows[:, 4:8] = (220, 40, 40, 255) primitives.draw_rects(renderer, rows)

docs.title: pyguara.graphics.protocols
docs.text:
Core protocols for the Rendering system.

This module defines the essential contracts (interfaces) that decouple the "What" (Renderable objects) from the "How" (The Renderer backend).

By adhering to these protocols: 1. Game entities don't need to know if they are being drawn by Pygame or OpenGL. 2. The Renderer doesn't need to know what an "Enemy" or "Player" is; it just knows it received something Renderable.

docs.title: Renderable
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

An object that provides all necessary data to be drawn on screen.

Any class implementing this protocol (Game Entities, UI Widgets, Particles) can be submitted to the RenderPipeline. This effectively acts as the data source for a draw call.

Note

In a pure ECS (Entity Component System), this might strictly be a 'SpriteComponent'. However, defining it as a protocol allows flexibility for non-ECS objects (like debug cursors or simple UI) to be rendered through the same pipeline.

docs.title: y_sort property
docs.text:
y_sort: bool

Whether world Y decides this object's depth instead of z_index.

The 2.5D rule: objects lower on the screen (higher Y) cover objects higher up, so a character walking down past a tree ends up in front of it with nobody maintaining a number.

docs.title: sort_offset property
docs.text:

Added to world Y before comparing, when y_sort is True.

An object's depth is its contact point with the ground, not its centre: without this a tall tree whose centre sits above a short character's centre draws behind the character even while the character stands in front of its trunk. Usually half the height.

docs.title: resize
docs.text:
resize(width: int, height: int) -> None

Adopt a new drawing size.

width and height are read-only, so before this there was no way to tell a renderer the window had changed -- and the ModernGL one builds its orthographic projection from them. A renderer left on the size it was constructed with maps the original pixel rectangle onto the new framebuffer, stretching the world by the ratio between the two aspect ratios: a circle came out an ellipse.

Implementations whose size is read from something else -- a pygame surface is its own size -- have nothing to store, and say so.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default width int

The new width in pixels.

required height int

The new height in pixels.

required

docs.title: begin_move
docs.text:
begin_move() -> None

Start a run of moves, such as a drag.

Lets an implementation read the window's position once instead of once per frame. That read is not free, and worse, it is asynchronous: a window manager applies a move when it gets to it, so a position read straight after one may still be the old one. Adding a delta to that stale value puts the window somewhere nobody asked for, and the correction next frame is the small wobble a hand-rolled drag is known for.

docs.text:
move_by(dx: int, dy: int) -> None

Move the window by a screen-space delta.

A delta rather than an absolute position: a window manager may place a window somewhere other than asked -- WSLg offsets by the decoration it would have drawn -- so reading back a position and setting an absolute one accumulates that error on every drag frame.

docs.title: push_clip
docs.text:
push_clip(rect: Rect) -> None

Restrict subsequent drawing to rect, in screen coordinates.

Nesting intersects: a push inside an active clip narrows to the overlap of the two, so a scroll container can live inside another. An empty intersection clips everything away.

Every push must be matched by a pop_clip(). A widget that draws between the two should do it in a try/finally, or an exception leaves the clip set for the rest of the frame.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default rect Rect

The region to clip to, in screen pixels.

required

docs.title: pop_clip
docs.text:
pop_clip() -> None

Undo the most recent push_clip().

Restores the clip to whatever was in force before that push, which may be another clip or none at all. A pop with nothing pushed is a no-op rather than an error: a widget that pops in a finally should not turn one bug into two.

docs.title: clip
docs.text:
clip(
    name: str,
    frame_width: int,
    frame_height: int,
    row: int = 0,
    count: int = 0,
    fps: float = 10.0,
    *,
    loop: bool = True,
    mode: PlaybackMode | None = None,
    loop_count: int = 1,
    frame_events: dict[int, tuple[str, ...]] | None = None,
    margin: int = 0,
    spacing: int = 0,
) -> AnimationClip

Build an AnimationClip from one row of the grid.

slice_grid() returns a flat row-major list, so building a clip meant slicing frames[8:16] by hand and getting the arithmetic right every time -- friction rather than architecture, and the one place a sprite sheet's layout leaks into game code.

A row, not an arbitrary span, because that is how sprite sheets are actually laid out: one action per row. Use slice_grid() plus a slice for anything stranger.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default name str

The clip's name, e.g. "walk_down".

required frame_width int

Width of a single frame in pixels.

required frame_height int

Height of a single frame in pixels.

required row int

0-based row index.

0 count int

How many frames to take from that row. 0 takes the whole row.

0 fps float

The clip's frame rate.

10.0 loop bool

Whether the clip loops. Ignored if mode is given.

True mode PlaybackMode | None

Explicit PlaybackMode, for ping-pong or play-N-times.

None loop_count int

How many loops LOOP_TIMES runs.

1 frame_events dict[int, tuple[str, ...]] | None

Frame index to event names, as AnimationClip takes them. Indices are relative to this clip, not to the sheet -- frame 0 is the first frame of the row.

None margin int

Blank border between the sheet edge and the grid.

0 spacing int

Blank gutter between adjacent frames.

0

Returns:

Type Description AnimationClip

The clip, with its frames already sliced.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the row is out of range, or the requested count exceeds what the row holds. Both mean the caller's idea of the sheet disagrees with the sheet, and a clip quietly short of frames animates wrongly rather than visibly failing.

docs.title: pyguara.graphics.backends.clipping
docs.text:
The nesting clip stack every UIRenderer backend shares.

UIRenderer.push_clip / pop_clip promise that a nested push intersects rather than replaces, and that a pop restores whatever was in force before. That is the whole of the semantics, it is identical for every backend, and the backends differ only in what they do with the resulting rectangle -- pygame sets it on a surface, GL would set a scissor, the headless one discards it. So it lives here once instead of three times.

docs.title: ClipStack
docs.text:
The stack of clip regions a single UI pass pushes and pops.

Holds effective rectangles -- each already intersected with the one below it -- so current is what a backend applies without further arithmetic, and a pop is a list pop rather than a recomputation.

docs.title: current property
docs.text:

The region in force, or None when nothing is clipped.

docs.text:

docs.title: push
docs.text:
push(rect: Rect) -> Rect

Narrow the clip to rect, intersected with the current one.

Intersecting is the only behaviour that lets a scroll container sit inside another: an inventory inside a scrolling sidebar must not draw outside the sidebar just because its own viewport is larger.

An empty intersection is kept as a zero-size rectangle rather than discarded. It clips everything away, which is correct -- none of the inner element is on screen -- and it keeps the stack's depth matching the caller's pushes, so the matching pop still lands in the right place.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default rect Rect

The region to clip to, in screen pixels.

required

Returns:

Type Description Rect

The effective region, after intersection.

A pop with nothing pushed is a no-op: a widget that pops in a finally should not turn one bug into two.

docs.title: pyguara.graphics.backends.headless_renderer

Headless graphics backend.

Used for server-side logic, unit tests, or CI/CD pipelines where no display exists. Unlike the Pygame backend under SDL_VIDEODRIVER=dummy, none of these classes ever touch pygame.display (or any other SDL video call), so they carry no SDL video dependency at all. Hosts the full composition-root trio a real backend needs -- HeadlessWindowBackend (IWindowBackend), HeadlessBackend (IRenderer), HeadlessUIRenderer (UIRenderer), and HeadlessTextureFactory (TextureFactory) -- in one module since each is a handful of no-op lines.

docs.title: pyguara.graphics.backends.surface_blending
docs.text:
Blending a translucent shape onto a pygame surface.

pygame.draw replaces the destination pixel, alpha included, where a translucent shape should composite into it. The helpers here draw the shape on a scratch surface and blit it, which composites. Every primitive goes through them: rects, circles, lines and polygons.

Font.render ignores a colour's alpha, so render_text bakes the alpha into the glyphs' pixels. That works whether the result is blitted or uploaded to the GPU.

docs.title: pyguara.graphics.backends.pygame.fallback_font
docs.text:
A pygame font that draws characters its face lacks from fallback faces.

SDL_ttf opens one file and draws a box for any character it lacks, and pygame does not say which those are. So the text is split into runs by the face that has each character -- the native extension reads the character maps, the same answer the wgpu renderer uses -- each run is rendered with its own pygame.font.Font, and the runs are set side by side on the default face's baseline.

With no fallbacks set, every call goes straight to the default face, so text that needs none renders exactly as before.

docs.title: close
docs.text:
close() -> None

Release the surface, then the window.

The GPU object is shared: the renderers hold frame.gpu too, so dropping this window's reference does not free it. It is told to let go of the window explicitly, before the window is destroyed, because a surface must not outlive its window. That call also waits for the GPU to finish its last frame, with or without a surface, so the process does not exit under a driver thread that is still rendering.

docs.title: pyguara.graphics.backends.wgpu.frame
docs.text:
What the wgpu window, world renderer and UI renderer share.

All three draw into one NativeGpu frame, in the order they are called, so they hold one GpuFrame between them: the native device, and the two caches that turn CPU-side pixels into GPU textures.

Text is rasterised in Rust (NativeFont) once per string, in white, cached as a texture and tinted by the instance colour when drawn.

Nothing is freed in the middle of a frame. An eviction queues the texture id, and after_frame frees it once the frame is rendered.

docs.text:
line_quad(
    start_x: float,
    start_y: float,
    end_x: float,
    end_y: float,
    width: int,
) -> tuple[float, float, float, float, float]

Turn a pygame-style line into the quad that covers the same pixels.

pygame does not draw a thick line as a rotated rectangle. It draws a one-pixel line and repeats it width times along the minor axis -- up and down for a mostly horizontal line, side to side for a steep one. So its thickness is measured along an axis, not across the line; an even width sits half a pixel towards positive on that axis; and both end pixels are drawn.

docs.title: pyguara.graphics.backends.wgpu.polygon
docs.text:
Turn a UI polygon into triangles for the GPU.

The wgpu UI renderer draws a polygon as one native mesh step: its fill triangulated by ear clipping, its outline as one ring of mitred quads, so a translucent outline is blended once at its corners.

Vertices are placed on pixel centres, where pygame's own edges run, so the two renderers agree inside a polygon and differ slightly along its edges.

docs.title: MITER_LIMIT module-attribute
docs.text:
MITER_LIMIT = 4.0

How far a corner's miter may reach, in half-widths, before it is cut.

A sharp corner's miter grows without bound -- at 10 degrees it is eleven half-widths long -- and draws a spike. Past the limit the corner is bevelled instead.

docs.text:
IRenderer on wgpu: the world renderer.

Every call here pushes one primitive into the native frame. Nothing is drawn until the window presents.

It matches the pygame renderer pixel for pixel where that is possible: a rectangle on the same pixels, a line through the same pixel centres, text at the same integer position. pygame names a pixel by its top-left corner and the GPU rasterises through pixel centres, so a circle or line at pygame's (x, y) is drawn here about (x + 0.5, y + 0.5).

docs.title: pyguara.graphics.backends.wgpu.shapes
docs.text:
ShapeBatch on wgpu.

A batch's rows are already the instance layout the shape shader reads (centre, padded half-size, rotation, colour, stroke, kind), so they go to the GPU as they are, one instanced draw for the whole batch.

A batched line is a capsule with rounded ends, and a batched circle's edge is a signed distance at the pixel centre. The renderer's per-primitive draw_line and draw_circle match pygame instead.

docs.title: SHAPES module-attribute
docs.text:
SHAPES = InstancedShader(
    "shapes",
    attributes=(
        Attribute("pos", "vec2"),
        Attribute("size", "vec2"),
        Attribute("rotation"),
        Attribute("color", "vec4"),
        Attribute("width"),
        Attribute("kind"),
    ),
    uniforms=(Uniform("u_projection", "mat4"),),
    wgsl="
struct Varying {
    @builtin(position) position: vec4<f32>,
    @location(0) local: vec2<f32>,
    @location(1) size: vec2<f32>,
    @location(2) color: vec4<f32>,
    @location(3) width: f32,
    @location(4) @interpolate(flat) kind: f32,
};

@vertex
fn vertex(@builtin(vertex_index) index: u32, shape: Instance) -> Varying {
    let local = quad_corner(index) * 2.0 * shape.size;
    let c = cos(shape.rotation);
    let s = sin(shape.rotation);
    // shape.vert's mat2(c, s, -s, c) * local: from +x towards +y.
    let rotated = vec2<f32>(c * local.x - s * local.y, s * local.x + c * local.y);
    var out: Varying;
    out.position = params.u_projection * vec4<f32>(rotated + shape.pos, 0.0, 1.0);
    out.local = local;
    out.size = shape.size;
    out.color = shape.color;
    out.width = shape.width;
    out.kind = shape.kind;
    return out;
}

fn sd_box(p: vec2<f32>, half_extent: vec2<f32>) -> f32 {
    let d = abs(p) - half_extent;
    return length(max(d, vec2<f32>(0.0))) + min(max(d.x, d.y), 0.0);
}

fn sd_segment(p: vec2<f32>, half_length: f32, half_width: f32) -> f32 {
    let q = vec2<f32>(clamp(p.x, -half_length, half_length), 0.0);
    return length(p - q) - half_width;
}

@fragment
fn fragment(in: Varying) -> @location(0) vec4<f32> {
    let shape = i32(in.kind + 0.5);
    let half_stroke = in.width * 0.5;
    var d: f32;
    if (shape == 0) {
        d = sd_box(in.local, in.size - vec2<f32>(half_stroke));
    } else if (shape == 1) {
        d = length(in.local) - (in.size.x - half_stroke);
    } else {
        d = sd_segment(in.local, in.size.x - in.size.y, in.size.y);
    }
    var alpha = step(d, 0.0);
    if (in.width > 0.0) {
        alpha = step(-in.width, d) * step(d, 0.0);
    }
    if (alpha <= 0.0) {
        discard;
    }
    return vec4<f32>(in.color.rgb, in.color.a * alpha);
}
",
)

A batch of rectangles, circles or capsules, as shape.frag draws them.

docs.text:
The wgpu backend's textures: RGBA bytes decoded in Rust, not pygame surfaces.

A texture on this backend is the pixels the GPU will be given, held once on the CPU: ImageTexture. Its loader decodes with decode_image (rust/src/imaging.rs) and its factory wraps bytes a caller already has -- a sprite sheet's cells, rasterised geometry. Neither imports pygame.

The pixels stay on the CPU after upload because the upload is lazy and per-frame cached (GpuFrame.image), and because a texture that outlives a device -- the window closed and reopened -- has to be uploadable again.

docs.text:
close() -> None

Release the surface, then the window.

The GPU object is shared: the renderers hold frame.gpu too, so dropping this window's reference does not free it. It is told to let go of the window explicitly, before the window is destroyed, because a surface must not outlive its window. That call also waits for the GPU to finish its last frame, with or without a surface, so the process does not exit under a driver thread that is still rendering.

docs.title: PlaybackMode
docs.text:
Bases: Enum

How a clip behaves when it reaches its last frame.

A single loop bool could only say "start over" or "stop", which leaves out the two things an idle animation and a one-shot both want: breathing back down rather than snapping to frame 0, and finishing N times rather than once or forever.

Attributes:

Name Type Description ONCE

Stop on the last frame.

LOOP

Jump back to frame 0 and keep going.

PING_PONG

Play forwards, then backwards, then forwards -- an idle bob or a breathing loop, where a hard cut back to frame 0 is visible as a hitch.

LOOP_TIMES

Loop loop_count times, then stop on the last frame.

docs.text:
A 2D Camera component that defines the viewable area of the game world.

It handles Zoom and Panning math. It does NOT render anything; it simply provides the transformation the renderer applies.

There is one world-to-screen transform: screen = world * zoom + screen_offset(viewport). world_to_screen, screen_to_world and get_view_bounds are built on it. Rotation is not supported.

The center of the camera in World Coordinates.

zoom float

The scale factor (1.0 = 100%, 2.0 = 200%).

The co-op camera. Call it every frame with the players' current positions; the camera centres their bounding box and picks the zoom that fits it, between min_zoom and max_zoom.

Framing and follow() are mutually exclusive -- both decide position, so holding both would make the result depend on the order of two lines inside update(). Starting one cancels the other. With adjust_zoom, framing also cancels an in-flight zoom_to(), which it would otherwise overwrite every frame.

How far out the camera will go before letting someone off screen.

0.1 max_zoom float

Ceiling, so one target does not zoom to infinity.

4.0 smooth_time float

Seconds of smoothing on position and zoom; 0 snaps.

0.0 adjust_zoom bool

False to centre the targets without touching zoom.

True

Type Description ValueError

docs.title: PlaybackMode
docs.text:
Bases: Enum

How a clip behaves when it reaches its last frame.

A single loop bool could only say "start over" or "stop", which leaves out the two things an idle animation and a one-shot both want: breathing back down rather than snapping to frame 0, and finishing N times rather than once or forever.

Attributes:

Name Type Description ONCE

Stop on the last frame.

LOOP

Jump back to frame 0 and keep going.

PING_PONG

Play forwards, then backwards, then forwards -- an idle bob or a breathing loop, where a hard cut back to frame 0 is visible as a hitch.

LOOP_TIMES

Loop loop_count times, then stop on the last frame.

docs.title: AnimationClip dataclass
docs.text:
Data for a single animation state (e.g., 'walk_down').

Attributes:

Name Type Description frame_events dict[int, tuple[str, ...]]

0-based frame index -> event name(s) fired when advance_animator() lands on (or catches up through) that frame. Consumed by AnimationSystem, which turns each fired name into an AnimationFrameEvent -- the mechanism kits/action_combat's ActiveFrameWindow uses to toggle a Hitbox's active frames without its own timer. Not fired for frame 0 by play_clip()'s initial-frame application; only by advance_animator()-driven frame transitions.

mode PlaybackMode | None

What happens at the last frame. Defaults to None, which means "whatever loop says" -- loop predates this and plenty of clips (and every prefab file) still set it.

loop_count int

How many loops LOOP_TIMES runs. Ignored otherwise.

frame_durations tuple[float, ...] | None

Seconds each frame is held, one per frame, for a clip whose frames are not all the same length. When set it decides the timing and frame_rate is not read.

    animator: Animator, dt: float

docs.title: Camera2D
docs.text:
A 2D Camera component that defines the viewable area of the game world.

It handles Zoom and Panning math. It does NOT render anything; it simply provides the transformation the renderer applies.

There is one world-to-screen transform: screen = world * zoom + screen_offset(viewport). world_to_screen, screen_to_world and get_view_bounds are built on it. Rotation is not supported.

Attributes:

Name Type Description position Vector2

The center of the camera in World Coordinates.

zoom float

The scale factor (1.0 = 100%, 2.0 = 200%).

docs.title: position property writable
docs.text:
position: Vector2

The centre of the camera in world coordinates.

While a view override is held this is the override, so that a game drawing by hand from camera.position follows the editor's view exactly as the render pipeline does. The game's own writes keep landing underneath, where release_view finds them.

docs.title: view_overridden property
docs.text:
view_overridden: bool

Whether something other than the game is driving the view.

docs.title: view_position property
docs.text:
view_position: Vector2

Where the camera actually looks this frame.

position plus the current shake displacement. Every transform -- screen_offset, and get_view_bounds through it -- is expressed against this, not against position, so a shake moves the picture without moving the camera: position stays the value follow(), frame_targets() or the game last set, and bounds clamping has a stable thing to clamp.

bounds: Rect | None

docs.title: zoom property writable

The scale factor: 1.0 is natural size, 2.0 twice as large.

The override while one is held, for the same reason position is.

Idempotent, so a drag can call it on every frame without having to track whether it already holds the view.

Keep the view inside a world box -- "do not show past the wall".

Clamped in update(), against position and not the shaken view, so a shake still shows at the edge of a room. When the view is larger than the box on an axis, the camera centres on the box.

Sized from the camera's fallback viewport, so a split-screen camera must declare its real size with set_viewport_size().

docs.title: frame_targets
docs.text:
frame_targets(
    targets: list[Vector2],
    padding: float = 0.0,
    min_zoom: float = 0.1,
    max_zoom: float = 4.0,
    smooth_time: float = 0.0,
    adjust_zoom: bool = True,
) -> None

Keep several points on screen at once, zooming to fit.

The co-op camera. Call it every frame with the players' current positions; the camera centres their bounding box and picks the zoom that fits it, between min_zoom and max_zoom.

Framing and follow() are mutually exclusive -- both decide position, so holding both would make the result depend on the order of two lines inside update(). Starting one cancels the other. With adjust_zoom, framing also cancels an in-flight zoom_to(), which it would otherwise overwrite every frame.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default targets list[Vector2]

World points to keep in view.

required padding float

World-space margin around their bounding box.

0.0 min_zoom float

How far out the camera will go before letting someone off screen.

0.1 max_zoom float

Ceiling, so one target does not zoom to infinity.

4.0 smooth_time float

Seconds of smoothing on position and zoom; 0 snaps.

0.0 adjust_zoom bool

False to centre the targets without touching zoom.

True

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If targets is empty, or the zoom range is not a positive interval.

docs.title: pyguara.graphics.components.geometry
docs.text:
Procedural geometric shapes that render like any other sprite.

Shapes rasterise themselves once into a Texture, cached until a property changes, so they take part in Z-sorting and batching exactly as a loaded sprite does. The alternative -- immediate-mode draw calls inside the render loop -- cannot be batched and defeats the pipeline.

Rasterisation produces plain RGBA bytes and hands them to a TextureFactory, so a shape works on whichever backend is running. This module imports no backend of its own.

docs.title: pyguara.graphics.lighting.cycle
docs.text:
Ambient light driven around a loop of keyframes -- a day/night cycle.

The mechanism only: interpolate an AmbientLight along a ring of keyframes by a normalised phase. What the keyframes mean (dawn, dusk) is the game's.

The cycle is opt-in per entity and needs an AmbientLight beside it. It overwrites that light's colour and intensity every tick it plays, so a transient flash is a LightSource, or playing = False for its duration. sample_cycle() is a free function over plain data, for a game that tints fog or UI by the same phase.

docs.text:
Defines the visual properties of a rendered object.

A material combines a shader (a SpriteShader, one WGSL function), an optional second texture (a mask, a ramp, a noise field) and uniform values by name. Materials are sorted by ID during batching to minimize shader/texture switches.

Example

FLASH = SpriteShader("flash", uniforms=(Uniform("amount"),), wgsl=...) sprite.material = Material(FLASH, uniforms={"amount": 0.0}) sprite.material.set_uniform("amount", 0.8) # on a hit

docs.text: The render pipeline: batching, the render system and the render graph.

docs.title: pyguara.graphics.pipeline.batch
docs.text: Logic for grouping render calls to minimize CPU/GPU overhead.

docs.title: Batcher
docs.text:
Group sorted render commands into draw batches.

Consecutive commands sharing a texture and a material become one batch, so a backend issues one draw call per group. Rotation, scale, tint and atlas source rect are optional parallel columns, filled only from the first command in a batch that needs one.

Grouping is by material_id, not object identity, so a copied or deserialised material batches with its original. The loop works on floats, not Vector2; see docs/guides/performance.md.

docs.title: create_batches
docs.text:
create_batches(
    sorted_commands: list[RenderCommand],
    camera: Camera2D,
    viewport: Viewport,
) -> list[RenderBatch]

Group compatible commands into batches to minimize draw calls.

Commands are grouped by (texture, material_id), and only consecutive ones -- the caller is expected to have sorted, which RenderQueue.sort does on (layer, sort_group, z_index, material_id).

A batch carries transform, tint and source-rect columns only when some command in it needs them, so a backend can keep a fast path for plain sprites. Those columns are either empty or exactly as long as destinations; nothing in between.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default sorted_commands list[RenderCommand]

The frame's commands, already sorted.

required camera Camera2D

Supplies the zoom and the world-to-screen offset.

required viewport Viewport

The region being drawn into.

required

Returns:

Type Description list[RenderBatch]

One batch per run of compatible commands, in command order.

docs.title: pyguara.graphics.pipeline.buffers
docs.text:
The standard framebuffer chain, and the format it carries.

A frame moves through four named buffers: world, lightmap, composite and post-processed. This module names them and the format each has. RenderGraph declares them on the manager at construction, and effects with their own scratch buffers declare theirs the same way, so a pass asking for a buffer by name gets the declared format.

docs.title: HDR_DTYPE module-attribute
docs.text:
HDR_DTYPE = 'f2'

16-bit float, so a value above 1.0 survives to be tonemapped.

bloom_composite.frag is where it is tonemapped: a knee at 0.8, identity below and asymptotic to 1.0 above. That choice is what let the range be brought in without re-tuning the demos lit against the old clamped pipeline -- a plain Reinhard maps the whole scale, and would have pulled every mid-tone in tamandua_murundus and mourisco_ressonancia down with it. See tests/integration/test_bloom_tonemap_pixels.py.

docs.title: STANDARD_CHAIN module-attribute
docs.text:
STANDARD_CHAIN: tuple[str, ...] = (
    WORLD_FBO_NAME,
    LIGHT_FBO_NAME,
    COMPOSITE_FBO_NAME,
    POST_PROCESSED_FBO_NAME,
)

The buffers RenderGraph declares as HDR when it is constructed.

docs.title: pyguara.graphics.pipeline.device
docs.text:
The render graph's view of the GPU.

A pass reads some buffers and runs one shader over the whole of another buffer, or many instanced quads into it, with a few uniforms and a blend mode. It describes that work as a FullscreenShader or an InstancedShader, its inputs by name, its uniform values and its target; GraphicsDevice.run and draw_instanced do it. WgpuDevice is the device.

Shaders are WGSL, with in.uv (0, 0) at the top left. The heat haze and the storm are the exception: they use v_uv with y up.

docs.title: Blend module-attribute
docs.text:
Blend = Literal['replace', 'alpha', 'add']

How a pass combines with what its output already holds.

alpha is what the passes draw with: straight-alpha blending, as every pass was approved with against ModernGL. add is the light accumulation. replace overwrites.

Record the format name is created with, before anything creates it.

Declaring is not allocating: the framebuffer is still built by the first get_or_create that needs it, at the declared format rather than the 8-bit default. That is what gives a chain of buffers one owner -- without it, the format is whichever caller happens to run first, and every other caller has to either pass the same dtype or accept what it finds.

docs.text:
Render graph - orchestrates multi-pass rendering.

The RenderGraph manages the sequence of render passes that compose the final frame. It provides access to shared resources like the FramebufferManager and coordinates pass execution.

docs.title: RenderGraph
docs.text:
Orchestrates the rendering pipeline by executing passes in order.

Holds a FramebufferManager and an ordered list of passes. A typical order for a 2D game with lighting and post-processing: LightPass (lights into the light buffer), CompositePass (world times light), PostProcessPass (bloom, vignette), FinalPass (blit to the screen).

The world itself is not a pass. Application._render_with_graph binds and clears the world buffer and lets the scenes draw into it before any pass runs.

sort() -> None

Sorts the queue in-place to ensure correct visual stacking.

Sorting order:

  1. Layer: background to UI.
  2. Sort group (Sprite.sort_group): coarse ordering within the layer.
  3. Depth (z_index): a y-sorted command carries its world Y here.
  4. Material ID: groups commands at equal depth for the batcher.

Defines the Viewport logic for screen-space rendering management.

This module provides the Viewport class, which defines the specific rectangular region of the OS window where the game world is drawn. While the Camera controls what you see (World Space), the Viewport controls where it appears on the screen (Screen Space).

docs.text:
Composite render pass - combines world and light map.

This pass multiplies the world texture by the light map to create the final lit scene. The result is either written to another FBO for post-processing or directly to the screen.

docs.title: COMPOSITE module-attribute
docs.text:
COMPOSITE = FullscreenShader(
    "composite",
    inputs=("u_world", "u_lightmap"),
    wgsl="
@fragment
fn fragment(in: Varying) -> @location(0) vec4<f32> {
    let world_color = textureSample(u_world, input_sampler, in.uv);
    let light_color = textureSample(u_lightmap, input_sampler, in.uv);
    // Light above 1.0 brightens, below darkens; the world's alpha is kept.
    return vec4<f32>(world_color.rgb * light_color.rgb, world_color.a);
}
",
)

World times light map, the same in both sources.

docs.title: pyguara.graphics.pipeline.passes.light_pass
docs.text:
Light render pass - renders dynamic lights to a light map.

This pass collects all lights in the scene and renders them to a light framebuffer using additive blending. The result is then composited with the world in the composite pass.

docs.title: LIGHTS module-attribute
docs.text:
LIGHTS = InstancedShader(
    "lights",
    attributes=(
        Attribute("pos", "vec2"),
        Attribute("radius"),
        Attribute("color", "vec3"),
        Attribute("intensity"),
        Attribute("falloff"),
        Attribute("kind"),
        Attribute("spot_dir"),
        Attribute("spot_cos_half"),
    ),
    uniforms=(Uniform("u_projection", "mat4"),),
    wgsl="
struct Varying {
    @builtin(position) position: vec4<f32>,
    @location(0) uv: vec2<f32>,
    @location(1) color: vec3<f32>,
    @location(2) intensity: f32,
    @location(3) falloff: f32,
    // Flat: the type is a discriminant, not a quantity.
    @location(4) @interpolate(flat) kind: f32,
    @location(5) spot_dir: f32,
    @location(6) spot_cos_half: f32,
};

@vertex
fn vertex(@builtin(vertex_index) index: u32, light: Instance) -> Varying {
    let corner = quad_corner(index);
    let scaled = corner * light.radius * 2.0;
    var out: Varying;
    out.position = params.u_projection * vec4<f32>(scaled + light.pos, 0.0, 1.0);
    out.uv = corner + vec2<f32>(0.5, 0.5);
    out.color = light.color;
    out.intensity = light.intensity;
    out.falloff = light.falloff;
    out.kind = light.kind;
    out.spot_dir = light.spot_dir;
    out.spot_cos_half = light.spot_cos_half;
    return out;
}

const TYPE_DIRECTIONAL: f32 = 2.0;
const TYPE_SPOT: f32 = 3.0;

@fragment
fn fragment(in: Varying) -> @location(0) vec4<f32> {
    let offset = in.uv - vec2<f32>(0.5, 0.5);
    let dist = length(offset) * 2.0;
    var attenuation = 1.0 - pow(clamp(dist, 0.0, 1.0), in.falloff);
    attenuation = max(attenuation, 0.0);
    attenuation = smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, attenuation);
    if (in.kind == TYPE_DIRECTIONAL) {
        attenuation = 1.0;
    } else if (in.kind == TYPE_SPOT) {
        let axis = vec2<f32>(cos(in.spot_dir), sin(in.spot_dir));
        var aligned = 1.0;
        if (dist > 0.0001) {
            aligned = dot(normalize(offset), axis);
        }
        let edge = (1.0 - in.spot_cos_half) * 0.15 + 0.0001;
        attenuation *= smoothstep(in.spot_cos_half - edge, in.spot_cos_half + edge, aligned);
    }
    return vec4<f32>(in.color * (attenuation * in.intensity), 1.0);
}
",
)

A quad per light: radial falloff, an even directional fill, or a cone.

Visual effects system for PyGuara.

Two layers live here:

  • Post-processing: PostProcessEffect and PostProcessStack, plus the shipped screen-space effects (bloom, heat haze, storm, vignette). These transform the finished frame.
  • Feedback: Sparks and Shaker, the small pooled primitives a game reaches for when something is hit. These are composed into a scene, as ParticleSystem is.

Procedural rain streaks, sheet lightning, and forked bolts.

docs.title: pyguara.graphics.vfx.shake
docs.text:
Screen shake: several overlapping impulses summed into one offset.

CameraShake is a single decaying impulse. Real feedback overlaps -- a kill lands while the previous explosion is still settling -- and running one shake at a time means the second impact either cuts the first short or is swallowed by it. Shaker keeps every live impulse and sums them.

The result is a plain pixel offset, which is deliberate: a scene drawing in world space adds it to the camera position, and one drawing in screen space adds it to what it draws. Neither has to own a camera to shake.

docs.title: pyguara.graphics.vfx.sparks
docs.text:
Coloured shape particles: sparks, embers, splashes, debris.

A pool of short-lived primitives drawn through IRenderer.draw_circle and draw_line, not as textured sprites. Use ParticleSystem when particles are sprites; a spark has no texture, takes a colour per primitive, and batches each shape type into one instanced draw.

The pool is held in Rust as arrays, and hands its primitives to a renderer that can take them through ShapeBatch. It has no Python implementation. See docs/guides/performance.md.

Example

sparks = Sparks() sparks.burst(position, Color(255, 180, 60), count=14, streak=True) sparks.update(dt) sparks.render(renderer, offset=shake_offset)

docs.text:
Rising heat and drifting dust as a screen-space post-process effect.

The shimmer is a refraction in the fragment shader, drawn over the finished frame, so its cost does not depend on how strong it is and nothing goes through the ECS or the batcher.

docs.text: haze.gust(0.6) # a dust kick that decays on its own

Rain and lightning as a screen-space post-process effect.

The rain is procedural in the fragment shader, drawn over the finished frame, so a downpour costs what a drizzle costs and nothing goes through the ECS or the batcher.

This effect owns how the weather looks; the game owns what it is doing. A strike is not scheduled here: the caller drives flash, bolt and the rest.

Example

storm.rain = 0.3 # a steady drizzle storm.update(dt) # advances the shader clock

docs.title: ... and when a strike lands:
docs.text: storm.strike(x=0.4) # a new bolt shape at 40% across the frame storm.flash = envelope # driven by the caller's own fade

docs.title: StormEffect
docs.text:
Bases: PostProcessEffect

Procedural rain streaks, sheet lightning, and forked bolts.

Attributes:

Name Type Description rain

Downpour amount, 0.0 (dry) to 1.0 (heavy). Scales both how many drops fall and how brightly they read.

rain_speed

Multiplier on fall rate. 1.0 is a steady vertical rain; raise it with wind for a squall.

wind

Streak slant. Positive leans the rain right, negative left. Roughly -0.5..0.5 stays believable.

rain_color

Linear RGB the streaks add to the frame.

flash

Sheet lightning, 0.0 to 1.0 -- a wash that lifts the whole frame. Drive this from an envelope; holding it high looks like a fade to white, not like lightning.

flash_color

Linear RGB of both the sheet wash and the bolt.

bolt

The bolt's own brightness, 0.0 to 1.0. Usually held for a few frames per strike, much shorter than flash.

bolt_x

Where the bolt falls, 0.0 (left edge) to 1.0 (right).

docs.title: pyguara.i18n.check
docs.text:
Hold every locale's strings against the source's.

What pyguara i18n check runs. It reports, per locale:

  • a key the source has and the locale lacks (it would show English);
  • a key the locale has and the source lacks (a typo, or a removed string);
  • placeholders that differ from the source's, form by form;
  • plural forms the locale's language needs and the entry lacks;
  • a file that will not load, or names a language with no plural rules;

and, as a warning, a file not yet reviewed by a native speaker.

docs.text:
Which plural form a count takes, per language: CLDR's rules, for integers.

A game counts things -- scrap, players, seconds -- so only integer counts are handled. Each rule is transcribed from the Unicode CLDR plural rules (https://www.unicode.org/cldr/charts/latest/supplemental/language_plural_rules.html) for the languages the engine has been asked to support; a language with no rule here is refused rather than given English's, which would be a plausible wrong answer.

docs.title: pyguara.input.coop
docs.text:
Local co-op: routes input devices to player slots.

InputManager resolves bindings the same way regardless of who's playing; PlayerRouter is the piece that decides which player a given device's input belongs to, and lets a game query the result. Initial assignment (keyboard is player 0, say) is the game's job -- assign() -- since the engine has no way to guess it. What genuinely needs engine mechanism is the dynamic part: an unassigned gamepad pressing a join button, and a gamepad disconnecting mid-session.

docs.text:

The gamepad button an unassigned controller presses to claim the next free player slot.

docs.title: assign
docs.text:
assign(
    device: InputDevice,
    controller_id: int | None,
    player: int,
) -> None

Explicitly bind a device to a player slot.

The usual way a game establishes its default player -- keyboard and mouse have no join gesture of their own, so this is how they (and a gamepad already connected at startup, if a game wants one to just work without pressing anything) get attributed at all.

Overwrites any previous assignment for (device, controller_id) silently; does not fire PlayerLeftEvent for whatever player it previously held, only a real disconnect does that.

docs.title: pyguara.kits
docs.text:
Opt-in kits: composable, genre-specific systems built on core mechanism.

pyguara/ core is genre-agnostic and never imports from here. A kit is systems, components and a thin facade, constructed and ticked by the game that wants it; nothing under pyguara/kits/ registers itself. A kit may depend on another kit if the dependency is explicit, acyclic and shallow; prefer core events at the seams.

This package imports nothing: a game imports pyguara.kits.<name>.

docs.title: pyguara.kits.action_combat
docs.text:
The action_combat kit: damage and health, plus Hitbox and Hurtbox.

Health, DamageDealt and the apply_damage() pipeline (crit, mitigation via kits/stats, invincibility) stand alone; kits/projectiles depends on them.

Hitbox, Hurtbox and HitboxSystem detect hits. A Hitbox entity carries a TriggerVolume, and "active frames" is that volume's active field, set by the game or by ActiveFrameSystem from AnimationFrameEvent. A Hurtbox has no shape: overlap is detected against the target's solid Collider.

docs.title: pyguara.kits.action_combat.damage
docs.text:
The damage pipeline: mitigation, invincibility, and Health mutation.

Combines kits/stats' pure formulas with Health's state into the one function a hit -- melee, projectile, hazard, DoT tick -- actually calls. Which stat means "defense" for a given DamageType is this kit's own vocabulary to impose (unlike kits/stats, which stays generic): "armor" for PHYSICAL, "resistance" for ELEMENTAL. A game not using those names supplies its own StatBlock with them, or passes stats=None to skip mitigation entirely.

A Hitbox entity also carries a pyguara.physics.trigger_volume.TriggerVolume -- Hitbox is combat metadata riding alongside it, not a replacement for its sensor-collider/entities-tracking machinery, which TriggerSystem already builds and maintains. Not a shape of its own: HitboxSystem detects overlap through a Hitbox's TriggerVolume sensor against the target's solid Collider, then checks for this component to confirm the target can be damaged, and reads team from it. docs.title: pyguara.kits.effects
docs.text:
The effects kit: the generic item, boon and equipment-module substrate.

Effect is a plain, overridable domain object with no fixed subtypes; categories are game data. EffectContainer is a data-only component holding a list of them. add_effect() and remove_effect() apply and remove them and handle stacking, and EffectSystem ticks active effects each frame. An effect subscribes to whatever event it cares about in its own on_apply(), through core event dispatch; this kit imports no other kit.

docs.title: EffectContainer dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: StrictComponent

Pure data: the effects currently active on an entity.

Attributes:

Name Type Description effects list[Effect]

Active Effect instances, in application order.

docs.title: StackingRule
docs.text:
Bases: Enum

How add_effect() handles an effect whose key is already present.

Attributes:

Name Type Description STACK

Add another instance alongside any existing ones (up to add_effect()'s max_stacks, if given).

REFRESH

Reset the existing instance's elapsed to 0 instead of adding a new one -- a re-applied buff extends its duration rather than stacking its magnitude.

IGNORE

Do nothing while an instance is already present.

REPLACE

Remove every existing instance sharing the key, then apply the new one.

docs.title: Effect
docs.text:
Base class for a stacking, time-limited or reactive gameplay effect.

Attributes:

Name Type Description key

Identity used by container.add_effect()'s stacking rules to decide whether two applications are "the same" effect. Defaults to the class name; override for two effects of the same class to be considered distinct (or two different classes to share stacking, if a game wants that).

duration

Seconds until this effect auto-expires, or None for permanent (removed only by an explicit remove_effect() call).

elapsed

Seconds since this effect was applied. update()'s default implementation advances this; a subclass overriding update() for its own tick behavior (damage-over-time, say) should call super().update(dt) to keep expiry working.

source

Whatever applied this effect, if anything -- an item id, an attacker entity id, a status name. Not used by this class itself; here for a subclass or key to key off.

Rarity/roll_rarity() and LootEntry/LootTable/roll_loot() build on pyguara.common.random.weighted_choice(), re-exported here. roll_rarity()'s luck adjustment has the same weight * (1 + luck) shape as kits.stats.apply_luck_to_chance, applied across a multi-way roll.

weighted_choice(
    rng: RandomStream, choices: Sequence[tuple[T, float]]
) -> T

Pick one item from choices, weighted by each entry's own weight.

Originated in kits/loot (drop tables); moved here once kits/procgen needed the same primitive for Wave Function Collapse's per-cell state pick -- a generic RNG utility, not a loot-specific one.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default rng RandomStream

Seeded stream driving the roll.

required choices Sequence[tuple[T, float]]

(item, weight) pairs. Weights need not sum to 1 -- each item's odds are its own weight over the total. A weight of 0 is never picked (in practice; only an exact floating-point boundary hit could select it, which does not happen).

required

docs.title: pyguara.kits.platformer_movement
docs.text:
Platformer input-to-motion policy: coyote time, jump buffer, wall jump.

A kit because this is one genre's vocabulary. The mechanism it stands on is in core: pyguara.physics.character_mover.CharacterMover, which sweeps a collider against solids with no gravity assumption. This kit and kits.topdown_movement are two policies over it.

Nothing here registers itself. A game that wants PlatformerController in its prefabs registers the component.

Example

container.get(ComponentRegistry).register(PlatformerController)

docs.title: pyguara.kits.platformer_movement.controller
docs.text:
Platformer controller component for 2D character movement.

This module provides a complete platformer movement solution with features like ground detection, jump mechanics, coyote time, jump buffering, wall sliding, and wall jumping. It's designed for responsive, game-feel-oriented character control in 2D platformer games.

Movement/jump logic lives in PlatformerSystem; this component only carries data plus a small set of side-effect-free query predicates (can_jump()/can_wall_jump()/is_wall_sliding()).

from pyguara.kits.platformer_movement.controller import PlatformerController, PlatformerInput

docs.text: player.add_component(PlatformerController( move_speed=200.0, jump_force=400.0, coyote_time=0.15, jump_buffer=0.1 ))

docs.title: In your input-to-system code, submit this tick's intent
docs.text: controller = player.get_component(PlatformerController) controller.pending_input = PlatformerInput(move=-1.0, jump=True)

docs.text:
System for managing platformer controller physics and state.

The PlatformerSystem updates PlatformerController components each frame, handling ground detection, movement, jumping, and wall mechanics.

Movement is driven by CharacterMover, not the physics solver: a character has no RigidBody/shape registered with the physics engine at all, only a CharacterBody (velocity, ground state, knockback) and a Collider used purely as a source of dimensions. docs.title: pyguara.kits.procgen
docs.text:
The procgen kit: BSP, WFC, graph, Delaunay, Poisson-disc and placement.

None of the algorithms has room or tile vocabulary:

  • bsp.py partitions plain Rect regions. dungeon.py is the roguelike recipe on top of it.
  • wfc.py collapses caller-defined states under adjacency rules.
  • graph.py and delaunay.py connect scattered points; the second only joins neighbours, so no edge crosses open space.
  • poisson.py picks spots with a minimum spacing, and placement.py decides what goes in each slot under the caller's rules.

A veto on putting one kind in one slot.

split_bsp(
    bounds: Rect,
    rng: RandomStream,
    min_leaf_size: int,
    max_depth: int | None = None,

Recursively split bounds into a binary tree of leaf regions.

Splits vertically (side-by-side children) when a region is wider than tall, horizontally (stacked children) when taller than wide, and picks randomly between the two for a near-square region -- the classic BSP dungeon-generator heuristic, avoiding a lattice of uniformly skinny rooms. required max_depth int | None

Stop splitting past this recursion depth, regardless of size. None (the default) splits until size alone stops it.

None

The tree's root, bounds itself as the top-level region.

docs.title: place_items
docs.text:
place_items(
    slots: Sequence[Slot],
    requests: Sequence[PlacementRequest],
    rules: Sequence[PlacementRule],
    rng: RandomStream,
    attempts: int = 8,
) -> PlacementResult

Assign kinds to slots, honouring every rule.

Greedy, randomised and retried; not a backtracking solver, so its running time is bounded. The whole assignment is attempted several times from a shuffled slot order and the best result kept. Whatever could not be placed is reported.

Requests are ordered by their Requires dependencies first, so a prerequisite is placed before its dependent, then by priority, then by count.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default slots Sequence[Slot]

The candidate spots.

required requests Sequence[PlacementRequest]

What to place, and how many.

required rules Sequence[PlacementRule]

The vetoes. Every rule is consulted for every candidate; one "no" is enough.

required rng RandomStream

Seeded stream. The same seed, slots, requests and rules give the same result.

required attempts int

How many shuffled orders to try before settling for the best found. 1 makes it a single greedy pass.

8

Returns:

Type Description PlacementResult

The assignment, plus whatever could not be placed.

Raises:

Type Description DependencyCycleError

If Requires rules form a cycle, which no ordering can satisfy -- a fact about the rule set rather than about this particular slot list, so it raises rather than being reported as unplaced.

ValueError

If attempts is below 1.

docs.title: poisson_disc_sample
docs.text:
poisson_disc_sample(
    bounds: Rect,
    min_distance: float,
    rng: RandomStream,
    max_attempts: int = 30,
) -> list[Vector2]

Scatter points within bounds, each at least min_distance apart.

Bridson's algorithm: grow outward from a random seed point, proposing candidates in the annulus between min_distance and 2 * min_distance around a random active point, accepting the first candidate that clears every existing point. An acceleration grid keyed by pyguara.common.grid.Cell (sized min_distance / sqrt(2) per side) keeps each spacing check local instead of scanning every prior point.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default bounds Rect

The region to fill.

required min_distance float

The minimum allowed distance between any two returned points. Must be positive.

required rng RandomStream

Seeded stream driving every random draw.

required max_attempts int

Candidate points tried around an active point before it's retired from further growth. Higher values pack tighter but cost more.

30

Returns:

Type Description list[Vector2]

The accepted points, in the order accepted. Roughly, but not

list[Vector2]

exactly, evenly spaced -- genuinely random within the spacing

list[Vector2]

constraint, not a lattice. Empty if bounds has no area.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

min_distance is not positive.

docs.title: generate_wfc
docs.text:
generate_wfc(
    width: int,
    height: int,
    states: Sequence[S],
    rules: Sequence[AdjacencyRule[S]],
    rng: RandomStream,
    weights: Mapping[S, float] | None = None,
    pinned: Mapping[Cell, S] | None = None,
    neighbor_fn: Callable[
        [Cell], Sequence[Cell]
    ] = neighbors4,
    max_attempts: int = 20,
) -> dict[Cell, S]

Generate a width x height grid by Wave Function Collapse.

Repeatedly collapses the lowest-entropy remaining cell to one of its possible states (weighted, via weights), then propagates that choice through rules to narrow every neighbor's possibilities. A rule set that paints a cell into zero possible states (a contradiction) restarts the whole grid and tries again, up to max_attempts -- still deterministic overall, since every attempt draws from the same rng in sequence.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default width int

Grid width, in cells.

required height int

Grid height, in cells.

required states Sequence[S]

Every state a cell may end up in. Must be non-empty.

required rules Sequence[AdjacencyRule[S]]

Adjacency constraints. A (state, direction) pair with no matching rule leaves that neighbor unconstrained in that direction.

required rng RandomStream

Seeded stream driving every collapse choice.

required weights Mapping[S, float] | None

Relative odds per state when a cell has several possibilities left. Defaults to uniform. A state missing from this mapping gets weight 1.0.

None pinned Mapping[Cell, S] | None

Cells forced to a specific state before generation starts, e.g. a fixed entrance tile. Every key must be in bounds and every value must be one of states.

None neighbor_fn Callable[[Cell], Sequence[Cell]]

Adjacency topology -- pyguara.common.grid.neighbors4 (the default) or neighbors8 for diagonal adjacency too.

neighbors4 max_attempts int

Retries allowed after a contradiction before giving up.

20

Returns:

Type Description dict[Cell, S]

Every in-bounds cell's final state.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

states is empty, or pinned names an out-of-bounds cell or a state not in states.

WfcContradictionError

Every attempt hit a contradiction.

docs.text:
Deciding what goes where, under rules the caller writes.

poisson_disc_sample(), generate_dungeon() and build_graph() produce candidate spots. This module decides which spot gets which kind of thing, under frequency, spacing, dependency and exclusion rules. A rule reads caller-defined string kinds and slot tags; nothing here knows what a room is.

Example

slots = [Slot(position=p, tags={"dead_end"}, group=floor) for p in spots] result = place_items( slots, [PlacementRequest("shop", count=2), PlacementRequest("boss", count=1)], [ MaxPerGroup("shop", limit=1), MinSpacing("boss", distance=400.0), RequiresTag("boss", {"dead_end"}), ], rng, )

docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

A veto on putting one kind in one slot.

A rule only ever says no. That is deliberate: a rule that could say "yes, definitely" would have to be weighed against the others, and then the answer would depend on their order. Vetoes commute, so a rule set has no ordering to get wrong, and a game can add one rule without re-reading the rest.
