docs.title: place_items
docs.text:
place_items(
    slots: Sequence[Slot],
    requests: Sequence[PlacementRequest],
    rules: Sequence[PlacementRule],
    rng: RandomStream,
    attempts: int = 8,
) -> PlacementResult

Assign kinds to slots, honouring every rule.

Greedy, randomised and retried; not a backtracking solver, so its running time is bounded. The whole assignment is attempted several times from a shuffled slot order and the best result kept. Whatever could not be placed is reported.

Requests are ordered by their Requires dependencies first, so a prerequisite is placed before its dependent, then by priority, then by count.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default slots Sequence[Slot]

The candidate spots.

required requests Sequence[PlacementRequest]

What to place, and how many.

required rules Sequence[PlacementRule]

The vetoes. Every rule is consulted for every candidate; one "no" is enough.

required rng RandomStream

Seeded stream. The same seed, slots, requests and rules give the same result.

required attempts int

How many shuffled orders to try before settling for the best found. 1 makes it a single greedy pass.

8

Returns:

Type Description PlacementResult

The assignment, plus whatever could not be placed.

Raises:

Type Description DependencyCycleError

If Requires rules form a cycle, which no ordering can satisfy -- a fact about the rule set rather than about this particular slot list, so it raises rather than being reported as unplaced.

ValueError

If attempts is below 1.

docs.title: pyguara.kits.procgen.poisson
docs.text:
Poisson-disc sampling: natural, minimum-spacing point placement.

Bridson's algorithm: every returned point sits at least min_distance from every other. Rules between kinds of placed item are placement.py's job.

docs.title: poisson_disc_sample
docs.text:
poisson_disc_sample(
    bounds: Rect,
    min_distance: float,
    rng: RandomStream,
    max_attempts: int = 30,
) -> list[Vector2]

Scatter points within bounds, each at least min_distance apart.

Bridson's algorithm: grow outward from a random seed point, proposing candidates in the annulus between min_distance and 2 * min_distance around a random active point, accepting the first candidate that clears every existing point. An acceleration grid keyed by pyguara.common.grid.Cell (sized min_distance / sqrt(2) per side) keeps each spacing check local instead of scanning every prior point.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default bounds Rect

The region to fill.

required min_distance float

The minimum allowed distance between any two returned points. Must be positive.

required rng RandomStream

Seeded stream driving every random draw.

required max_attempts int

Candidate points tried around an active point before it's retired from further growth. Higher values pack tighter but cost more.

30

Returns:

Type Description list[Vector2]

The accepted points, in the order accepted. Roughly, but not

list[Vector2]

exactly, evenly spaced -- genuinely random within the spacing

list[Vector2]

constraint, not a lattice. Empty if bounds has no area.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

min_distance is not positive.

docs.title: pyguara.kits.procgen.wfc
docs.text:
Wave Function Collapse: constraint-propagation grid generation.

States are caller-defined hashable values (a tile kind, a biome id) and adjacency is the AdjacencyRules the caller supplies.

The next cell to collapse is chosen through a heap; _attempt carries the invariant that makes the heap sound. The selection order decides which draw from rng lands where, so changing it changes the grid a seed produces. That is a breaking change for every world already generated.

docs.title: WfcContradictionError
docs.text:
Bases: RuntimeError

Every attempt narrowed some cell to zero possible states.

docs.title: AdjacencyRule dataclass
docs.text:
One allowed neighbor pairing.

Attributes:

Name Type Description from_state S

The state occupying a cell.

to_state S

A state allowed in the neighbor reached by direction.

direction Cell

The offset from the from_state cell to that neighbor, e.g. (1, 0) for "to the east". Directions are not implied reciprocal -- a symmetric constraint needs its own rule for each direction.

docs.title: generate_wfc
docs.text:
generate_wfc(
    width: int,
    height: int,
    states: Sequence[S],
    rules: Sequence[AdjacencyRule[S]],
    rng: RandomStream,
    weights: Mapping[S, float] | None = None,
    pinned: Mapping[Cell, S] | None = None,
    neighbor_fn: Callable[
        [Cell], Sequence[Cell]
    ] = neighbors4,
    max_attempts: int = 20,
) -> dict[Cell, S]

Generate a width x height grid by Wave Function Collapse.

Repeatedly collapses the lowest-entropy remaining cell to one of its possible states (weighted, via weights), then propagates that choice through rules to narrow every neighbor's possibilities. A rule set that paints a cell into zero possible states (a contradiction) restarts the whole grid and tries again, up to max_attempts -- still deterministic overall, since every attempt draws from the same rng in sequence.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default width int

Grid width, in cells.

required height int

Grid height, in cells.

required states Sequence[S]

Every state a cell may end up in. Must be non-empty.

required rules Sequence[AdjacencyRule[S]]

Adjacency constraints. A (state, direction) pair with no matching rule leaves that neighbor unconstrained in that direction.

required rng RandomStream

Seeded stream driving every collapse choice.

required weights Mapping[S, float] | None

Relative odds per state when a cell has several possibilities left. Defaults to uniform. A state missing from this mapping gets weight 1.0.

None pinned Mapping[Cell, S] | None

Cells forced to a specific state before generation starts, e.g. a fixed entrance tile. Every key must be in bounds and every value must be one of states.

None neighbor_fn Callable[[Cell], Sequence[Cell]]

Adjacency topology -- pyguara.common.grid.neighbors4 (the default) or neighbors8 for diagonal adjacency too.

neighbors4 max_attempts int

Retries allowed after a contradiction before giving up.

20

Returns:

Type Description dict[Cell, S]

Every in-bounds cell's final state.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

states is empty, or pinned names an out-of-bounds cell or a state not in states.

WfcContradictionError

Every attempt hit a contradiction.

The progression kit: experience, levels, the pick, and the magnet.

Three things: the experience and level substrate, the upgrade offer, and the pickup magnet. The level-up UI, the upgrade content and any item model stay with the game.

  • Nothing here knows what an upgrade does. Upgrade.apply is a callable the game writes.
  • Nothing here knows what a level is worth. grant_experience() counts levels into Experience.pending_levels and dispatches LeveledUp; spending them is the game's.

docs.title: MagnetSystem
docs.text:
Pulls Attracted entities toward nearby Magnets and collects them.

Queries the shared SpatialHash around each magnet rather than walking every pickup on the field. Entities are expected to be tracked in it the usual way (pyguara.spatial.SpatialTracked + SpatialIndexSystem); this system never inserts into it itself.

Collection dispatches PickupCollected and marks the pickup inactive. Destroying the entity is left to the game, which may want to pool it, play something on it, or fade it out first.

docs.title: pyguara.kits.projectiles
docs.text:
The projectiles kit: pooled projectiles checked against the spatial hash.

Projectiles are plain pooled objects, not ECS entities. Each tick, ProjectileSystem checks a shot's whole step against the shared SpatialHash, nearest target first and then by id. A shot reaches a target at its edge: its hit_radius plus the target's Hurtbox.radius. A hit calls kits.action_combat.apply_damage() unless on_hit= replaces it. solids= stops a shot at the first wall in its path, and on_end= is told why each projectile stopped.

docs.title: pyguara.kits.projectiles.net
docs.text:
Shots over the network: each sent once, and flown by every client itself.

Imported on its own; the kit does not import it, so a single-player game loads no networking. The host sends each shot once, as a reliable event, and each client flies it on its own ProjectileSystem. The host alone decides hits, and sends where a shot ended when it stops early. A client's own shots appear when fired and are matched to the host's copy by ProjectileKey. See docs/systems/networking.md.

Example

register_projectiles(schema, kinds, position=..., velocity=...) ProjectileHost(projectiles, replication, app) # host ProjectileClient(projectiles, dispatcher, replication, dt) # client

docs.title: pyguara.kits.spawn
docs.text:
The spawn kit: a schedule- and pacing-gated wave/encounter director.

SpawnDirector never knows what is being spawned: a SpawnEntry's factory is an opaque callable the game builds. Tower-defence waves and continuous horde pressure are the same mechanism with different Wave parameters and a different schedule.

docs.title: SpawnDirector
docs.text:
Releases queued waves' entries as the schedule, pacing and cap allow.

Three independent gates:

  • Schedule: schedule_at() holds a wave until the director's clock reaches a point in the run; queue_wave() queues one immediately, behind whatever is already waiting.
  • Pacing: a wave's interval caps how fast its entries release.
  • Alive cap: nothing releases while alive_count() is at alive_cap.

The clock is the director's own accumulated dt.

docs.text:
elapsed: float

Seconds of update() this director has seen.

This is the "at this point in the run, this much" shape: a horde that thickens, a boss at four minutes. A wave whose time has already passed queues on the next update().

A SpawnEntry.factory is an opaque zero-argument callable that does the spawning. This module only decides when it may happen.

Attributes:

Minimum seconds between releasing one entry and attempting the next. 0 imposes no pacing delay -- the whole wave releases in one tick unless the alive cap stops it.

Seconds to wait, once this wave becomes the active one, before its first entry can release.

docs.title: SpawnDirector
docs.text:
Releases queued waves' entries as the schedule, pacing and cap allow.

Three independent gates:

  • Schedule: schedule_at() holds a wave until the director's clock reaches a point in the run; queue_wave() queues one immediately, behind whatever is already waiting.
  • Pacing: a wave's interval caps how fast its entries release.
  • Alive cap: nothing releases while alive_count() is at alive_cap.

The clock is the director's own accumulated dt.

Attribute/stat containers, damage typing, and resist/mitigation math.

StatBlock wraps a pyguara.common.modifiers.ModifiableValue per stat. Nothing here is registered in the container or wired into the ECS: a game constructs StatBlock components and attaches them.

docs.text:
apply_luck_to_chance(
    base_chance: float, luck: float
) -> float

Scale a chance (dodge, block, crit, ...) by a luck-like modifier.

base_chance * (1 + luck) -- luck=0.0 leaves the chance unchanged; luck=0.25 raises it by a quarter. Clamped to [0.0, 1.0] since a chance outside that range isn't meaningful to a caller rolling against it (random.random() < chance).

docs.title: mitigation_from_defense
docs.text:
mitigation_from_defense(
    defense: float, scaling: float
) -> float

Return the fraction of damage defense mitigates, as a diminishing curve.

defense / (defense + scaling) -- 0.0 at zero defense, approaching but never reaching 1.0 as defense grows, so no amount of stacking ever makes a hit deal zero damage. scaling sets how much defense is needed to reach a given mitigation fraction; a game commonly derives it from the defender's level or the attacker's own offensive stat, but this function has no opinion on that -- it just takes the number.

Name Type Description Default defense float

Defense value to convert, typically effective_defense()'s result.

required scaling float

The defense value at which mitigation reaches 50%. Must be positive.

required

Mitigation fraction, 0.0-1.0. Multiply incoming damage by

float

1 - mitigation_from_defense(...) to get the damage that lands.

docs.title: pyguara.kits.topdown_movement
docs.text:
Top-down movement policy: actor-vs-actor soft separation.

Pushes overlapping actors gently apart using the spatial hash, which is what a top-down game wants. Like kits.platformer_movement, it is a policy over pyguara.physics.character_mover.CharacterMover, which is in core.

Nothing here registers itself.

docs.title: TopDownBody dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: StrictComponent

A character moved by CharacterMover, with actor-vs-actor separation.

The top-down sibling of CharacterBody/PlatformerController: the same swept collide-and-slide against solids via CharacterMover, but no gravity, ground state, or jump -- an 8-dir top-down mover doesn't have any of those -- plus separation_radius, which PlatformerController has no equivalent of, since platformer characters don't gently push each other apart.

Attributes:

Name Type Description velocity Vector2

Current velocity in pixels/second, in world space. Nothing here integrates it from input; a control or AI system sets it directly each tick, the same way a RigidBody's velocity is set directly rather than accumulated internally.

separation_radius float

Half of this actor's "personal space". Two actors are pushed apart by TopDownSystem once the distance between them is less than the sum of their two radii. Zero (the default) opts this actor out of separation entirely, in both directions -- it neither pushes others nor is pushed by them.

moved_elsewhere bool

Something else steps this body, such as a player controller or network prediction calling step_body itself. TopDownSystem then leaves its movement alone, so it isn't moved twice in a tick. Separation still applies.

docs.title: DirectionalAnimationSystem
docs.text:
Keeps each DirectionalAnimator pointing where its body is going.

Reads velocity from TopDownBody when the entity has one, because that is the kit's own mover; otherwise from the distance the Transform moved since the last tick, so a character driven by a tween, a pathfinder or a script still faces the right way.

An entity with a DirectionalAnimator and no Animator is skipped rather than treated as an error: a game may well attach the facing to something it draws itself.

docs.text:
Letting a networked client predict a top-down character.

pyguara.net knows nothing about movement, so this is what connects the two. It only matches pyguara.net.prediction.PredictedBody's shape, and imports nothing from the network package.

velocity_of runs on both machines, on a command that came over the network on one of them. Velocity must be a pure function of the command, or a replay has nothing to re-run, and it must limit what it returns, because the command is untrusted on the host.

docs.title: pyguara.kits.topdown_movement.system
docs.text:
System driving TopDownBody: solid collision plus actor separation.

Solid collide-and-slide reuses CharacterMover exactly as PlatformerSystem does -- it is already generic, with no gravity assumption, so an arbitrary (including 8-directional) velocity slides along walls the same way platformer motion does. Actor-vs-actor separation is the genuinely new mechanism CharacterMover doesn't provide: two actors closer than the sum of their separation_radius are pushed directly apart, positionally, rather than blocked like a solid.

A growing/shrinking chain of grid cells following a head.

Genre-agnostic mechanism, not just a snake's body: a Tron-style light-cycle trail, a rope/tail follow, a visual combo chain all need the same "advance the head, grow on demand, detect self-overlap" shape. No snake vocabulary lives here -- games/true_coral is this kit's first consumer, built entirely on top via its own components/systems.

docs.title: EngineLogger

A logging.Logger wrapper adding categories, context and event output.

Level methods accept a category and arbitrary keyword arguments; the keywords become structured fields on the record, reachable by handlers and carried into OnLogEvent.

docs.title: pyguara.net
docs.text:
Networked multiplayer: a listen server and the players who join it.

Opt-in, so a single-player game imports none of this. Importing it is always safe, even with no native extension. A session is what needs one, and fails with a clear message when it starts.

Everything arriving from the network is untrusted. The Rust core authenticates packets and survives hostile ones, but it does not make a decoded value sensible, so code above this package bounds-checks lengths, ids and enums itself. See docs/systems/networking.md.

Read it from inside advance, to act as the host does on that tick, such as firing a shot numbered by it. tick can't tell you: one step may advance several ticks to catch up, and a correction replays past ones from inside handle_message. None outside an advance.

docs.title: pyguara.net.prediction
docs.text:
Your own character responding at once, while the host stays in charge.

The client runs its own character immediately and sends what it did as commands, each naming the host tick it applies to. The host applies one command per tick and sends back the exact state. A state "at tick N" includes every command before N. If the client's prediction for that tick differs, it takes the host's state and replays the newer commands. The host accepts commands, never positions.

Lateness, clock lead and the smoothing of corrections are described in docs/systems/networking.md.

docs.title: pyguara.net.replication
docs.text:
Keeping every client's world matching the host's.

The host owns the simulation. Each snapshot it reads the replicated fields of every tracked entity and sends them, and clients draw what they receive, about 100 ms behind, interpolating toward the newest. Snapshots are complete states, so a client's world converges after any loss. Spawns, despawns and game events registered on the schema travel reliably and are applied on the same delayed timeline.

Replication's reliable messages share Channel.EVENTS with the game's; their first byte is at or above FIRST_RESERVED_KIND.

docs.title: pyguara.net.schema
docs.text:
What crosses the wire for each component, and how it is packed.

A game names the components it replicates and how to quantise each field. Nothing else is sent, and the same schema on both sides decides how bytes are read:

schema = ReplicationSchema()
schema.register(Transform, position=QuantisedVector(step=0.25), rotation=Angle())
schema.register(Health, current=UInt16(), max_health=UInt16())

Every value is an integer on the wire, so a non-finite float cannot arrive. A value that does not fit saturates and is counted rather than wrapping, because wrapping would teleport an entity across the map, and that would look like a network bug.

docs.title: pyguara.net.session
docs.text:
Invites, version checks, and who is in the game.

Two machines that disagree about the rules should never start playing, so a client carries its versions in the connection's user data and the host refuses a mismatch aloud. Nothing in the game layer hears from a peer until the host has admitted it.

A wrong protocol id or a wrong key is silent at the network layer, by design: an unauthenticated reply is what a forged packet would want. So those show up here as a timeout, and the message says what to check.

docs.title: pyguara.net.simulated
docs.text:
A seeded, in-process network that drives the real Rust core.

This sits below the reliability layer, so a test exercises the code that ships with no sockets, no threads and no sleeps, and a failure replays from its seed. It proves the logic. It cannot prove how a real connection behaves, or whether playing over one feels good.

network = SimulatedNetwork(seed=1, conditions=LinkConditions(loss=0.2))
host = network.add_host(key)
client = network.add_client(key, host_address=network.address_of(host))
network.advance(1 / 60)

docs.title: pyguara.net.simulated_steam
docs.text:
A stand-in for Steam, so a game can test its Steam path with no Steam.

SimulatedSteamCloud plays Steam's servers and SimulatedSteam one player's NativeSteam. Everything above it (the Steam core, the transport, the lobby, the sessions) is the real code. It keeps session requests, friends-only capped lobbies and member events. Delivery is instant, lossless and in order.

Example

cloud = SimulatedSteamCloud() host = SteamNetwork(cloud.add_player(1001), clock=clock) guest = SteamNetwork(cloud.add_player(1002), clock=clock)

docs.title: pyguara.net.steam
docs.text:
Online play through Steam: the transport, and the hub that drives it.

SteamTransport is a Transport, so HostSession and ClientSession run over it unchanged. Messages go through Valve's relays. SteamNetwork owns Steam, the SteamLobby and the transport; call update() once a frame before the session's poll(), and flush() after the frame's fixed updates. A player is admitted by being in the host's lobby. The game ships steam_api beside its executable. See docs/systems/networking.md.

Example

network = SteamNetwork.open() network.lobby.host(max_players=4) for event in network.update(): if isinstance(event, LobbyOpened): session = HostSession(network.host_transport(3), versions) elif isinstance(event, LobbyJoined): session = ClientSession(network.join_transport(versions.encode()))

docs.title: pyguara.net.steam_lobby
docs.text:
Steam lobbies: who may join a hosted game, and where a guest connects.

A host opens a friends-only lobby. Each member who enters becomes MemberAdmitted and each who leaves MemberRemoved. A guest enters the lobby and then connects to its owner, which LobbyJoined names.

SteamLobby is sans-IO: the caller feeds it every tuple NativeSteam.run_callbacks() returns and acts on the events it gives back. Everything from a lobby or a friend's rich presence is untrusted: parse_lobby_id is strict, and a join request is only reported.

docs.title: pyguara.net.transport
docs.text:
Moving whole messages between peers: the protocol, and the UDP backend.

A Transport is what the session layer needs from a network and no more, so a Steam transport can sit behind it later. The Rust core does the work: this module only adapts it. See rust/src/net/core.rs.

Poll a transport once a frame. It never raises because of what a peer sent: hostile bytes are dropped below this layer, and a core that fails says so with TransportFailed.

docs.title: pyguara.persistence
docs.text:
Data persistence system.

Provides save/load functionality with: - Multiple serialization formats (JSON, MessagePack, binary) - Integrity verification via checksums, with fallback to a backup copy - Schema migration support for versioned save files - Pluggable storage backends, including the per-user data directory

docs.title: CONTAINER_FORMAT_VERSION module-attribute
docs.text:
CONTAINER_FORMAT_VERSION = 1

Version of the blob framing: one JSON header line, newline, payload.

Distinct from a save's save_version (the game's schema) and from version (the engine build). The framing changed once already with no field to detect it by, which is the hole this closes while it is still v1 -- a reader that cannot recognise the container must refuse it rather than misread the payload inside.

docs.title: PersistenceManager
docs.text:
Coordinator for the data persistence subsystem.

Orchestrates serialization, integrity checking and storage, acting as the facade the rest of the engine uses to save and load data.

A save is written as a single blob: a one-line JSON metadata header, a newline, then the serialized (and optionally compressed) payload. The storage backend only has to make that one blob durable, so there is no window in which metadata and payload can disagree.

Name Type Description storage

docs.title: FileStorageBackend
docs.text:
Storage backend that saves each key as one file on the local disk.

Each key maps to a single {key}.save file under base_path, written to a temporary file and renamed, so a crash mid-write never corrupts the previous value. Each write keeps the previous value as {key}.save.bak, which PersistenceManager falls back to when the primary will not decode.

Keys must be filesystem-safe as given: alphanumerics, _ and -. Any other key raises ValueError.

docs.title: SaveMetadata dataclass
docs.text:
Metadata recorded alongside a stored object.

Serialised into the header of every save blob and re-read on load; the load path uses format/compressed to reverse the encoding and checksum to verify integrity.

Attributes:

Name Type Description version str

The engine version string when the data was saved.

timestamp datetime

When the data was saved (timezone-aware, UTC).

data_type str

The class name of the stored object.

checksum str | None

SHA-256 hash of the stored payload bytes, for integrity verification. Covers the payload exactly as written to disk (after compression, if any). Saves written before this was SHA-256 carry a 32-character MD5 digest instead, and are still read; the length tells the two apart. Note that a checksum detects corruption, not tampering -- it travels in the same header as the payload it describes, so a rewritten save can carry a matching digest.

save_version int

Integer schema version, for migration tracking.

format str

The SerializationFormat value the payload is encoded in.

compressed bool

Whether the payload bytes are gzip-compressed.

format_version int

Version of the container -- the header/payload framing itself, as opposed to save_version (the game's schema) or version (the engine build). A reader that does not recognise it cannot safely guess at the payload, so it refuses instead. Absent in saves written before the field existed, which are read as 1.

CONTAINER_FORMAT_VERSION = 1

Version of the blob framing: one JSON header line, newline, payload.

Distinct from a save's save_version (the game's schema) and from version (the engine build). The framing changed once already with no field to detect it by, which is the hole this closes while it is still v1 -- a reader that cannot recognise the container must refuse it rather than misread the payload inside.

docs.title: UnsupportedSaveFormatError
docs.text:
Bases: Exception

A save's container format is newer than this build understands.

Kept distinct from the corruption path on purpose. A save like this is not damaged -- it is valid and was written by a later build, which is what a player sees after downgrading. Treating it as corrupt would quarantine a perfectly good save and promote an older backup over it, so recovery is deliberately not attempted for this one.

docs.title: pyguara.persistence.quick_save
docs.text:
Saving during play, without stalling a frame.

PersistenceManager.save_data serializes and fsyncs on the calling thread. QuickSaver does that work on a worker thread and writes only the newest value for a key, so a burst of events costs one write. The storage underneath writes atomically, so a crash loses at most the last min_interval and never corrupts a save.

Example

saver = QuickSaver(persistence, min_interval=1.0) saver.request("character", character.to_save_data()) # each event saver.flush() # end of a run saver.close() # at shutdown

docs.title: QuickSaver
docs.text:

Hand over a value you will not mutate. It is serialized later, on another thread, so a live object changed in the meantime would be saved half-updated.

docs.title: Serializer
docs.text:
Serialises game data to JSON or MessagePack, and back.

There is deliberately no pickle format. A save file names its own encoding in its header, so supporting pickle meant a file could ask to be unpickled -- and pickle.loads on bytes the engine did not write executes whatever those bytes say. The checksum was no obstacle, travelling in the same attacker-written header. JSON and MessagePack both decode to inert data.

docs.title: FileStorageBackend
docs.text:
Storage backend that saves each key as one file on the local disk.

Each key maps to a single {key}.save file under base_path, written to a temporary file and renamed, so a crash mid-write never corrupts the previous value. Each write keeps the previous value as {key}.save.bak, which PersistenceManager falls back to when the primary will not decode.

Keys must be filesystem-safe as given: alphanumerics, _ and -. Any other key raises ValueError.

docs.title: SaveMetadata dataclass
docs.text:
Metadata recorded alongside a stored object.

Serialised into the header of every save blob and re-read on load; the load path uses format/compressed to reverse the encoding and checksum to verify integrity.

Attributes:

Name Type Description version str

The engine version string when the data was saved.

timestamp datetime

When the data was saved (timezone-aware, UTC).

data_type str

The class name of the stored object.

checksum str | None

SHA-256 hash of the stored payload bytes, for integrity verification. Covers the payload exactly as written to disk (after compression, if any). Saves written before this was SHA-256 carry a 32-character MD5 digest instead, and are still read; the length tells the two apart. Note that a checksum detects corruption, not tampering -- it travels in the same header as the payload it describes, so a rewritten save can carry a matching digest.

save_version int

Integer schema version, for migration tracking.

format str

The SerializationFormat value the payload is encoded in.

compressed bool

Whether the payload bytes are gzip-compressed.

format_version int

Version of the container -- the header/payload framing itself, as opposed to save_version (the game's schema) or version (the engine build). A reader that does not recognise it cannot safely guess at the payload, so it refuses instead. Absent in saves written before the field existed, which are read as 1.

docs.title: pyguara.persistence.migrations
docs.text:
Migration registry module.

This module collects all migrations for the persistence system. Add your migrations here or import them from submodules.

Usage

docs.title: Define migrations using the decorator
docs.text:
from pyguara.persistence.migration import register_migration

@register_migration(from_version=1, to_version=2, description="Example migration") def migrate_v1_to_v2(data: dict) -> dict: # Transform data from v1 to v2 format return data

docs.title: Or define migrations manually and add to the registry
docs.text:
from pyguara.persistence.migration import Migration, get_global_registry

def my_migration(data: dict) -> dict: return data

get_global_registry().add(Migration( from_version=2, to_version=3, migrate_fn=my_migration, description="Another migration" ))

docs.text:
Bases: BaseComponent

Physics joint component connecting two RigidBodies.

A Joint connects this entity's RigidBody to another entity's RigidBody, constraining their relative motion according to the joint type.

JointSystem creates the backend constraint once both entities have a RigidBody whose body exists in the engine, retrying on later ticks until then. It destroys the constraint when either entity is removed, or when this Joint component is removed from its entity. Removing an entity's RigidBody while keeping the Joint is not tracked -- drop the Joint too.

Push ECS state into the engine, ahead of anything that queries it.

Drains pending teardowns, creates bodies for entities new to the engine, and mirrors a kinematic body's position and rotation from its Transform. Call it before a system that queries the engine in the same tick (SolidSystem, a character's probes), so the query sees this tick's kinematic positions. update() also calls it.

docs.title: pyguara.physics.bounds
docs.text:
The world-space box a Collider actually occupies.

One function, because four places were each deriving it and three of them derived it differently. Collider.offset is documented as a "local offset from the RigidBody center", and physics/debug_draw.py applied it while the physics engine's BOX shape and every mover probe did not -- so the debug overlay drew a collider in one place and the simulation used another.

Callers pass their own default half-extents: a platformer character, a top-down one and a moving solid have deliberately different fallbacks when no Collider is attached, and this is not the place to pick between them.

docs.title: pyguara.physics.character_mover
docs.text:
Move a character by sweeping it and stopping flush against what it hits.

The mover steps the character itself and stops it the moment the next step would overlap a solid, so it never penetrates geometry. This is the model of Celeste's Actor and Solid.

Position is kept to whole pixels. A float remainder accumulates the motion that has not yet added up to a pixel, so nothing is lost to rounding. Every whole pixel stepped is tested, so a fast character cannot tunnel. It does not rotate or handle slopes. See docs/physics/character-movement.md.

docs.title: MoveResult dataclass
docs.text:
What a move ran into.

Attributes:

Name Type Description position Vector2

Where the character ended up. Always whole pixels.

remainder Vector2

Sub-pixel motion not yet spent, to be passed back into the next call so it accumulates rather than being discarded.

hit_x bool

True if horizontal motion was stopped by something.

hit_y bool

True if vertical motion was stopped by something.

blocking_x int | str | None

Entity that stopped horizontal motion, or None.

blocking_y int | str | None

Entity that stopped vertical motion, or None.

grounded bool

True if this call's downward motion was stopped -- the character landed or is resting against something below it. False on a tick where nothing moved it downward at all (e.g. already resting, with velocity clamped to zero), even though it may still be on the ground; continuous "is grounded" state is probe()'s job, not this field's.

docs.title: CharacterMover
docs.text:
Sweeps a character's box through the world one whole pixel at a time.

Axes are resolved separately, which is what produces sliding: a character walking into a wall keeps its vertical motion, and one landing while running keeps its horizontal motion.

docs.title: probe
docs.text:
probe(
    position: Vector2,
    half_extents: Vector2,
    direction: Vector2,
    entity_id: int | str | None = None,
) -> int | str | None

Report what, if anything, is one pixel away in direction.

A contact check that does not move or depend on velocity -- Celeste's OnGround() is exactly CollideCheck(Position + Vector2.UnitY), an overlap test one pixel below, not a raycast. Ground/wall detection built on a raycast has to work around the query's own geometry (a swept circle can reach back into the caster); a probe built from the same overlap primitive as move() can't have that problem, because it is the same test a step would make.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default position Vector2

The character's current centre.

required half_extents Vector2

Half width and half height of its box.

required direction Vector2

Which side to probe; only each axis's sign matters, so Vector2(0, 1) probes one pixel below and Vector2(-1, 0) probes one pixel to the left.

required entity_id int | str | None

The character, excluded from the test.

None

Returns:

Type Description int | str | None

The entity id found there, or None if that pixel is clear.

docs.title: pyguara.physics.collision_system
docs.text:
Collision callback routing system.

This module provides the CollisionSystem, which bridges the physics engine's collision reports to PyGuara's event system. It translates low-level physics callbacks into high-level game events that can be subscribed to by game systems.

The CollisionSystem is registered as a singleton in the DI container and automatically wired to the physics engine during application bootstrap.

Architecture

Physics engine → CollisionSystem → EventDispatcher → Game Systems

Example

docs.title: Collision system is automatically registered during bootstrap
Subscribe to collision events in your scene or system:
docs.text:
def on_enter(self): self.event_dispatcher.subscribe(OnCollisionBegin, self._on_collision)

def _on_collision(self, event: OnCollisionBegin) -> None: print(f"Collision: {event.entity_a} <-> {event.entity_b}") print(f"Impact: {event.impulse}")

docs.title: CollisionSystem

Bridges the physics engine's collision reports to the event system.

The CollisionSystem maintains state about active collisions and triggers, ensuring that events are dispatched correctly and consistently. It's designed to be called by the physics engine's collision handlers.

docs.title: CharacterBody dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: BaseComponent

A character moved by CharacterMover, not the physics solver.

Replaces RigidBody for a platformer character: there is no shape registered with the physics engine at all, so the character cannot detect its own collider (the self-detection bug class this audit found for ground rays becomes structurally impossible rather than guarded against) and solver friction is never asked to carry or push it -- SolidSystem/SolidMover do that explicitly instead.

Attributes:

Name Type Description velocity Vector2

Current velocity in pixels/second. PlatformerSystem integrates gravity into this itself, since nothing else does for an entity with no physics body.

grounded bool

Whether the character is currently resting on something. Set every tick from CharacterMover.probe(), not from MoveResult.grounded -- a resting character often has zero vertical velocity, and a move of zero distance never attempts a step to report blocked.

riding int | str | None

Entity id of the MovingSolid currently carrying this character, or None. Lets SolidSystem recognise the same platform across ticks rather than re-detecting a rider fresh every frame.

squished bool

Set when a solid pushed this character somewhere with no free space at all. The game decides what that means; nothing here clears it automatically.

external_velocity Vector2

A knockback velocity overriding normal input control while external_velocity_timer is running.

external_velocity_timer float

Seconds remaining on the current knockback. Ticks down to zero in PlatformerSystem.update().

docs.title: MovingSolid dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: BaseComponent

Marks an entity whose motion should carry and push actors.

A MovingSolid is still an ordinary RigidBody/Collider as far as the physics engine is concerned (so genuinely dynamic bodies -- debris, ragdolls -- keep colliding with it normally); SolidSystem additionally moves any CharacterBody resting on or in the way of it by the same delta each tick it moves, using SolidMover.

docs.title: Pushable dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: BaseComponent

Marks a MovingSolid a character can shove, not just ride or block on.

When CharacterMover finds its sweep blocked by a Pushable entity, it asks SolidMover to move that entity by the remaining delta first: if the pushable can move, the character continues behind it; if the pushable is itself blocked, the character stops too.

docs.title: pyguara.physics.debug_draw
docs.text:
Draw physics colliders on top of the world, to see what the solver sees.

A sprite and the collider under it are separate pieces of data that nothing forces to agree. When they disagree, the symptom is visual -- a character that looks like it is standing inside the floor, or floating above it -- and no amount of reading component values tells you which of the two is wrong. This draws the colliders so the two can be compared directly.

It draws outlines only, through IRenderer, so it works on any backend and needs no debug support from one.

docs.title: pyguara.physics.events
docs.text:
Physics-related event definitions.

This module defines events emitted by the physics system, including collision events (for solid bodies) and trigger events (for sensor volumes).

Events are dispatched through the EventDispatcher and can be subscribed to by game systems and components.

Usage

from pyguara.physics.events import OnCollisionBegin

def on_collision(event: OnCollisionBegin) -> None: print(f"Collision between {event.entity_a} and {event.entity_b}") print(f"Impact force: {event.impulse}")

event_dispatcher.subscribe(OnCollisionBegin, on_collision)

docs.title: CollisionEvent dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: Event

Base class for collision events between solid physics bodies.

Collision events are fired when two non-sensor colliders interact. They provide detailed information about the collision including contact points, normals, and impulse forces.

Attributes:

Name Type Description entity_a str

ID of the first entity involved in the collision.

entity_b str

ID of the second entity involved in the collision.

point Vector2

World coordinates of the collision contact point.

normal Vector2

Surface normal at the collision point (pointing from A to B).

impulse float

Magnitude of the collision impulse (impact force).

timestamp float

Time when the event occurred (seconds since epoch).

source Any | None

Entity that triggered the event (collision system).

docs.title: OnCollisionBegin dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: CollisionEvent

Fired when two bodies START colliding.

This event is triggered on the first frame of contact between two physics bodies. Use this to respond to initial impacts (e.g., play sound effects, apply damage, spawn particles).

Example

def on_collision_start(event: OnCollisionBegin) -> None: if event.impulse > 100: # Play crash sound for hard impacts audio.play_sound("crash.wav")

docs.title: OnCollisionEnd dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: CollisionEvent

Fired when two bodies STOP colliding.

This event is triggered when two bodies separate after being in contact. Useful for cleanup logic or state changes when objects are no longer touching.

Note

impulse is typically 0.0 for collision end events since no force is applied during separation.

Example

def on_collision_end(event: OnCollisionEnd) -> None: # Stop sound effect when objects separate audio.stop_sound("friction_loop.wav")

docs.title: OnCollisionPersist dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: CollisionEvent

Fired each frame while two bodies remain in contact.

This event is triggered every physics step (typically 60 FPS) while two bodies are touching. Use this for continuous effects like friction sounds or cumulative damage over time.

Warning

This event fires frequently (60+ times per second) for sustained contact. Avoid expensive operations in handlers.

Example

def on_collision_persist(event: OnCollisionPersist) -> None: # Apply continuous friction damage if event.impulse > 50: apply_damage(event.entity_a, damage=0.1)

Base class for sensor/trigger volume events.

Trigger events are fired when entities enter, exit, or remain inside trigger volumes (sensor colliders). Unlike collision events, trigger events don't involve physical forces or contact points.

docs.title: OnTriggerEnter dataclass

Bases: TriggerEvent

Entity ENTERS a trigger volume.

Fired when an entity first enters a sensor collider (trigger volume). Use this for gameplay mechanics like checkpoints, collectibles, zones, and proximity detection.

Example

def on_checkpoint_enter(event: OnTriggerEnter) -> None: if event.other_entity == player_id: save_checkpoint(event.trigger_entity) show_message("Checkpoint activated!")

docs.title: pyguara.physics.joint_system
docs.text:
System that turns Joint components into live physics constraints.

Joint is a plain data component; on its own it does nothing. JointSystem is what reads it, asks the physics engine to create the matching constraint once both connected bodies exist, and tears the constraint down again when either entity -- or the Joint component itself -- goes away.

Like PhysicsSystem, this is an opt-in system: a game that uses joints creates one and ticks it each fixed step, after PhysicsSystem.update() so that both bodies have been registered with the backend.

Usage

joint_system = JointSystem(engine, entity_manager, event_dispatcher)

def fixed_update(self, fixed_dt: float) -> None: self.physics_system.update(fixed_dt) self.joint_system.update(fixed_dt)

docs.title: JointSystem
docs.text:
Creates and destroys physics constraints for Joint components.

A Joint lives on one entity and names a second by id. The constraint is created once both entities have a RigidBody whose backend body exists; until then the joint is pending and retried on the next update(). The backend handle is stored on Joint._joint_handle and in a table keyed by owner id.

Attributes:

Name Type Description _engine

The physics engine backend.

_entity_manager

EntityManager for resolving the target entity.

_dispatcher

EventDispatcher, subscribed for EntityDestroyed.

_handles dict[str, Any]

Owner entity id -> backend joint handle, for live joints.

docs.text:

Create pending constraints and drop ones whose component is gone.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default delta_time float

Fixed timestep in seconds (unused; the constraint, once created, is stepped by the engine).

required

Destroy every constraint this system created.

Mirrors PhysicsSystem.cleanup(); call it when tearing a scene down so no constraint outlives its space.

docs.title: pyguara.physics.joints
docs.text:
Physics joint components and utilities.

This module provides joint/constraint components that connect RigidBodies and constrain their relative motion. Joints are essential for creating complex physical systems like ragdolls, vehicles, rope chains, and mechanical contraptions.

A Joint is pure data. JointSystem (pyguara.physics.joint_system) is what turns it into a live constraint in the backend, once both connected entities have a RigidBody; a game that uses joints must create and tick a JointSystem alongside its PhysicsSystem.

Usage

from pyguara.physics.joints import Joint, create_pin_joint, create_spring_joint

docs.title: Create a pin joint (revolute)
docs.text: entity_a.add_component(create_pin_joint( target_entity_id=entity_b.id, anchor_a=Vector2(0, 10), anchor_b=Vector2(0, -10) ))

docs.title: Create a spring joint
docs.text: entity_a.add_component(create_spring_joint( target_entity_id=entity_b.id, rest_length=100.0, stiffness=500.0, damping=20.0 ))

docs.title: Joint dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: BaseComponent

Physics joint component connecting two RigidBodies.

A Joint connects this entity's RigidBody to another entity's RigidBody, constraining their relative motion according to the joint type.

JointSystem creates the backend constraint once both entities have a RigidBody whose body exists in the engine, retrying on later ticks until then. It destroys the constraint when either entity is removed, or when this Joint component is removed from its entity. Removing an entity's RigidBody while keeping the Joint is not tracked -- drop the Joint too.

Attributes:

Name Type Description joint_type JointType

Type of constraint (PIN, DISTANCE, SPRING, SLIDER, GEAR, MOTOR).

target_entity_id str

ID of the entity to connect to.

anchor_a Vector2

Local anchor point on this entity's body.

anchor_b Vector2

Local anchor point on target entity's body.

min_distance float

Minimum distance (for DISTANCE/SLIDER joints).

max_distance float

Maximum distance (for DISTANCE/SLIDER joints).

stiffness float

Spring stiffness coefficient (for SPRING joints).

damping float

Spring damping coefficient (for SPRING joints).

max_force float

Maximum force the joint can apply (0 = infinite).

collide_connected bool

Whether connected bodies can collide with each other.

_joint_handle Any | None

Internal physics engine handle (managed by PhysicsSystem).

pyguara.physics.materials
docs.text:
Physics material presets for common surfaces.

This module provides pre-configured PhysicsMaterial instances for common surfaces and gameplay scenarios. These presets offer realistic physical properties and improve developer ergonomics by eliminating the need to manually tune friction, restitution, and density values.

Usage

from pyguara.physics.materials import Materials

player.add_component(Collider( shape_type=ShapeType.BOX, dimensions=[32, 64], material=Materials.PLAYER ))

ground.add_component(Collider( shape_type=ShapeType.BOX, dimensions=[800, 32], material=Materials.GROUND ))

docs.title: MaterialConstants dataclass
docs.text:
Common physics material presets.

All materials are frozen dataclass instances to prevent accidental modification. Each preset is configured with realistic friction, restitution (bounciness), and density values.

Attributes:

Name Type Description DEFAULT

Generic material with moderate friction and no bounce.

WOOD

Wooden surfaces with moderate friction and slight bounce.

METAL

Metallic surfaces with lower friction and minimal bounce.

STONE

Stone/concrete surfaces with high friction and minimal bounce.

RUBBER

Rubber surfaces with very high friction and bounce.

ICE

Icy surfaces with minimal friction and no bounce (slippery).

GLASS

Glass surfaces with minimal friction and high bounce (brittle).

SUPER_BALL

Highly bouncy material for game mechanics.

PLAYER

Typical player character material with controlled movement.

GROUND

Standard ground/platform material with no bounce.

docs.title: PhysicsSystem
docs.text:
The bridge between the ECS world and the physics engine.

It synchronizes the state of ECS 'Transform' components with the underlying physics simulation bodies.

Architecture: Self-Sufficient System (Pull Pattern) - Queries entities internally via EntityManager - Compatible with SystemManager orchestration

docs.title: sync_kinematic_transforms
docs.text:
sync_kinematic_transforms() -> None

Push ECS state into the engine, ahead of anything that queries it.

Drains pending teardowns, creates bodies for entities new to the engine, and mirrors a kinematic body's position and rotation from its Transform. Call it before a system that queries the engine in the same tick (SolidSystem, a character's probes), so the query sees this tick's kinematic positions. update() also calls it.

The question a character mover asks before committing a step: "if I were here, would I be inside something, and if so, what?" docs.text:
Move a solid, carrying and pushing whatever it touches.

CharacterMover moves a character under its own control. This moves one that is not driving: riding a platform, or shoved by one.

Riders are found by their position before the solid moves and carried by the same delta. Anything else the solid's new footprint overlaps is pushed clear along the axis the solid is moving. An actor is placed, not swept, and then checked against everything but that solid; one that is not clear has been squished, which is reported for the game to decide. This mirrors Celeste's Solid.MoveHExact/MoveVExact.

docs.title: pyguara.physics.trigger_volume
docs.text:
Trigger volume components for zone-based gameplay mechanics.

Trigger volumes are sensor colliders that track which entities are inside them. They're essential for implementing checkpoints, collectibles, damage zones, teleporters, and any gameplay mechanic that activates when entities enter an area.

A TriggerVolume only emits events when three systems are running: PhysicsSystem (steps the simulation), CollisionSystem (routes sensor contacts to trigger events) and TriggerSystem (updates the component state, and gives the entity the sensor Collider plus a static RigidBody it needs to enter the simulation at all).

Usage

from pyguara.physics.trigger_volume import TriggerVolume

docs.title: Create a checkpoint trigger. No Collider or RigidBody needed --
TriggerSystem adds both. Add your own KINEMATIC RigidBody instead if
the trigger must move with a platform.
docs.text: checkpoint = entity_manager.create_entity() checkpoint.add_component(Transform(position=Vector2(400, 300))) checkpoint.add_component(TriggerVolume( shape_type=ShapeType.BOX, dimensions=[100, 100], tags={"player"} # Only trigger for player entities ))

docs.title: Check what's inside
docs.text: if checkpoint.trigger_volume.contains_entity(player.id): save_checkpoint()

docs.title: pyguara.random.service
docs.text:
Deterministic, hierarchical random-number service.

RandomService owns a root seed and hands out named child RandomStreams derived from it, so two runs with the same root seed produce the same sequence for the same stream name, and one stream's draws do not disturb another's.

Child seeds come from hashlib.sha256(f"{root_seed}:{name}"), not hash(name), which is salted per process. get_state() and restore_state() cover the root seed and every stream requested so far; any other stream is re-derived from the root seed when asked for.

docs.title: ResourceManager
docs.text:
Orchestrate the loading, caching, and lifecycle of game resources.

  • load() is a cache-get: a miss reads from disk and caches. The resource sits in the cache unpinned (reference count 0).
  • acquire() and release() pin and unpin, and must be balanced. A release() that drops the count to 0 evicts at once.
  • unload_unused() evicts every resource whose count is 0, and unload(path, force=True) evicts regardless of the count.
  • reload() re-reads a cached resource, keeping its count.
Example

A .meta sidecar (hero.png.meta for hero.png) supplies import settings to a loader that supports metadata:

{
    "type": "texture",
    "filter": "nearest",
    "premultiply_alpha": true
}

index_directory(
    root_path: str, recursive: bool = True
) -> None

Scan a directory and maps filenames to their full paths without loading them.

This allows requesting assets by name (e.g., 'hero') instead of full path (e.g., 'assets/chars/hero.png'), mimicking Godot's resource system.

Two files that share a stem (chars/hero.png and fx/hero.png) would both claim the bare name hero. pump(budget_ms: float = DEFAULT_PUMP_BUDGET_MS) -> int

Advance queued loads, spending at most budget_ms.

Call once per frame on the thread that owns the device context -- uploads happen here. Work is started only while the budget holds, but a single item is never interrupted part-way, so one slow upload can overrun it; see Budget.

Requests whose decode is still running on a worker are skipped without consuming budget, so a pump never blocks on a thread.

docs.title: pyguara.resources.async_load
docs.text:
Asynchronous resource loading: a thread pool where it pays, a budget elsewhere.

ResourceManager.pump(budget_ms) completes pending work on the main thread until the budget is spent. It serves every loader and is where device uploads happen. A loader that declares threaded_decode also has its decode phase run on a worker, which pays only for a decode that releases the GIL; see docs/guides/performance.md.

A worker only turns a path into bytes. Call load(), load_async() and pump() from one thread; there is no cache lock.

docs.text:
Bases: IResourceLoader, Protocol

A loader that separates file decode from device upload.

Decoding a file is CPU work on bytes; creating a GPU texture belongs to the main thread. So ResourceManager may run decode() on a worker and always runs upload() on the thread that owns the device.

docs.title: pyguara.resources.manager
docs.text:
Central Asset Management System.

This module provides the ResourceManager, which acts as the single source of truth for all game assets. It handles: 1. Caching (Flyweight pattern) to prevent duplicate loading. 2. Loader delegation based on file extensions (Strategy pattern). 3. Type safety validation using Generics. 4. Asset metadata via .meta sidecar files for import settings.

docs.title: ResourceManager
docs.text:
Orchestrate the loading, caching, and lifecycle of game resources.

  • load() is a cache-get: a miss reads from disk and caches. The resource sits in the cache unpinned (reference count 0).
  • acquire() and release() pin and unpin, and must be balanced. A release() that drops the count to 0 evicts at once.
  • unload_unused() evicts every resource whose count is 0, and unload(path, force=True) evicts regardless of the count.
  • reload() re-reads a cached resource, keeping its count.
Example

A .meta sidecar (hero.png.meta for hero.png) supplies import settings to a loader that supports metadata:

{
    "type": "texture",
    "filter": "nearest",
    "premultiply_alpha": true
}

index_directory(
    root_path: str, recursive: bool = True
) -> None

Scan a directory and maps filenames to their full paths without loading them.

This allows requesting assets by name (e.g., 'hero') instead of full path (e.g., 'assets/chars/hero.png'), mimicking Godot's resource system.

Two files that share a stem (chars/hero.png and fx/hero.png) would both claim the bare name hero. That is ambiguous, so the bare-stem entry is dropped and a warning is logged naming both paths; the unambiguous full-name keys (hero.png) are always kept. Resolve the clash by loading the colliding asset via its full name or path.

Call once per frame on the thread that owns the device context -- uploads happen here. Work is started only while the budget holds, but a single item is never interrupted part-way, so one slow upload can overrun it; see Budget.

Requests whose decode is still running on a worker are skipped without consuming budget, so a pump never blocks on a thread.

docs.title: pyguara.resources.meta
docs.text:
Asset import metadata system.

This module provides a .meta file sidecar system for defining import settings on assets. Meta files allow customization of how assets are loaded without modifying the original files.

Example

For hero.png, create hero.png.meta:

{
    "type": "texture",
    "filter": "nearest",
    "mipmaps": false,
    "premultiply_alpha": true
}

For bgm.ogg, create bgm.ogg.meta:

{
    "type": "audio",
    "stream": true,
    "volume_db": -3.0
}

docs.title: size_bytes property
docs.text:
size_bytes: int

Roughly how much memory this resource occupies.

What ResourceManager's cache budget counts. An estimate: the real figure is in a backend's allocator, often on the GPU.

Zero means "unknown", not "free". A resource of unknown size is neither counted towards the budget nor evicted to satisfy it. Subclasses that can estimate should; Texture does.

docs.title: release
docs.text:
release() -> None

Free whatever this resource holds outside Python's heap.

A no-op by default. ResourceManager calls it on every eviction, so a resource backed by a driver allocation (a GPU texture) frees it here; the garbage collector cannot.

Implementations must be idempotent, since eviction and an explicit teardown can both reach the same resource, and must leave the object safe to repr and to drop afterwards.

Bases: ABC

Abstract base class for all game scenes.

Manages the lifecycle of a specific game state (Menu, Gameplay, etc).

docs.title: render
docs.text:
render(
    world_renderer: IRenderer, ui_renderer: UIRenderer
) -> None

Frame render logic.

The default submits every entity carrying a visible Sprite to self.render_system, then flushes. With a Transform, Sprite.position is an offset from it. If that Transform has interpolate=True, the position drawn is lerp(previous_position, position, self.render_alpha). An entity with only a Sprite is drawn at the sprite's own position.

Override to add manual draws, calling super().render(world_renderer, ui_renderer) first.

Fixed-rate update for physics and deterministic game logic.

Called at a fixed rate (60 Hz by default) whatever the display framerate. For each active scene, in order:

  1. Snapshot previous_position for every Transform with interpolate=True, before any system moves it.
  2. Tick the scene's own SystemManager.
  3. Call the scene's fixed_update().
  4. Flush the scene's EntityManager.

docs.title: render
docs.text:
render(
    world_renderer: IRenderer,
    ui_renderer: UIRenderer,
    alpha: float = 1.0,
    *,
    before_each: Callable[[], None] | None = None,
) -> None

Render current scene and transition effects.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default world_renderer IRenderer

World rendering interface

required ui_renderer UIRenderer

UI rendering interface

required alpha float

How far the current frame sits between the last two fixed steps (accumulator / fixed_dt), for Transform.interpolate entities. Set on each scene as render_alpha immediately before that scene's render() runs, rather than threaded as a Scene.render() parameter -- every one of the 9 demos already overrides that exact two-parameter signature, so adding a third would force a mechanical change across all of them for a value only the base default combination uses.

1.0 before_each Callable[[], None] | None

Called immediately before every scene's render(), bottom of the stack to the top. Application uses it to re-bind the world render target: a scene that runs a render-graph pass itself leaves that pass's output buffer bound, and without this the scene stacked above it would draw its whole frame into that buffer instead of the world -- which is how a garden pushed over its title screen drew nothing at all.

None

docs.title: cleanup
docs.text:
cleanup() -> None

Tear down every live scene, LIFO, exiting each exactly once.

Persistent layers go first (they draw on top), then the current scene (entered last), then the stack top-down. A scene that a transition has started entering but not yet made current is included too, so an application shutting down mid-fade does not leave it holding its world.

docs.title: CircularWipeTransition
docs.text:
Bases: Transition

An iris wipe: a circular hole that closes on the centre and reopens.

The scene stays visible inside a circle centred on the window. The circle contracts to nothing, covering the frame from the corners inwards, and then expands again over the new scene.

The cover is drawn at config.color, opaque by default as in WipeTransition and SlideTransition. A translucent colour is honoured; see circular_cover_points.

Attributes:

Name Type Description segments

Sides in the polygon approximating the circle. See DEFAULT_WIPE_SEGMENTS for why 64.

render(
    world_renderer: IRenderer, ui_renderer: UIRenderer

Frame render logic.

The default submits every entity carrying a visible Sprite to self.render_system, then flushes. With a Transform, Sprite.position is an offset from it. Fixed-rate update for physics and deterministic game logic.

Called at a fixed rate (60 Hz by default) whatever the display framerate. For each active scene, in order:

  1. Snapshot previous_position for every Transform with interpolate=True, before any system moves it.
  2. Tick the scene's own SystemManager.
  3. Call the scene's fixed_update().
  4. Flush the scene's EntityManager.

docs.text:
render(
    world_renderer: IRenderer,
    ui_renderer: UIRenderer,
    alpha: float = 1.0,
    *,
    before_each: Callable[[], None] | None = None,
) -> None

Render current scene and transition effects.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default world_renderer IRenderer

World rendering interface

required ui_renderer UIRenderer

UI rendering interface

required alpha float

How far the current frame sits between the last two fixed steps (accumulator / fixed_dt), for Transform.interpolate entities. Set on each scene as render_alpha immediately before that scene's render() runs, rather than threaded as a Scene.render() parameter -- every one of the 9 demos already overrides that exact two-parameter signature, so adding a third would force a mechanical change across all of them for a value only the base default combination uses.

1.0 before_each Callable[[], None] | None

Called immediately before every scene's render(), bottom of the stack to the top. Application uses it to re-bind the world render target: a scene that runs a render-graph pass itself leaves that pass's output buffer bound, and without this the scene stacked above it would draw its whole frame into that buffer instead of the world -- which is how a garden pushed over its title screen drew nothing at all.

None

docs.title: cleanup
docs.text:
cleanup() -> None

Tear down every live scene, LIFO, exiting each exactly once.

Persistent layers go first (they draw on top), then the current scene (entered last), then the stack top-down. A scene that a transition has started entering but not yet made current is included too, so an application shutting down mid-fade does not leave it holding its world.

docs.title: pyguara.scene.serializer
docs.text:
Scene serialization logic.

A scene file holds everything needed to rebuild an authored world, in a shape a person could have typed. Beyond components, it stores each entity's tags, its enabled state, its ChildOf owner and its spatial Transform parent.

Resources are written as {"__resource__": path} and resolved on load by the texture_resolver the bootstrap injects. A path that will not resolve skips the component with a warning.

A dunder-ish key rather than a plain "path": component fields are written under their own names, and a component with a genuine path: str field would otherwise be indistinguishable from a resource handle.

docs.title: pyguara.scene.transitions
docs.text:
Scene transition effects system.

This module provides visual transition effects when switching between scenes, including fade, slide, wipe, and zoom effects with customizable easing.

Example

from pyguara.scene.transitions import FadeTransition, TransitionManager

transition_manager = TransitionManager() fade = FadeTransition(duration=0.5) transition_manager.start_transition(fade, from_scene, to_scene, on_complete)

docs.title: In update loop:
docs.text: transition_manager.update(dt)

docs.title: In render:
docs.text: transition_manager.render(renderer, ui_renderer)

docs.title: DEFAULT_WIPE_SEGMENTS module-attribute
docs.text:
DEFAULT_WIPE_SEGMENTS = 64

Sides in the polygon approximating a circular wipe's edge.

At 64 the error against a true circle is sub-pixel at any window size the engine is likely to see: the worst case is the sagitta of one chord, r * (1 - cos(pi / 64)), which is 0.9 px at the 735 px radius a 1280x720 window needs. Doubling it halves that and doubles nothing that matters -- the cost is one polygon either way -- but 64 is already below what a viewer can see on a moving edge.

docs.text:

    screen_width: int,
    screen_height: int,
    segments: int = DEFAULT_WIPE_SEGMENTS,
) -> float

Return the radius at which a wipe's cover vanishes entirely.

Not the half-diagonal, which is the intuitive answer and leaves a visible artefact. An inscribed polygon touches the circle at its vertices and falls inside it everywhere else, so a 64-gon of radius exactly the half-diagonal still cuts the corners off: measured, 2131 of a 1280x720 window's pixels stayed covered at what should have been full reveal -- four dark slivers, at the one moment the effect is supposed to be invisible. Scaling by 1 / cos(pi / segments) puts the polygon's edges through the corners instead.

docs.title: circular_cover_points
docs.text:
circular_cover_points(
    center_x: float,
    center_y: float,
    radius: float,
    screen_width: int,
    screen_height: int,
    segments: int = DEFAULT_WIPE_SEGMENTS,
) -> list[tuple[int, int]]

Return one polygon covering the screen except a circular hole.

The cover is a single self-touching outline: round the window rectangle, in along a seam to the circle, round the circle in the opposite winding, and back out along the same seam. A scanline fill leaves the hole empty, and the two coincident seam edges cancel.

One polygon is used, not a fan of quads, so a translucent cover is blended once everywhere and shows no seams.

required center_y float

Radius of the revealed circle. Clamped at both ends: at or below zero the whole window is covered, and at or above fully_revealed_radius nothing is.

docs.title: stop
docs.text:
stop() -> None

Stop the coroutine immediately.

Closes the underlying generator, so any finally blocks or context managers open inside the scripted sequence run their cleanup now rather than whenever the generator is garbage collected. Idempotent, and never raises: a generator that swallows the injected GeneratorExit (by yielding again) is reported and left for the garbage collector.

docs.title: CoroutineManager
docs.text:
Manages multiple coroutines.

Handles starting, updating, and stopping coroutines.

A scripted sequence that raises is contained: it is stopped and reported according to error_strategy, and the other coroutines still run this frame. Coroutines may safely start or stop coroutines (including themselves) from inside their own body during update().

Example

manager = CoroutineManager() coro = manager.start_coroutine(my_sequence())

docs.title: FixedStepTicker
docs.text:
A count of fixed-timestep steps, so a sequence can wait on one.

The coroutine manager is ticked from the variable-rate update, so a sequence has no inherent notion of the fixed step. This is the shared counter that bridges them: the engine advances it from Application._fixed_update, and WaitForFixedUpdate watches it.

A counter rather than a flag, so two instructions created in the same frame both see the next step rather than racing to consume one signal.

stop() -> None

Stop the coroutine immediately.

Closes the underlying generator, so any finally blocks or context managers open inside the scripted sequence run their cleanup now rather than whenever the generator is garbage collected. docs.title: pyguara.spatial
docs.text:
Non-physics spatial queries for PyGuara.

SpatialHash, the underlying value type, lives in pyguara.common.spatial and knows nothing of the ECS. SpatialTracked and SpatialIndexSystem here wire it to entities: attach SpatialTracked to anything a spatial query needs to find that has no physics body, and run SpatialIndexSystem each tick to keep the hash current.

The physics-backed equivalent -- point_query, region_query, overlap_circle, etc. on IPhysicsEngine -- already covers entities that do have a physics collider; this module exists for the ones that don't.

No distance test: a key anywhere in the cell counts, so what comes back depends on where the cell boundaries fall. That makes it the one query whose result is sensitive to cell_size.

docs.title: pyguara.studio
docs.text:
PyGuara Studio: the companion authoring application.

Studio runs the engine, opens a project, and lets a developer author content visually. Everything it writes is a file a person could have written by hand. Every change to authored state becomes an EditCommand on a CommandStack, whoever asked for it; see ADR 0001.

Importing this package does not import Dear ImGui, so the JSON-lines transport (pyguara studio ops) runs without it. The panels and the editor layer are imported from their own modules.

transaction(label: str) -> Iterator[None]

Group every command applied inside the block into one entry.

What a multi-select edit needs: moving twelve entities is twelve commands that must undo together, because undoing a third of a move is not a state the user was ever in.

An exception inside the block reverts whatever did apply and re-raises, so the world is left as it was and nothing reaches the history. An empty block adds nothing.

coalesce_with(previous: EditCommand) -> EditCommand | None

Merge this command into previous, or decline.

What keeps a gizmo drag from filling the undo stack with one entry per mouse-motion event. A drag issues a SetField per frame; the stack asks each to fold into the last, so the whole drag undoes in one step -- which is what a user means by "undo that move".

Declining is the default and the safe answer: a merge is only correct when the pair describes one continuous gesture on the same target.

docs.title: EditError
docs.text:

A command cannot be applied, and nothing was changed.

Raised by apply() before it mutates anything, so a failed command never leaves half an edit behind and is never pushed onto the stack. The message is shown to whoever asked for the edit -- a human in a toast, an agent as a tool error -- so it names what was wrong and, where there is one, the valid alternative.

docs.title: pyguara.studio.attach
docs.text:
Putting the editor layer, and Studio on top of it, into an application.

attach_editor installs the ImGui context, the input routing, the render pass and two panels over live engine state. attach_studio calls it and adds the operation registry, the journal, the command stack and the rest of the panels. Both are opt-in.

Nothing here imports Dear ImGui at module scope, because the JSON-lines transport loads this module. A session is bound to one scene's EntityManager, so StudioAttachment rebuilds it on each scene switch.

Example

app = create_application() studio = attach_studio(app.container) app.run(MyScene("game", dispatcher))

docs.title: DEFAULT_LAYOUT_REGIONS module-attribute
docs.text:
DEFAULT_LAYOUT_REGIONS: dict[str, tuple[str, ...]] = {
    "left": ("Hierarchy",),
    "right": ("Inspector", "Components", "Config"),
    "bottom": (
        "History",
        "Journal",
        "Commands",
        "Resources",
    ),
    "top": ("Play",),
    "centre": ("Viewport",),
}

Where Studio's panels open, by window title.

The arrangement every editor converges on, for the reason they converge: the hierarchy is a list you scan down one side, the inspector is a column of fields opposite it, and the thing you are actually working on gets the middle. History, the journal and the palette share the bottom as tabs -- all three are consulted rather than watched.

Applied once. A developer who drags a panel elsewhere keeps it there; without any layout at all every window opens at the same default position, stacked on top of the others.

Plain titles rather than a DockLayout, under the module docstring's rule: a module-level from pyguara.studio.layer import DockLayout here is what made the dependency-free JSON-lines transport need ImGui, and this constant is the one piece of the layout a caller reads without one.

FinalPass.input_fbo_name is the authority -- it names the buffer the finished frame was composed into -- and this is the fallback for a graph that has no final pass, which is what the offscreen capture tooling runs with.

docs.text:
Whether Dear ImGui is importable, resolved once here.

imgui_bundle.imgui needs no OpenGL binding to create a context or build a frame; the draw data is rasterised by WgpuImGuiRenderer. The test suite asserts the flag is true on a dev install, so the editor cannot switch itself off unnoticed.

Importing this module imports imgui_bundle when it is installed, so it is not a cheap probe. Anything the agent transport loads must import it inside a function; see pyguara/studio/attach.py.

docs.text:
release() -> None

Release the editor layer with the graph that drives it.

The layer owns an ImGui context and, through its renderer, GL programs, buffers and textures built on this graph's context. The graph releases every pass it holds (Application.shutdown() calls RenderGraph.release()), so routing the layer's teardown through here is what keeps those from outliving the context they came from.

EditorLayer.release() is idempotent, so a caller that also releases the layer itself is fine.

Titles docked to the left edge.

right tuple[str, ...]

Titles docked to the right edge.

bottom tuple[str, ...]

Titles docked along the top, above everything else -- where a transport bar belongs.

centre tuple[str, ...]

Titles filling what is left, which is the largest region.

right_ratio float

How much of the remaining width the right edge takes.

How much of the remaining height the bottom takes.

How much of the remaining height the top takes, or None to size it to exactly one row of controls. A fixed fraction cannot do that: the row's height depends on the UI scale, and a strip that fits at 1.0 clips the row at 1.25.

docs.text:
Studio's menus.

An entry that changes the scene goes through the operation registry, the surface an agent drives. So a person choosing Entity > Create Empty and an agent calling create_entity share one path, one history and one journal, and a menu can only offer what an operation offers.

The menus are Scene (file commands), Edit (undo and redo), Entity, View (panels and layout), Run (play controls) and Agent (the approval mode and the journal).

docs.title: pyguara.studio.sceneio
docs.text:
Saving, loading and emptying the open scene.

Studio's session owns a world and a history; it does not own the scene object or the serializer, and both live in the engine container. This is the small piece that joins them, so the operations can offer Save and Open without reaching into the container themselves -- a handler that did would work in the editor and fail in every test that builds a session by hand.

Without one, StudioSession.scene_io is None and the operations say what is missing rather than failing somewhere deeper.

The editor's shared "which entities are being looked at" state.

Held by id, not by Entity, so a selection cannot keep a destroyed entity alive. Panels resolve the ids against the live world every frame; an id that no longer resolves reads as nothing selected.

A selection is an ordered set with a primary. Order is insertion order, and the primary is the most recently added id: the one a gizmo anchors to and the Inspector shows fields for.

docs.title: pyguara.studio.session
docs.text:
One editing session: a world, its history, its journal, its rules.

Everything that edits a scene goes through a StudioSession. It owns the EntityManager being edited, the CommandStack, the Journal, and the approval mode, which decides whether an edit applies at once, waits for a person, or is only described.

In PLAN mode an edit is applied, its diff captured, and then reverted, so the caller gets the real consequence and the world ends as it started.

docs.title: EditorMode
docs.text:
Bases: str, Enum

Whether the scene is being edited or the game is being played.

The scene being edited and the game being run are not the same thing at the same time: Play snapshots the world, Stop restores it, and an edit made while playing is refused.

docs.title: EDIT class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
EDIT = 'edit'

Nothing simulates. The scene is the thing on screen, and it is editable.

docs.title: PLAY class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
PLAY = 'play'

The game runs. Edits are refused rather than silently lost, and Stop puts the scene back as it was.

docs.title: ApprovalMode
docs.text:
Bases: str, Enum

How an edit requested by an actor is handled.

A str enum so it crosses a JSON boundary without an encoder hook -- the mode is part of an agent's reply, so it has to.

docs.title: AUTO class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
AUTO = 'auto'

Apply it. The default for a human at the keyboard.

docs.title: ASK class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
ASK = 'ask'

Hold it for a person to approve or reject.

What to run an unfamiliar agent under: every edit becomes a queued PendingEdit carrying the diff it would produce, so the reviewer sees the consequence rather than the request.

docs.title: PLAN class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
PLAN = 'plan'

Describe it and change nothing.

Implemented by applying the edit, capturing the diff and reverting, so the description is the real consequence and not a guess at it.
