docs.title: pyguara.studio.theme
docs.text:
How the editor looks.

  • Neutral greys and one accent, used only for what is selected or active.
  • Rounded corners and generous padding.
  • Scaled to the window: scale_for derives a factor from the window size, and a caller can override it.

docs.title: ACCENT module-attribute
docs.text:
ACCENT = (0.26, 0.59, 0.98)

The one colour that means "this one". Everything else is a grey.

docs.title: REFERENCE_WIDTH module-attribute
docs.text:
REFERENCE_WIDTH = 1536.0

The window width at which the UI is drawn at 1:1.

Chosen so a 1080p window lands on 1.25 rather than 1.0: ImGui's built-in font is a 13px bitmap designed for a debug overlay, and at 1920 wide it is small enough to squint at. A 1280-wide window stays at 1.0, since below that the answer is fewer panels rather than smaller text.

docs.title: MIN_SCALE module-attribute
docs.text:
MIN_SCALE = 1.0

Never shrink. Below this the font stops being legible, and a small window wants fewer panels rather than smaller text.

docs.title: MAX_SCALE module-attribute
docs.text:
MAX_SCALE = 3.0

Beyond this the chrome eats the screen on any display sold today.

docs.text:

Return a UI scale that keeps the editor legible at width.

Derived from the window rather than from the OS's DPI setting, which SDL does not report reliably across the platforms this runs on -- and which is the wrong question anyway: what matters is how much room the panels have, not how dense the pixels are.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default width int

The window width in pixels.

required height int

The window height in pixels, used only to avoid scaling up a window that is wide and short.

required

A title bar the editor draws itself.

Opt-in, through display.borderless. It needs a backend that offers window controls, and the resizable flag, since removing the OS frame removes its resize edges.

Dragging moves the window by the pointer's offset from where the bar was grabbed, not by its delta since the previous frame. The pointer position is relative to the window being moved, so a frame-to-frame delta cancels itself. No absolute position is set, because a window manager may place a window somewhere other than asked.

Three concerns live here:

docs.title: pyguara.studio.agent.harness
docs.text:
The closed loop: open a scene, edit it, run it, look at the result.

A harness binds a StudioSession (edits as undoable, journaled commands), Application.begin() and step() (frames advanced by the caller) and the capture path of tools/agent_view.py.

A headless application gets FixedClock, so every frame is one sixtieth of a second and two runs of one script produce the same frames. A capture reads the buffer the renderer drew into. It does not prove a window appeared; see docs/guides/agent-visual-inspection.md.

docs.title: pyguara.studio.agent.instructions
docs.text:
Generating the instruction files coding agents actually read.

AGENTS.md is the canonical file. The per-tool files are thin shims that import it: CLAUDE.md (an @AGENTS.md line, since Claude Code does not merge the two), GEMINI.md and .cursor/rules/*.mdc. AGENTS.override.md is never written; that name is the user's.

Generated regions are fenced by markers. Regeneration replaces what is between them and leaves every other byte of the file alone.

The instruction to the reader is in the marker itself, because the person who needs it is looking at the file, not at this module.

docs.title: pyguara.studio.agent.journal
docs.text:
An append-only record of every edit, and who asked for it.

The undo stack is a position: an undo moves it. The journal is a log, and an undo is another entry in it, so it answers "what was done, in order".

Written as JSON Lines, one object per entry, so a session that crashes mid-write leaves every complete line readable. Entries carry an actor, which tells a person's edit from an agent's. It is provenance, not a permission.

Every mutation Studio performs is an EditCommand on a CommandStack -- whether it came from a panel, the command palette, or an agent over MCP.

docs.title: DEFAULT_LIMIT module-attribute
docs.text:
DEFAULT_LIMIT = 256

How many undo entries to keep.

Finite because an editing session is long and a command holds the state it captured -- DestroyEntity keeps a whole subtree alive for as long as it is undoable. Dropping the oldest entry is the standard trade: a developer who wants to undo 300 edits wants the file they saved, not the stack.

docs.title: pyguara.studio.commands.base
docs.text:
The edit command: the one way authored state changes in Studio.

Everything that mutates a scene (a gizmo drag, a palette entry, an agent's tool call) produces an EditCommand and hands it to a CommandStack. See ADR 0001.

A command captures its own inverse when it is applied: SetField records the old value as it writes the new one. So a command instance is a record of one application, and apply() twice without a revert() between raises.

docs.title: pyguara.studio.commands.entity
docs.text:
The concrete edits: entities, components, fields, hierarchy, tags.

Each command makes its change through the EntityManager's own API and knows what to put back. Every field write ends with notify_component_changed().

EntityManager.remove_entity cascades through ChildOf, and a removed entity cannot be re-added. So DestroyEntity snapshots the whole subtree before removing anything (every entity, its components, tags, enabled state and parent link) and undo rebuilds it.

docs.title: HANDLE_FIELDS module-attribute
docs.text:
HANDLE_FIELDS: tuple[str, ...] = ('_body_handle',)

Fields holding a live engine object, which a copy gets as None.

A RigidBody carries the physics backend's body. Copying it is wrong twice over -- the backend still owns the original, and the copy would point at a body that is not its own. As None, the physics system builds the copy a fresh one, as it does for any entity it has not seen. Not copied at all, since a native world cannot be.

docs.title: DuplicateEntity
docs.text:
Bases: EditCommand

Copy an entity and everything it owns, under fresh ids.

Ctrl+D, and the most-used way to build a level: place one platform well and make twenty. The copy keeps the original's parent, so a duplicated child lands beside its sibling rather than at the root.

The ids are minted once, at the first apply, and reused by every later redo. Minting again would give the redo different ids from the undo that preceded it, and anything holding one -- a selection, an agent's next call -- would be pointing at an entity that no longer exists.

The engine had no command stack of any kind before this; pyguara/tools and the ImGui Inspector both mutate components in place, so nothing was reversible. Studio routes every edit through here instead.

Bound to one EntityManager for its lifetime. A history that spans a scene switch would be undoing commands into a world that never saw them applied, so StudioSession builds a new stack per scene rather than carrying one across.

docs.title: DEFAULT_LIMIT module-attribute
docs.text:

How many undo entries to keep.

Finite because an editing session is long and a command holds the state it captured -- DestroyEntity keeps a whole subtree alive for as long as it is undoable. Dropping the oldest entry is the standard trade: a developer who wants to undo 300 edits wants the file they saved, not the stack.

docs.title: pyguara.studio.mcp.availability
docs.text:
Whether the MCP SDK is importable, resolved once here.

The SDK is a transport, not the contract: the operation surface also runs over pyguara.studio.ops.stdio, which needs only the standard library. If this import fails, only the MCP front end is unavailable. mcp is in the dev extra, and the test suite asserts the flag is true there.

The check is for the 2.x shape of the SDK, which renamed FastMCP to MCPServer and moved the low-level handlers to constructor callbacks, so a 1.x install reads as "wrong version".

docs.text:
The MCP front end over Studio's operation surface.

A thin adapter. Every operation, its schema and its error text live in pyguara.studio.ops; this module presents them as Model Context Protocol tools. It validates nothing and writes no error message, so it cannot disagree with the JSON-lines front end.

Built on the SDK's low-level Server, which takes an explicit inputSchema; the schemas already exist. Results go back as JSON text and as structured content. Field names are the SDK's Python-side ones (input_schema, structured_content, is_error).

docs.title: pyguara.studio.model
docs.text:
The read model: what Studio and an agent see when they look at a scene.

Three layers, sharing one value vocabulary:

  • values -- encoding component field values to JSON and back, shape- compatible with what SceneSerializer writes.
  • schema -- what a component's fields are, their types and whether they can be set. Drives the Inspector, the schema browser, and the JSON Schema an agent reads.
  • snapshot -- a scene at one instant, and the diff between two.
  • projectmap -- the budgeted inventory an agent reads first.

The operations Studio ships with.

The edit history, as a list you can rewind to a point in.

What makes undo legible rather than a key you press hopefully. A stack of labels tells you what you did; clicking one tells you where to go back to. That second part -- "undo to here" -- is the reason the panel exists at all, since a plain Ctrl-Z needs no window.

Entries are listed oldest-first so an index stays put as new edits arrive at the end. A newest-first list renumbers everything on every edit, which makes the row a user is reaching for move while they reach for it.

The command palette: a person calling the operations an agent calls.

A front end onto OperationRegistry, so an operation cannot be available to an agent and missing here.

Arguments are typed as JSON, in the shape the schema browser shows and scene files use; no form is generated. entity_id defaults to the primary selection. The result, including the diff, is shown underneath.

scene_tree on a real scene is far larger than a panel, and rendering all of it costs a frame to produce something nobody reads.

docs.title: pyguara.studio.panels.play
docs.text:
Play, pause and step the game without leaving the editor.

The panel drives Application.paused, time_scale and its frame loop; it runs no loop of its own.

Play copies the whole world into a WorldSnapshot and lets the game run, and Stop puts that copy back. While playing, an edit is refused. Pause and Step are for watching a running game.

docs.title: MAX_TIME_SCALE module-attribute
docs.text:
MAX_TIME_SCALE = 4.0

Fastest the panel will run the game.

Past this, a fixed-timestep loop spends the whole frame in _fixed_update catching up and the display stops responding -- the spiral physics.max_frame_time exists to clamp, reached deliberately from the editor instead of accidentally from a lag spike.

docs.title: pyguara.studio.panels.resources
docs.text:
The project's assets: what is indexed, what is loaded, and what is in one.

Two scrolling lists share a filter. Selecting a row previews the resource, and two buttons act on it: Spawn builds an entity from a data file, and Reload re-reads a loaded resource from disk.

Everything the panel does is the resources operation, so a spawn is on the session's history and journal and obeys the approval mode. The listing is re-read every REFRESH_FRAMES frames and after each action.

docs.title: pyguara.studio.panels.schema
docs.text:
What components exist, and what each one's fields are.

Reads the same ComponentSchema the Inspector's widgets and an agent's JSON Schema come from, so the three cannot describe a component differently. A browser over a second, hand-maintained list of components is a browser that is wrong.

Practical use, in order of how often: finding the name to type into a prefab file, checking whether a field is settable before trying, and reading an enum's members -- which is the one thing nothing else on screen tells you.

docs.title: pyguara.studio.viewport
docs.text:
The scene viewport: the rendered frame, with editing on top of it.

panel is the ImGui panel -- pan, zoom, grid, selection, marquee -- shown over the render graph's own framebuffer, so what the viewport shows is by construction what the game shows.

picking is the geometry underneath it, deliberately free of GL, ImGui and any window, so it can be tested against a real world directly.

docs.text:
screen_to_world(
    camera: Camera2D,
    panel_point: Vector2,
    panel: Rect,
    target: Rect,
) -> Vector2

Map a point in a viewport panel to world coordinates.

Two mappings, composed. A Studio viewport shows a framebuffer rendered at the game's resolution, scaled into whatever size the panel happens to be, so a click has to be scaled back to framebuffer space before the camera can be asked about it. Skipping that step is how a viewport picks correctly only when the panel is exactly the render size.

required

The world position under the cursor.

docs.title: sprite_bounds
docs.text:
sprite_bounds(
    transform: Transform, sprite: Sprite | None
) -> Rect | None

Return a sprite's world-space box, or None when it has no size.

Measured from the texture rather than assumed: a 16x16 coin and a 256x256 backdrop are both pickable at their real size. The sprite's own position is an offset from the transform, and scale multiplies both the sprite's and the transform's.

Rotation is ignored. The box is axis-aligned, which makes a rotated sprite's box slightly generous -- the right trade for picking, where being a few pixels forgiving is a feature.

docs.title: pyguara.studio.viewport.gizmo
docs.text:
The transform gizmo: dragging an entity rather than typing at it.

One drag is one undo entry:

  1. On drag begin, the starting transform of every selected entity is recorded.
  2. While dragging, components are written directly.
  3. On release, the starting values are put back and one CompositeCommand is applied through the session. A command captures its inverse when applied, so it must see the old values.

Escape cancels: the recorded values go back and no command is applied.

docs.title: HANDLE_GRAB_RADIUS module-attribute
docs.text:
HANDLE_GRAB_RADIUS = 9.0

How close, in panel pixels, the cursor must be to grab a handle.

In pixels rather than world units deliberately: a handle is a screen-space affordance, and one that shrank as you zoomed out would become ungrabbable at exactly the point you most want to drag something a long way.

docs.title: pyguara.studio.viewport.panel
docs.text:
The scene viewport: the rendered frame, with editing on top of it.

An ImGui panel showing the render graph's own framebuffer as an image, with pan, zoom, a grid, selection and a marquee drawn over it.

The frame is rendered at the game's resolution and scaled into the panel, so a coordinate crosses two mappings: panel to framebuffer, then framebuffer to world. picking.screen_to_world and picking.world_to_panel are that pair. Pan and zoom drive the scene's own Camera2D.

docs.title: pyguara.studio.viewport.picking
docs.text:
Working out which entity is under the cursor, or inside a marquee.

Two sources:

  • Physics: IPhysicsEngine.point_query for a click, and region_query then overlap_box_all for a marquee.
  • Sprite bounds: an axis-aligned box per visible sprite, from its transform and texture, for entities with no collider.

Everything here is geometry over the ECS, with no ImGui and no window.

docs.title: DEFAULT_PICK_SIZE module-attribute
docs.text:
DEFAULT_PICK_SIZE = 16.0

Half-extent, in world units, for an entity with no measurable bounds.

An entity with a Transform and nothing else still has to be clickable -- a spawn point, a trigger marker, an empty used as a parent. A fixed box is honest about being arbitrary, where gizmos.py's identical constant was indistinguishable from a measurement.

docs.title: pyguara.systems
docs.text: System management for orchestrating game logic.

docs.title: SystemManager
docs.text:
Holds a scene's systems and updates them in a fixed order.

Each scene owns one of these; there is no global instance. Systems run in ascending priority order, so a lower number updates earlier.

Note

The direction is the opposite of EventDispatcher, where a higher priority runs first. Systems are a pipeline -- input before physics before rendering -- so ascending reads naturally as a sequence; event handlers compete for the same event, where "most important first" is the natural reading.

Example 
systems = SystemManager()
systems.register(PhysicsSystem(engine, dispatcher), priority=100)
systems.register(AISystem(entity_manager), priority=200)
systems.initialize()

systems.update(dt)   # physics, then AI

docs.title: register
docs.text:
register(
    system: Any,
    priority: int = DEFAULT_PRIORITY,
    system_type: type[Any] | None = None,
) -> None

Add a system to the update order.

If initialize() has already run, the new system is initialised immediately. That covers a system registered in on_enter(), which runs after the scene initialises its manager.

Several systems may share a key. They all update, but get_system() and unregister() then reach only the most recently registered, which is logged. Give each a distinct system_type to keep them addressable.

Parameters:

The system to add. Must expose update(dt).

required priority int

Update order; lower runs earlier.

Key for get_system(). Defaults to the system's own class. Pass it when several systems share a base class, or to register against an interface.

None

docs.title: pyguara.systems.phases
docs.text:
Named points in a scene's update order.

Phase is an IntEnum, so a phase is a priority: register(system, priority=Phase.LOGIC) mixes with raw ints, and Phase.LOGIC + 10 means "just after".

The values are 100 apart and match the bands the engine uses. Scene registers Tween at 120, Steering at 150, AI at 200, AudioSource at 250 and Animation at 300.

Example

systems.register(poison, priority=Phase.LOGIC) systems.register(death, priority=Phase.LOGIC + 10) # after poison

docs.title: pyguara.tilemap
docs.text:
A genre-agnostic tilemap data structure: layers, tilesets, and Tiled import.

physics/tilemap.py's merge_tile_rects is the collision-geometry half of this; TileLayer.collision_rects() calls it directly rather than duplicating tile merging here.

docs.title: TileLayer
docs.text:
A dense width x height grid of global tile ids.

Knows nothing of tilesets or Tilemap -- collision_rects() takes a property lookup as a parameter rather than reaching for one, so this stays a plain grid a Tilemap composes rather than a piece that depends on it.

Return the global tile id at cell, or EMPTY_GID if none.

docs.title: set_tile
docs.text:
set_tile(cell: Cell, gid: int) -> None

Set the global tile id at cell.

Invalidates the cached collision_rects() result -- the next call re-merges, since a changed tile can change which rectangles cover the solid area.

docs.title: pyguara.tilemap.ldtk_loader
docs.text:
Load an LDtk (.ldtk) project into the same Tilemap the Tiled loader builds.

  • An LDtk file holds many levels: load_ldtk returns one Tilemap per level.
  • LDtk tile ids are per tileset. Global ids are synthesised by laying the tilesets end to end, so Tilemap.properties_for works.
  • LDtk tile layers are sparse; the dense TileLayer grid is filled from them, and an unplaced cell is EMPTY_GID.
  • An IntGrid layer gets a synthetic tileset.

Level backgrounds and entity references between levels are not read.

docs.title: pyguara.tilemap.spawning
docs.text:
Turn a map's objects into entities, through prefabs.

The loaders stop at data; this module is where a map meets the ECS. A loader says an object has type "Bat", and the game says which prefab that means.

In Tiled, a custom property named Component.field overrides that field on the spawned entity (Health.max = 30, or deeper, Transform.scale.x = 2). Any other property stays on SpawnedObject.source.properties.

Example

map_ = load_tmx("levels/cave.tmx") spawned = spawn_objects( map_, factory, {"Bat": bat_prefab, "Door": door_trigger_prefab}, ignore_types={"CameraBounds"}, )

docs.text:
spawn_objects(
    tilemap: Tilemap,
    factory: PrefabFactory,
    prefabs: Mapping[str, PrefabData],
    *,
    layers: Iterable[str] | None = None,
    ignore_types: Collection[str] = (),
    offset: Vector2 | None = None,
    include_hidden: bool = False,
) -> list[SpawnedObject]

Spawn an entity for every typed object on a map.

All or nothing: every object is checked before the first is spawned, and a map with a mistake raises with the whole list. An object with no type is skipped. A type with no prefab is an error unless it is in ignore_types.

The entity's Transform is placed at the object's centre. A sized rectangle or a circle also sets the shape of any Collider or TriggerVolume in the prefab, unless a Component.field property states it. A polygon or polyline cannot be a collider and raises.

Added to every position, for a room placed inside a larger world.

Load a Tiled (.tmx) map into a Tilemap.

Reads embedded and external (.tsx) tilesets; tile layers encoded as CSV, as base64 (uncompressed, gzip or zlib) or as <tile gid="..."> elements; layers nested inside <group>; and <objectgroup> object layers.

Refused, each with an error naming it: non-square tiles, zstd compression, and infinite maps (<data> split into <chunk> elements).

docs.title: GID_FLAG_MASK module-attribute
docs.text:
GID_FLAG_MASK = 536870911

Keeps the tile id and discards Tiled's three orientation flags.

Tiled packs horizontal (0x80000000), vertical (0x40000000) and diagonal (0x20000000) flips into a gid's top bits. Unmasked, a horizontally flipped tile 1 arrives as 2147483649, no Tileset's range contains it, and Tilemap.properties_for returns {} -- so a flipped wall silently stops being solid, and only in the places the author happened to mirror a tile. The flags themselves are not yet exposed; masking them is what makes the tile id usable at all.

A widget that can scroll its own contents.

An optional capability, tested with isinstance; UIElement.handle_event() keeps its three-argument form.

layout(available_rect: Rect, renderer: UIRenderer) -> None

Overrides UIElement.layout: the container first resolves its own rect (its constraints against available_rect, if any), then measures every visible child and stacks them along direction, distributing free space per alignment on the main axis and either centring or stretching them on the cross axis. Nested containers are laid out recursively afterwards.

docs.title: GridContainer
docs.text:
Bases: UIElement

Lays children out in a fixed number of columns, row by row.

What BoxContainer cannot do: an inventory, an ability bar, a crafting grid. Children flow left to right and wrap, so adding one never requires rewriting the layout.

Column width is uniform -- the content width split columns ways, minus spacing -- because that is what a slot grid means. Row height is the tallest child in that row, or row_height when the grid wants square cells regardless of content.

docs.text:

A viewport that clips its contents and scrolls them.

Children are laid out at their full extent, shifted by the scroll offset, and clipped to this element's rect.

They are shifted during layout, not during render, so each child's rect is where it is drawn and hit-testing agrees with the pixels.

Implements base.Scrollable, so UIManager routes the wheel here when the cursor is anywhere inside.

docs.title: ColorScheme dataclass
docs.text:
Standardized color palette using Color objects.

Two layers. The base five colours plus two overlays are the shorthand a theme is written in. The semantic roles below them (surfaces, a text hierarchy, edges, action states) are what components read.

Every semantic role the caller does not name is derived from the base colours. derive() also refuses an unknown role by name; the presets and pyguara.ui.design_system build theirs with it.

Build a full scheme from the base colours, then apply overrides.

This is the difference between a preset that only names five colours and one whose surfaces, edges and action states all belong to the same palette. Pass a role in overrides to state it outright -- which is what a design system does, having chosen every value deliberately rather than by rule.

docs.title: pyguara.ui.builder
docs.text:
Declarative construction of UI trees.

Opt-in sugar over the imperative API: the builder makes the same add_child() calls, with the parent threaded through a context manager. on_click= assigns UIElement.on_click. add() and nest() take any UIElement subclass and keep its type, so custom widgets work in a builder.

Example

with UIBuilder(ui_manager) as ui: with ui.box(Vector2(80, 288), Vector2(260, 220), spacing=14) as column: ui.label("Main Menu", font_size=44) ui.button("Start Game", on_click=self._on_start) ui.button("Quit", on_click=self._on_quit)

ui_manager.set_focus(column.children[0])

Overrides UIElement.layout: the container first resolves its own rect (its constraints against available_rect, if any), then measures every visible child and stacks them along direction, distributing free space per alignment on the main axis and either centring or stretching them on the cross axis. docs.text:
Bases: UIElement

Lays children out in a fixed number of columns, row by row.

What BoxContainer cannot do: an inventory, an ability bar, a crafting grid. Children flow left to right and wrap, so adding one never requires rewriting the layout.

Column width is uniform -- the content width split columns ways, minus spacing -- because that is what a slot grid means. Row height is the tallest child in that row, or row_height when the grid wants square cells regardless of content.

docs.title: ScrollContainer
docs.text:
Bases: UIElement

A viewport that clips its contents and scrolls them.

Children are laid out at their full extent, shifted by the scroll offset, and clipped to this element's rect.

They are shifted during layout, not during render, so each child's rect is where it is drawn and hit-testing agrees with the pixels.

Implements base.Scrollable, so UIManager routes the wheel here when the cursor is anywhere inside.

How far the contents are scrolled, in pixels. Never negative.

docs.title: max_offset property
docs.text:

The furthest this viewport can scroll.

Zero when the contents fit, which is what makes scroll_by() return False and hand the wheel back to whatever is underneath.

docs.text:
content_extent: int

The size of the contents along the scrolling axis, as last laid out.

docs.title: scroll_by
docs.text:
scroll_by(dx: float, dy: float) -> bool

Scroll by a wheel delta.

Wheel y is positive away from the user, which is a request to move the content down and therefore the offset up -- hence the negation. Getting this backwards is the single most noticeable bug a scroll view can have.

Parameters:

Horizontal notches.

required dy float

Vertical notches.

required

docs.title: pyguara.ui.rich_text
docs.text:
Inline styling: a markup parser, and wrapping that keeps each run's style.

Pure functions over a measuring callback, like text_layout. Plain text stays with wrap_text.

The markup is BBCode-style: [b], [i], [color=#e2621f] and [size=24], each closed as [/b] and so on. Tags nest and must close in order. [[ is a literal [. A malformed string raises MarkupError, so pass anything a player typed through escape_markup first.

docs.title: pyguara.ui.text_case
docs.text:
Upper and lower case that are right in Turkish.

str.upper() follows Unicode's default mapping, which is wrong in Turkish and Azerbaijani: there, i capitalises to İ (dotted) and ı (dotless) to I, so "iptal".upper() must be "İPTAL", not "IPTAL" -- a different word to a Turkish reader. Everything else is str.upper() unchanged.

The language is set engine-wide, from the game's locale, and the UI's own case changes (a design-system button's uppercase) go through here.

docs.title: pyguara.ui.text_layout
docs.text:
Breaking a string into the lines a renderer will actually draw.

Pure functions over a measuring callback: wrapping needs to know how wide a candidate line is and nothing else from a renderer, so it can be tested against a fake.

A renderer's get_text_size measures a single line and ignores newlines, while draw_text honours them. Splitting the text here and drawing one line per call makes the measured size and the drawn size agree.

docs.title: wrap_text
docs.text:
wrap_text(
    text: str, width: int | None, measure: MeasureWidth
) -> list[str]

Break text into the lines that fit width.

Explicit newlines always split, width or no width -- they are the author asking for a break rather than the layout discovering one. A run of them produces empty lines, which are kept: a blank line between paragraphs is content.

Greedy, not minimum-raggedness. A Knuth-Plass-style optimal break reads better in a book and is not worth a per-frame dynamic program for a HUD; nothing here precludes adding one later behind the same signature.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default text str

The string to break. \\r\\n and \\r are normalised to \\n first, so a file read in text mode on one platform and binary on another wraps the same way instead of leaving a stray glyph at every line end.

required width int | None

The line width in pixels, or None to split on explicit newlines only -- which is what an auto-sizing label wants, since its own width is whatever the text turns out to be.

required measure MeasureWidth

Measures a candidate line's pixel width.

required

Returns:

Type Description list[str]

At least one line; "" wraps to [""], not to [], so a caller

list[str]

can rely on the line count being the height in lines.

docs.text:
caret_index_at(
    text: str, offset: int, measure: MeasureWidth
) -> int

Return the caret index nearest offset pixels into text.

A caret sits between characters, so the answer is a boundary. The left half of a glyph puts the caret before it and the right half after.

Linear in the length of the text, measuring each prefix. Bisection is not used: with kerning, prefix widths need not be monotonic.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default text str

The string the caret is being placed in.

required offset int

Pixels from the start of the text. Values outside the text clamp to the ends rather than being an error -- a drag that leaves the widget is an ordinary thing to do.

required measure MeasureWidth

Measures a prefix's pixel width.

required

Returns:

Type Description int

An index in 0..len(text).

docs.title: pyguara.ui.theme_presets
docs.text:
Pre-built UI theme presets.

This module provides ready-to-use theme configurations for common use cases. All themes can be customized by cloning and modifying specific properties.

Each preset names only the base colours and lets ColorScheme.derive() fill the semantic roles -- surfaces, the text hierarchy, action states -- from them.

Example

from pyguara.ui.theme_presets import Themes from pyguara.ui.theme import set_theme

docs.title: Use dark theme
docs.text: set_theme(Themes.DARK)

docs.title: Customize a preset
docs.text: my_theme = Themes.LIGHT.clone() my_theme.colors.primary = Color(255, 0, 0) set_theme(my_theme)

docs.title: ThemeConstants
docs.text:
Accessor for the pre-built theme presets.

Each attribute access returns a fresh copy of the preset, so callers cannot corrupt the canonical definition for the rest of the process:

>>> my_theme = Themes.DARK          # already a private copy
>>> my_theme.colors.primary = Color(255, 0, 0)
>>> Themes.DARK.colors.primary     # unaffected
Color(r=70, g=130, b=180, a=255)

Pass one straight to set_theme(Themes.DARK) when you want it verbatim.

docs.title: ColorScheme dataclass
docs.text:
Standardized color palette using Color objects.

Two layers. The base five colours plus two overlays are the shorthand a theme is written in. The semantic roles below them (surfaces, a text hierarchy, edges, action states) are what components read.

Every semantic role the caller does not name is derived from the base colours. derive() also refuses an unknown role by name; the presets and pyguara.ui.design_system build theirs with it.

docs.title: derive classmethod
docs.text:
derive(
    *,
    primary: Color | None = None,
    secondary: Color | None = None,
    background: Color | None = None,
    text: Color | None = None,
    border: Color | None = None,
    **overrides: Color,
) -> ColorScheme

Build a full scheme from the base colours, then apply overrides.

This is the difference between a preset that only names five colours and one whose surfaces, edges and action states all belong to the same palette. Pass a role in overrides to state it outright -- which is what a design system does, having chosen every value deliberately rather than by rule.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default primary Color | None

The brand/action colour.

None secondary Color | None

The supporting accent, also the default focus ring.

None background Color | None

The canvas the UI sits on.

None text Color | None

The body text colour, and the far end of the contrast range every surface is lifted towards.

None border Color | None

The default edge colour.

None **overrides Color

Any role named here wins over the derived value.

{}

Returns:

Type Description ColorScheme

A scheme with every role populated.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

If overrides names something that is not a role.

docs.title: pyguara.ui.design_system
docs.text:
The PyGuara design system: brand tokens, themes, and the Cerrado look.

  • tokens: the brand palette, raw colours.
  • themes: cerrado_dusk() and cerrado_day(), ordinary UIThemes mapping those tokens onto the engine's semantic colour roles.
  • components and skin: a bevelled edge, a stamp shadow and the brand's button colourways.

Setting the theme re-skins every stock component. Use BevelButton or BevelPanel only where the raised edge is wanted.

Example

from pyguara.ui import set_theme from pyguara.ui.design_system import cerrado_dusk

set_theme(cerrado_dusk())

Identifiers are ASCII: the family is Guará, and the name is GUARA_500. Component dimensions are not tokens; each component keeps its own defaults.

docs.title: Animation
docs.text:
PyGuara's animation code comes in two independent halves:

Half Module Animates Tweening pyguara.animation any number or sequence of numbers over time Sprite animation pyguara.graphics.components.animation a Sprite's texture, frame by frame

They share nothing but the name. Pick whichever fits; a project often uses both.

docs.title: Tweening
docs.text:
A Tween interpolates a value from start_value to end_value over duration seconds, shaped by an easing function.

from pyguara.animation import Tween, TweenManager, EasingType

tween = Tween(
    start_value=(0.0, 0.0),
    end_value=(100.0, 50.0),
    duration=1.0,
    easing=EasingType.EASE_OUT_QUAD,
)
tween.start()

# every frame:
tween.update(dt)
x, y = tween.current_value

docs.title: Endpoint types
docs.text:
The two endpoints must have the same shape, and current_value comes back as the type that went in:

Endpoints current_value two numbers float two Vector2 Vector2 two Color Color, channels rounded and clamped two equal-length tuples tuple two equal-length lists list

That the type survives matters because the usual destination is an attribute: writing a plain tuple to transform.position is a bug that surfaces as an AttributeError several frames later, nowhere near the tween.

Color tweening is first-class — hit-flash white, poison tint, corpse fade — and overshooting easings are safe, because Color's own constructor clamps.

A mismatched or unsupported endpoint raises at construction, not mid-playback: a tween is usually built a long way from where it is ticked, and a shape error reported at tick time names a frame rather than a call site.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
Call Effect start() begin (or restart from the top) pause() / resume() freeze / unfreeze; update() still returns "alive" stop() reset to IDLE; update() becomes a no-op until start() update(dt) advance; returns False once the tween has completed

Read-only: current_value, progress (0–1), is_playing, is_complete.

docs.title: Delay, loops, yoyo
docs.text:
• delay — seconds to wait after start() before the first movement. Applied once; loop repeats do not re-wait.
  • loops — 0 plays once, -1 loops forever, N plays once and then repeats N more times (N + 1 playthroughs total).
  • yoyo — on each loop, swap the direction instead of snapping back to the start, so the value ping-pongs.
  • on_update(value) fires every frame the tween moves; on_complete() fires once, only at final completion (never on an intermediate loop, never on an infinite loop).

A single update(dt) whose dt spans several whole loops resolves one loop boundary and carries the remaining time forward, catching up over the next few frames rather than firing every boundary at once. Clamp dt upstream if a lag spike must not stutter a tween.

docs.title: TweenManager
docs.text:
TweenManager owns a bag of tweens, ticks them, and drops each one when it completes.

from pyguara.animation import Tween, TweenManager

manager = TweenManager()
manager.add(tween)   # returns the tween, for chaining
tween.start()

# in your system's update():
manager.update(dt)

Nothing in the engine updates a TweenManager for you — call manager.update(dt) from a system or scene you own. For tweening an entity's properties, reach for tween_property() instead; that path is ticked for you. Two Tween instances are equal only when they are the same object, so a manager can hold many identically configured tweens (five enemies flashing white) without them aliasing each other. pause_all(), resume_all(), stop_all(), clear(), tween_count and active_tweens round out the surface. stop_all() also clears; a tween that is add()ed but never start()ed (or is stop()ped) stays in the bag until you remove() or clear() it.

docs.title: Easing
docs.text: pyguara.animation.easing provides EasingType and 31 functions across the usual families — quad, cubic, quart, quint, sine, expo, circ, elastic, back, bounce, each in in / out / in-out. Call one directly, or go through ease(t, easing_type), which clamps t to [0, 1] first. Elastic and back deliberately overshoot outside [0, 1]; the rest stay within it.

docs.title: Tweening entity properties
docs.text:
from pyguara.animation import tween_property

tween_property(entity, "transform.position", to=target,
               duration=0.3, easing=EasingType.EASE_OUT_QUAD)

That is the whole of it. TweenSystem is registered on every scene's SystemManager (priority 120), so the value is written every tick and the binding is dropped when it finishes.

Before this, tweening one property was about forty lines per effect: hold a reference, own a TweenManager, tick it in a system you wrote, read current_value, write it back.

docs.title: Paths
docs.text:
The first segment names a component the way entity.transform does; the rest walk attributes from there.

tween_property(entity, "transform.position", to=Vector2(100, 0), duration=0.4)
tween_property(entity, "sprite.color", to=Color(255, 0, 0), duration=0.1)
tween_property(entity, "transform.rotation", to=3.14, duration=1.0)

The write replaces the final attribute rather than mutating it, which is the only approach that works for a value type: Vector2 is immutable, and Color's channels are clamped on construction.

A path that does not resolve raises PropertyPathError at the call, not later. A tween that quietly does nothing is worse to debug than one that refuses to start.

docs.title: What a second tween does
docs.text:
The start point is read from the property itself, so a call interrupting an earlier tween of the same path begins from wherever it had got to — which is what makes a knockback retargeted mid-flight look continuous rather than snapping back.

By default a new tween replaces any tween already running on that exact path. Two tweens writing one property every frame is never what anyone wanted: the last writer wins and the result depends on binding order. Pass replace=False if you really mean both.

stop_property(entity, "transform.position")   # leaves the value where it got to
stop_tweens(entity)                           # everything on this entity

docs.title: Why a scene system, not a global manager
docs.text:
An app-wide TweenManager outlives the scene whose entities it animates, and goes on writing to components of entities that no longer exist. That is the same leak #55 fixed for coroutines. A scene-owned system cannot have it: the scene's SystemManager.cleanup() takes the tweens with it.

Priority 120 puts it first in the engine band, before steering, AI and the scene's own update — otherwise every reader is one frame behind the animation it can see on screen.

docs.title: Timelines
docs.text:
Chaining through nested on_complete callbacks stops being readable past two steps, and cannot express "these two at once, then that one" at all. Combat juice is naturally a timeline.

from pyguara.animation import Timeline

(Timeline()
    .then(wind_up)
    .wait(0.05)
    .call(spawn_hitbox)
    .parallel(knockback, screen_shake)
    .then(recover)
    .start())

A Timeline ticks with the same update(dt) -> bool contract a Tween has (the Animatable protocol), so a TweenManager holds either without knowing which, and a timeline can be a step inside another timeline.

Method Does then(animatable) Run it, then continue wait(seconds) Pause call(fn) Call it, in order with the steps around it parallel(*animatables) Run them together; finish with the slowest

loops follows Tween.loops: 0 once, -1 forever, N extra repeats. on_complete fires once, after the last loop. stop() halts every step, so an interrupted parallel group does not leave its members running, and does not fire on_complete.

Two timing rules:

  • Leftover time carries into the next step, in the same call. Five 1 ms steps would otherwise take one frame each — 83 ms at 60 Hz for 5 ms of animation.
  • A step that takes no time runs in the same call too, so then(tween).call(spawn_hitbox) does not fire the callback a frame after the tween it belongs to. At most one full pass over the steps happens per call, so a looping timeline of nothing but callbacks misbehaves rather than hanging the frame.

An empty timeline is complete, not stuck: a game building one from a filtered list of effects should not hang when the filter matches nothing.

docs.title: Sprite animation
docs.text:
A clip is an ordered list of textures plus a frame rate. An Animator plays one clip at a time and writes the current frame onto a Sprite.

Animator is a data-only component — the clip table and the playback cursor — so the behaviour that moves that cursor is free functions beside it, the same split Transform/set_parent and Health/apply_damage use. Import them from the same module.

from pyguara.graphics.components.animation import (
    AnimationClip,
    Animator,
    add_clip,
    play_clip,
)

animator = Animator(sprite)
add_clip(animator, AnimationClip("run", run_frames, frame_rate=12.0, loop=True))
add_clip(animator, AnimationClip("hit", hit_frames, frame_rate=20.0, loop=False))

play_clip(animator, "run")             # no-op if "run" is already playing
play_clip(animator, "run", force_reset=True)  # restart from frame 0

AnimationClip rejects an empty frame list or a non-positive frame_rate at construction. advance_animator(animator, dt) catches up every whole frame the dt covers, so a lag spike or a host slower than the clip's frame_rate does not drop frames or drift behind. A clip that ends, ONCE or LOOP_TIMES, stops on its last frame; is_finished then reports True (and is_playing False). play_clip() with an unknown clip name logs a warning and does nothing.

docs.title: Playback modes
docs.text:
loop could only say "start over" or "stop". mode says more:

PlaybackMode At the last frame ONCE Stop there LOOP Back to frame 0 PING_PONG Play backwards, then forwards again LOOP_TIMES Loop loop_count times, then stop

PING_PONG is what an idle bob or a breathing loop wants: the hard cut back to frame 0 is visible as a hitch. It walks frame by frame rather than computing the destination, so a lag spike still fires every frame event it crossed, including the turn at the far end.

loop remains the serialized form and mode is derived from it when nothing set one, so an existing clip or prefab file keeps working. Setting both inconsistently resolves in mode's favour — it is the more specific statement.

docs.title: Playback speed
docs.text:
animator.playback_speed = 2.0    # haste
animator.playback_speed = 0.0    # hitstop

A multiplier over the clip's own frame_rate, so a haste or slow buff is one field rather than a faster copy of every clip. Zero holds the cursor without clearing is_playing, which is what a hitstop wants: the animation resumes where it was instead of restarting. A negative speed holds too — running a clip backwards is PING_PONG's business, and a negative multiplier is far more likely a sign flip in a buff calculation.

docs.title: Building clips from a sheet
docs.text:
sheet = SpriteSheet("assets/hero.png", texture_factory)
walk = sheet.clip("walk_down", 32, 32, row=1, count=8, fps=12.0)

slice_grid() returns a flat row-major list, so building a clip meant slicing frames[8:16] by hand — the one place a sheet's layout leaked into game code. A row, not an arbitrary span, because that is how sheets are laid out: one action per row. A row past the end, or a count larger than the row, raises: a clip quietly short of frames animates wrongly rather than visibly failing.

frame_events indices are relative to the clip, not to the sheet.

docs.title: Frames of different lengths
docs.text:
AnimationClip("attack", frames, frame_durations=(0.08, 0.08, 0.25, 0.05))

frame_durations holds each frame for its own time, in seconds, one per frame: a wind-up that lingers, a strike that snaps. When it is set it decides the timing and frame_rate is not read. Catch-up, frame events, the playback modes and playback_speed all work as they do at a fixed rate; a ping-pong holds each frame for its own time in both directions. A list of the wrong length, or with a duration that is not positive, raises.

docs.title: Importing from Aseprite
docs.text:
from pyguara.graphics.aseprite import load_aseprite

sheet = load_aseprite("assets/hero.json", texture_factory)
add_clip(animator, sheet.clip("idle"))
add_clip(animator, sheet.clip("attack"))

In Aseprite, File > Export Sprite Sheet with JSON Data ticked writes an image and a JSON file. load_aseprite() reads the pair, through pyguara.assets, so it works from a pack too.

In Aseprite In the engine A tag One AnimationClip, under the tag's name A frame's duration That frame's entry in frame_durations; a plain frame_rate when every frame of the tag is as long Direction: forward, reverse LOOP, with the frames reversed for reverse Direction: ping-pong, ping-pong reverse PING_PONG A repeat count on a tag LOOP_TIMES with that count No tags at all One looping clip of every frame, named after the file "Trim" on export Each frame is put back on a canvas of the sprite's size, so a clip's frames stay aligned

Both JSON layouts, "Array" and "Hash", are read. The image is looked for beside the JSON under the file name the JSON gives, whatever folder the artist exported from; image_path= names it outright.

sheet.frames and sheet.durations hold the whole timeline, for a game that builds its own clips. sheet.clip(name) raises a KeyError that lists the tags there are.

What it refuses, with an AsepriteFormatError that says what to change: a JSON file that is not a sprite sheet export, a frame outside the image (the JSON and image are from different exports), a rotated frame, and a ping-pong tag with a repeat count, which the engine has no playback mode for.

A tag's clip loops unless it has a repeat count. For an attack that plays once and then reports is_finished, give the tag a repeat of 1 in Aseprite.

docs.title: State machine
docs.text:
AnimationStateMachine sits on top of an Animator: one state per clip, with transitions between them.

from pyguara.graphics.components.animation import (
    AnimationState,
    AnimationStateMachine,
    AnimationTransition,
    TransitionCondition,
    add_state,
    set_default_state,
    transition_to,
)

fsm = AnimationStateMachine(sprite, animator)
add_state(fsm, AnimationState("idle", idle_clip))
add_state(
    fsm,
    AnimationState(
        "attack",
        attack_clip,
        transitions=[
            AnimationTransition(
                "attack", "idle", TransitionCondition.ANIMATION_END
            )
        ],
        on_complete=lambda: print("attack done"),
    ),
)
set_default_state(fsm, "idle")   # enters the state and starts its clip

transition_to(fsm, "attack")     # manual switch; returns False if already there
  • AnimationState carries on_enter, on_exit and on_complete callbacks. on_complete fires once when a non-looping clip finishes, not every frame it then sits on its last frame; re-entering the state re-arms it.
  • AnimationTransition.condition is either ANIMATION_END (fires once the state's clip finishes) or IMMEDIATE (fires on the tick after the state is entered — useful for a one-shot intro that hands off to a loop). priority breaks ties; the highest-priority eligible transition wins, and at most one transition fires per update.
  • current_state_name reports where the machine is.

docs.title: AnimationSystem
docs.text: AnimationSystem is registered automatically on every Scene's SystemManager (priority 300) and ticked at the fixed timestep. Each tick it calls advance_state_machine() on every AnimationStateMachine, then advance_animator() on every standalone Animator whose entity does not also have a state machine (the machine drives its own animator). You do not call it, and you should not advance animators a second time from scene code.

docs.title: Directional animation (kit)
docs.text:
Every game this engine targets is top-down, and every top-down character has N actions × 4 or 8 facings. pyguara.kits.topdown_movement carries that:

from pyguara.kits.topdown_movement import (
    DirectionalAnimator, DirectionalClipSet, DirectionalAnimationSystem,
)

clips = DirectionalClipSet(actions=("idle", "walk", "attack"), ways=8)
for name in clips.every_clip_name():
    add_clip(animator, sheet.clip(name, 32, 32, row=rows[name]))

entity.add_component(DirectionalAnimator(clips, action="walk"))
scene.system_manager.register(DirectionalAnimationSystem(em), priority=500)

Names follow the usual convention ("walk_down", "attack_up_left"), so a game lists only the exceptions in overrides. A 4-way set maps a diagonal onto its left/right cardinal rather than up/down: a profile view reads as a three-quarter view far better than a back view does.

facing_from_vector(v, ways=8) is the piece everyone writes by hand, with the two details everyone gets wrong first:

  • Screen Y grows downward, so a negative Y is up.
  • A zero vector returns None, not a default. A stopped character must keep facing where it last faced; snapping to DOWN on every halt is the other classic bug — which is why DirectionalAnimator.facing is stored rather than recomputed.

The system reads velocity from TopDownBody when there is one, and otherwise from how far the Transform moved since the last tick, so a character driven by a tween, a pathfinder or a script still faces the right way. It asks for the clip every frame and relies on play_clip() ignoring a re-request for the clip already playing, so walking in a straight line does not restart the cycle sixty times a second.

The action is the game's business; the system only ever changes the facing.

A kit rather than core: 8-way facing is a genre's vocabulary, and nothing in pyguara.graphics should know what "down" means.

docs.title: Audio System
docs.text: pyguara.audio plays music and sound effects, with optional spatial (position-aware) playback and a bus hierarchy for grouped volume control. Game code never touches pygame's mixer directly.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
1. IAudioSystem (pyguara.audio.audio_system) — the backend contract: music streaming, one-shot and looping SFX, spatial placement, buses, per-sound mix updates, and the optional capabilities below. PygameAudioSystem is the shipped implementation; it is registered as a singleton by the application bootstrap.
  2. AudioManager (pyguara.audio.manager) — a convenience wrapper over IAudioSystem that loads clips by path through the ResourceManager, tracks the current music track, and forwards volume calls. Also a bootstrap singleton.
  3. AudioSourceSystem (pyguara.audio.audio_source_system) — the ECS system that drives AudioSource / AudioEmitter / AudioListener components. A scene registers it automatically (priority 250).
from pyguara.audio import AudioManager

audio = container.get(AudioManager)
audio.play_music("music/theme.ogg", loop=True)
sound = audio.play_sfx("sfx/jump.wav", volume=0.8)

docs.title: Choosing a backend
docs.text:
AudioConfig.backend is native, the default, or pygame; the environment variable is PYGUARA_AUDIO_BACKEND. There is deliberately no auto, because it would give the same game different capabilities on different machines, and native fails at startup if the extension cannot be imported -- which is what a checkout with no Rust toolchain, or nothing built yet, will see, and why pygame is kept.

To rule the native mixer out while debugging, set PYGUARA_AUDIO_BACKEND=pygame, which needs the pygame extra.

NativeAudioSystem decodes with symphonia and mixes in Rust (rust/src/mixer.rs), writing to the sound card through cpal -- no pygame.mixer, and no pygame at all. The policy is the default backend's, so a game hears the same mix: buses, spatial attenuation and pan, 32 voices with lower priorities stolen first. On top of it:

  • Pitch is continuous, and changes duration. A voice steps through its clip by its pitch, so 2.0 is an octave up and half as long, and 1.003 is 1.003 -- nothing is rendered or cached per pitch. The range is 0.25 to 4.0, and outside it raises ValueError.
  • Interpolation is linear, so a large upward pitch aliases. Inaudible at a few percent, and not meant for wide pitch sweeps.
  • Loop points wrap in the mixer, sample-exact, in the same loop that plays the voice: an intro, then loops laps of the region (-1 forever). No update() is needed for them and a frame stall cannot reach them.
  • Bus volumes reach sounds already playing. pygame fixed a channel's loudness when it started; here moving the SFX slider moves a loop under way.
  • Music decodes off the frame, on a worker thread, and starts when ready, fading in; is_music_playing() is true while it decodes.
  • It also reads .flac, which the default backend's loader does not.
  • A clip must come through NativeSoundLoader, which bootstrap registers for this backend, given the system's mixer: clips are converted to the rate the mixer runs at, which on a device is the device's own. A clip from another loader raises TypeError.
  • With no output device it runs silent, on a clock. Sounds still end when they would have, as pygame's dummy driver did, and the boot log says so. NativeAudioSystem.output reads device: <name>, silent: <why> or offline.

output="offline" is a mixer that advances only when mixer.render(frames) is called. The tests and tools/audio_capture.py (capture_native) use it to measure what would have reached the speaker.

Measured, 44.1 kHz stereo Start a pitched voice, and stop it 4 us Mix one 60 Hz frame (735 samples) of 32 voices 0.12 ms, on the audio thread Load and convert one second of audio 1.3 ms A clip in memory 353 KB per second (stereo float), once

The device is cpal on Windows and macOS. On Linux it is ALSA, loaded with dlopen when a mixer opens the device rather than linked: a linked libasound.so.2 made the whole extension fail to import on a machine without it (a slim container, a server), taking every native store with it. Now a missing ALSA is one more reason the mixer is silent, and says so. It plays 16-bit stereo at 48 kHz to ALSA's default device, which on a desktop is PipeWire's or PulseAudio's plugin; PYGUARA_ALSA_DEVICE names another (null takes samples with no card, which is how tests/test_native_alsa.py runs the path). A build without the audio-output cargo feature has no device and always runs silent.

symphonia is MPL-2.0: file-level copyleft, fine to link unmodified from an MIT engine, but the wheel distributes it.

docs.title: Optional capabilities
docs.text:
Three features cannot be expressed by every mixer: per-play pitch, loop points inside a clip, and DSP on a bus. PygameAudioSystem, the default, expresses none of them; NativeAudioSystem expresses the first two. Each is declared through AudioCapability and declined by raising UnsupportedAudioCapability, so a request a backend cannot honour fails where it was made.

from pyguara.audio import AudioCapability

if AudioCapability.PITCH in audio.capabilities:
    audio.play_sfx("sfx/hit.wav", pitch=random.uniform(0.9, 1.1))
else:
    audio.play_sfx("sfx/hit.wav")

Every capability has a request that means not asked for — pitch=1.0, loop_start=None, an empty effect list — so code that uses none of them runs on any backend. A no-op that accepted pitch=1.2 and played at the original speed would report success for a sound that is wrong, with nothing for the caller to check; this is the same reasoning that made ShapeType.SEGMENT raise instead of returning None.

Capability What it adds PygameAudioSystem NativeAudioSystem PITCH pitch= on either play_sfx no — the mixer resamples at load and plays at its own rate yes LOOP_POINTS loop_start= / loop_end= no — Channel.play takes a loop count and nothing else yes BUS_EFFECTS set_bus_effects(bus, [...]) no — a channel's only processing is a left/right gain pair no — needs the device, see below

Loop points from a .meta sidecar warn instead of raising. AudioMeta carries loop_start / loop_end, and those are the asset describing itself rather than a call site asking for something. An incapable backend logs once per clip and loops the whole file: refusing would let one line of metadata silence a sound that worked before anybody wrote it. An explicit argument still raises. A malformed range (negative, or inverted) raises ValueError on every backend, before the capability is consulted — the same bad input should read the same way everywhere.

Bus effects are a settled seam, not a shipped feature: LowPassFilter, HighPassFilter and Reverb are descriptions a backend interprets, applied in list order. Nothing implements them yet, which is why asking for one raises and get_bus_effects reports () rather than the chain you handed it — holding a chain that will never be applied would describe an effect nobody can hear.

docs.title: Music
docs.text:
play_music(path, loop=True, fade_ms=1000) streams one track at a time from disk (pygame's mixer.music). stop_music, pause_music, resume_music and is_music_playing control it; get_current_music() returns the path AudioManager last started, or None.

Music volume follows the music bus and the master bus: changing either re-applies immediately to the playing stream.

docs.title: Sound effects and handles
docs.text:
play_sfx(clip, volume, loops, priority, bus, pitch, loop_start, loop_end) plays a clip and returns a SoundHandle, or None if the clip is invalid or every channel is busy with an equal-or-higher priority sound.

  • A handle is opaque. Its token is minted per play, never reused in a process, and means nothing to a caller. stop_sfx, is_sound_active and set_sound_mix all take one; a handle whose sound has ended resolves to nothing, so they become no-ops rather than acting on a stranger.
  • That is the point. A mixer channel number is recycled the instant its sound ends, so stop_sfx(7) on a channel int held for a few frames stopped whatever had taken channel 7 over. Channel 0 was also falsy, so if channel_id: dropped a real sound.
  • loops: 0 plays once, -1 loops forever, n repeats n extra times.
  • priority (AudioPriority.LOW…CRITICAL): when no channel is free, a new sound steals the channel of the lowest-priority sound below its own priority. Same-or-higher priority sounds are never interrupted.

Loudness and stereo pan are applied to the channel, never to the Sound object — the ResourceManager hands every concurrent play of one clip the same Sound, so setting its volume would bleed across all of them.

docs.title: Limiting one sound
docs.text:
Ten hits landing in one frame start ten copies of the same clip at once, which sounds like one hit, much louder. AudioManager.set_sfx_limit caps it:

audio = container.get(AudioManager)
audio.set_sfx_limit("sfx/hit.wav", max_voices=4, min_interval=0.03)
  • max_voices is the most copies playing together. A copy stops counting once is_sound_active says it has ended.
  • min_interval is the seconds between two starts, in real time.
  • A play over the limit is dropped, and play_sfx returns None. It isn't queued, which would be heard late, and it doesn't cut off a copy already playing.
  • The limit is per clip path. play_sfx_clip reads it from the clip.
  • Calling it with both arguments at their defaults removes the limit. get_sfx_limit returns what is set.

docs.title: One-shot lifecycle
docs.text: A one-shot sound finishes on its own with no callback. IAudioSystem exposes is_sound_active(handle), which is True only while that exact sound is still playing — it returns False once the sound has ended or its channel has been recycled by an unrelated sound. AudioSourceSystem calls it every frame to reconcile AudioSource state; you rarely call it directly.

docs.title: Placeholder sounds
docs.text:
Before any real sounds exist, pyguara.audio.placeholder builds short stand-ins (a thud, a blip, a hiss) from simple tones and noise, and writes them as .wav files the game loads like any other. When a real recording arrives it replaces the file, with no code change.

From code, the functions combine like this:

from pyguara.audio.placeholder import envelope, mix, rng_for, sine, transient, write_wav

rng = rng_for("hit")
hit = envelope(mix(transient(0.03, 0.5, rng), sine(140.0, 0.12, 0.6)), decay_rate=20.0)
write_wav(Path("assets/audio/hit.wav"), hit)

From data, the same tree as JSON. Each node is an object with one key, naming a function, holding that function's arguments; envelope and concat take what they wrap as of, and mix takes a list:

{"hit": {"envelope": {"decay_rate": 20.0, "of": {"mix": [
    {"transient": {"duration": 0.03, "amplitude": 0.5}},
    {"sine": {"freq": 140.0, "duration": 0.12, "amplitude": 0.6}}]}}}}

pyguara sounds data/sounds.json assets/audio/
Node Arguments sine, square freq, duration, amplitude (1.0) sweep freq_start, freq_end, duration, amplitude (1.0) noise, transient duration, amplitude envelope of, attack (0.005 s), decay_rate (8.0) concat of (a list), gap (0.01 s) mix a list
  • Every recipe is checked before anything is written. A mistake names its place in the tree and the closest valid name, for example hit > envelope > of > mix[1] > sine: unknown argument 'frq'; did you mean 'freq'?
  • The output is deterministic. Noise is seeded by the sound's own name, so editing one sound leaves every other file byte-identical, and a rebuild with no edits changes nothing. --seed rerolls all of them.
  • Files are mono, 16-bit, 22,050 Hz. Anything past full scale is clipped.

Quintal do Cerrado's assets/audio/generate_placeholder_sfx.py is a worked example in code.

docs.title: Spatial audio
docs.text:
Attach components to entities that also carry a Transform:

Component Purpose AudioListener Marks the "ears" (usually the camera/player). One active listener per scene; its position drives every spatial calculation. AudioSource A persistent or looping sound that follows its entity. spatial=True (default) attenuates and pans it by distance to the listener, updated every frame while it plays. AudioEmitter A fire-and-forget one-shot at the entity's position. remove_after_play=True (default) drops the component once it has played. 
entity.add_component(Transform(position=Vector2(400, 300)))
entity.add_component(AudioSource(clip_path="sfx/engine_loop.wav", loop=True))
entity.get_component(AudioSource).play()   # or auto_play=True / play_on_awake=True

auto_play fires once, when the source is first processed; a one-shot that ends is not restarted (use loop=True for that, or call play() again). AudioSource.is_playing reflects reality — it goes back to False when a non-looping sound ends.

docs.title: SpatialAudioConfig
docs.text:
Controls the distance model (AudioSourceSystem.set_spatial_config, or PygameAudioSystem.set_spatial_config):

Field Meaning reference_distance Distance (world units) within which volume is 100%. Must be > 0. max_distance Distance at which the sound is silent. Must be > reference_distance. rolloff_factor How fast volume falls between the two (1.0 ≈ realistic inverse-distance; < 1 slower). Must be >= 0. pan_strength Stereo spread from horizontal offset (0.0 mono … 1.0 full). Must be >= 0.

Out-of-range values raise ValueError at construction — an inverted or zero range is a divide-by-zero in the pan maths and a hard volume cliff in the attenuation maths, not a soft degradation.

docs.title: Buses and volume
docs.text:
Four buses in a fixed hierarchy: master → sfx / music / voice (AudioBusType). Effective volume walks the chain (bus.volume × … × master.volume); a muted bus contributes 0.

audio_system.set_bus_volume(AudioBusType.SFX, 0.5)
audio_system.set_bus_muted(AudioBusType.MASTER, True)

Buses are volume-only on the shipped backend. set_bus_effects is the seam for DSP; see Optional capabilities.

set_master_volume / set_sfx_volume / set_music_volume are shorthands for the master / sfx / music buses.

!!! note "Known limitation" A bus or master volume change re-applies to the music stream and to spatial SFX (which are re-mixed every frame), but not to already-playing non-spatial SFX — those keep the volume they were started with until they end. Set bus volumes before triggering sounds, or drive important sustained sounds through an AudioSource.

docs.title: Backend notes
docs.text:
A machine with no audio output still runs. If the mixer can't open, because the device is missing or disabled, both backends log a warning and fall back to SDL's dummy driver. Everything keeps working and nothing is heard, so a game doesn't need to handle this itself.

PygameAudioSystem wraps pygame.mixer (pygame-ce), which pip install 'pyguara[pygame]' installs. It allocates 32 channels by default. shutdown() stops all audio and releases the device; it is idempotent and is called from Application.shutdown().

It reports AudioCapability.NONE, and the three things it cannot do are the reason a second backend is wanted rather than a longer feature list on this one — see #72, whose P1 "sound variation" needs PITCH.

For headless use (tests, CI) set SDL_AUDIODRIVER=dummy before the mixer initialises — playback then advances in real time but produces no sound.

docs.title: Command-Line Tools
docs.text:
pyguara.cli is the offline toolbox — things you run from a shell against a project on disk, never from inside a running game. It installs one console script:

[project.scripts]
pyguara = "pyguara.cli:main"

main is a Click group of sub-commands:

Command What it does pyguara new Create a project that runs: one scene, an entry point, an assets folder. pyguara build Package a game into a standalone executable (wraps PyInstaller). pyguara dist Generate per-store upload scripts and platform icons. pyguara atlas Pack a folder of sprites into one texture atlas + JSON metadata. pyguara sounds Build placeholder sound effects from a JSON recipe file, one .wav each. pyguara studio Studio's agent surface: ops, mcp and instructions. See Studio and Agent Integration. 
pyguara --help
pyguara --version
pyguara build --help
pyguara atlas --help

build and atlas exit non-zero on failure (1 for a usage/tool error, the PyInstaller exit code for a failed build), so they compose in scripts and CI.

docs.title: pyguara new
docs.text:
pyguara new my-game
cd my-game
python -m my_game

Creates my-game/ and writes into it:

File What it is my_game/__main__.py The entry point: the window's title and size, then pyguara.run(MainScene) my_game/scenes.py One scene, with a component and a box that moves at the fixed rate pyproject.toml The project, depending on the engine version that created it, with a my-game script assets/ Empty, for textures, sounds, fonts and data AGENTS.md and its shims What pyguara studio instructions writes; --no-instructions leaves them out

The package is the name in lower case with hyphens as underscores. A name that could not be imported is refused, as is one that would shadow pyguara or a standard library module. So is a target directory that already has something in it; --directory puts the project somewhere other than ./NAME.

No file edits sys.path: python -m my_game runs from the project folder, and pip install -e . adds a my-game command. Run either from the project folder: the engine reads config/ and assets/ and writes logs/ and saves/ relative to the working directory.

docs.title: pyguara build
docs.text:
Compiles an entry script and its assets into a distributable bundle.

# onedir bundle (default) into dist/
pyguara build games/guara_falcao/main.py --output dist/guara_falcao

# one self-contained file, custom name and icon
pyguara build games/true_coral/main.py --onefile --name TrueCoral \
    --icon games/true_coral/assets/icon.ico

docs.title: How it runs
docs.text:
build shells out to PyInstaller through the current interpreter — python -m PyInstaller …, not a bare pyinstaller on PATH — so it works inside a uv/venv install where the console script may not be exported. import PyInstaller failing prints an install hint and exits 1; you need the build extra:

uv sync --extra build      # or: pip install -e .[build]

docs.title: Asset bundling
docs.text:
With no -a/--assets, build looks next to the entry script for a folder named assets, resources, or data (any case) and bundles the first it finds. Pass -a one or more times to be explicit; each becomes a PyInstaller --add-data entry preserving the folder name at runtime.

A default set of hidden imports (pygame, numpy, PIL, msgpack, …) is always passed so the frozen build finds the engine's backends; add project-specific ones with --hidden-import.

docs.title: Asset packs
docs.text:
--pack bakes the asset folders (auto-detected or given with -a) into one file, <name>.pak, and bundles that instead of the folders. An install then holds one asset file rather than hundreds:

pyguara build main.py --pack
  • Each folder keeps its own name inside the pack (assets/sprites/hero.png), the path --add-data would have given the loose file. Paths the game's code builds, such as Path(__file__).parent / "assets" / ..., find it unchanged.
  • The frozen game mounts every .pak in its bundle on its first asset read, through pyguara.assets. There is nothing to call. Run from source, nothing is mounted and the loose files are read.
  • Already-compressed files (PNG, JPEG, OGG, MP3, FLAC) are stored as they are; everything else is deflated. Hidden files and __pycache__ are left out; .meta sidecars are kept.
  • The pack is reproducible: the same folders bake to the same bytes.
  • A game's own file reads must go through pyguara.assets too (assets.read_text(path) rather than open(path)), or they will not find packed files. See docs/systems/resources.md, "Packed assets".

docs.title: Crash reports
docs.text:
A build is --windowed by default, so it has no console: an unhandled exception closes the window and the player sees nothing else. Install the crash reporter first thing in the entry script, before the application is built, so a failure at startup is caught too:

from pyguara.crash import install_crash_reporter

install_crash_reporter("Guara & Falcao")
app = create_application()

A crash then writes crash-<date>-<time>-<pid>.txt under crashes/ in the player's data directory: ~/.local/share/<game> on Linux, under %LOCALAPPDATA% on Windows, ~/Library/Application Support/<game> on macOS. It holds the traceback, the pyguara and Python versions, the platform, whether the build is frozen, the native store, the renderer and the GPU, and anything the game added with pyguara.crash.note(key, value), such as the level. The newest 20 are kept. Where there is a console, the report's path is printed and the traceback still follows.

It is opt-in because the folder is named after the game. Ctrl+C is not a crash, and an exception in a background thread, which does not end the program, is not reported. A report contains paths from the player's machine, home directory included, so it is theirs to send.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default Notes -o, --output dist/ Bundle destination. -n, --name entry-script stem Executable / bundle name. --onefile / --onedir --onedir Single file vs. a directory. --windowed / --console --windowed Hide the OS console on launch. --icon — Any format Pillow reads; converted to the host's. --bundle-id — macOS bundle identifier, e.g. com.studio.game. -a, --assets auto-detect Repeatable. Asset directories to bundle. --add-data — Repeatable. Raw src<sep>dst PyInstaller spec. --hidden-import — Repeatable. Extra modules to force-include. --clean off Wipe the PyInstaller cache first. --debug off --debug=all. --pack off Bake the asset folders into one <name>.pak instead of bundling them loose. --dry-run off Print the PyInstaller command and stop.

After a successful build, the generated build/ work directory and the <name>.spec file are removed from --output. The reported Output: path points at the executable — for --onedir that is <output>/<name>/<name>[.exe], one level inside the bundle directory.

docs.title: Icons
docs.text:
--icon takes any image Pillow can read, and converts it to the format the host toolchain needs — .ico on Windows, .icns on macOS, .png elsewhere — into the PyInstaller work directory, not the shipped bundle. This matters because PyInstaller converts nothing and fails on Windows given a .png, so a project with one logo.png could not be built there. Pass an already-correct file and it is used untouched.

PyInstaller cannot cross-compile, so "the host" and "the target" are the same thing: a Windows .exe is built on Windows. pyguara dist icons writes all three formats at once if you want them committed.

Use --dry-run to see exactly what would be executed without needing PyInstaller installed:

pyguara build main.py --onefile --dry-run

docs.title: pyguara dist
docs.text:
Generates the per-store scripts that take a built game to players. It writes scripts and never uploads: that needs steamcmd or butler, a store account, and for Steam a Steam Guard code, none of which belongs inside a game engine.

pyguara dist icons logo.png --out build/icons
pyguara dist steam --app-id 480 --depot-id 481 --content dist/MyGame
pyguara dist itch --target studio/my-game --content dist/MyGame --version 0.1.0

docs.title: pyguara dist icons
docs.text: Writes icon.ico (multi-size: 16, 32, 48, 64, 128, 256 — Windows picks one per context, and a single-size file is a blurry taskbar icon), icon.icns and icon.png from one source image. Sizes larger than the source are skipped rather than upscaled.

docs.title: pyguara dist steam
docs.text:
Writes a content-builder script set into --out (default dist/steam/):

file what it is scripts/app_build_<appid>.vdf the build: which depots, which branch scripts/depot_build_<depotid>.vdf the depot: which files go in it upload.sh / upload.bat steamcmd +run_app_build around the above dev/steam_appid.txt development only — see below README.md the manual steps, including Steam Guard

Two defaults are deliberate. Preview is 1, because a wrong ContentRoot produces a completely successful build of the wrong files and the only sign is the file list. SetLive is empty, because naming a branch there publishes to customers the moment the upload finishes.

steam_appid.txt is never put in the content root, and the depot script excludes it by name as well. It overrides the App ID Steam supplies and makes SteamAPI_RestartAppIfNecessary return false, so a customer who launches the executable directly plays with no Steam client attached — no overlay, no achievements, no cloud saves, and no error. Copy it next to the executable while testing locally only.

One known uncertainty, stated in the generated README too: the depot script's root key is DepotBuildConfig, which is what the SDK's bundled samples and working upload pipelines use, while Valve's documentation page spells the same block DepotBuild. If steamcmd rejects the file, diff it against sdk/tools/ContentBuilder/scripts and trust those.

docs.title: pyguara dist itch
docs.text:
Writes push.sh wrapping butler push <dir> user/game:channel.

The channel name is not cosmetic: itch.io reads it to decide which platform an upload is for, and one naming no platform is tagged for none and offered to nobody — while butler reports success. So a channel that matches none of win, windows, mac, osx, linux, android is refused, with the list in the error. Several in one name is fine, as butler's own example win-linux-mac-stable shows. With no --channel, the host platform's name is used.

docs.title: pyguara atlas
docs.text:
Packs every image in a directory into one atlas texture using a shelf-packing algorithm (sprites sorted tallest-first, laid into horizontal rows), and writes JSON metadata the engine's ResourceManager.load_atlas reads back.

pyguara atlas -i assets/sprites/ -o build/atlas.png -m build/atlas.json
pyguara atlas -i assets/sprites/ -o build/atlas.png -s 4096 -p 4

Supported inputs: .png, .jpg, .jpeg, .bmp, .tga (non-RGBA images are converted). The scan is one directory deep, not recursive.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default Notes -i, --input (required) Directory of source sprites. -o, --output (required) Atlas PNG path. -m, --metadata — JSON metadata path. Omit to skip. -s, --size 2048 Atlas is a square size × size. -p, --padding 2 Transparent gutter around each sprite.

docs.title: Metadata shape
docs.text:
{
  "atlas_size": [2048, 2048],
  "padding": 2,
  "sprite_count": 3,
  "regions": {
    "player": { "x": 2, "y": 2, "width": 64, "height": 64,
                "original_size": [64, 64] }
  }
}

A region's name is the source filename without extension. sprite_count always equals len(regions).

docs.title: Failures are loud
docs.text:
The generator refuses ambiguous or impossible input rather than producing a subtly wrong atlas:

  • Stem collision. hero.png and hero.jpg in the same folder both want the region name hero. This raises ValueError naming the offending files — rename or remove one.
  • Sprite doesn't fit. A sprite larger than --size in either dimension (plus padding) raises — increase --size or shrink the sprite. (Width used to slip through and get silently cropped.)
  • Output inside the input. generate() excludes the resolved -o/-m paths from its own scan, so re-running with the atlas written back into the sprite folder does not ingest the previous atlas. Still cleaner to keep build output in its own directory.

docs.title: Two ways to invoke it
docs.text: pyguara atlas … and python -m pyguara.cli.atlas_generator … run the same Click command with the same options — the module entry point delegates straight to it.

docs.title: pyguara sounds
docs.text:
