Builds placeholder sound effects, so a game has audio to wire up before it has real assets.

pyguara sounds data/sounds.json assets/audio/
pyguara sounds data/sounds.json assets/audio/ --seed 7

RECIPES is a JSON object mapping each sound's name to its recipe: a tree of tones, noise and envelopes, in the format pyguara.audio.placeholder documents. Every recipe is checked before anything is written, and a bad one fails the command without leaving a partial set behind. --seed is shared by every sound; change it to reroll their noise.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: tests/test_build_tool.py covers argument assembly and the --dry-run / missing-PyInstaller paths with Click's CliRunner (a real PyInstaller run is not exercised). tests/test_atlas_tool.py covers load_images / pack / generate, the collision and size guards, and round-tripping the metadata through ResourceManager.load_atlas.

docs.title: Dev Tools
docs.text:
pyguara.dev holds development-only helpers. Today that is asset hot-reload: edit a texture, tilemap or data file on disk and the running game re-imports it without a restart.

It does not hot-reload Python code. An earlier HotReloadManager that reloaded modules at runtime was removed — it was never wired into the loop, reloaded on a background thread, and could not migrate instance state. Live code reload is a product decision the engine has not taken.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
Off by default. Enable it on the Application:

app = create_application()
app.enable_asset_hot_reload()      # optional poll_interval, default 0.5s
app.run(MyScene("main", event_dispatcher))

SandboxApplication calls enable_asset_hot_reload() for you, so a sandbox build has it from the start. The call is idempotent; there is no disable() — Application.shutdown() stops the watcher.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
AssetReloadWatcher wraps a PollingFileWatcher and bridges it to ResourceManager.reload():

  1. On start(), and periodically after, it reconciles its watch set with the ResourceManager cache — every cached resource whose path is a real file on disk is watched. Assets loaded later are picked up; evicted ones are dropped.
  2. The polling thread detects a modified file (mtime or size change) and queues the resource's cache key. It does not reload anything itself.
  3. Application._update() calls watcher.drain() once per frame, on the main thread. drain() calls ResourceManager.reload(key) for each queued asset, de-duplicating repeated changes to one reload, and returns the keys it reloaded.

The queue-then-drain split is deliberate: ResourceManager is not safe to mutate from under a running frame, so the reload always happens on the loop thread, never the watcher thread.

docs.title: The stale-reference caveat
docs.text:
reload() swaps the cache entry. Code that already holds the previous resource instance keeps that stale object — reload does not mutate it in place. Re-load() after a change to pick up the new instance:

class MyScene(Scene):
    def update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        # cheap: a cache hit unless the asset was just reloaded
        self._tiles = self.container.get(ResourceManager).load("level1", TileMap)

An asset held only through acquire() (never re-load()ed) will not visibly change until something re-fetches it.

docs.title: PollingFileWatcher
docs.text:
The watcher is usable on its own for any "run this when a file changes" need:

from pyguara.dev import PollingFileWatcher

watcher = PollingFileWatcher(poll_interval=0.5)
watcher.watch("assets/levels/1.json", on_level_changed)
watcher.watch_directory("assets/shaders", rebuild_shader, pattern="*.glsl")
watcher.start()
...
watcher.stop()

It polls modification time and size — cross-platform, no native dependency, not instantaneous. A change callback runs on the polling thread and may call back into the watcher (watch(), unwatch(), watched_count); the watcher fires callbacks with its lock released so that cannot deadlock. An exception from one callback is logged and does not stop the others or the poll loop.

check_now() runs one poll cycle synchronously and returns the changed paths — useful in tests or a manually pumped loop instead of start().

docs.title: Capability gaps
docs.text: Polling only — no inotify / FSEvents / ReadDirectoryChangesW backend, so detection lags by up to poll_interval and a burst of rapid saves is coalesced rather than debounced. The watch set follows the resource cache, so an asset that is not loaded yet is not watched (no "watch the whole assets/ tree" mode). These, and the stale-holder problem reload() leaves, are tracked under issue #40.

docs.title: Developer Tools
docs.text:
PyGuara ships an in-game developer overlay (pyguara.tools) drawn on the engine's own backend-agnostic UIRenderer -- no external GUI toolkit. It is a debug and inspection surface. A full scene-authoring application (level editor, animation editor, agentic authoring harness) is tracked separately as #53.

An earlier Dear ImGui editor (pyguara/editor) was removed: its pygame integration hard-imports OpenGL.GL, PyOpenGL was never a dependency, so it had never executed. Its useful parts were rebuilt as the tools below.

A second, working ImGui layer now exists beside them -- the ImGui editor layer -- drawing through the engine's own wgpu device instead of PyOpenGL. It lives in pyguara.studio, with the authoring application built on it; there is no pyguara/editor package any more. The two surfaces are independent: attaching the editor layer changes nothing about the overlay, and the overlay remains the only dev surface on the Pygame backend.

docs.title: Enabling the overlay
docs.text:
SandboxApplication wires the overlay in automatically:

from pyguara.application.bootstrap import create_sandbox_application

app = create_sandbox_application()
app.run(MyScene("main", app._event_dispatcher))

Press F12 to toggle the whole overlay, then a function key per tool.

Key Tool Purpose F1 PerformanceMonitor FPS, frame timing, counts F3 EventMonitor Rolling log of recent engine events F4 PhysicsDebugger Collision shape wireframes F8 ShortcutsPanel This table, in-game (read live from the ToolManager)

ShortcutsPanel builds its table from ToolManager.iter_shortcuts() at render time, so it stays in step with whatever SandboxApplication registered rather than a hand-kept copy.

docs.title: What the overlay does not do, and where it went
docs.text:
F2, F5, F6, F7 and F9 are unbound, and the gaps are deliberate rather than a renumbering: a developer reaching for the old key finds nothing there instead of something else.

Was Does what Now F5 HierarchyTool List entities, click to select Studio's Hierarchy panel F2 EntityInspector Inspect and live-edit components Studio's Inspector panel F9 TransformGizmo Translate/rotate/scale handles Studio's viewport gizmo F6 ConfigInspector Live-edit GameConfig, S to save Studio's Config panel F7 AssetsTool Browse resources, spawn from a DataResource Studio's Resources panel

The first three were duplicates, and the weaker of the two copies. Studio's gizmo is 814 lines against 353: it has drag state, handle hit-testing, axis locking, snapping and one undo entry per drag, where the overlay's drew arrows and read Q/W/E. Its Inspector routes an accepted edit through set_field, so the change lands on an undo stack and in an audit journal; the overlay's wrote straight onto the component. Keeping both meant two ways to change the world, only one of which kept a record.

The last two were not duplicates, and removing them removed capability. Both have since been rebuilt in Studio, as the Config and Resources panels. They went with the rest because they were built on the same widget layer, pyguara/tools/tweakable.py, and that layer is why none of these were good enough to keep: nothing in the overlay scrolls — a grep for scroll or wheel across the package returned nothing, so a list longer than its panel simply ran off the bottom — and its number editor stepped by a hard-coded 1.0 when you clicked the left or right half of a row, which cannot express a 0.5 damping value at all. Studio has a scrolling dockable surface, and its number fields take any value.

Screen-space only. PhysicsDebugger draws using Transform.position as a screen coordinate -- no camera transform. It lines up only with the camera at the origin at zoom 1. The world-to-screen unification (issue #23) is the fix.

docs.title: Authoring, as opposed to diagnosing
docs.text:
The overlay reports; it does not author. Everything that changes the world now lives in PyGuara Studio, which is attached explicitly and needs the wgpu backend:

from pyguara.application.bootstrap import create_application
from pyguara.studio import attach_studio

app = create_application()
attach_studio(app.container)
app.run(MyScene("game", app._event_dispatcher))

On the Pygame backend there is no authoring surface, and that is the honest statement of the trade. Studio and the editor layer need the GL context the render graph owns, and a Pygame window is a software surface with none. What that backend keeps is this overlay: frame timing, the event stream, collision wireframes and the shortcut table -- enough to debug a running game, not enough to build a scene in one.

Scene save/load remains available programmatically through SceneSerializer (save_scene / load_scene), and EntityManager.clear() is the supported way to empty a world before reloading -- it fires subscribe_entity_removed callbacks and flushes cached queries.

docs.title: Writing a custom tool
docs.text:
Subclass Tool and register it. Draw with the UIRenderer primitives (draw_rect, draw_line, draw_circle, draw_polygon, draw_text, draw_texture) -- never a GUI library.

from pyguara.tools.base import Tool
from pyguara.graphics.protocols import UIRenderer
from pyguara.common.types import Color, Rect, Vector2


class SpawnCounter(Tool):
    def __init__(self, container):
        super().__init__("spawn_counter", container)
        self._rect = Rect(20, 20, 200, 40)

    def update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        pass

    def render(self, renderer: UIRenderer) -> None:
        count = sum(1 for _ in self._entity_manager.get_all_entities())
        renderer.draw_rect(self._rect, Color(0, 0, 0, 200), 0)
        renderer.draw_text(
            f"Entities: {count}",
            Vector2(self._rect.x + 8, self._rect.y + 10),
            Color(255, 255, 255),
            16,
        )

import pygame

app = create_sandbox_application()
app._tool_manager.register_tool(SpawnCounter(app.container), pygame.K_F10)

Registering a name that is already taken replaces the old tool (its render-order slot and shortcut are dropped first). ToolManager.unregister_tool(name) removes a tool and calls its Tool.on_removed() hook -- override that to undo anything __init__ acquired, such as an EventDispatcher subscription (EventMonitor does). SandboxApplication.shutdown() clears every tool this way before the engine tears down.

Tool._entity_manager resolves the active scene's EntityManager on every access. Before the first scene switch there is no world, so it returns a single throwaway empty manager -- fine to read, but a tool that mutates the world in that window is writing into an orphan no scene will ever see. Return True from process_event to stop an event reaching the game.

docs.title: The ImGui editor layer
docs.text:
A second dev surface, pyguara.studio: Dear ImGui panels drawn as a render pass over the finished frame. It needs the wgpu backend and is opt-in.

from pyguara.application.bootstrap import create_application
from pyguara.studio import attach_editor

app = create_application()
attach_editor(app.container)
app.run(MyScene("game", app._event_dispatcher))

attach_editor gives you the layer and nothing else: a context, the input routing, the render pass, and a Hierarchy and an Inspector over live engine state. PyGuara Studio is this plus a session -- an operation registry, a command stack, an audit journal and the rest of the panels -- and attach_studio calls attach_editor to get it. Ask for the layer when you want to look at the world, and for Studio when you want to change it and keep a record.

The two used to be separate packages, pyguara/editor and pyguara/studio, with ten imports and a panel subclass crossing between them. They are one package now. What is a boundary is the pyguara.tools overlay above: it draws through UIRenderer, needs no ImGui, and works on the Pygame backend, which has no GPU device for this layer to draw into.

attach_editor returns the EditorLayer, and registers it in the container so game code can reach it. It returns None -- logging why -- when the editor cannot run: ImGui is not installed, or the backend has no GPU render graph. It does not half-install.

It works on both create_application() and create_sandbox_application(), which draw a frame the same way. That was briefly not true: SandboxApplication used to override _render() wholesale and never executed a single render-graph pass, so the editor attached and was then never drawn -- and the sandbox also skipped lighting, compositing and post-processing on the GPU backend. It now overrides the _render_overlays() hook instead and inherits the frame loop, so an overlay adds itself without restating how a frame is drawn.

docs.title: Why wgpu-only
docs.text: The editor rasterises ImGui's draw data through the native wgpu frame the RenderGraph's device owns, as one mesh step per frame. The Pygame backend has none: its PygameRenderGraph is a stub with no device, and the window it opens is a software surface. On that backend attach_editor declines and the pyguara.tools overlay above stays the dev surface.

docs.title: Why not imgui_bundle.python_backends
docs.text:
Those backends import OpenGL.GL. An undeclared PyOpenGL dependency is exactly what made the first editor dead code, so the renderer here (pyguara.studio.wgpu_renderer.WgpuImGuiRenderer) draws through the frame the renderer is already using rather than standing up a second graphics stack. pyguara.studio.availability.IMGUI_AVAILABLE records whether ImGui imported, and a test asserts it is True, so the editor cannot quietly switch itself off again.

ImGui itself stays optional, and the thing that keeps it so is an import rule rather than a flag: nothing the agent transport loads -- pyguara.studio, pyguara.studio.ops.*, pyguara.studio.session, pyguara.studio.attach -- may import Dear ImGui at module scope, so pyguara studio ops runs on an install without it. Now that the layer and Studio share a package that is one unguarded import away at all times, and tests/studio/test_attach.py asserts it in a fresh interpreter: not that the transport still works without ImGui, but that it never asked for it.

docs.title: Panels
docs.text:
Panel Shows HierarchyPanel The entity tree, over the ECS parent/child relation; click to select InspectorPanel The selected entity's components, with editable fields

Both read PanelContext, which carries the active scene's EntityManager (or None when no scene is active yet) and the shared Selection. The inspector edits bool, int, float, str, Vector2 and Color fields and draws anything else read-only. A frozen=True component is drawn read-only rather than assigned to, and every accepted edit ends with EntityManager.notify_component_changed() so anything mirroring the component -- physics bodies, render batches, the spatial index -- is told.

Where an accepted edit goes depends on who attached the panel. Under attach_editor it is the direct write above, which is all a layer with no history can honestly do. Under attach_studio the panel is given the attachment, and every accepted field becomes the same set_field operation an agent calls -- so it lands on the same undo stack, in the same journal, and under the same approval mode. That used to be a StudioInspectorPanel subclass in the other package, overriding the one method that writes; with both in pyguara.studio it is one class and a constructor argument.

docs.title: Custom panels
docs.text:
from pyguara.studio.panels.base import EditorPanel, PanelContext


class EntityCount(EditorPanel):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__("Entity Count")

    def draw(self, context: PanelContext) -> None:
        from imgui_bundle import imgui

        imgui.begin(self.title)
        if context.entity_manager is None:
            imgui.text_disabled("No active scene.")
        else:
            total = sum(1 for _ in context.entity_manager.get_all_entities())
            imgui.text(f"Entities: {total}")
        imgui.end()

layer = attach_editor(app.container, panels=[EntityCount()])

draw() runs between new_frame() and render(), and only while the panel is visible. Pair every begin() with an end() unconditionally -- Dear ImGui owes an End even for a collapsed window.

docs.title: Input
docs.text: EditorLayer.process_event() takes the engine's own events -- the editor never imports pygame -- and returns True when ImGui is using that kind of input, so the caller can stop the event reaching the game. Scroll and typing arrive as MouseWheelEvent and TextInputEvent, which the window backends translate from SDL alongside the existing key and mouse events.

docs.title: Input System
docs.text: pyguara.input is the translation layer between hardware (keyboard, mouse, gamepad) and the semantic actions your game logic reacts to. Game code listens for "jump", never for a key code, so the same logic survives rebinding and works across devices.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Backend (IInputBackend) — abstracts the joystick subsystem so the manager can run headless in tests. The bootstrap picks the one that matches the renderer: NativeInputBackend (gamepads through gilrs) on wgpu, the default, PygameInputBackend on pygame, and NullInputBackend, which has no devices, on the headless application.
  2. Raw events — InputManager.process_event() ingests the engine's own keyboard, mouse and text events, which the window backend (winit on wgpu, SDL on pygame) has already translated; InputManager.update() polls gamepad state once per frame.
  3. Binding lookup — KeyBindingManager maps (device, code) in the active context to action names.
  4. Action dispatch — an OnActionEvent is published for game logic; OnRawKeyEvent / OnMouseEvent are published in parallel for the UI layer.

InputManager is registered as a singleton by the application bootstrap, so a scene resolves it from the container:

from pyguara.input import ActionType, InputDevice, InputManager
from pyguara.input.keys import SPACE

input_manager = container.get(InputManager)
input_manager.register_action("jump", ActionType.PRESS)
input_manager.bind_input(InputDevice.KEYBOARD, SPACE, "jump")

Use the constants in pyguara.input.keys (SPACE, A, LEFT, F1, …), not pygame constants — game code never imports the backend.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
register_action(name, action_type, deadzone=0.1) defines what an action is:

ActionType Fires when PRESS the input goes down RELEASE the input comes up HOLD the input goes down and when it comes up (value 1.0 then 0.0) ANALOG a bound gamepad axis moves (value is the post-deadzone axis position)

An ANALOG action only responds to a bound axis; a digital key bound to one produces nothing. Likewise a PRESS/RELEASE/HOLD action bound to an axis does nothing — axes drive ANALOG only.

docs.title: Bindings
docs.text:
input_manager.bind_input(InputDevice.KEYBOARD, SPACE, "jump")
input_manager.bind_input(InputDevice.GAMEPAD, GamepadButton.A.value, "jump")

A key may carry several actions and an action may have several keys. The manager owns a KeyBindingManager; reach it for queries and rebinding through the rebinding API below.

docs.title: Contexts
docs.text:
A context is the current input mode. Only bindings registered for the active context resolve, so one key drives different actions in gameplay and in menus:

from pyguara.input import InputContext
from pyguara.input.keys import RETURN

input_manager.bind_input(InputDevice.KEYBOARD, SPACE, "jump", InputContext.GAMEPLAY)
input_manager.bind_input(InputDevice.KEYBOARD, RETURN, "confirm", InputContext.MENU)

input_manager.context = InputContext.MENU        # property
input_manager.set_context(InputContext.GAMEPLAY) # imperative alias

The manager starts in InputContext.GAMEPLAY. Contexts are GAMEPLAY, UI, MENU, DEBUG. Changing to a different context publishes an InputContextChangedEvent (old_context, new_context); setting the context it already holds is a no-op and publishes nothing. A binding registered for a context that is never made active never fires.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
All input events carry timestamp (set at construction) and source (the manager that emitted them).

Event Fields OnActionEvent action_name, context, value OnRawKeyEvent key_code, is_down, modifiers OnMouseEvent position, button, is_down, is_motion InputContextChangedEvent old_context, new_context GamepadButtonEvent controller_id, button, is_pressed GamepadAxisEvent controller_id, axis, value, previous_value 
def on_action(self, event: OnActionEvent) -> None:
    if event.action_name == "jump" and event.value > 0.5:
        self.player.jump()

docs.title: Gamepads
docs.text:
InputManager.update() drives an owned GamepadManager (also reachable as input_manager.gamepad) that polls device state, applies deadzones, and publishes GamepadButtonEvent / GamepadAxisEvent on change. Bound InputDevice.GAMEPAD actions are driven off those events; gamepads are not read from the window's event queue.

from pyguara.input import GamepadAxis, GamepadButton

pad = input_manager.gamepad
if pad.get_button(0, GamepadButton.A):
    ...
move_x = pad.get_axis(0, GamepadAxis.LEFT_STICK_X)
pad.rumble(0, low_frequency=0.4, high_frequency=0.4, duration_ms=200)

controller_id is a stable slot number ("player 1" is 0). It is pinned to one physical device by its backend's device id (SDL's on pygame, gilrs's on wgpu) for as long as that device is plugged in, so unplugging one controller never renumbers the others. A slot is freed on disconnect and reused by the next controller to connect. GamepadConfig (constructor argument) tunes deadzone, trigger_deadzone, axis_sensitivity and vibration_enabled.

A game sees its gamepads only while its window has focus. On the wgpu backend pads are read through gilrs, whose Windows backend (Windows.Gaming.Input) delivers input only to the process that owns the foreground window; pygame's SDL ignores an unfocused pad by default too, so this is not new. Alt-tabbed out, buttons read as released and sticks as centred.

This bites a test script: one that reads NativeGamepads from a console with no window of its own sees nothing, and on Windows the focused terminal takes the input instead (Windows Terminal switches tabs on the bumpers). Open a window and keep it focused while probing a pad.

docs.title: Rebinding and persistence
docs.text:
KeyBindingManager supports runtime rebinding with conflict handling and JSON-serializable export:

from pyguara.input import ConflictResolution, KeyBindingManager, RebindResult

bindings: KeyBindingManager = input_manager.bindings
result, conflict = bindings.rebind(
    "jump", InputDevice.KEYBOARD, RETURN, InputContext.GAMEPLAY,
    resolution=ConflictResolution.SWAP,
)
ConflictResolution Behaviour when the target key is taken ERROR (default) raises ValueError SWAP the two actions trade keys UNBIND the conflicting action loses its binding ALLOW both actions share the key

rebind() returns (RebindResult, BindingConflict | None). RebindResult is SUCCESS, SWAPPED or UNBOUND — there is no CONFLICT value, because ERROR raises instead of returning. A SWAP of an action that had no prior binding has no key to trade back and returns UNBOUND.

data = bindings.export_bindings()   # dict, ready for json.dump
bindings.import_bindings(data)       # replaces all current bindings
bindings.reset_to_defaults()         # clears every context

docs.title: Localisation
docs.text:
Player-visible text lives in one file per language, not in the code. Code names a key; the engine finds the text for it in the player's language.

class Hud(Scene):
    def on_enter(self) -> None:
        self.title.text = self.tr("title")
        self.waiting.text = self.tr("room.waiting", player=host_name)

    def update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        self.scrap.text = self.tr("hud.salvage", count=self.salvage)

docs.title: The files
docs.text:
locales/<locale>.json, one per language, UTF-8, named by BCP 47 tag: en.json, zh-Hans.json, pt-BR.json. Each is a flat object of keys:

{
  "_meta": {"reviewed": false, "translator": "machine draft"},
  "title": "Рекламатор",
  "room.waiting": "Ожидание {player}...",
  "hud.salvage": {
    "one": "{count} обломок",
    "few": "{count} обломка",
    "many": "{count} обломков",
    "other": "{count} обломка"
  }
}
  • The source locale (en by default) is the reference. Every key the game uses must be there.
  • A placeholder is {name}, optionally with a format spec: {ratio:.0%}. A translator may move it anywhere in the sentence. Nothing else is allowed ({0}, {player.name}, {x!r}), because a translation file is data from outside the code and str.format could otherwise walk the attributes of what is passed in. A file that tries is refused when it loads.
  • A plural entry is an object of CLDR forms: zero, one, two, few, many, other. other is required. Pass count=, an int, and the form is picked by the language's rule. A language without plurals (Chinese, Japanese, Korean) may give a plain string.
  • _meta.reviewed: false marks a translation no native speaker has signed off yet. A file without it counts as reviewed.

docs.title: Plural forms by language
docs.text:
Languages Forms a translation must give Notes en, de, tr one, other one is exactly 1 es, it one, other many is optional, for exact millions fr, pt one, other 0 is singular too; many optional, as above ru one, few, many, other 1, 21: one. 2-4, 22: few. 5-20, 25: many zh, ja, ko other No plural forms

Another language is refused until its rules are added to pyguara/i18n/plurals.py, rather than given English's.

docs.title: What a lookup does
docs.text: Situation Result The key is in the current locale Its text Only the source has the key The source's text, and one warning in the log per key and locale The source lacks the key MissingStringError: code asking for text nobody wrote A plural form the entry lacks The other form A placeholder with no value KeyError

docs.title: Choosing the language
docs.text:
The i18n config section:

Setting Default locale "" A tag such as "pt-BR". Empty uses the operating system's directory "locales" The folder of locale files. Without it, nothing is loaded source "en" The language the game is written in

directory is read through pyguara.assets, so locales/ can ship in a pack. A relative path is relative to the working directory, which a player's shortcut decides, so a built game should set it from where its own files are, as it does for any other asset.

The locale asked for is narrowed to the closest one there is a file for: an exact match, then (for Chinese) the same script, then the same language in another region (pt-PT gets pt-BR), and otherwise the source.

A game on Steam should use the language the player chose there:

from pyguara.i18n import best_locale, locale_from_steam

steam_locale = locale_from_steam(steam_language)        # "schinese" -> "zh-Hans"
translator.locale = best_locale(steam_locale or "", translator.available, source="en")

Setting translator.locale while the game runs dispatches LocaleChanged; a screen built from keys rebuilds its text when it hears it. Case changes in pyguara.ui.text_case follow the locale from startup and on every change, so upper("i") is "İ" in Turkish.

Outside a scene, take the Translator from the container, app.container.get(Translator), and pass it to what needs it.

docs.title: Checking the files
docs.text:
pyguara i18n check locales/
pyguara i18n check locales/ --require-reviewed     # for a release build

It compares every locale with the source and reports keys that are missing or stray, placeholders that differ, plural forms the language needs and the entry lacks, and files that will not load. A translation not yet reviewed is a warning, or a failure with --require-reviewed. The exit status is 1 on any error.

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
pyguara.net connects one hosting player's game to the players who join it: the transport and session move messages and decide who may play, and replication keeps every client's world matching the host's. Prediction does not exist yet, so a client's own character still moves only when the host's snapshot says so.

It is opt-in. A single-player game imports none of it, and importing it needs no native extension: only starting a session does.

docs.title: Hosting and joining
docs.text:
from pyguara.net import (
    Channel, ClientSession, HostSession, Invite, MessageReceived, PlayerJoined,
    UdpTransport, Versions,
)

versions = Versions(engine="0.6.0", game="1.0", content_hash=my_content_hash)

# The host makes an invite and shares its string with its friends.
invite = Invite.create("203.0.113.5", 7777)
print(invite)  # pyguara://203.0.113.5:7777#...
host = HostSession(UdpTransport.host(invite.key, invite.port), versions)

# A player joins with that string.
invite = Invite.parse(text_from_a_friend)
client = ClientSession(
    UdpTransport.client(
        invite.key, secrets.randbits(63), invite.host, invite.port, versions.encode()
    )
)

Poll once a frame. Neither session raises because of what a peer sent.

for event in host.poll():
    if isinstance(event, PlayerJoined):
        host.send(event.peer, Channel.EVENTS, welcome_bytes)
    elif isinstance(event, MessageReceived):
        handle(event.peer, event.channel, event.data)

A player whose engine version, game version, content hash or protocol differs is refused, and Refused.reason names both sides. A wrong invite is deliberately silent at the network layer, so it shows up as Left after 10 seconds, with a message saying to check the invite.

An invite is a secret. Anyone holding it can join, and anyone who also recorded the session's handshake can read that session. Make a new one per session. repr(invite) leaves the key out, so it does not end up in a log by accident. Players also see each other's IP addresses on a direct connection, and a game should say so.

docs.title: Over Steam
docs.text:
Online play between friends goes through Steam rather than invites: no port forwarding, traffic is relayed through Valve's network, and no player sees another's IP address. The sessions are the same; only the transport differs.

from pyguara.net import ClientSession, HostSession, SteamNetwork
from pyguara.net.steam_lobby import JoinRequested, LobbyFailed, LobbyJoined, LobbyOpened

network = SteamNetwork.open()        # finds steam_api, starts Steam, reaches the relays
network.lobby.host(max_players=4)    # or: network.lobby.join(lobby_id)

# Once a frame, before the session:
for event in network.update():
    if isinstance(event, LobbyOpened):
        session = HostSession(network.host_transport(max_clients=3), versions)
        network.lobby.invite()       # the overlay's invite dialog
    elif isinstance(event, LobbyJoined):
        session = ClientSession(network.join_transport(versions.encode()))
    elif isinstance(event, JoinRequested):
        ...                          # an invite accepted mid-game: the game decides
    elif isinstance(event, LobbyFailed):
        show(event.reason)
# ... the session's poll, the fixed updates, the session's sends ...
network.flush()                      # send them now rather than next frame

pyguara.net.simulated_steam.SimulatedSteamCloud stands in for Steam in tests: give each player's SimulatedSteam to a SteamNetwork and the transport, lobby and sessions above it are the real code.

Being in the host's friends-only lobby is what admits a player. Members entering and leaving become allow and revoke on the host's transport, and a Steam session from anyone else is never accepted. A player who leaves the lobby is dropped from the game. Friends see "Join Game" on the host and on every guest, which is Steam's friends-only rule.

A game Steam launches to join a lobby gets +connect_lobby <id> on its command line: lobby_from_args(sys.argv) reads it, and the game calls network.lobby.join with it.

steam_api is Valve's library and this engine cannot ship it. Take steam_api64.dll (or libsteam_api.so) from the Steamworks SDK's redistributable_bin and put it beside the game: pyguara dist steam --steam-api <path> copies it into the built game, and in development PYGUARA_STEAM_API names it. During development Steam also needs the app ID, from steam_appid.txt in the working directory or SteamAppId; 480 is Valve's test app. Never ship steam_appid.txt -- pyguara dist steam keeps it out of the depot.

There is no network thread on Steam: Steam's API is pumped from the frame. A stalled frame delays acknowledgements as well as game state, well inside the 10-second timeout.

docs.title: Channels
docs.text:
Channel Delivery Use it for COMMANDS Unreliable Per-tick input. Repeat recent ticks in each message, so one loss costs nothing SNAPSHOT Unreliable, may reorder State. Carry a tick, and drop anything older than you have EVENTS Reliable, ordered Damage, deaths, drops, spawns. See Game events LEVEL Reliable, ordered, lowest priority Large transfers CONTROL Reliable, ordered The session's own. A client's messages here are ignored

Channels are not ordered against each other, so an event can overtake the snapshot it depends on.

Keep unreliable messages under about 1,100 bytes. A larger one is split into slices, and losing one slice loses the whole message. Split a large snapshot into several messages that each decode alone.

send returns False rather than raising when a message is not accepted: no such peer, or over the channel's limit. On a reliable channel that means a backlog, and the largest single message is half the channel's limit: about 512 KiB on EVENTS and 8 MiB on LEVEL.

docs.title: Replication
docs.text:
The host simulates. Clients draw what they receive, about 100 ms behind, so there is always a newer snapshot to interpolate toward.

schema = ReplicationSchema()   # the same on host and client, in the same order
schema.register(Transform, position=QuantisedVector(step=0.25), rotation=Angle())
schema.register(Health, current=UInt16(), max_health=UInt16())

# Host
replication = ReplicationHost(entity_manager, schema, session.send)
app.add_step_hook(HostDriver(app, session, replication))
enemy.add_component(Replicated("enemy"))             # everyone sees it
drop.add_component(Replicated("drop", owner=slot))   # only that player does

# Client: a name from the network can only choose among these
replication = ReplicationClient(entity_manager, schema, {"enemy": make_enemy, "drop": make_drop})
app.add_step_hook(ClientDriver(session, replication, on_event=handle_game_message))

Run nothing that simulates on a client: no AI, flocking or spawning. To see all of this running:

uv run python games/net_horde/main.py                      # both sides, one window
uv run python games/net_horde/main.py --host               # one window
uv run python games/net_horde/main.py --join "pyguara://"  # the other

Things that will catch you out:

  • Field range. A 16-bit QuantisedVector at step 0.25 reaches about 8000 units from the origin. Use wide=True for more. A value that doesn't fit saturates, and is counted in ReplicationHost.saturated().
  • A reliable message of your own must start with a byte below FIRST_RESERVED_KIND, 0xE0.
  • Per-player drops on the host's own screen. The host's world holds everyone's, so its renderer and effects must filter by Replicated.owner. A client's world never holds anyone else's, since they are never sent.
  • Teleports. A jump over snap_distance, 256 units by default, is drawn at once rather than as motion. Shorter ones slide.
  • A component needs to exist on the client's entity, from its spawner, or its state is ignored.
  • Pass digest_every= while developing. The host then sends a hash of the state, and ReplicationClient.digests_mismatched above 0 is a real desync.

docs.title: Game events
docs.text:
Hits, kills and heals have to agree on every screen, so the host sends them as events and each client dispatches them to its own game. Register an event on the same schema, with a codec per field, and the host's relay sends every registered type as the game dispatches it:

schema.register_event(
    HitLanded,
    target=EntityRef(),                       # arrives as the client's own entity id
    amount=Quantised(step=0.01, wide=True),
    damage_type=EnumField(DamageType),
    killed=Flag(),
)
schema.register_event(SkillUsed, user=EntityRef(), skill=Choice(SKILL_NAMES))

# Host: the game dispatches as always, and its own screen reacts as before.
relay = EventRelay(dispatcher, replication, app)

# Client: the same presentation code reacts, since it listens to the same events.
replication = ReplicationClient(entity_manager, schema, spawners, on_event=dispatcher.dispatch)
  • An event lands with the snapshot it belongs to. It goes out reliably, in order with spawns and despawns, and a client applies it when its delayed view reaches the event's tick. A hit number appears as the health drops, and a kill still names the enemy, although the host removed it the same tick.
  • EntityRef names replicated entities only. It travels as the network id and arrives as the client's id for that entity, or None if it isn't replicated or is already gone. An entity spawned the same tick can be named: sending an event announces pending spawns first.
  • A client builds the event from the sent fields alone, so every other field of the dataclass needs a default. Registering one without a default, or a field the class doesn't have, raises at once.
  • Choice sends a string from a fixed list, such as a skill's name, by its position. Both sides list the same values in the same order; the fingerprint includes them, so a client with a different list refuses rather than misreading.
  • For one player only, pass slot_of= to the relay, or slot= to ReplicationHost.send_event.
  • Don't relay what a client predicts. A client's own hop or shot already played when the player pressed the button, and the host's copy arrives about a round trip later. Leave those events unregistered, or have the client ignore its own. Shots have this built in: see Shots.
  • Events don't reach a player who joins later. They describe moments, not state.

docs.title: Shots
docs.text:
Bullets are not replicated: hundreds of them read every snapshot would use up the budget. The host sends each shot once, as a reliable event, and every client flies it on its own ProjectileSystem. The host alone decides what a shot hits. It lives in the projectiles kit, as pyguara.kits.projectiles.net, since core never imports a kit:

from pyguara.kits.projectiles.net import (
    ProjectileClient, ProjectileHost, register_projectiles,
)

# Both sides, on the same schema.
register_projectiles(
    schema, SHOT_KINDS,
    position=QuantisedVector(step=0.25, wide=True),
    velocity=QuantisedVector(step=0.25),
)

# Host: the game's own ProjectileSystem, with its real on_hit. Fire through the relay.
shots = ProjectileHost(projectiles, replication, app)
shots.spawn("bolt", origin, velocity, slot=player_slot, life=0.8, hit_radius=6, payload=shot)

# Client: a display-only ProjectileSystem. Dispatch the host's events to it.
replication = ReplicationClient(world, schema, spawners, on_event=dispatcher.dispatch)
shots = ProjectileClient(display_projectiles, dispatcher, replication, TICK_SECONDS)
# Each frame, after the network update:
shots.update(frame_time)

A client draws from projectile.payload, a NetShot carrying the shot's kind.

  • A shot costs bytes once, when fired. 24 bytes of event, about 34 on the wire. When one stops early, at a target, at a wall or by ProjectileSystem.clear(), the host sends where it stopped, 15 bytes more. One that runs out of life ends by itself on both sides. With 200 bullets in flight a client receives exactly what it does with none (tests/test_net_projectiles.py).
  • Shots fly on the delayed timeline. A shot leaves its shooter where the client draws the shooter, and moves with the delayed view's clock rather than the frame's, so it keeps pace with the interpolated world while that clock is corrected.
  • A player's own shots show at once. Call ProjectileClient.fire from the character's advance, where the host's game calls ProjectileHost.spawn with that player's slot, with the tick PredictionClient.advancing names. Not PredictionClient.tick: one step advances several ticks when the client catches up, and a correction replays past ticks from inside handle_message, so only advancing is the tick being simulated. A shot is named by ProjectileKey(slot, tick, index), so the host's copy is recognised and not shown twice. Both sides must fire a tick's shots in the same order. Give ProjectileClient the PredictionClient as prediction, so it numbers each advance's shots afresh: then a replay firing a shot again is ignored, since it's already showing. Without it, a replay of the tick last fired on looks like more shots on that tick.
  • Prediction can be wrong about a skill being ready. A shot shown that the host never fired is taken away half a second after the host's would have arrived, and counted in mispredicted. One the host fired that the client didn't show appears from the network, late, and is counted in unpredicted. Either one staying above zero means the client's idea of cooldowns or energy differs from the host's.
  • On a client, an own shot stops at the first opposing target it reaches, for display only. That needs the display system to have a spatial index of what the client draws. Other players' shots pass through until the host says they stopped. A shot can look as if it touched a target and did nothing, which is the accepted trade: damage comes only from the host, as game events.
  • The host's ProjectileSystem must leave on_end free, since the relay takes it. Stopping shots by setting active = False bypasses it, so a client never hears. Use ProjectileSystem.clear().

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
Measured with tools/net_phase0.py, on a horde of real components with three clients, per frame at 60 Hz with 20 Hz snapshots. Reproducible, but not from a shipping game.

Entities Host Client Per client, at 20 Hz 200 0.22 ms 0.82 ms 0.35 Mbit/s 500 0.55 ms 2.7 ms 0.88 Mbit/s 1,000 1.13 ms 6.0 ms 1.77 Mbit/s

A client spends more than the host because it decodes and interpolates, but it isn't running the simulation. Python's garbage collector is the remaining hitch: a full collection took up to 23 ms, which makes the worst frame about 20 ms where it would otherwise be about 4. That run held four worlds in one process, so a real client should be smaller, but measure it in a real game.

docs.title: Prediction
docs.text:
Your own character runs at once. Its commands go to the host, each naming the host tick it applies to, and the host sends back the exact state. If that differs from what the client predicted for that tick, the client goes back to the host's state and replays the newer commands. A state "at tick N" includes every command before N.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Move:
    x: float = 0.0
    y: float = 0.0

commands = CommandSchema(Move, x=Quantised(step=1 / 64), y=Quantised(step=1 / 64))

def velocity_of(command: Move) -> Vector2:   # runs on both machines
    direction = Vector2(command.x, command.y)
    if direction.magnitude > 1.0:            # untrusted on the host
        direction = direction.normalize()
    return direction * SPEED

# Host
prediction = PredictionHost(commands, Move(), session.send)
app.add_step_hook(HostDriver(app, session, replication, prediction=prediction))
character.add_component(Replicated("player", controller=slot))
prediction.bind(slot, TopDownPrediction(character, mover, velocity_of))
# In fixed_update, for each remote player, before TopDownSystem runs:
body.velocity = velocity_of(prediction.take(slot, app.fixed_tick))

# Client
prediction = PredictionClient(commands, Move(), session.send)
replication = ReplicationClient(
    entity_manager, schema, spawners,
    predicted_components=(Transform,),
    on_controlled=lambda entity: prediction.bind(
        entity and TopDownPrediction(entity, mover, velocity_of)
    ),
)
app.add_step_hook(ClientDriver(session, replication, prediction=prediction))
# In fixed_update:
prediction.step(command_from_keys())

The client needs its own copy of the solids for the mover to query. The host's own player just uses the keys: it has no one to predict for.

Things that will catch you out:

  • Velocity has to be a pure function of the command. Anything else it reads, such as a timer, has to be in the state capture returns, or a replay comes out differently.
  • Only the movement is predicted. TopDownSystem's separation push needs other actors, so it arrives as a correction. Expect visible corrections while pressed against something the client doesn't simulate: phase 0 measured 10-19 px in constant contact before smoothing.
  • After the fixed updates, Transform holds what's shown, which can include a fading correction. Read it in a fixed update for the simulated position.
  • The first moment after joining isn't predicted well. The client starts with a guess at its lead, and commands sent before that settles get corrected.
  • Other players' characters are drawn about 100 ms behind. They're interpolated like everything else.

PredictionClient.corrections should stay flat while you walk around walls with nothing pushing you. If it climbs, the host and client are stepping differently, which is a bug.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
Measured with the test harness on one machine, at a simulated 100 ms round trip.

Client, per frame, standing still, including the message 18 us Host, per player, per tick 4 us Replay of 6 ticks while moving, from phase 0 0.28 ms Longest replay one correction can cause 120 ticks Command message, 60 a second 47 bytes State message, 20 a second 40 bytes A client's upload, on the simulated link 26 kbit/s

Over 30 seconds of walking and hitting walls, with five seeds, after the first 3 seconds:

Network Corrections Commands late Lead over the host 100 ms 0 0 8 ticks 100 ms, 2% loss 0 0 8-9 ticks 200 ms, 30 ms jitter, 2% loss 0 0 12 ticks 160 ms, 30 ms jitter, 20% loss 0 2-6 10-12 ticks

A simulated network proves the logic. Whether it feels immediate has to be judged by a person, which is what games/net_horde is for.

docs.title: Everything from the network is untrusted
docs.text:
The Rust core authenticates packets and survives hostile ones, but it does not make a decoded value sensible. An invited player can send any bytes in a valid message. So in your own decoders:

  • Bounds-check lengths, ids and enums.
  • Reject non-finite floats.
  • Clamp and validate commands on the host: move vectors, cooldowns.
  • Treat a decoding failure as dropping the message, never as an exception in the frame loop.
  • Never unpickle network data.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
SimulatedNetwork drives the real Rust core through a seeded fake wire, with an explicit clock. There are no sockets, threads or sleeps, and a failure replays from its seed.

network = SimulatedNetwork(seed=1, conditions=LinkConditions(latency=0.05, loss=0.02))
host = network.add_host(key)
client = network.add_client(key, network.address_of(host), versions.encode())
network.advance(1 / 60)

These suites need the extension built, and fail rather than skip without it. A simulation proves the logic. It cannot prove how a real connection behaves or whether playing over one feels good, so see the network probe for testing between two machines.

See docs/adr/0007-networking-model.md for why it works this way.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
pyguara.persistence is the save/load layer: it turns an object graph into a durable file on disk and back, verifies it has not been corrupted, and migrates old save files forward as your schema changes.

from pyguara.persistence import PersistenceManager

pm = container.get(PersistenceManager)

pm.save_data("slot_1", {"level": 3, "hp": 100})
state = pm.load_data("slot_1")            # -> {"level": 3, "hp": 100} or None

The bootstrap wires a PersistenceManager backed by a FileStorageBackend rooted at ./saves and a MigrationManager at current_version=1.

docs.title: save_data / load_data
docs.text:
save_data(key, data, save_version=1, compress=False, fmt=JSON) Serialize, checksum, and write one blob. Returns True only if the bytes reached storage. load_data(key, verify_integrity=True) Read, verify, deserialize, migrate. Returns the object, or None if the key is absent, the blob is corrupt, or a migration failed.

data may be any JSON-friendly graph; Vector2, Color and Rect are recognised and round-trip as themselves. A dict is the only top-level shape that migrations apply to.

  • fmt — SerializationFormat.JSON (default, human-readable), MSGPACK (compact binary, same value-type support as JSON), or BINARY (pickle — handles arbitrary objects but only load a BINARY file you trust; deserializing a pickle runs code).
  • compress — gzip the payload before writing. Transparent on load (the header records it).
  • save_version — the schema version stamped into the file, read back by the migration step.

load_data never raises for a bad file: a missing key, a truncated blob, a failed checksum, or a failed migration all log and return None.

docs.title: Saving during play
docs.text:
save_data serializes and fsyncs on the calling thread, so calling it from gameplay stalls a frame. QuickSaver does that work on a worker thread and writes only the newest value per key, at most once per min_interval:

saver = QuickSaver(pm, min_interval=1.0)
saver.request("character", character_as_plain_data())   # each time something changes
saver.flush()                                           # at the end of a run
saver.close()                                           # at shutdown

Hand over a value you won't mutate. It is serialized later on another thread, so a live object could be saved half-updated. A crash loses at most the last min_interval, and storage writes atomically, so it can't corrupt a save.

Save size save_data on the main thread request Worst frame with quick saves 4 KB 4.2 ms about 5 us 1.5 ms 74 KB 14.8 ms about 4 us 5.3 ms 1.5 MB 356 ms about 3 us 6.6 ms

Worst frame is against 0.5 ms with no saves, writing as often as every 50 ms, in WSL2 on an SSD. Windows is unmeasured. The remaining stall is the GIL, since the JSON encoder holds it while serializing, so keep quick-saved data small, and prefer several small keys to one large one.

docs.title: On-disk format
docs.text:
Each key is stored as one file — saves/<key>.save for the file backend — laid out as a single-line JSON metadata header, a newline, then the payload bytes:

{"version":"0.5.0","timestamp":"2026-09-08T17:02:37+00:00","data_type":"dict","checksum":"87f0…","save_version":1,"format":"json","compressed":false}
{
  "level": 3,
  "hp": 100
}

Metadata and payload share one file so there is no window in which they can disagree — the write either lands whole or not at all. The checksum is an MD5 of the payload bytes exactly as written (after compression, if any); load_data(verify_integrity=False) skips the comparison.

docs.title: Storage backends
docs.text:
PersistenceManager talks to a StorageBackend — a plain key → blob store:

class StorageBackend(Protocol):
    def save(self, key: str, blob: bytes) -> bool: ...
    def load(self, key: str) -> bytes | None: ...
    def delete(self, key: str) -> bool: ...
    def list_keys(self) -> list[str]: ...

FileStorageBackend(base_path="saves") is the built-in implementation. It writes atomically (temp file, fsync, os.replace, then an fsync of the directory) and sweeps orphaned .tmp_* files left by a crashed write on startup.

Keys must be filesystem-safe as given — letters, digits, _ and -. A key containing a space, a dot, or a path separator is rejected with ValueError rather than silently rewritten: "slot 1" and "slot/1" would otherwise both collapse onto slot1 and overwrite each other.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text:
When a loaded save's save_version is older than the MigrationManager's current_version, load_data walks the registered migrations in order and applies each one before returning.

from pyguara.persistence import register_migration

@register_migration(from_version=1, to_version=2, description="hp -> health")
def _v1_to_v2(data: dict) -> dict:
    data["health"] = data.pop("hp")
    return data

A migration function takes the data dict, mutates and returns it. The MigrationManager threads one dict through the whole chain (1 → 2 → 3 → …), so a migration sees the output of the previous step.

  • Register via @register_migration (collected in the global registry, which the bootstrap drains into the manager) or MigrationManager.register(Migration(...)) directly.
  • to_version must be greater than from_version, both >= 1, and no two migrations may share a from_version.
  • The chain must be contiguous from the save's version to current_version — a gap raises ValueError (caught by load_data, logged, returns None).
  • No downgrades. Loading a save whose version is newer than current_version fails rather than guessing.
  • A migration that raises is wrapped in MigrationError with the failing step; the partly-migrated data is discarded.

MigrationManager.needs_migration(v) and has_migration_path(v) let you check ahead of a load.

docs.title: Scenes
docs.text: SceneSerializer (pyguara.scene) is the higher-level entry point for saving a whole scene's entities and components; it serializes each entity to a dict and hands the result to PersistenceManager.save_data. See the Scenes page for that layer.

docs.title: Prefab System
docs.text: pyguara.prefabs turns a data description of an entity — components and their field values, optional inheritance, optional child entities — into a live entity in a scene's EntityManager. Prefabs can be built in memory or loaded from .prefab / .prefab.json / .prefab.yaml files.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
1. PrefabData (pyguara.prefabs.types) — the template: a name, a components dict ({ComponentName: {field: value}}), an optional extends path, an optional children list, tags, and a version.
  2. ComponentRegistry (pyguara.prefabs.registry) — maps a component name to its class so {"Transform": {...}} can be turned into a Transform instance. The bootstrap registers every core engine component (Transform, Tag, RigidBody, Collider, the AI/animation/audio components, PrefabInstance, …) on a process-global registry, exposed through DI as ComponentRegistry.
  3. PrefabLoader / PrefabCache (pyguara.prefabs.loader) — read a file into PrefabData. PrefabLoader is also registered with the ResourceManager for the .prefab extension. PrefabCache adds a path→PrefabData cache and is the DI-registered singleton.
  4. PrefabFactory (pyguara.prefabs.factory) — instantiates a PrefabData into an entity. One is created per scene in Scene.resolve_dependencies(), bound to that scene's EntityManager and with its resolver wired to PrefabCache.load, so extends and children paths resolve against files on disk.
from pyguara.prefabs import PrefabData

goblin = PrefabData(
    name="Goblin",
    components={
        "Transform": {"position": {"x": 100, "y": 80}},
        "Tag": {"name": "enemy"},
    },
)
entity = self.prefab_factory.create(goblin)

docs.title: The component registry
docs.text:
registry.create(name, data) builds one component:

  • Dataclass components are filled field by field. {"x": ..., "y": ...} dicts become Vector2; an Enum field accepts a member name (case-insensitive) or a raw member value.
  • A key that matches no field raises ValueError. A typo in a prefab ("colour" for "color") is an authoring error, caught at instantiation rather than surfacing later as a missing value.
  • Transform has a custom __init__ and is not a dataclass, so it goes through a built-in deserializer. clear() wipes user registrations and re-seeds the built-ins, so a cleared registry can still round-trip Transform once it is re-registered.

Register your own components with the class or the decorator:

from pyguara.prefabs import register_component

@register_component
class Health(BaseComponent):
    current: int = 100
    maximum: int = 100

docs.title: Inheritance — extends
docs.text:
extends names another prefab (by resolver path). Parent components are resolved first, then the child's components are deep-merged over them: nested dicts merge key by key, so a child can override Transform.position.x alone and inherit y and scale.

A resolver is required for extends to do anything — the per-scene factory has one. An extends chain that refers back to a prefab already being resolved raises ValueError naming the cycle (a -> b -> a) instead of recursing until the stack runs out.

docs.title: Children
docs.text:
PrefabData.children is a list of PrefabChild(prefab, offset, name, overrides). Each child is instantiated as its own entity and its Transform is parented to the parent entity's Transform (set_parent(..., keep_world_transform=False)):

  • The child's authored position is treated as local to the parent.
  • offset ({"x": .., "y": ..}) is added to that local position.
  • Moving the parent entity moves the children with it.

A child needs a resolver to be found (the per-scene factory has one); without one, children are skipped with a warning. A child with an offset but no Transform component logs a warning and the offset is ignored.

docs.title: Instantiation and metadata
docs.text:
factory.create(prefab, entity_id=None, overrides=None, source_path=None) returns the entity. overrides is a second deep-merge layer applied after inheritance. Every created entity gets a PrefabInstance component recording prefab_path (the source_path, or prefab.name for an in-memory prefab) and the instance_overrides that were applied.

factory.create_from_path(path, ...) resolves the path through the resolver and passes it as source_path, so instances carry the real file path.

A component whose data cannot be built (unknown field, bad enum value, type mismatch) makes create() raise rather than return a half-populated entity. An unregistered component name is skipped with a warning — register it if it is meant to be there.

docs.title: File format
docs.text:
{
  "name": "Goblin",
  "version": 1,
  "extends": "enemies/base_enemy.prefab.json",
  "tags": ["enemy", "melee"],
  "components": {
    "Transform": { "position": { "x": 0, "y": 0 } },
    "Health": { "current": 30, "maximum": 30 }
  },
  "children": [
    { "prefab": "fx/torch.prefab.json", "name": "torch", "offset": { "x": 8, "y": -4 } }
  ]
}

PrefabLoader accepts .prefab.json, .prefab.yaml / .prefab.yml (when PyYAML is installed), and .prefab (format auto-detected). A file whose top-level value is not a mapping raises ValueError. If name is omitted the file stem is used.

docs.title: Spawning from a map
docs.text:
spawn_objects turns the objects on a Tiled or LDtk map into entities. The map says what an object's type is, and the game says which prefab that means:

from pyguara.tilemap import load_tmx
from pyguara.tilemap.spawning import spawn_objects

level = load_tmx("levels/cave.tmx")
spawned = spawn_objects(
    level,
    factory,
    {"Bat": bat_prefab, "Door": door_prefab},
    ignore_types={"CameraBounds"},  # read through `level.objects(...)` instead
)
for item in spawned:
    item.entity, item.source  # the entity, and the MapObject it came from

It lives in its own module, not pyguara.tilemap, so reading a map never imports the ECS.

Rule Why All or nothing. Every object is checked first, and MapSpawnError lists every problem with nothing spawned A mistake should not leave half a level in the world An object whose type has no prefab raises A silently unspawned enemy is found by noticing a room is empty. Use ignore_types for what the game handles itself An object with no type is skipped It names nothing Transform goes at the object's centre A collider is centred on its transform. Tile objects, whose corner is the bottom left, and rotated objects are handled A sized rectangle or a circle shapes any Collider or TriggerVolume in the prefab So a door is the size it was drawn A polygon or polyline on a prefab with a collider raises Collider.dimensions cannot carry vertices, and a bounding box would collide where nothing is drawn Objects and layers hidden in the editor are skipped include_hidden=True to spawn them

Properties. A custom property named Component.field overrides that field, and can go deeper (Health.max = 30, Transform.scale.x = 2). It beats the object's own shape, and a component or field that does not exist raises. Any other property is the game's own, on item.source.properties.

offset= moves everything, for a room placed inside a larger world.

docs.title: Replay System
docs.text: pyguara.replay records the input event stream of a session frame by frame and plays it back, re-driving the game loop from the recorded frame timings. It is meant for bug repro, regression tests, and sharing a run.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Application owns the whole surface — you do not construct a ReplayRecorder or ReplayPlayer yourself:

app = create_application()
app.run(scene)                       # ... play normally ...

seed = app.start_recording(seed=42, description="boss fight bug")
# ... frames pass; every input event is captured ...
data = app.stop_recording()          # -> ReplayData
app.save_recording(data, "runs/boss")  # -> writes runs/boss.replay.gz

app = create_application()
app.load_replay("runs/boss.replay.gz")   # starts playback immediately
app.run(scene)                            # the replay drives input; real
                                          # input is swallowed until it ends

Recording and playback are mutually exclusive: start_recording() while a replay is loaded, or load_replay() while recording, raises RuntimeError.

Internally Application frames each recorder frame around poll_events() (begin_frame / end_frame), feeds ReplayRecorder from InputManager.process_event / the gamepad callbacks, and on playback pumps each recorded frame's events back through InputManager.process_replayed_event, which re-runs them through the same binding logic a live event takes.

docs.title: What is captured
docs.text:
Per frame: frame_id, timestamp, delta_time, and an ordered list of RecordedInputEvent — keyboard up/down (with held modifiers), mouse up/down/move (with position and modifiers), and gamepad buttons/axes. Session metadata: seed, start_scene, engine version, UTC recorded_at, duration, frame count, description.

ReplayRecorder.record_action() also exists for a game that wants to record a synthetic high-level action directly (AI- or script-driven), replayed via the ACTION branch of process_replayed_event.

docs.title: Determinism — what reproduces, what does not
docs.text:
On playback Application.run() takes each frame's duration from the recording (ReplayPlayer.peek_delta()) instead of the wall clock, so the fixed-step accumulator count, _update() deltas, tweens, particles and WaitForSeconds all advance exactly as they did while recording, on any machine and at any render rate.

Reproduces:

  • bound actions and the raw OnRawKeyEvent / OnMouseEvent stream (position and modifiers included), so both gameplay and UI interactions replay;
  • everything downstream of those that is a pure function of input + time — fixed-step physics, animation, coroutine waits, camera smoothing.

Does not reproduce, today:

  • RNG. The seed is recorded and exposed as ReplayPlayer.seed, but nothing reseeds a random source on playback — there is no engine RNG service yet (tracked in the roguelike-core issue). A game that seeds its own RNG from player.seed on load will replay; one that calls random.* on the global module state will not.
  • Anything a game reads from outside the input+time envelope directly: time.time() / datetime.now(), the filesystem, the network, thread scheduling.
  • Floating-point results across different CPU/BLAS builds.
  • Starting state. The game must rebuild an identical initial world; the regression test seeds both runs from one template Entity via Entity.clone().

docs.title: File format
docs.text: JSON, gzip by default. The on-disk format follows the extension: .replay.gz is gzip, .replay is plain, a path with neither gets one appended per the compress argument. ReplaySerializer.get_metadata(path) returns just the metadata block for a save/replay menu. load() refuses a file whose metadata.version exceeds ReplaySerializer.SUPPORTED_VERSION — there is no migration layer.

docs.title: API surface
docs.text:
Call Purpose Application.start_recording(seed=None, description="") begin capture; returns the seed Application.stop_recording() end capture; returns ReplayData Application.save_recording(data, path, compress=True) write to disk Application.load_replay(path) load and start playback save_replay(data, path, compress=True) / load_replay(path) module-level serializer helpers ReplaySerializer.get_metadata(path) read the metadata block only

ReplayPlayer exposes two playback models for a caller driving its own loop (the Application path uses the first):

Call Model advance_frame() + peek_delta() one recorded frame per host frame; host steps its clock by the recorded delta update(dt) wall-clock; consumes every frame whose timestamp has elapsed; honours playback_speed

Plus seek_to_frame, pause_playback / resume_playback, progress, current_frame / total_frames, is_playing / is_paused / is_finished, and add_event_handler for a callback per replayed event.

docs.title: Resource Management
docs.text:
The ResourceManager (pyguara.resources) is the central asset hub: one cache, one place that knows how to turn a file path into a typed engine object.

from pyguara.resources import ResourceManager, Texture

manager = container.get(ResourceManager)
hero = manager.load("assets/chars/hero.png", Texture)

docs.title: Loading and caching
docs.text:
load(path_or_name, resource_type) resolves the path, returns the cached instance on a hit, or runs the registered loader on a miss and caches the result. It is type-safe: asking for a Texture when the file loaded as an AudioClip raises TypeError immediately (on the miss and on a later cache hit with a mismatched type).

Loaders are registered per extension (the Strategy pattern). The bootstrap wires:

Loader Extensions Produces JsonLoader .json, .manifest, .config DataResource PygameImageLoader (pygame backend) / NativeImageLoader (wgpu, decoded in Rust) .png, .jpg, .jpeg, .bmp, .tga Texture (PygameTexture / ImageTexture) NativeSoundLoader (native mixer, the default) / PygameSoundLoader (audio.backend: pygame) .wav, .ogg, .mp3, and .flac on the native mixer AudioClip PrefabLoader .prefab, .prefab.json, .prefab.yaml PrefabData (see Prefabs)

Registering a second loader for an extension logs a warning and wins.

docs.title: Naming: index_directory
docs.text:
index_directory(root) scans a tree and lets you load an asset by its bare name instead of its full path:

manager.index_directory("assets")
hero = manager.load("hero", Texture)          # -> assets/chars/hero.png

Both the stem (hero) and the full filename (hero.png) are indexed. If two files under the tree share a stem (chars/hero.png and fx/hero.png), the bare name is ambiguous: it is dropped and a warning names both paths. The full-name keys still work, so load the colliding asset as "hero.png" or by its full path.

docs.title: Lifecycle: reference counting
docs.text:
A load() is a cache get, not a claim. The resource enters the cache unpinned (reference count 0), and a repeated load() of the same asset does not change that.

Call Effect acquire(name) +1. Pin the resource so unload_unused() cannot evict it. release(name) −1. Must balance an acquire(). Dropping to 0 evicts immediately. Releasing something at 0 raises ValueError. unload_unused() Evict every resource at count 0. Call it between scenes. Returns the count freed. unload(name, force=True) Evict now, whatever the count. unload(name) Decrement like release(), but tolerant: a no-op if the name is unknown.

acquire() / release() on an unloaded name raise KeyError.

So the pattern for an asset a scene must hold for its whole life is load() then acquire() in on_enter(), and release() (or a blanket unload_unused()) in on_exit().

docs.title: Cache budget
docs.text:
unload_unused() is all-or-nothing and manual, so a long run that visits many floors accumulates every texture it ever touched until something thinks to call it. A budget makes the ceiling a property of the manager instead of a thing every scene must remember:

manager.set_cache_budget(256 * 1024 * 1024)   # None is unbounded (the default)

Enforced after every load, least-recently-used first. A cache hit counts as use, so a texture you keep drawing stays.

Three rules decide what gets evicted:

  • A pinned resource is never evicted, whatever the budget says. acquire() means "I am using this"; a cache that evicted it anyway would hand the next load() a second instance while the first is still being drawn. A budget smaller than what is pinned is therefore exceeded, and said so in the log once rather than every frame.
  • The resource just loaded is never evicted to make room for itself.
  • A resource of unknown size is left alone. Evicting it frees an unknown amount, which is not a step towards a target.

docs.title: size_bytes, and what "unknown" means
docs.text:
The budget counts Resource.size_bytes, an estimate: the real figure lives in a backend's allocator and often on the GPU, where Python cannot see it.

Resource Estimate Texture width × height × 4 — every backend here uploads RGBA BlobResource exactly len(data) TextResource the encoded length, not len(text) anything else 0, meaning unknown

Zero means unknown, not free. A resource that cannot estimate is neither counted towards the budget nor evicted to satisfy it, so the figure undercounts rather than guessing. In practice it is a texture budget, which is where the memory is. Override size_bytes on a resource that can do better.

set_cache_budget(0) keeps nothing unpinned — a real thing to want between levels.

docs.title: Hot reload: reload
docs.text:
reload(name) re-runs the loader for a cached resource, re-reading its .meta sidecar too, and swaps the new instance into the cache. The reference count is preserved.

Callers that already hold the previous instance keep that stale object — reload() swaps the cache entry, it does not mutate the old object. Call load() again after a reload to pick up the new one. This is what the asset hot-reload loop in Dev Tools does.

docs.title: .meta sidecar import settings
docs.text:
An asset hero.png can carry a sibling hero.png.meta (JSON) describing how to import it. A meta-aware loader receives the parsed settings; the resolved object is also attached to the resource as resource.import_meta for systems that need it after load.

{ "type": "texture", "filter": "nearest", "premultiply_alpha": true }

type may be omitted when the extension implies it (.png → texture, .ogg → audio). Unknown fields are ignored; an invalid file logs a warning and is treated as "no meta". The MetaLoader caches by path and re-reads when the file's mtime changes; MetaLoader.invalidate(path) forces a re-read and save_meta() writes one back.

Meta type Fields What currently consumes it TextureMeta filter, premultiply_alpha, srgb, mipmaps, wrap_s, wrap_t Both image loaders apply premultiply_alpha, and both carry filter on the texture, which the wgpu renderer honours (nearest ↔ linear) and the pygame renderer cannot. mipmaps/wrap_* are not applied yet. AudioMeta volume_db, load_mode, loop_start, loop_end, normalize The audio system applies volume_db as a per-asset gain per play. load_mode: stream warns (clips are always fully decoded — use play_music). loop_*/normalize are not applied yet. SpritesheetMeta frame_width, frame_height, margin, spacing, filter SpriteSheet.slice_from_meta(meta) reads the grid geometry (margin/spacing included). filter is not applied.

docs.title: Atlases
docs.text: load_atlas(texture_path, json_path) loads a packed-sprite texture plus a JSON region map and returns an Atlas. It acquire()s the underlying texture so unload_unused() will not pull it out from under the atlas; drop it with unload(texture_path, force=True). A malformed region map raises InvalidMetadataError with line/column info.

docs.title: Files the engine does not interpret
docs.text:
Not every asset is a texture, a sound or a parsed document. A shader is a string; a font file or a packed table is a pile of bytes. A game that wanted one used to go around ResourceManager entirely, losing the index, the cache, the reference counting and the hot reload with it.

shader = manager.load("sprite.vert", TextResource).text
font_bytes = manager.load("inter.ttf", BlobResource).data

Both are registered by bootstrap. TextLoader claims the shader stages (.vert, .frag, .geom, .comp, .glsl); BlobLoader claims .bin, .dat, .ttf and .otf. Neither claims .txt or .md — a game's prose is content a game loads on purpose, and claiming those engine-wide would make the choice for it:

manager.register_loader(TextLoader(extensions=(".txt", ".md")))

Neither claims an extension a real loader owns, either: a blob loader claiming .png would quietly win the registration race and hand a texture request a pile of bytes.

!!! note "No font resource yet" BlobResource gets a .ttf into the cache; it does not give you something you can draw with. A usable font is a backend object (pygame's Font, or a GL glyph atlas) and so needs a factory protocol the way a texture does — and both UI renderers currently own private font caches that would have to be unified first. That is a design, not a loader, and it is still open on #272.

docs.title: Packed assets: pyguara.assets
docs.text:
Every engine loader reads files through pyguara.assets, never open(), so a shipped game can keep its assets in one pack (a ZIP) instead of hundreds of loose files:

from pyguara import assets

assets.mount_pack("Reclaimer.pak", root=game_dir)
  • A path keeps its meaning. The pack holds paths relative to root. A path asked for, absolute or relative to the working directory, is looked up in the pack only if it lies under that root. So load("assets/hero.png"), the folder index and .meta files work the same, loose or packed, and index_directory() lists packed files under the paths they would have on disk.
  • Packs are consulted before the disk, the last mounted first. A file in no pack is read from disk, so a development checkout needs no pack at all, and a patch pack can override files in a base pack.
  • Packs are read-only. Saves, settings and logs are written to disk.
  • Pygame's music player keeps streaming a loose track from disk. A packed track is read into memory first. The native mixer decodes whole tracks either way.
  • What goes through it: every ResourceManager loader (images on both renderers, sounds, JSON, text, blobs), .meta files, the folder index, atlases, prefabs, sprite sheets, Tiled and LDtk maps, themes, music, locale files (pyguara.i18n and pyguara i18n check) and fallback fonts.

A loader of your own should read with assets.read_bytes(path), assets.read_text(path) or assets.open(path). One that calls open() itself still works for loose files, but not packed ones.

docs.title: Introspection
docs.text: get_cache_stats() returns {"resource_count", "total_references", "total_bytes", "budget_bytes", "resources": {path: {"type", "ref_count", "size_bytes"}}} — useful for a debug overlay or a leak check between scenes.

docs.title: Scripting System
docs.text: pyguara.scripting runs coroutines — Python generator functions that yield control back to the engine — so sequential, time-based game logic can be written as a straight-line function instead of a state machine or a chain of callbacks. The model is close to Unity's coroutines.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
The bootstrap registers a single CoroutineManager as a DI singleton, and Application ticks it once per frame from _update() — the variable-rate step, alongside UI and tweens, so sequences look smooth rather than being frame-reproducible. Reach it from a scene through the container:

from pyguara.scripting import CoroutineManager

class MyScene(Scene):
    def on_enter(self) -> None:
        self._coroutines = self.container.get(CoroutineManager)
        self._coroutines.start_coroutine(self.intro())

    def intro(self):
        yield from ...  # see below

Because the manager is app-wide, coroutines are not stopped when a scene exits. A sequence that outlives its scene keeps ticking against entities that may no longer exist — keep the Coroutine handles a scene starts and stop_coroutine() them in on_exit(), or call stop_all() if the manager is effectively scene-private.

docs.title: Wait instructions
docs.text:
A coroutine controls its own timing by yielding a WaitInstruction:

Yield Resumes when WaitForSeconds(seconds) that much game time has elapsed WaitUntil(predicate) predicate() first returns truthy WaitWhile(predicate) predicate() first returns falsy None (a bare yield) next frame another Coroutine, or a generator that sub-sequence has finished

Convenience factories wait_for_seconds(), wait_until() and wait_while() return the matching instruction.

from pyguara.scripting import wait_for_seconds, wait_until

def wave_sequence(spawner, enemies):
    print("wave starting")
    yield wait_for_seconds(2.0)

    spawner.spawn_wave()
    yield wait_until(lambda: len(enemies) == 0)

    print("wave cleared")

docs.title: Nested sequences
docs.text:
Yielding another coroutine or a raw generator suspends the parent until the child completes, then resumes the parent in the same frame:

def cutscene():
    yield pan_camera_to(boss)          # a generator function call
    yield wait_for_seconds(0.5)
    yield boss_intro_lines()           # another one
    hud.show()

WaitForSeconds timing is frame-granular: the frame that yields the instruction is not counted, and time elapsed past the duration is not carried into the next wait, so a long chain of short waits drifts by up to a frame each. Use WaitUntil against a clock you own if a sequence must hit a wall time exactly.

docs.title: Managing coroutines
docs.text:
CoroutineManager:

  • start_coroutine(generator) -> Coroutine — begins running it next update(); the returned handle is what you stop.
  • stop_coroutine(coroutine) -> bool — stops and drops one; False if it was already gone (a finished coroutine removes itself).
  • stop_all() — stops and drops every coroutine.
  • active_count / active_coroutines (a copy) — introspection.

Stopping a coroutine closes its generator, so finally blocks and with statements inside the sequence run their cleanup immediately rather than whenever the generator is garbage-collected:

def show_dialogue(box):
    box.open()
    try:
        yield wait_until(box.dismissed)
    finally:
        box.close()          # runs even if the coroutine is stopped early

Coroutines may call start_coroutine(), stop_coroutine() and stop_all() from inside their own body during update() — including stopping themselves.
