The pass iterates a snapshot: a coroutine stopped mid-frame is skipped, one started mid-frame is carried forward and first runs next frame, and no sibling is skipped by the mutation. (A coroutine that stops itself from inside its body cannot have its generator closed at that instant; its finally blocks then run at GC.)

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
What happens when a coroutine body raises is governed by the manager's error_strategy (pyguara.errors.ErrorHandlingStrategy), the same knob EventDispatcher and DIContainer use:

Strategy Behaviour RAISE (default) log the traceback, stop the offender, re-raise LOG log the traceback, stop the offender, carry on IGNORE stop the offender silently

Under every strategy the failing coroutine is stopped and removed, and the other coroutines still run that frame — one bad sequence cannot strand the rest or corrupt the manager's list. An exception inside a nested sequence is handled the same way at the top-level coroutine.

from pyguara.errors import ErrorHandlingStrategy
from pyguara.scripting import CoroutineManager

manager = CoroutineManager(error_strategy=ErrorHandlingStrategy.LOG)

docs.title: PyGuara Studio
docs.text:
The companion authoring surface: a dockable editor over a running game, and the same operations exposed to a coding agent.

Studio is opt-in. A shipped game never attaches it and pays nothing for it.

from pyguara.application.bootstrap import create_application
from pyguara.studio import attach_studio

app = create_application()
attach_studio(app.container)
app.run(MyScene("game", dispatcher))

docs.title: Trying it
docs.text:
Six demos already use the wgpu backend, and tools/studio_demo.py opens any of them with Studio attached:

uv run python tools/studio_demo.py                       # guara_falcao
uv run python tools/studio_demo.py tamandua_murundus
uv run python tools/studio_demo.py guara_falcao --mode ask
uv run python tools/studio_demo.py guara_falcao --borderless

main.py and the remaining demos run on the Pygame backend, where Studio declines rather than half-installing.

attach_studio builds on attach_editor, so it needs wgpu for the same reason: it draws through the GPU device the render graph owns, and the Pygame backend's window is a software surface with none. On that backend it declines and logs why, and pyguara/tools remains the dev surface there. See Editor Tools.

docs.title: The one idea
docs.text:
Every change to authored state becomes an EditCommand on a CommandStack, whoever asked for it — a panel, the command palette, or an agent.

  human UI      command palette      agent (MCP / JSON-lines)
      |                |                        |
      +----------------+------------------------+
                       |
                  ops registry
                       |
               EditCommand objects
                       |
               CommandStack --> Journal
                       |
                 EntityManager

That single seam is why undo/redo, a reviewable audit journal, diffable agent edits and a deterministic edit-run-check loop are one mechanism rather than four. See ADR 0001.

docs.title: Panels
docs.text:
Panel What it is for Viewport The rendered frame, with pan, zoom, a grid, selection, marquee and the transform gizmo over it Hierarchy The entity tree, with a filter and same-prefix grouping Inspector The selected entity's components, edited by reflection Play Pause, resume, single-step and slow the running game History Every edit, oldest first. Clicking a row rewinds to it Journal What was done and who asked, plus the approval queue Components Every registered component, its fields and its enum members Config The engine configuration by section, edited in place and saved on request Resources The files the resource manager has indexed and the ones it has loaded, with a preview, Spawn and Reload Commands A person calling the operations an agent calls

Panels open docked -- hierarchy left, inspector, components and config right, viewport centre, play on top, history/journal/commands/resources tabbed below.

docs.title: Finding an entity
docs.text:
An ECS scene has none of the pressure a Godot scene has to hang a level's tiles off a parent, so a generated level arrives as hundreds of flat siblings. The demo this was reported from put 252 rows in the Hierarchy panel, 232 of them tiles.

Two answers, both from Godot's Scene dock:

  • A filter box. Typing narrows the list to what is being worked on.
  • Grouping. Runs of siblings sharing a name prefix -- everything up to the first numeric segment, so tile_0_0 through tile_19_11 are all tile -- fold into one row once there are four or more of them. 252 rows become twelve.

The grouping is display only: no entity is named tile, nothing is reparented, and the row says so on hover. A row that looked like a parent and was not would be a worse lie than the long list it replaced.

Selecting an entity anywhere else -- clicking in the viewport, an agent's operation -- scrolls the panel to it and opens the group holding it.

The panel reads and selects; it does not edit. Every change goes through an operation, so it lands on one history and in one journal.

docs.title: The view is yours, and selection reaches what is behind
docs.text:
Panning takes the camera. Studio shows the game's own framebuffer, so there is exactly one camera and panning has to move it -- and a game whose follow system writes it every tick wins. Measured: a pan put the camera at (-97, 178) and forty frames later the follow system had it at (204, 387), so the click that followed landed on whatever had moved under the cursor. That is what "the middle button broke selection" was.

So the viewport takes the view, as Godot's and Unity's editor views are separate from the game's camera. The game keeps writing where it wants the camera; those writes are recorded and not displayed. The toolbar says which it is -- Following the game, or Free view with a Follow game button that hands it back, resuming wherever the game had got to rather than where the view was left.

Clicking again reaches what is behind. Picking returns everything under the point, front-most first, and clicking the same spot walks back through the stack -- the only way to select a background tile under a platform, and how Godot's editor reaches a node behind another one. Clicking somewhere else starts at the front again.

Physics still contributes candidates, because a collider is a deliberate statement about an entity's extent where a sprite box is inferred from an image. It no longer decides: point_query orders by how deeply the point is enclosed, which has nothing to do with what is on top, and clicking the player used to hand back the platform it was standing on.

The HUD is not entities. It is UIManager widgets with their own tree, their own layers and their own hit testing, drawn over the frame; no amount of entity picking reaches it. A click that lands on one now says so, rather than silently clearing the selection, which is indistinguishable from a click that missed. Editing the game's runtime UI is not something Studio does.

docs.title: Edit, then play
docs.text:
The lifecycle every editor has, and the one Studio did not. Studio attaches in edit mode: the scene is loaded and nothing simulates.

Edit Play The game stopped running Edits everything refused, naming Stop The scene is what you see is a copy, restored on Stop

Press Play and Studio copies the whole world and lets the game run. Press Stop and that copy goes back, exactly as it was when Play was pressed. Pause and Step are about watching a running game, not editing one, and live inside Play.

Three engines, one agreement: Godot runs the game in its own process, Unreal in its own world, Unity in the same world and discards the changes on Stop. The scene you edit and the game you run are not the same thing at the same time. Studio used to attach to a running game and edit it live -- Unity's case without the discard -- and that is where every confusing symptom came from: a gizmo drag overwritten by the controller on the next tick, a pan reclaimed by the follow system, an edit outlived before it could be seen.

Editing is refused while playing rather than discarded. Unity allows it and throws it away, which everyone treats as a footgun; refusing costs nothing and the message says to press Stop.

WorldSnapshot is what makes Stop mean something. It does not go through SceneSerializer, which silently skips any component the registry does not know -- which is every component a game defines unless it registered them, and the stated reason there was no reset before. It copies the live components instead, the way the command stack already captures a subtree, so a component it has never heard of is copied exactly as well as one it has. Measured on guara_falcao: 252 entities, 14 ms each way, nothing lost.

Two details that are easy to get wrong and are tested:

  • Copied, not referenced. Holding the live component means the game mutates the very object the snapshot is meant to restore, and Stop puts back exactly what play left behind.
  • Engine handles are cleared. A copied RigidBody._body_handle points at a body the backend removed with the entity. Cleared, the physics system builds a fresh one, which is what it already does for an entity it has not seen.

run_frames is not Play. An agent stepping a stopped game frame by frame is editing, not playing, and its edits are allowed throughout -- which is the whole point of the edit/run/check loop.

docs.title: Why an edit may not show
docs.text:
Reported as "the controls over an entity's components do not seem to have any effect". Driving the whole loop and measuring it separates three things that look identical from the outside:

What happened How to tell The edit was refused A toast says so, naming the correction. Before, it was a log line nobody saw The edit landed, and the game overwrote it The Viewport says Running in amber. Whatever drives the entity -- a controller, a physics body, a follow system -- writes its transform again on the next tick. Pause and the edit stands The edit landed, and nothing draws from that component The world changed and the frame did not. A game that draws by hand from its own data renders the same picture whatever the component says

The third is not a Studio bug and cannot be fixed from here: a component is authored state, and only a game that renders from it will show a change to it. Every demo in games/ draws by hand, so editing a Sprite's colour changes the component and nothing else. Entities those demos do draw from their Transform -- the player, the tiles -- move when moved.

the_edit_lifecycle_works in tests/studio/_attach_scenarios.py drives the whole loop against a real demo with the game paused, and asserts the frame actually changed. Paused, because a running game changes the frame every tick and a pixel comparison would say nothing.

docs.title: Everything goes through an operation, including the Inspector
docs.text:
attach_editor installs an InspectorPanel with no attachment, and one with no attachment writes straight onto the component -- right for a layer with no session behind it. In Studio that was a second way to change the world: a field typed into it reached no history, appeared in no journal, and applied even in plan mode, which is supposed to change nothing.

So attach_studio installs an InspectorPanel that has the attachment, and that one sends every accepted field through set_field -- the same operation an agent calls. One seam, one history, one record, which is the premise the whole design rests on, and it had a hole in it exactly where most editing happens.

This was a StudioInspectorPanel subclass while the editor layer was a separate package: a class whose entire body overrode one method across a package boundary. The boundary is gone and so is the subclass. It is now one class, and where an edit goes is a constructor argument -- which is the honest shape, because a direct write is not a lesser version of the operation path, it is what an editor with no history can do.

docs.title: Editing the configuration
docs.text:
The Config panel lists every section of GameConfig, the engine's and the ones a game registered, and draws each setting with a widget for its type: a checkbox, a number field, a text field committed on Enter, a colour picker, or a list of an enum's members. A float is a drag field; Ctrl+click types an exact value. It opens hidden, from View.

An accepted edit is the config operation, which has three verbs:

Verb Does get Reports every section, or one, with each setting's type, value, default and an enum's valid names set Changes one setting, as an edit on the same history as the scene's save Writes the configuration file

set writes through ConfigManager.update_setting(), so the value is type-checked and validated, and a refusal comes back with the manager's reason. Because it is an edit like any other, it undoes, it is journaled, plan mode describes it without making it, and it is refused while the game is playing.

Four things to know:

  • Changing a setting does not make a subsystem re-read it. The write dispatches OnConfigurationChanged; whatever read the value once at startup keeps the old one until the next launch. Save, then restart.
  • Nothing reaches the file until save. Saving leaves the history alone, so an edit can still be undone afterwards, and the file then holds the value from before the undo until it is saved again.
  • A setting an active profile sets is shown and not editable. save writes such a setting with the value underneath the profile, and the profile stays applied.
  • A planned edit announces itself twice. plan mode applies an edit and reverts it, and both writes dispatch OnConfigurationChanged.

A setting that holds None has no widget in the panel; set accepts a value for it, and null to clear it again.

docs.title: Browsing resources
docs.text:
The Resources panel shows two lists under one filter: every resource currently loaded, with its type and size, and every file ResourceManager.index_directory() mapped. Both scroll. It opens hidden, from View. Selecting a row previews it, and two buttons act on it. All of it is the resources operation:

Verb Does list Reports the indexed files, each with the names that load it, and the loaded resources. Takes a filter and a limit preview Describes one resource; a data file comes with its contents spawn Creates an entity from a data file, as one undoable edit reload Re-reads a loaded resource from disk

A data file is whatever loads as a DataResource: .json, .manifest and .config. spawn reads its top-level keys. Each one that names a registered component, with an object of fields, becomes that component, built through the ComponentRegistry as a scene file's are:

{
  "Transform": {"position": {"x": 40, "y": 50}},
  "Tag": {"name": "Crate"}
}

The entity is named after the file (crate, then crate_2) unless entity_id says otherwise, and carries a ResourceLink to the file.

Things to know:

  • Keys that are not components are reported, not hidden. The reply lists them under skipped, and the panel's toast names them.
  • One component that cannot be built refuses the whole spawn. Nothing is created, and the error names the component.
  • Previewing a data file loads it, and it stays in the cache. Previewing anything else never loads it: a texture is described only if the game already loaded it.
  • reload is not undoable, and code holding the old resource object keeps it; see Resources.
  • The panel reads the listing again every 30 frames and after each action, so a file loaded by the game appears within half a second.

docs.title: The camera the gizmo trusts
docs.text:
Scene.camera is the camera the scene renders with, and everything that turns a world position into a screen one from outside the frame reads it: the Viewport panel, picking, and the transform gizmo.

A scene that overrides render() and draws with a camera of its own has to assign it there. Nothing fails if it does not -- the frame looks right, because the scene is using the camera it meant to. Only the editor is wrong, and quietly: guara_falcao drew the gizmo hundreds of pixels from the entity it belonged to, over the game's own pause button. tests/test_demo_bootstrap_conventions.py now refuses a demo that builds a camera and never assigns it.

docs.title: The arrangement
docs.text:
Applied once, not on every resize, and then left to ImGui. Three consequences, all of them what a docking editor is expected to do:

  • A splitter you drag stays dragged.
  • Widening the window widens the viewport, not the side docks. They keep the width they were given. Rebuilding the tree on each resize -- which is what this used to do -- forced them back to a percentage instead, so on a 21:9 display the hierarchy took a third of the screen and clipped its text anyway.
  • The arrangement survives a restart. ImGui's own settings file carries it, in <project>/.pyguara/studio-layout.ini -- a tool's state rather than the project's, out of the way and easy to delete. .gitignore carries it. The bare editor and every test write nothing: persistence is opt-in through EditorLayer.set_settings_file, and Studio is what opts in.

View > Reset Layout is the one action that discards both a saved arrangement and whatever has been dragged since.

docs.title: The menus
docs.text:
Studio's menu bar is built over the operation registry, not over the editor's internals. An entry that changes the scene calls the same operation an agent calls over MCP or JSON lines, so a person choosing Entity > Create Empty and an agent calling create_entity take one path, land in one history, and read the same way in the journal.

Menu What is in it Scene Save, Open, New, and Quit Edit Undo, Redo, Duplicate, Delete Entity, Deselect Entity Create Empty, Add Component, Enable/Disable View The panels, and Reset Layout Run Pause/Resume, Step, the time-scale presets Agent The approval mode, Approvals, Journal, and the commands that let an agent in Help The documentation link, and About

The names follow Godot and Unity where they agree -- Scene is Godot's File, Entity is this engine's word for Godot's Node and Unity's GameObject -- because a menu bar is not the place to be original. Agent has no equivalent in either, and is the point of Studio.

The same menus are drawn into the editor's own title bar when the window is borderless, and into ImGui's main menu bar when it is not. One list, two places, so the two can never disagree about what the editor offers.

What is greyed out is greyed out for a reason. Save and Open need a session that can reach the serializer, which one built by hand has no container for; the menu disables them rather than offering an action that fails. Nothing in the bar reaches around an operation to do its work, so there is no state a person can reach that an agent cannot.

docs.title: The window
docs.text:
Two display flags decide what the operating system gives the editor, and both default off so a shipped game is unaffected:

display. What it does resizable The user can size the window, and the window system reports it. Without it the window manager may still let the frame be maximised -- WSLg does -- while nothing in the engine is told, and the editor carries on drawing at the starting resolution into a corner of a much larger window borderless Removes the OS title bar, so the editor draws its own

borderless is what the grey Windows-classic frame around the editor was. With it set, attach_editor installs a TitleBar: the panel menu at the left, the window title centred, and minimise/maximise/close at the right, in the editor's own palette -- the arrangement Godot and VS Code use, and for the same reason. The icons are stroked onto the draw list rather than written as text, because ImGui's built-in font carries Basic Latin and nothing else.

Set only where the backend offers window controls. Window.chrome answers that: it hands back the backend when it satisfies IWindowChrome and None otherwise, and the editor leaves the OS bar alone in the second case. A borderless window whose buttons do nothing is worse than the frame it replaced.

Close goes through the window's event queue rather than destroying the window: the button is pressed from inside a frame that is still being drawn, and the application runs the same shutdown it runs for the OS's own button.

Keep resizable on wherever borderless is: removing the frame removes the OS's resize edges with it.

docs.title: Who the window belongs to
docs.text:
ctx.screen.viewport means where the game's frame goes. With keep_aspect the render graph narrows it to the letterbox, so the game and its HUD land inside their own frame however the window is dragged.

The editor is not the game: it owns the whole window, and its pass sets the window viewport for its own draw and puts the letterbox back afterwards -- back, because the game's UI composites after the graph runs and belongs inside the frame rather than on the bars.

Getting that wrong is not subtle. Inheriting the letterbox squeezed every panel by the ratio between the two: on a 2000x876 window that is a horizontal scale of 0.73, which reads as compressed text and a round sun in the Viewport panel drawn as an ellipse taller than wide. An ultrawide display makes it worse -- at 21:9 more than a quarter of the window is bars.

docs.title: Viewport
docs.text:
Studio owns the screen. On attach it disables the final blit, so the game is not also drawn full-screen behind the panels, and redirects the game's UI compositing into the buffer the viewport shows -- so the HUD appears over the game, inside the viewport, instead of over the editor's panels. release_screen() puts all of it back.

The frame is letterboxed, not stretched: a docked panel is almost never the render target's shape, and a stretched view means a sprite lined up in the editor is wrong everywhere else. Every coordinate mapping uses the drawn image's rectangle rather than the panel's, or a click would be offset by the width of the bars.

Pan with the middle button or space-drag; zoom with the wheel, anchored on the cursor. Click to select, ctrl-click to add, drag to marquee. Enclose switches the marquee between selecting what it touches and only what it fully contains.

Picking consults the physics engine first where there is one — point_query is written for exactly this and orders results most-deeply-enclosing first — and otherwise measures each sprite's real bounds from its texture, transform scale and offset. An entity with no sprite and no collider still gets a fixed box, so a spawn point or an empty used as a parent remains clickable.

docs.title: Gizmo
docs.text:
Q translate, W rotate, E scale. Drag an arrow to constrain to an axis, the centre handle to move freely. Snap rounds to the grid step in absolute world space — snapping the delta would leave an entity that began off-grid off it forever. Rotation snaps in degrees, since a grid is a distance and means nothing to an angle. Escape cancels a drag, leaving neither a change nor a history entry.

One drag is one undo entry, spanning the whole drag. Components are written directly while dragging, for live feedback with no history churn; on release the starting values are restored and a single command is applied. The restore is not redundant: a command captures its inverse when applied, so one applied against a world already holding the final values would record "from final to final" and undo nothing.

docs.title: The operation surface
docs.text:
Around twenty operations, reachable three ways. The registry is shared, so an operation cannot be available to one caller and missing from another.

# JSON lines on stdio -- no extra dependency.
pyguara studio ops

# Model Context Protocol -- needs the `studio` extra.
pyguara studio mcp
Group Operations Discovery list_operations, project_overview, list_components, component_schema Reading scene_summary, scene_tree, get_entity, find_entities Editing create_entity, destroy_entity, duplicate_entity, add_component, remove_component, set_field, set_parent, set_enabled, set_tags Running run_frames, capture_frame Session history, journal, approvals, scene, config, resources

scene carries four verbs behind an "operation" argument -- save, open, new and list -- as history does. The flat surface is budgeted, because a client's tool limit is spent on the verbs used every minute, and saving is not one of them.

Two of those four clear the undo history, and say so: opening, because every command on the stack describes a world that no longer exists, and saving, because undoing past a save leaves the file and the world disagreeing with nothing on screen to show it. Emptying the scene does not -- it is a destroy of every root inside one transaction, so it stays a single undoable entry.

Each declares a risk class — read, edit, run or write_disk — so a caller can express "read anything, ask before writing" without enumerating operations.

Rarer work sits behind history and approvals, which take an operation argument, rather than becoming another dozen entries. A client has a limit on how many tools it will present, and an agent's accuracy falls as the list grows.

docs.title: Approval modes
docs.text:
Mode Behaviour auto Apply the edit. The default for a person at the keyboard ask Queue it with the diff it would make, for someone to approve plan Describe it and change nothing

plan is not a prediction: the edit is applied, the diff captured, and the edit reverted, so the reported consequence is the real one. Destroying an entity names every id the ownership cascade would take with it.

pyguara studio ops --mode ask --journal .studio/journal.jsonl

docs.title: The harness
docs.text:
A closed loop for an agent with no window: open a scene, edit it, run it, look at the frames, check what moved.

from pyguara.studio.agent.harness import open_headless
from games.guara_falcao.bootstrap import configure_game_container
from games.guara_falcao.scenes import GameScene

harness = open_headless(
    GameScene,
    container_factory=configure_game_container,
)
harness.step(30)
capture = harness.capture("frame")
print(capture.blank, capture.world_flat)

"Headless" means no window, not the headless backend. create_headless_application() registers no texture loader, so any scene that loads an image dies before it finishes entering — and a real demo is almost entirely images. The harness boots the normal bootstrap under an SDL driver that needs no display, dummy, and PYGUARA_WINDOW=offscreen, under which the wgpu backend opens no window and renders offscreen.

Runs are deterministic: the harness installs FixedClock and seeds RandomService itself, so the same script twice produces the same frames. That is what makes "run it again and diff" an answer.

A capture reports whether the composed frame and the world buffer behind it are a single flat colour. They are separate because a composed frame carries the UI, so a dead world render path still leaves a HUD on screen and the frame is never flat.

!!! warning "What a capture proves" It reads the buffer the renderer drew into, which proves the render path works. It does not prove a window appears on screen. Those have already diverged in this engine, when vsync silently promoted the display to an OpenGL surface that never presented software blits — the captures looked perfect and the real window was blank. See Visual Inspection.

docs.title: Instruction files
docs.text:
Studio generates the files coding agents read, from the project itself.

pyguara studio instructions          # write them
pyguara studio instructions --check  # fail if stale, for CI

It writes a canonical AGENTS.md and thin shims that import it: CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md and .cursor/rules/pyguara.mdc. Generated regions are fenced, and nothing outside them is touched — an instruction file is mostly hand-written knowledge, and a generator that overwrites it is one nobody runs twice.

See the agent integration guide.

docs.title: What is deliberately absent
docs.text:
• Reset-to-where-play-began. It would mean restoring the whole world, and SceneSerializer skips any component the registry does not know — which is every component a game defines unless it registered them. A reset that quietly dropped the player's controller is worse than none. Save before playing and load afterwards instead.
  • Generated argument forms in the palette. A form would be nicer for scalars and hopeless for a nested dataclass. Arguments are JSON, which is the shape the schema browser shows and the scene files use.
  • Prefab override editing and the animation timeline. Issues #51 and #37 respectively; Studio consumes their data models rather than defining them.

docs.title: Declarative UI Builder
docs.text:
UIBuilder builds a UI tree the way the imperative API builds one, with the parent threaded through a with block instead of a local variable. It is opt-in sugar, not a replacement: every screen already written against add_child() keeps working untouched, and the builder produces an indistinguishable tree.

from pyguara.common.types import Vector2
from pyguara.ui import UIBuilder

with UIBuilder(ui_manager) as ui:
    with ui.box(Vector2(270, 288), Vector2(260, 220), spacing=14) as column:
        ui.label("Main Menu", font_size=44)
        ui.button("Start Game", size=Vector2(260, 52), on_click=self._on_start)
        ui.button("Quit", size=Vector2(260, 52), on_click=self._on_quit)

ui_manager.set_focus(column.children[0])

The same screen, written by hand, is what the builder above expands to:

column = BoxContainer(Vector2(270, 288), Vector2(260, 220), spacing=14)
title = Label("Main Menu", Vector2(0, 0), font_size=44)
column.add_child(title)
start = Button("Start Game", Vector2(0, 0), Vector2(260, 52))
start.on_click = self._on_start
column.add_child(start)
quit_button = Button("Quit", Vector2(0, 0), Vector2(260, 52))
quit_button.on_click = self._on_quit
column.add_child(quit_button)
ui_manager.add_element(column, UILayer.CONTENT)

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• No callback mechanism of its own. UIElement.on_click is a bare attribute, so on_click= is that same assignment and nothing more. The function you pass is the function stored.
  • No theme wiring. UIElement.__init__ calls get_theme() unconditionally, so an element themes itself the moment it exists.
  • No fixed widget vocabulary. See Custom widgets.

docs.title: Mounting
docs.text:
A builder given a UIManager mounts its roots when the with block ends:

with UIBuilder(ui_manager) as ui:        # mounted on exit
    ...

Without one it builds a detached tree, which roots hands back:

with UIBuilder() as ui:
    ...
for root in ui.roots:
    ...                                   # place it yourself
ui.mount(ui_manager)                      # or mount it later

A block that raises mounts nothing. Half a menu on screen is harder to diagnose than no menu, and the exception already says what went wrong.

Only top-level elements are roots -- a nested element is drawn by its parent.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
Roots mount at the builder's layer (UILayer.CONTENT by default). layer() scopes a different one, so one builder can produce a backdrop and its content:

with UIBuilder(ui_manager) as ui:
    with ui.layer(UILayer.BACKDROP):
        ui.add(Scrim(800, 600, strength=0.32))
    with ui.box(...) as column:
        ...

docs.title: Custom widgets
docs.text:
A game's own elements are the normal case, not the exception -- guara_falcao builds its screens out of BevelPanel, BevelButton and Scrim. add() takes any UIElement and returns it with its own type intact; nest() does the same and descends into it:

with UIBuilder(ui_manager) as ui:
    with ui.nest(BevelPanel(Vector2(140, 96), Vector2(520, 132))) as plate:
        ui.label("GUARÁ & FALCÃO", font_size=44, width=520, align=TextAlign.CENTER)
    with ui.box(Vector2(270, 288), Vector2(260, 220), spacing=14):
        ui.add(BevelButton("Play", Vector2(0, 0)), on_click=self._on_play)

A container factory attaches its element when it is called, not when the with block is entered, so ui.panel(...) on its own adds a childless panel rather than silently adding nothing.

docs.title: Factories
docs.text:
Containers Leaves box(), panel(), navbar(), canvas() label(), button(), checkbox(), slider(), text_input(), progress_bar(), image() nest(element) — any element add(element) — any element

Positions default to the origin: a child's position is overwritten by its container's layout pass before it is ever drawn, so passing one is noise. Sizes default to the component's own default where it has one.

checkbox(), slider() and text_input() take on_change; everything clickable takes on_click.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
UIBuilderError is raised when a builder is used in a way that cannot be meant, rather than quietly producing a tree nobody will see:

  • adding before the with block, or after it
  • reusing a builder (they are single-use; build one tree each)
  • mount() with no manager anywhere
  • attaching an element that already has a parent, which would silently remove it from the tree it is already in

docs.title: Rich text
docs.text:
RichLabel draws inline styling, in BBCode-style markup:

ui.rich_label(
    "[b]Tamanduá[/b] takes [color=#e2621f]12 fire[/color] damage",
    width=420,
)
Tag Does [b]...[/b] Bold [i]...[/i] Italic [color=#rrggbb]...[/color] Colour, with an optional alpha pair [size=24]...[/size] Font size [[ A literal [

Tags nest and must close in order. A string that does not parse raises MarkupError when it is set, rather than drawing its own tags at the player.

Anything a player typed goes through escape_markup. Otherwise a name with a [ in it raises, and one with [size=500] in it restyles the dialogue:

from pyguara.ui.rich_text import escape_markup

label.text = f"[b]{escape_markup(player_name)}[/b] joined"

It wraps by the same rules as Label. A word may span several styles, and a break keeps the style on both sides. A line is as tall as its largest run, and runs of different sizes share a bottom edge, which is close to a shared baseline but not exact, because a renderer reports a line's height and not a font's ascent.

docs.title: Languages written without spaces
docs.text: Label and RichLabel break Chinese and Japanese between characters, since neither puts spaces between words, and Latin text inside them stays whole. They follow the kinsoku rules: a line never starts with closing punctuation (。, 」, ！), a small kana (ッ, ょ) or ー, and never ends with an opening bracket (「, （). Korean puts spaces between words and wraps on them, as English does. pyguara.ui.text_layout.break_offsets(word) says where a space-free word may break.

docs.title: Upper case in Turkish
docs.text:
str.upper() turns i into I, which is wrong in Turkish and Azerbaijani, where it is İ (and ı is the one that becomes I). The design system's uppercase buttons go through pyguara.ui.text_case, which gets it right once told the language:

from pyguara.ui import text_case

text_case.set_case_language("tr")
text_case.upper("iptal")    # "İPTAL"

Label is unchanged and is the one to use for plain text. Every run in a RichLabel is its own text draw, so a line of five styles costs five.

Bold and italic come from UIRenderer.draw_text(..., bold=, italic=), so a custom renderer has to accept them. They use whatever faces the system's font provides.

docs.title: UI Design System
docs.text:
The PyGuara design system is content for the UI system, not a second one. It is a brand palette, two themes built from it, and the two pieces of drawing a theme cannot express. Every stock component -- Button, Panel, Checkbox, Slider, ProgressBar, TextInput -- renders in the design system's colours without knowing it exists, because they read the same semantic roles the themes define.

from pyguara.ui import set_theme
from pyguara.ui.design_system import cerrado_dusk

set_theme(cerrado_dusk())

That is the whole integration. Two themes ship: cerrado_dusk() (violet ground, Guará action) and cerrado_day() (sand ground, deepened Guará). Each call returns a fresh UITheme, so mutating one never affects the next caller.

docs.title: Semantic colour roles
docs.text:
ColorScheme has two layers. The base five -- primary, secondary, background, text, border -- are the shorthand themes have always been written in. The semantic roles are what components actually read:

Group Roles Surfaces surface_canvas, surface_card, surface_raised, surface_inset Text text_heading, text_body, text_muted, text_faint, text_on_primary, text_on_disabled Edges edge, edge_strong, focus_ring Actions action_primary, action_primary_hover, action_primary_press, action_secondary, action_disabled

The roles exist because the base five had to be overloaded: secondary meant the accent and the hover fill and the focus ring and a checkbox's tick, and a placeholder was drawn in the border colour because it happened to be dim enough. A design system cannot be stated in that vocabulary.

docs.title: Deriving a scheme
docs.text:
Name only what you care about and let the rest follow:

from pyguara.common.types import Color
from pyguara.ui.types import ColorScheme

colors = ColorScheme.derive(
    primary=Color(226, 98, 31),
    background=Color(29, 22, 32),
    text=Color(242, 230, 210),
)

Surfaces are lifted by interpolating towards the theme's text colour, which lightens them in a dark theme and darkens them in a light one, so one rule serves both. text_on_primary is chosen by luminance, so a pale action colour gets dark text. Any role passed explicitly wins over the rule; an unknown role name raises rather than being silently dropped.

ColorScheme(...) derives by the same rule, so the two agree on any palette. derive() is the one to prefer, because it names the valid roles when it refuses a typo.

docs.title: Tokens
docs.text: pyguara.ui.design_system.tokens holds the brand palette as plain Color values, grouped by family: Guara, Sand, Rock, Wood, Verdant, Roxo, Water, Falcao. Nothing there says what a colour is for -- themes.py does that. Component dimensions deliberately live with the components, not here.

docs.title: What needed code
docs.text:
Two things are geometry rather than colour, so they could not be theme values:

from pyguara.common.types import Vector2
from pyguara.ui.design_system import BevelButton, BevelPanel, Skins

play = BevelButton("Play", Vector2(40, 40))
sage = BevelButton("Options", Vector2(40, 100), skin=Skins.SAGE)
card = BevelPanel(Vector2(16, 16), Vector2(400, 300), shadow=True)

BevelButton is the stock Button -- same sizing, focus traversal and click handling -- plus a raised edge that inverts when pressed, a face that drops a pixel while held, and an upper-cased label applied at render time (self.text keeps what you passed). Without a skin it follows the active theme's action colours, so it stays correct under any theme.

ButtonSkin covers the brand colourways that are not "the theme's primary action": Skins.SAGE, Skins.WOOD, Skins.GUARA. Each carries its own pressed colour, so a green button does not flash orange on click. A disabled button ignores its skin and falls back to the theme -- disabled is a theme-wide look, and it draws neither bevel nor shadow, since it is not raised.

docs.title: Why the bevel is opaque
docs.text: The obvious bevel is white at low alpha on the top edge and black on the bottom. It does not work: both UI backends draw through pygame.draw, which replaces the destination pixel including its alpha rather than blending. On the pygame backend the surface is opaque, so a 45/255 white lands as solid white; on the (since retired) ModernGL backend the overlay was SRCALPHA, so the same call punches a transparent hole in the element. bevel_edges() mixes the highlight into the fill colour on the CPU instead, which gives the same result on both backends and is deterministic enough to assert in a test.

docs.title: Seeing it work
docs.text:
games/guara_falcao is the worked example: a title screen, a HUD, a pause menu and an options panel, all skinned by cerrado_dusk() and none of them holding a colour of their own.

uv run python tools/agent_view.py guara_falcao --gl --frames 40 --shot 39

It is also where the pieces that are not colour get exercised — UILayer.HUD under UILayer.OVERLAY, the focus ring scoped to the topmost layer so Tab cannot leave an open modal, LayoutConstraints anchoring the HUD to the corners, and the options panel's theme row calling set_theme() live, which re-skins the panel the switch is sitting in.
